evidence.fact: Miro's AI OKR Assistant creates tailored OKRs for a department after the user adds company context and sets deadlines.
Zensai Perform & Engage 365 offers a 'Suggest OKRs' AI feature that drafts goals at the team or department level.

Kollabe's OKR generator takes a department, a mission and a timeframe, then produces objectives with measurable key results and suggested initiatives. These tools draft goals, but a manager still decides on and commits to them.

AI takeoff tools from vendors such as ConstructConnect and Trimble use computer vision to detect, count and measure items on digital drawings. Vendors say this can cut takeoff time by up to 80%. Turning those quantities into a priced bid still depends on the firm's own cost data, assemblies and scope judgment.

Vendors claim AI takeoff is 80–98% accurate on clean commercial drawing sets. Accuracy is weaker on scanned sheets and dense MEP sets. Scope interpretation, pricing judgment and risk allocation are still done by people.
No license is required to work as a cost estimator. Certifications from ASPE, AACE and ICEAA are voluntary.

Forestry advisory tools that combine remote sensing with AI already exist. Södra and Terra Labs' AI planner builds forest management plans, and Finnish chatbot-style advisors combine forest data, costs and legal requirements into recommendations. These tools speed up advisory work but are not meant to replace foresters.
In Alabama, anyone who gives forest management recommendations for hire on land they do not own must be registered with the state Board of Registration for Foresters.
California's Board of Forestry says that offering forestry recommendations on forested land without a Registered Professional Forester's expertise and stamp violates the Professional Foresters Law.

Research on deep learning for tree segmentation and species classification from LiDAR is well developed (e.g. transformer classifiers, interactive segmentation pipelines). An agent can write code, run analyses and draft protocols for these methods. The main limit is that individual trees in point clouds must still be labelled to provide ground-truth data, which slows this work down.

Licensing applies to professional forestry practice and recommendations in some states, such as California's RPF signature and stamp rules. These rules do not cover developing measurement or identification methods, so a human signature is not legally required for this task.
Many states do not regulate foresters at all, so licensing barriers vary by state and are limited.

Remote refraction apps such as Opternative, myRx and Warby Parker's Virtual Vision Test can support prescription renewals. A licensed physician still issues or approves each prescription, and the tests only cover narrow patient groups. They are not comprehensive exams.

Under the FTC Contact Lens Rule, a prescriber fits the lenses, releases the prescription at the end of the fitting and keeps signed confirmations. Under the FTC Eyeglass Rule, the prescriber hands over the prescription after an eye exam that includes a refraction. This makes a licensed prescriber accountable for the work.

Online refraction can renew prescriptions with physician approval, but fitting, supplying and adjusting eyeglasses and contact lenses means handling the patient and the device in person. An agent can only help with digital sub-steps such as drafting the prescription, choosing lenses and placing orders.

Consumer AI apps and research prototypes, such as an avatar breathing coach and an SMS or web yoga e-coach, can guide relaxation and breathing exercises. None of them covers recreational therapy practice or clinician-supervised instruction in sports, dance or art.

In Utah, a TRS licence requires a current NCTRC CTRS certification plus a documented practicum. Some states, including New Hampshire, also license recreational therapists, so a human professional is accountable for treatment delivery.

New Hampshire requires a degree, fieldwork supervised by a CTRS and the NCTRC exam to practise. This in-person clinical role involves demonstrating activities and adapting them to the patient as they go.

O*NET lists this as a core sonographer duty: preparing the patient, explaining the procedure, moving the patient onto the table, cleaning the skin, applying gel and positioning the patient. Nearly all of these steps are hands-on work done with the patient in the room.

Commercial conversational AI (for example, Patient Prism) can give radiology exam preparation instructions and answer patients' questions before the exam. That covers only the explaining part of the task. The vendor's claims have not been independently evaluated.

Studies of AI-generated information about abdominal ultrasound find that it is fast, but its accuracy and reliability are still uncertain. A commentary recommends using chatbots only to supplement human patient education.

Axon Draft One already writes draft incident reports from body-cam audio and saves roughly 40% of report-writing time. Officers still have to attest to each report, and it then goes through sergeant review and records review.

At Arvada PD, officers review, edit and finalize every AI-drafted report, and supervisors review and approve all submitted reports. The AI is treated as a support tool, and humans remain responsible for accuracy.

California SB 524 (Penal Code 13663, in effect since 1 January 2026) requires AI-assisted police reports to carry a disclosure and an officer's signature confirming the facts, and the first AI draft must be kept.

Jail management systems already automate parts of the release check. Tyler's DeKalb deployment halved release processing time and removed duplicate warrant data entry, and other systems recheck charges and warrants (NCIC) at release. Because warrant databases are split across agencies, a human still has to cross-check.
Deschutes County jail policy names the shift supervisor as the final safeguard in the release process. The supervisor must sign the Release Authorization Form before an inmate is released.
In Bexar County, two supervisors must approve each release, and staff who authorize a wrongful release can be disciplined. Legal accountability therefore stays with human supervisors.
The main salon platforms (Fresha, Boulevard, Vagaro, Mindbody) can keep a client's card on file and take deposits automatically. That lets software settle a bill without anyone at the counter.
Boulevard offers a self-checkout kiosk and an AI receptionist. Third-party AI receptionists connect to Vagaro's API to find clients, book appointments and take deposits.

The vendor sources say AI tools handle booking and deposits, but they don't confirm fully automatic checkout after a visit. Taking cash, making change and helping clients with tap or chip payments at the till still need a person there.

Commercial AI skin-analysis tools already scan a face from a photo, detect about 15 skin concerns such as redness, wrinkles and texture, and then generate a personalised product routine with explanations.

Consumer AI skincare apps recommend products based on skin type and explain which ingredient targets which concern, although they state their advice is informational only. The salon version of this task still depends on in-person skin assessment, demonstrating how to apply products and building client trust during the service.

State cosmetology boards regulate skin-care services, meaning the physical treatments, under the license. Makeup demonstrations and product advice are not described as acts only a licensee may perform, so no human sign-off is required to recommend products.

AI agents settle many routine retail and e-commerce inquiries on digital channels with no human involved. Vendors claim 76–92%, but independent benchmarks put it nearer 14–50%. About 22% of AI-handled tickets are passed to a human, and 58% of consumers are not fully comfortable with AI support.

In-store AI kiosks such as CJ Olive Young's 2026 rollout can answer product, stock and navigation questions in several languages. They are fixed kiosks, though. Greeting shoppers on the floor and handling complaints face to face are still done by staff and supervisors.

Other in-store AI tools, like Skechers' Luna kiosk, mostly support shoppers and store associates with information and suggestions. They do not stand in for the supervisor who handles customers in person on the floor.

Shelf-scanning robots such as Simbe's Tally and Walmart's scanners find out-of-stock items, wrong prices and label problems on shelves. They give information to store associates, but people still do the physical cleaning and organizing. These are robots, which the reference AI agent does not have.
In 2026, agentic AI in retail is used for customer support, pricing and clienteling. It is described as a tool that helps associates, not as something that sells on the sales floor.
Walmart says its in-store inventory robots check shelves but will not replace store workers. The physical shelf work and selling face to face still need people.
Retorio sells retail-focused AI roleplay in which virtual customers push back, object and surprise trainees during objection-handling and upselling practice. This is vendor marketing.

Born Digital's AI roleplay tools for store and call-center staff score tone, accuracy, empathy, policy compliance and how the situation was resolved, so an agent could run the practice and feedback steps on its own. This is vendor marketing.

RetailDoc's SalesRX offers AI roleplay training for retail associates. Its customer case study reports that 99% of associates said they improved, which is a self-reported vendor figure. The supervisor still has to watch live sales on the floor and coach in person.

Existing AI returns agents check the order, test eligibility against written policy, work out the refund or store credit and update the order and payment systems. Policy exceptions are escalated to a human, so they still need human judgment.

Retail planning software already uses AI to split top-level open-to-buy budgets across product and location groups and to adjust replenishment automatically. Logile markets AI-built store labor budgets.

In-store refund and void approvals rely on manager overrides tied to named user accounts. Loss-prevention experts recommend a second approval for higher-value refunds. This is an internal control set by each retailer, not a legal or licensing requirement, and approvals can already be done remotely from a mobile device.
Gecko says its AI voice agents for equipment rental answer calls 24/7, collect rental details, quote from live inventory, take bookings and take payment during the call. This is a vendor claim.

OneAI says its car-rental agent checks live availability, quotes total prices including taxes and fees, and books reservations during the call. The vendor's own case figures show bookings from about 38% of contacts.
SendSquared says its AI voice agent checks live availability in the property system, quotes prices and writes confirmed reservations back. It markets this for its Guesty integration.
One vendor's AI agent connects to Booqable rental software. It reads live inventory to check availability and can create bookings and look up customers. Staff still handle the physical logistics.
Rently's AI agent on WhatsApp answers questions about availability, pricing and requirements, and records reservations in the rental system. Complex requests and VIP customers go to human staff.
Bookyt's rental chatbot matches a customer's question to the rental offering, asks for any missing details, and points to booking. This covers much of the discussion about type, quality and quantity.

Rental technician job postings describe the work as hands-on: setting bindings to the boot and to safety standards (sometimes with certification), fitting boots with a foot sizer, and checking gear for damage before and after rental.
Texada (vendor-reported, launched March 2026) offers AI damage detection that compares check-out and check-in photos. A person still has to take the photos and do any repair or adjustment.
Record360's 360AI is human-in-the-loop: the AI flags possible damage and people make the final call, so it only assists with the inspection step.
Conversational-commerce AI agents already greet online shoppers proactively, answer questions and recommend products to identify needs. Fin puts the 2026 market at about $10–14B.
Gorgias says proactive AI engagement drove 50% of conversation-driven purchases during BFCM 2025, which shows AI handling the greet-and-qualify step in digital channels. This is vendor data.

Agentic commerce tools such as Salesforce Agentforce Commerce work in digital storefronts. On the shop floor, greeting and reading customers face to face needs physical presence, which a bodiless agent lacks, so its role there is limited to helping staff (product lookup, suggestions).

Microsoft Brand Agents bring the advice a store associate would give into a chat on the retailer's website, including guidance, upselling and cross-selling. Google, OpenAI, Shopify and PayPal are building similar conversational shopping where customers compare and buy in one place.

In stores, AI copilots and voice-headset assistants support human associates by giving them product, inventory and recommendation data in real time. The associate still serves the customer face to face and physically finds the items.

Manhattan Active Omni's Store Associate Agent answers natural-language questions about inventory and customer behavior, so an agent can handle the 'locate or obtain' step through software. Gaps in universal carts, APIs and product data still limit full deployment.

Salesforce made its Agentforce Commerce Shopper Agent generally available in mid-2026 (June 24 or July 6; the sources give different dates). The agent answers consumer product questions, helps them find products and handles checkout on the retailer's own storefront.

The agents connect directly to inventory, order and customer data, so they can explain products and deal with service questions without passing the customer to a person. Commentators warn that answers drawn from the product catalogue can still be wrong, and no independent accuracy data was found.

Salesforce says AI influenced 20% of global online sales ($262B) during the 2025 holiday season. These are vendor figures. In physical stores, showing how a product works and building trust face to face still needs a person on the floor.

Endless-aisle and POS software (Shopify POS, Aptos, NewStore, Salesforce Retail Cloud, Retail Express) gives sales associates a view of stock across the whole chain. The associate can place a special order or send the order to the location that holds the item. This is digital work an agent can do through computer use.

Google's agentic 'Let Google Call' feature, built on Duplex, phones nearby stores on its own to check stock, price and promotions, then texts or emails a summary. So the 'call other stores' sub-step is already automated.
Vendors say retail voice agents connect to inventory and CRM systems to handle questions about product availability and order status. Most of the performance claims come from the vendors themselves.

Intuit's 2026 QuickBooks agents read time data, draft pay runs and draft journal entries for wages, taxes and benefits. They are human-in-the-loop by design and need owner approval before anything posts, so the setup sub-steps can be automated but still need human review.

AI agents can pull employee compensation data from payroll records, quarterly reports and tax filings to calculate exposure bases for insurance policies. This shows that mapping insurance data to bookkeeping records is technically within an agent's reach.

The NAIC Producer Licensing Model Act requires a licence only to sell, solicit or negotiate insurance. Administrative work only indirectly tied to sales is exempt, so integrating a policy into bookkeeping is not a licensed act.

AI travel chatbots and agents already put together information tailored to the traveler's itinerary and nationality. This includes visa and entry rules, transit requirements, local customs and etiquette, so the main step of assembling the information is automated.

No-code AI agents automatically check visa and entry eligibility by nationality and destination and alert users when requirements change. Guidance for travel agents still advises checking AI drafts against official sources.

IATA Timatic gives travel agents passport, visa and health requirements for over 220 countries, online or by API. That makes the authoritative regulation data digitally reachable, so an agent can send it to the customer by email or in a document instead of handing over a printed brochure.

Commercial AI agents pull data from invoices, check it, match it to purchase orders and send it for approval. Vendors claim they can read messy handwriting, but I found no independent test of handwriting accuracy. They report 95%+ accuracy overall and say line items are harder to read than header fields.

Payroll AI agents (Deloitte's listing on AWS Marketplace) check timesheets, worker classification and tax withholding, and flag errors before payroll runs. This covers the 'work with pay records' sub-step.
Invoice-processing agents check that data matches existing records and send a person a review request when something looks wrong. A human still reviews the exceptions.

PackageX Mailroom says its AI and machine vision read package labels from a photo, match items to recipients, send email, SMS or WhatsApp alerts and record proof of pickup. This automates the logging and notification steps, though the claims come from the vendor's own materials.
The app lets staff batch-scan packages and notify all recipients with one tap. A person still has to physically receive, scan, sort and hand over the items.

Independent reviews mostly repeat the vendor's description. Vendors pitch self-service workflows as a way to reduce front-desk work, not as autonomous handling of physical mail, which an agent without a body cannot do.

Vendor pages describe AI agents that run program enrollment from start to finish. They ask qualifying questions, send eligible applicants on to enrollment, offer waitlists or other programs to the rest, and follow up automatically by email or SMS. These are marketing claims and have not been independently checked.

The same vendor offers agents for government health-program enrollment. They pre-screen applicants on household income, family size and participation in other programs, and they collect registration details.

A guide on automating financial aid recommends that AI handle screening, flagging, document requests and status outreach, while humans make the final eligibility or award decisions. Low-confidence cases should go to a human, and every automated decision should be logged.

AI receptionist products for law firms answer inbound calls, run intake and conflict checks against the case-management system, and book consultations. They send urgent matters to an on-call attorney and do not give legal advice, so a human still takes the sensitive or judgment-heavy calls.
In 2026 there are many AI voice agents built for law firms that work as 24/7 virtual receptionists. Examples include Smith.ai, Lindy and Voiceflow, and some combine AI with human staff.

The FCC's February 2024 ruling places AI-generated voices under the TCPA's rules for an 'artificial or prerecorded voice'. Some outbound calls therefore need consent and must identify the caller. This is a rule on how calls are made, not a ban, and it does not require a human to make the calls.

Commercial AI record-retrieval platforms for law firms say they automate authorization validation, sending requests to US providers, follow-up, and sorting the records that come back. They also connect to case-management tools like Clio. These are vendor claims and say human oversight is still needed.

Releasing medical records needs a HIPAA authorization signed by the patient or a qualified personal representative, or else a subpoena or court order. A human has to supply this step, and an attorney cannot sign it just because they are on the case.

Retrieval guides for lawyers say the process starts only once a HIPAA-compliant authorization, subpoena, or court order is in place. After that, requests go to each provider's records department and have to be followed up until the records arrive.

AI tools such as S7 PLC Buddy, which uses Claude, can read live PLC diagnostics over the network and suggest likely causes. The vendor notes that the operational data agents need is spread across separate systems like SCADA, historians and fleet software.
Agent products for field technicians combine live readings, error logs and maintenance history to help with troubleshooting, but a technician still does the hands-on work.

Under NFPA 70E, touching energized parts with probes or test equipment counts as energized work. It must be done by a qualified person physically present with the right PPE, so diagnosing with meters and scopes needs someone on site.

Commercial retail space-planning software (LEAFIO) builds planograms automatically from sales data, ABC analysis, turnover and user-defined rules, and auto-calculates facings. These are vendor claims.
DotActiv markets AI planogram generation with batch creation of size variants that follow layout rules, plus an LLM category-management assistant. These are vendor claims.

Retail layouts are bound by occupancy, egress width and travel-distance code rules, such as the 75-ft sprinklered mercantile limit cited from IBC Table 1006.2.1 in a practitioner forum. A human with knowledge of the actual site still has to check compliance and fit before the layout is built in the store.

Atlassian's Jira Service Management ships Rovo agents. A Service Triage agent sets urgency and priority and recommends request types. An Ops Guide agent helps limit incident impact and runs post-incident reviews. This covers the workflow analysis and prioritization sub-steps (vendor claim).

A consultancy built a custom Rovo agent that prioritizes backlog work items in place of manual review. This shows that setting priorities can be partly delegated end to end, but a manager still accepts the result and enforces it with staff (consultancy case study; results not shown).

Rovo agents are positioned to automate triage and routine requests so IT teams can do higher-value work. Directing staff, setting deadlines people will meet, and enforcing standards still need human managerial authority and trust (vendor event listing).

Microsoft Planner's Project Manager agent, in preview, drafts status report emails and summaries of progress, milestones, blockers and next steps from plan data. People can then co-edit the reports in Loop and share them.
Atlassian shows how to build a Rovo agent that pulls Jira and Confluence data to write project health, milestone and risk summaries for PMOs and executives.

These products produce draft reports for people to review and edit before sharing. A manager still has to check accuracy, interpret context and approve the result, which is the review half of this task.

Commercial EHS platforms such as Notify Spark (launched October 2025), Benchmark Gensuite and EHS4Safety already use AI to handle accident reports, root-cause analysis and workers' compensation workflows. That covers the documentation, analysis and reporting steps.

Employers must collect information from injured employees, witnesses and treating health professionals and finish OSHA Form 301 within 7 days. An employer's designated representative can complete the form, so the law does not appear to require a specific licensed signer. The accident-scene inspection and in-person witness interviews still need a human on site.

A state workers' compensation report can count as an equivalent form if it captures the required information. That lets an agent draft one report that covers both the insurer and OSHA filings from the facts it gathers.

Industry commentary from 2026 says agentic AI can take a learning objective to a finished course: it analyzes source material, structures the content, builds personalized learning paths, role-plays and rubrics, and loads the course into an LMS. This evidence is mostly vendor or industry commentary, not independent outcome studies.

Courses on AI-powered instructional design for L&D professionals stress that human expertise is still essential for learning strategy and quality. These are marketing listings, not evidence of outcomes.

Canada's Job Bank lists Manager, Training and Development as not regulated. US career guides describe certification such as ATD or ISPI as voluntary, so no licence is generally required. A few roles, such as security training, have employer-specific credential requirements.

The rules for registered apprenticeship programs (29 CFR 29.5) are a published checklist: a written plan, work-process schedules, related-instruction outlines, equal-opportunity compliance under 29 CFR part 30 and a complaint contact. An agent can map program documents against these items.

State sample standards tie each program provision to a specific 29.5(b) subsection, so checking documents for compliance can largely be automated. Judging how a program actually runs, such as on-the-job supervision and apprentice interviews, still needs a human.

Commercial compliance agents already track mandatory training completion and certification expirations and run gap analyses across HR, policy and training records. This is a vendor's claim, not an independent test. I found no dedicated AI product for apprenticeship compliance review.

Pactum's AI chatbot runs supplier negotiations with Walmart's long-tail vendors on its own, within a value function that analysts define. Results go straight into ERP/CRM, and 3 out of 4 suppliers said they preferred it to a human. Its scope is still limited to commodity items, though.

In 2026, agentic procurement tools from Pactum, Keelvar, Arkestro and SAP Ariba contact and negotiate with hundreds of suppliers at once inside preset guardrails. Strategic contracts and escalations stay under human review.

Vendors and analysts describe tiered oversight: agents act alone on low-value spend, while a person picks among options for strategic sourcing and records why. That fits partial delegation rather than full delegation.

SAP released a rebuilt Ariba with built-in agent features in March 2026 and plans to add 11 Joule agents across Ariba and Fieldglass during 2026. Coupa has more than 20 role-based agents and launched Coupa Compose to build and run agents, and its September 2026 release lets agents run sourcing and payment workflows on their own.

Analysts say the 'autonomous' label is overstated. Cross-module agent workflows still need testing, and approval limits remain a barrier, so a human still sets the rules and approves configuration changes.

Governance guidance tells firms to set spending thresholds, list the decisions that need human review and keep explainable audit trails. These come from internal delegation-of-authority rules and the EU AI Act's high-risk rules, not from any licence that requires a human signature.
O*NET lists this as a Food Service Manager task: cooking, clearing tables and serving food and drinks when needed. All of it is hands-on physical work in the kitchen and dining room.
Restaurants that automate serving or bussing use dedicated robots such as Bear Robotics' Servi. That is physical hardware, outside the reference technology of software-only AI agents with no body.
Restaurant automation trends for 2026 point to robots, not software agents, as the answer to labor shortages in cooking and service.

Vendor pages say hotel revenue-management systems (RoomPriceGenie, PricingService.ai, RoomRaccoon/Pricepoint) set room rates on their own from competitor prices, booking pace and occupancy, push them to the PMS and channel manager, and offer an autopilot mode. These are vendor claims, not independent results.

Hotel budgeting tools such as Otelier TruePlan pull actuals from PMS, POS and accounting systems and use pre-built drivers to cut budget build time. Building the budget still needs input from department heads, and the owner or GM must approve how funds are split between departments.
Vendor buyer's guides say AI budgeting and forecasting software automates driver-based forecasts and budget updates. I found no evidence of fully autonomous budget approval or fund allocation.

Operto ONE runs seven AI agents across front-of-house and back-of-house hotel work. A supervisory layer decides whether each agent drafts, recommends or acts, depending on how confident it is. The agents coordinate tasks, but managers still oversee them.

Apaleo and THE FLAG run an agentic AI in live hotel operations that creates tasks for departments on its own, such as extra beds or cots. It saves about 3.5 hours a week of task creation. It routes and coordinates operational work but does not replace managers conferring with each other.

Sirma's Marta agent links to the PMS, revenue and operations systems. It updates plans and sends tasks to the right teams, which covers the information-sharing part of coordination. Decisions and negotiation between managers stay with humans.

Agentic AI in hotels is being used to coordinate housekeeping scheduling, guest requests, distribution and revenue management. Agents can query the property management system and open maintenance tickets, but only about 1 in 10 chains uses agents at scale, and the specific savings figures come from vendor blogs.

Vendor material says agents check the property management system in real time and either answer a request or start a workflow such as a maintenance ticket. Inspecting and fixing the problem is still left to staff on site.
Lodging manager job postings include physically inspecting the facility, rooms and grounds, doing preventive maintenance, landscaping and overseeing check-in and check-out.

Paradox's hospitality platform and its Olivia assistant already handle high-volume hotel hiring from front desk to housekeeping. Olivia screens applicants with knockout questions, schedules interviews against recruiter calendars, sends reminders, and produces offer letters and onboarding documents.
Third-party reviews say Olivia also coordinates video interviews and hiring events, so an agent can run most of the pipeline end to end. A human still usually decides who gets hired.

NYC Local Law 144 requires a bias audit, a published audit summary, and notice to candidates, who can ask for an alternative selection process. This, together with employer liability for hiring decisions, keeps a human accountable for the final choice. The EU AI Act also classes hiring AI as high-risk with human oversight duties, but my searches did not confirm this.

Code for America and Anthropic built a SNAP Policy Navigator that answers policy questions with cited sources, but the eligibility decision stays with humans. This shows AI can handle the research and interpretation steps of eligibility policy work.

Research on Rules as Code found that LLMs are useful for summarizing and interpreting SNAP and Medicaid policy but not ideal for implementing strict formulas such as benefit calculations, so humans still need to review the work.
Human service agency standards give policy-setting responsibility to the volunteer board, so deciding policy and being accountable for it stays with people.

AI needs-assessment generators can build a framework that pulls together census and demographic data, service utilization records, survey instruments and engagement strategies. They produce plans and templates, not finished analyses of the data.

A 2026 academic paper describes using AI for pattern detection, classification, prioritization and decision support on community-needs survey data to guide program planning. This shows the analysis sub-steps can be automated, though it is a research method rather than a deployed product.

Census figures are the standard population source for needs assessments but do not give an exact count of a community. Program needs assessments still rely on direct input from community members, which calls for human engagement and judgment to interpret.

Vendors sell purchase-order tracking agents. These agents read open PO records, supplier emails, receipts and invoices, label the status of each order and draft chase notes for a buyer to review. A human review step is still built in.
Dynamics 365 ERP MCP servers let AI agents reach live ERP purchasing and inventory data directly. Other vendor agents connect to SAP, Oracle and NetSuite and log every PO action for audit.

Supplier performance agents pull delivery, quality and cost data from ERP records and score suppliers against targets automatically. Vendors still stress human approval for important supplier decisions.

Vendor material describes ITAM, procurement and MDM pipelines (an HRIS trigger, then an asset request, then Jamf/Intune enrollment) that automate the digital side: reading orders, matching the hardware to the role, and setting up the device. Each new hire automatically triggers an asset request in the ITAM platform.

In zero-touch deployment, devices ship from the vendor already configured, which cuts down the technician's hands-on setup. Physical checks and handling still happen at the vendor or depot. The agent has no body, so it cannot look over the hardware itself.
IT provisioning and asset roles still involve hands-on prep and inspection of hardware before it is handed to users. No law or licence requires a human to sign off on this.

Oracle Autonomous Database and Data Safe already automate routine security work: security patching (Oracle says without downtime), encryption, user and security assessments, activity monitoring and data masking. Customers still have to classify their data and check that access policies match their rules.
Oracle says its autonomous database applies security patches automatically and encrypts network traffic automatically. Both claims come from Oracle's own materials.

Agents with database access can change permissions, and reported incidents include an agent running a destructive query on a production database. Guidance therefore calls for least-privilege access and human oversight, so a human still has to review and approve security changes before they are used.

Vendors sell AI agents for aerospace task management and team collaboration. Their own pitch says the agents handle repetitive tasks while humans review and approve the output. That means the agents help with scheduling, tracking and status reporting, but they do not direct engineering staff.

In 2026, NASA and Airbus are using agentic AI to automate design-variant generation and design-to-cost workflows. This automates the technical work being supervised, not the coordination of the people doing it.

The FAA appoints qualified individuals (Designated Engineering Representatives, who must hold an engineering degree under 14 CFR 183.29) to find that engineering data meets airworthiness standards. This puts accountability for design and test outcomes on humans.

Coats Digital released GSD RealMotion in August 2026. It is an AI tool that turns shop-floor video into method studies and is designed to work alongside its existing GSDCost system. The vendor (not independent testing) says it cuts a 45-minute manual timing exercise to about 15 minutes. So AI speeds up key steps, but someone still has to film on the floor and check the results.

A proposed framework for AI-assisted MODAPTS calls for checking AI-generated standards against stopwatch or video time studies, with manual recoding when they differ by more than ±5%. That means a human still has to validate the work before standards are used.

In the US, industrial engineers usually don't need a PE license because many states have an industrial exemption. A license is generally needed only for stamping designs. So in most cases, no law or license requires a human to sign off on internal labor standards or cost systems.
O*NET lists 'confer with customer representatives to review schematics and answer questions pertaining to installation of systems' as a task of Mechanical Drafters (17-3013.00).

AI tools in 2026 index CAD files, PDFs and scanned drawings and return source-cited answers to technical questions. This automates retrieval and drafting of answers, but vendors describe these as tools for internal engineering teams, not as agents that hold customer meetings on their own.

Electrical CAD software (WSCAD ELECTRIX AI 2026) has built-in assistants that answer technical installation questions such as wire sizing. This supports partial automation of answering questions about schematics.

Sketch-to-CAD and drawing-to-CAD AI tools in 2026 handle simple geometry from digital sketches or images. Complex parts still need human cleanup, and engineers review and approve the output. These tools help digitally but do not draw sketches by hand, trace onto paper or run copiers.

Turiya AI reads drawings supplied as images or PDFs and generates CAD code and 3D models. Engineers stay in control and review the results, so the tool supports digital reproduction steps rather than physical tracing or copying.
Drafter certification (ADDA Certified Drafter) is voluntary, and no general license is needed to draft, trace or reproduce drawings.

A 2025 WSP case study presented at IAIA describes an AI workflow for environmental baseline studies. It flags outdated datasets, fills gaps with remote sensing and uses text and data mining. This shows that agents can do the desk-based design and data-gathering steps.

A November 2025 ISEP advice note says AI adoption in environmental impact assessment is still uneven. A June 2026 UK scoping report includes a statement disclosing its AI use. Together they show AI assisting EIA scoping while practitioners keep responsibility for the work.

Under US agency NEPA rules, such as the Interior rule at 43 CFR 46.107, a Responsible Official must independently evaluate contractor-prepared environmental work, give written concurrence and remain responsible for the documents. A human therefore has to review and sign off.

Celanese's JO.AI agents are used across about 50 plants. They handle shift checklists, flag anomalies and draft work orders. Operators and managers still direct the work, so the agents help supervision rather than replace it.
ControlRooms released a multi-agent system in September 2026 that handles detection, advice, logging and shift handover summaries. The vendor stresses that humans stay in the loop to oversee safety.

OSHA's process safety rule (PSM, 29 CFR 1910.119) requires trained operators and an employee participation plan. Directing production in hazardous chemical processes happens on the plant floor and relies on people supervising people in person.

State environmental agencies increasingly run permitting and public notices through electronic systems. Louisiana's 2026 SB 99 gives emailed and electronic notices the same legal weight as mailed ones. An agent can handle these digital channels.

RCRA permit and closure documents have to be placed in publicly accessible locations near the facility or at agency offices, and notices go out to facility mailing lists. Some distribution is still on paper or in person.
Some state programs, such as Maryland's, still ask for hard copies and use mail alongside email. This leaves physical sub-steps for a human, or for a print-and-mail service.

Commercial AI tools such as Mentalyc and TherapyFuel already draft the written plan from session notes or chart diagnoses. They write the goals, objectives and interventions and track progress on each goal. Vendors say the output is a draft that the clinician must review using their own clinical judgment.

Illinois' Wellness and Oversight for Psychological Resources Act (2025) bars AI from making therapeutic decisions on its own. It also bars AI from producing treatment plans or recommendations unless a licensed professional reviews and approves them, with fines of up to $10,000 per violation.

Comparisons of AI tools for therapists in 2026 describe them as documentation and drafting aids that leave the clinical reasoning to the therapist. Carrying out the plan means delivering therapy, which depends on direct contact with clients and the trust built there.

Integrated library systems already handle circulation, patron, inventory and serials records and produce reports in software, so an agent with access to the ILS could compile and update these records through the software itself.
Automated circulation modules keep transaction records, overdue notices, item status (lost, missing, withdrawn), stock verification and report generation, so much of the record-keeping is digital.

Physical stock-taking and equipment checks are still done with handheld RFID readers or shelf scanning. That is the physical input a human (or robot) has to supply before the records can be checked against what is on the shelves.
Library systems already let patrons pay fines online through PayPal or card. Payments post to the patron's account automatically, so collection needs no staff action.
Patrons can choose which fines to pay and pay part of a fine through self-service online portals.
Library chatbots answer routine fine and account questions. Judgment calls, such as disputes or waivers, still go to a human, and in-person cash payments at the desk need someone physically there.

UT Austin's open-source AI-assisted cataloging project builds metadata from images of items, searches OCLC WorldCat for matching records and has an LLM score each match. Catalogers still review the matches before batch upload, so a human stays in the loop.
OCLC already uses machine learning at scale on WorldCat bibliographic records. It ran AI de-duplication of records in 2025 and later extended it to all formats and languages.

A May 2026 industry post (secondary source) says OCLC added AI suggestions for classification and subject headings to Record Manager and Connexion, saving up to about 20 minutes per title in pilots. It also says OCLC's Bibliographic Formats and Standards now explains how to record AI-generated metadata, which implies human oversight.

In December 2025 OCLC added AI suggestions for DDC and LCC classification numbers and LCSH subject headings to Record Manager and Connexion. Catalogers accept or ignore each suggestion and verify it. Pilot libraries reported saving up to 20 minutes per title (OCLC's own figure).

When tested on LCSH, Sears, LCC, DDC and Cutter assignment, ChatGPT and Copilot gave headings that were not specific enough, used unauthorized terms, and built malformed synthetic headings. The authors recommend using them as aids, with human review.

A DCMI 2026 paper reports that LLMs produce LCSH strings that look plausible but break policy. It proposes connecting Claude through MCP to Library of Congress linked-data APIs to check authority headings, so agent pipelines that validate their own output are possible but a human still checks the result.

Elicit, Consensus, Scite and Scopus AI already search the scholarly literature, build literature matrices and write summarized literature reviews with real citations. This covers the main sub-steps of compiling bibliographies and preparing abstracts.

These tools rely mainly on abstracts and open-access full text, and their vendors warn that they can hallucinate or produce inaccurate summaries. A human still has to check the citations and the abstracts before they are used.

Current tools cover large indexes of papers (over 138 million for Elicit and over 250 million for Consensus) and offer deep literature review features. The task is fully digital and needs no physical presence or licensed sign-off.

Existing AI tools such as aiScout (ai.io), Hudl, Sportlogiq and Wyscout already analyze athlete video, score drills and generate performance data and scouting reports. This covers the record-review and much of the skill-assessment work.

A 2024 study of English academy scouts found no significant difference between ratings made in person and from video. However, scouts still considered in-person viewing more accurate, and it carries real time and travel costs.

Scouts still value live viewing for intangibles (work ethic, leadership, body language, off-ball behaviour) and use in-person events and tryouts. Evaluating physical fitness on site requires being there. No search result showed a licensing rule requiring a human scout.

AI agents bought a Czech ad campaign from start to finish, linking Omnicom Media and publisher MAFRA through an MCP gateway and the Ad Context Protocol (AdCP). This is the vendor's own account and has not been independently checked.

At Cannes 2026, Yahoo DSP's Agent Network, TikTok's Symphony Agent and others launched agents that buy and sell ads. A PubMatic executive warned that reliability problems would be common in agent-run media buying.
AdCP was launched in October 2025 with a Media Buy protocol built on MCP. In the first live agent-run media buy, a human approved the purchase.

Raman systems like PharmID Verify check what is inside IV bags, syringes and vials, but the vendor describes them as helping pharmacists with final checks. The work still needs someone physically handling the product, and the verification is the pharmacist's.

A pilot study in 2016 found Raman testing of compounded preparations had a 100% positive predictive value. These are instrument tests run on physical samples, not tasks an agent can do with software alone.

Under USP <795> and state rules (for example N.J.A.C. 13:39-11A.10), the licensed compounding pharmacist is responsible for the identity, strength, quality and purity of ingredients and preparations, including inspecting them and reviewing the Certificate of Analysis.

Epic's Chart with Art: Nursing, live at Mount Sinai and other systems in 2026, drafts the end-of-shift care plan notes from chart data (vitals, flowsheets, medications) and from ambient capture at the bedside. Drafts go into the chart only after the clinician reviews them. Mercy reported note time falling from 3.5 minutes to about 32 seconds (a vendor-reported figure).

Under the College of Nurses of Ontario documentation standard, effective February 2026, nurses may use AI for documentation. They remain accountable for everything entered into the record and must review and verify all AI-generated content.
BCCNM standards require nurses to sign each entry in the client record to show accountability, whether the entry was written by hand or generated electronically.

Manufacturer services such as Sysmex BeyondCare and Ortho's Remote Monitoring Center already do remote calibration, QC monitoring and predictive alerts. Software can therefore take over the data side (QC trend review, scheduling, alerting), but a human still loads calibrators and reagents and does the hands-on maintenance on site.

A clinical-analyzer QC patent describes analyzers sending calibration and QC data and alarms over a network to manufacturer service servers for statistical analysis. This means only some data and diagnostic sub-steps can be done remotely.

CLIA 42 CFR 493.1255 requires labs to perform and document calibration verification at least every 6 months and after major preventive maintenance. CMS surveys cite labs that miss this, so qualified lab personnel remain accountable.

Commercial agentic RCM products say they check eligibility, assemble prior-authorization packets, fix denials and track appeals. They also say humans stay in the loop for key decisions and that unclear cases are escalated for manual review. These are vendor claims and have not been independently verified.

Pharmacy billing technicians spend much of their time on payer rejections, eligibility checks and prior authorizations, including talking with insurance companies. All of this is digital or done by phone.

Technician billing work is covered by state board of pharmacy rules and employer policy. The material found did not show a rule requiring a licensed person to sign claim submissions. Pharmacist verification applies to dispensing, not to billing.

Under nursing or medical direction, psychiatric aides give hands-on routine care. This includes help with bathing, dressing, grooming, feeding and toileting, physical checks, and restraining patients to prevent injury.
A California DDS duty statement for this type of role lists helping individuals with feeding, toileting, grooming and appearance. All of these require physical presence.

Pennsylvania's Office of Developmental Programs warns that AI companion bots pose privacy, emotional and safety risks for people with intellectual disabilities. This means software can only play a limited supporting role, such as caregiver chatbots or activity prompts.

Under 42 CFR 482.13(e)-(f), only trained, authorized staff may restrain a patient, and only when the patient's immediate physical safety is at risk. That staff must be trained to apply restraints safely, watch for distress such as positional asphyxia, and de-escalate. In practice this means trained people physically handle and watch the patient.

AI video and wearable systems that predict aggression or agitation on psychiatric wards are still small pilots or proofs of concept. At most they send alerts. None of them can physically restrain or help a patient.
Legal and ethical reviews urge caution before using AI-CCTV monitoring on mental health wards, citing privacy and consent. This limits AI to a narrow advisory role.

In O*NET-based job descriptions, psychiatric aides walk with patients to and from exams and treatments, keep them in assigned areas, and may restrain violent patients. This is physical, in-person supervision that an agent without a body cannot do.
Aides watch patients for unusual or harmful behaviour and physically restrain or help them to prevent injury. Escorting depends on being there in person and building trust with the patient.

Aides work under nursing and medical staff. No specific licence requires a human to sign off on escorting, but the task cannot be done without physical presence. Software can only help at the edges, such as scheduling or transport logistics.

Qualcomm's NRF 2025 demo shows a smart pharmacy kiosk that helps shoppers find items, book flu shots and get health information. This means an agent can do the product lookup and give directions without a person.

CJ Olive Young (July 2026) has an AI avatar kiosk that checks stock, finds products in the store and recommends items in eight languages. Shoppers can serve themselves, but the kiosk does not walk them to the shelf or greet them in person.

Intel lists an AI chatbot kiosk for pharmacy stores, so locating products with conversational AI is a real product category. The physical parts, greeting someone on the floor and walking them to the shelf, still need a human.

Pharmacy software such as Cegedim Pharmacy Manager's 'Fast Labelling' already fills in the patient, product, directions and quantity from an electronic prescription, so most label preparation is software-driven typing and printing. An agent using the computer could do the remaining data entry and trigger the print.

In pharmacy automation such as Parata Max, integrated printers already produce labels with patient details, medication, dosage instructions, barcodes and regulatory data without anyone typing them. Someone still has to handle the printed label and attach it to the container.

State rules (for example Arizona R4-23-1104 and Mississippi Art. XL) let technicians type and print labels but require a pharmacist to verify their accuracy and hold that pharmacist responsible for the data entered. A human review step therefore stays in place.
Pharmacy software already produces the reorder lists from PAR or min/max levels. That covers the digital step before restocking but not putting stock on the shelves.
In this job description, aides restock shelves throughout the pharmacy and refill supplies to set inventory levels. Both are hands-on duties done under pharmacist supervision.
O*NET lists restocking storage areas and replenishing shelves as a separate task from receiving and inventorying medications.

Pharmacy inventory software already handles the main record-keeping steps. It automatically reconciles wholesaler invoices so staff don't have to match paper invoices against packing slips by hand, and it keeps purchase orders and inventory levels up to date. An agent working in the browser could run these screens from start to finish.

Pharmacy management systems update a running inventory count from electronic wholesaler data (EDI) and invoices, and can track stock by lot and expiry date. Most of the data entry is structured digital work that an agent can do.

For controlled substances, the buyer has to record how many containers actually arrived and the date they arrived. Someone has to physically count the delivery, and only an authorized registrant can sign Form 222 or use a CSOS certificate. This keeps a human involved for checking deliveries and for the controlled-substance steps, even though the aide's routine record entry doesn't require a licence.
JailTracker's jail management software sends automated alerts about inmate appointments and transfers, and its scheduler module keeps staff up to date on scheduled inmate activities and appointments.
InCustody schedules inmate visitation appointments, keeps visitor history and enforces visitation rules, so the rule-based booking step is already software-driven.

A Virginia regional jail moved visitation scheduling from handwritten weekly logs to online self-booking, which shows the scheduling work itself is digital and needs no physical presence. Officers still oversee security limits such as keep-away orders, lockdowns and movement.

Jail management systems already handle booking records, charges, bond and holds, and they auto-fill arrest and charge data from connected CAD/RMS or arrest-report systems. This automates much of the data entry and updating.
Arrest information can be pulled into the jail system to fill in cases, charges and bond details, and staff can update charges, court dates and inmate records in real time.

Identification needs in-person steps by corrections deputies: Live Scan fingerprinting, photos, and documenting scars and tattoos. Checking identity against NCIC and state databases happens inside restricted criminal-justice (CJIS) systems.

Corrections scheduling tools such as VCS COSS, UKG TeleStaff and InTime automate shift rotations, post assignments, overtime and compliance with minimum staffing, but they are rules-based and assist the supervisor rather than replace them.

Housing sergeants act as first-line supervisors on the unit. They brief staff at the start of each shift, make sure officers follow post orders, conduct inmate counts and step in on disciplinary problems, all of which require being physically present in the facility.

Corrections sergeants are sworn positions in a defined chain of command. They supervise, direct, discipline and evaluate officers, which puts personnel and security accountability on a human supervisor.

Commercial visitor-management and access-control systems already handle pre-registration, face-matched check-in with liveness detection, badge issuing and entry/exit audit trails, in some cases without reception staff. The remaining work is mostly physical: intercepting tailgaters, inspecting bags or vehicles and confronting people.
Face-recognition visitor modules let administrators set when and where each visitor may enter and can enroll unexpected visitors on-site, which automates the authorization step.

US states license security guards individually (for example California's Guard Card, Texas Level II and Tennessee). In many states a person cannot work as a contract security officer without a state license.

Restaurant inventory software sold by vendors (Crunchtime/Fourth iQ 2.2) is said to forecast when key items will run out and send '86' alerts for missing ingredients. An agent could do this reconciliation, forecasting and shortage reporting from POS and inventory data.
Bar loss-detection software such as BarGuard is described as comparing poured amounts against sold amounts, flagging likely over-pours or missing items, and sending reorder notices automatically.

Counting stock still means a person walks the cooler, freezer, dry storage and bar, counts or weighs bottles and checks kegs. An agent with no body cannot do this step, so a human must stay involved. Source is vendor content.
Line cook work during service means grilling, sautéing, prepping mise en place and plating by hand. Cooking robots are limited to narrow fast-food uses and cannot yet adapt to unexpected variables.
As of October 2026, cooking robots still cannot handle unexpected variables on the fly, and some deployments have failed. In any case, the reference agents have no robotic body.
Several states, including Illinois, require anyone handling food in a restaurant to hold an accredited food handler certificate. This is a credential tied to a person.

Machines that peel produce automatically, such as the Minerva Omega onion and potato peeler at up to 240 kg/h, are mechanical kitchen equipment. They are not software AI agents, so the reference technology, which has no body, cannot run or replace them.
Peeling machines sold to restaurants, like the Cancan 1323, still need a person to load, run and unload them. Washing, peeling, cutting and seeding produce all means handling it physically.

Commercial vegetable prep machines such as the IMC MF5 are electromechanical tools. The task is manual or machine-assisted work, so an agent that only uses software can do nothing meaningful here beyond things like recipe or cut-spec lookup.

Kitchen automation in 2026 runs on dedicated robot hardware such as Appetronix arms for portioning, plating and salad or bowl assembly. Software-only agents can't do it, and the search found no system aimed at making hors d'oeuvres.
Automated micro kitchens cover only fixed modules (frying, baking, salads, stir-fry), and they are physical robotic systems, not AI agents.

Cooking robots like SoftBank's STEAMA and FLAMA need physical hardware on site. That confirms the task means handling food in person; a software agent can only help with recipes, scaling and prep lists.

Kitchen display systems already pace items by cook time so they reach the expo window together. For example, a 20-minute steak is fired before a 12-minute salmon, and shorter-cook items are held back. This automates the scheduling part of the task.

Toast POS has a 'fire by prep time' item-pacing setting that sends items to stations based on their cook times. It relies on configured cook times, not on what is actually happening at the grill, so the cook still adjusts in real time.
KDS vendors offer course pacing, fire timing and course-hold functions with set gaps between courses, which shows the sequencing logic can be done in software.
Automating food plating and delivery to tables needs dedicated robotic hardware, such as SoftBank's STEAMA/FLAMA cooking robots or delivery robots. A software-only AI agent can't do this.
Getting a plated dish to a customer's table takes physical robotic systems like overhead rails or mobile robots with arms. Even these robots are still described as limited spot solutions.
A patent on robotic service systems describes placing dishes directly at a customer's table as a physical problem that robotics still needs to solve.

AI voice and kiosk ordering (Square's AI kiosk launched in October 2026; Taco Bell drive-thru voice AI is in more than 100 locations) handles order taking and payment. It does not do the physical packaging or hand food to customers.
Taco Bell says more than 100 locations in 13 states use voice AI at the drive-thru. This software takes the order, but the food is still assembled and handed over by people.
Food Code rules require hands-on handling of ready-to-eat food with utensils or gloves. Packaging and serving are physical tasks, though the code does not require a human to sign anything.

O*NET lists 'Carry food supplies, equipment, and utensils to and from storage and work areas' as a core task for Food Preparation Workers (35-2021.00), with importance 87. The task is about physically moving items around a kitchen.

The occupation does hands-on, non-cooking food prep and stocking work in a physical kitchen. A software-only agent with no robotic body cannot move supplies, so its only possible contribution is a minor side job like inventory lists.

Kitchen display system (KDS) expo screens only handle the information side of the hand-off. They flag front-of-house staff when all items in an order are done, but a person still carries the plates to the pass.
Expo screens list each dish as it finishes so servers don't have to check whether it is ready. That covers the coordination messages, not the physical passing of food.
Kitchen staff mark items done by 'bumping' them on the KDS, which tells servers the food is ready. The software tracks status but never moves the food.
Automated meat cutting depends on physical robots: a six-axis arm with 3-D machine vision is used to cut beef hocks in processing plants. That is industrial robotics, not a software agent.
Research systems that cut pork carcasses into primal cuts need fixtures, saws and robot arms. The task is physical manipulation of the meat.
Fully automatic primal cutting of pig half carcasses uses a vision-positioned saw. This is specialised hardware that a software-only agent cannot operate in a typical kitchen.

Vendors say their bar ID-scanning software runs more than 75 automated checks on each ID and flags suspicious documents. They claim it detects up to 95% of fake IDs when paired with UV/IR/hologram hardware. These are vendor claims with no independent testing found.

Some systems combine document scanning with AI facial age estimation (Yoti) to catch good fakes. Software can do the authenticity and age-calculation steps, but someone still has to take the physical card and match the face to the photo at the bar.

States such as California require ID checkers to complete Responsible Beverage Service training. Their 'diligent inspection' defense, and North Carolina's point-of-sale carding with server liability, put legal responsibility on a human server.
AI ordering systems combine voice recognition, a large language model and QR codes so customers can order without an app. They can take drink orders end to end through a kiosk or a phone.

Robotic and kiosk bars take orders by tablet, touchscreen or voice commands. A UK commentary says these systems are not a full replacement for human bartenders, and some chains say they will not adopt them.

State rules require bar staff to refuse alcohol to anyone under 21 or apparently intoxicated, which means checking ID and judging intoxication in person. Bars also face dram shop liability for serving such patrons.

Self-pour beer walls and robotic dispensers (iPourIt, Pubinno, PourMyBeer) handle draft dispensing with hardware, RFID cards and POS links, not software-only AI agents. Guests still pour, or a staff member checks ID in person, so the physical serving stays with people or machines.
Pubinno sells AI-powered devices and robotics that automate draft beer dispensing. That shows the automation that exists needs a physical body, which the reference agents do not have.

California requires bartenders and other alcohol servers to hold Responsible Beverage Service certification, which includes training on checking IDs. Other states have similar rules, so a human must be accountable for serving alcohol.

By 2026, voice AI agents (SoundHound at Red Lobster and Five Guys, plus Aldelo's POS voice agent) take restaurant phone and drive-thru orders end to end and send them to the POS. However, accuracy failures have occurred, including McDonald's ending its IBM order-taking test in 2024.

With QR-code table ordering, diners browse, order and pay on their phones and the order goes straight to the kitchen and POS. Some restaurants have dropped servers for order-taking, but most keep staff in a hybrid model.
Vendors describe QR or app ordering as removing the server's job of bringing menus and taking orders. Staff are still needed at the table to deliver food and help guests.
Toast's help article describes the server printing an itemized receipt and leaving it with the guest. Guests can also view the itemized check on their phone, so the POS already builds the check.
Voice AI ordering agents connect to POS systems such as Toast, Square and Clover. They send captured orders and modifiers into the POS, where pricing and totals are handled.
With QR ordering, guests add items straight onto the same check in the POS, so no server has to enter them. Splitting checks and printing them happen on the floor.

Several vendors (Spatula, Perklist, Nora Neo, Mimiway, QRSur) offer AI menu assistants that diners open from a table QR code. They say these answer menu, ingredient and allergen questions and recommend dishes, wine pairings and add-ons in many languages. These are vendors' own descriptions and have not been independently checked. Some say the assistant only uses allergen data the restaurant has confirmed, so a human still has to maintain and confirm that data.
Vendors present AI menu assistants as taking over routine questions so staff can focus on in-person hospitality. Handing over menus at the table and reading guests in person still need a human there.

The 2022 FDA Food Code (§3-602.12(C)) requires written notice of major allergens for unpackaged food, and the notice can be electronic. These searches found no rule requiring a licensed human to answer menu questions. One Illinois bill would require menus to tell allergic guests to notify a waiter, but the results don't confirm it was enacted.

Flipdish's AI phone agent takes orders and suggests specials, sides and drinks to callers, then sends confirmed orders to the POS. This shows AI can tell customers about specials over remote channels.
Pos Dish's QR and digital menus feature seasonal specials and new dishes, so table-side digital channels can carry the specials information instead of a server.
Dynamu AI, an 'AI waiter' for full-service dine-in restaurants reached by QR code, is still in early pilots. Spoken, in-person delivery at the table still mostly needs a human server.

The robots that help with bussing (Bear Robotics Servi, Pizza Ranch units) are physical carts. Humans still load the dirty dishes, and the robots carry them to the dish room. That makes them robotics, not software agents, and they still don't wipe tables.
Even a purpose-built autonomous bussing robot (Smile Robotics) is much slower than a human at clearing tables. This shows the task depends on physical manipulation.
Restaurants deploy robots to carry dirty dishes to the dish room, which is entirely physical work. An agent that acts only through software has nothing to act on.

Payment at restaurant tables is being automated by dedicated pay-at-table hardware such as NCR Voyix Aloha Pay-At-Table and the tabletop kiosks Chili's uses. These are fixed systems that replace the task, not a general AI agent doing the worker's job.

Self-checkout and self-order kiosks with AI features, such as Partner Tech's Paula, need physical card terminals or tabletop devices. Accepting payment at the counter means being there in person to handle cash, cards and receipts, which a software-only agent cannot do. It can only help with the digital steps in the POS system.

Vendor reports say 66% of US consumers prefer self-service kiosks to staffed checkouts (a figure from the vendor itself). This shows how payment is moving to kiosks rather than to agents running the register.
Generative AI menu tools suggest dishes, flavor pairings, prices and menu descriptions from consumer-demand data and simple inputs, so an agent can produce the material staff would discuss.

Some AI menu tools connect to POS systems to pull sales and inventory data, but Toast advises operators to check AI-generated menus for practicality and cost before using them, so a human still reviews the result.

AI menu planning is sold as support for the people deciding the menu (data analysis and suggestions), not as a replacement for the staff discussion. The conversation itself and the host's first-hand guest feedback stay with humans.
The assistance porters give to passengers with reduced mobility is hands-on and in person: staff meet them at call points, help with check-in, and walk them all the way to their seat on the aircraft.
Autonomous wheelchairs are only at an early stage. Rome Fiumicino's four are run by assistance staff, and Dubai's is still being tested. Both are robotics, which the reference AI agents do not have.

The digital help now available comes from apps such as Be My Eyes and Aira, which use AI and remote agents for information and navigation. That only adds to in-person escort and baggage handling; it does not replace them.

Washoe County, Nevada licensing rules say a caregiver who counts toward the staff-to-child ratio must be physically in the room with the child, close enough to step in. Maine requires that all children can be seen or heard at all times and that sleeping children are checked in person every 30 minutes.

State licensing rules, such as Arizona's, set required staff-to-children ratios by age (1:5 for infants) that count only qualified human staff, and programs get cited when ratios or supervision fall short.
Childcare software such as Brightwheel handles side admin work: daily reports to parents, attendance and billing. The care itself is not done in software.
Caring for Our Children defines cleaning as physically removing dirt with soap, water and friction, then sanitizing surfaces. This is hands-on handling of objects.
Childcare guidance says mouthed and shared toys must be cleaned and sanitized at least daily or whenever soiled. Some guidance says after each use, with a separate bin for mouthed toys.
Sanitizers must be EPA-registered and used as the label says, including dilution and contact time. Licensing sets the standards but does not require a licensed person to do the cleaning.

Digital tools automate developmental screening steps such as ASQ-3 delivery and scoring, and there are AI video-based screening apps for parents. But screening flags still need professional judgement and are meant to start a conversation, not stand alone.

Childcare programs use ASQ to identify developmental and social-emotional concerns, and it depends on adults directly observing the child. An agent can score the questionnaires or draft messages, but it cannot watch children in the room.

Childcare providers are mandated reporters for abuse. Developmental concerns are raised with parents through direct conversations, meetings, email or phone, which is a trust-based, in-person part of the job.

Childcare platforms such as Brightwheel already have digital daily reports where staff log naps, meals, bathroom use and activities, and the app compiles them into summaries for families. They also include tools for observations and assessments against state standards.

Childcare software vendors now offer AI that turns teachers' brief observations into narrative updates and translations, but a teacher must approve each post before it is published. Practitioner guidance says AI should only tidy what a person observed, and that medication, accident and safeguarding records should never be written by AI.

Licensing rules require each dose of medication to be logged with the child's name, the dose, the date and time, and the staff member who gave it. California's medication chart has a staff signature line for each entry, so a human must perform and attest to it.

CDC guidance says sterilizing and sanitizing are hands-on jobs: washing bottles after every feeding, boiling or soaking items, or using a dishwasher's sanitize cycle, then air-drying them. A software-only agent can't do any of this.

Childcare standards (Caring for Our Children / Head Start) say caregivers must mix formula following the parent's or manufacturer's instructions and label bottles with the child's name and the date and time. All of these are physical steps done by staff, so AI could at most help look up guidance.
To prepare formula safely you have to boil water, mix by shaking or swirling, and refrigerate bottles and throw them out on time. Every step means handling the bottles directly.

ChatCPR is an open-source AI tool from UC San Diego, Johns Hopkins and UPMC. It talks bystanders through CPR and did better than human 911 dispatchers in early testing (May 2026). This is help to a human who does the CPR, not a replacement, so it supports L1 at most.
A test with 21 people used a voice chatbot to guide untrained users through CPR. Only 33% of them gave high-quality CPR. In every case a human had to do the chest compressions with their own hands.
Most states require child-care providers to hold first aid and CPR certification. This is a training rule for the caregiver, and it assumes a person on the spot gives the care by hand.

Caregiver apps such as Daily Nanny produce daily and weekly reports from logged naps, feeds, diapers and activities. These can support a parent check-in, but the nanny still has to log the data and hold the conversation.

Kidscare AI advertises AI journaling and milestone tagging to improve communication with parents about a child's development. This helps with preparation, but the content still comes from the caregiver's own firsthand observations.
Some systems, such as MyKidReports, generate the daily report automatically at checkout. That automates written updates, not the regular two-way meeting in which a nanny and parents build trust.

AI activity planners such as Kidtivity Lab and Taskade's Children's Activity Planner can generate age-appropriate games, crafts and activity plans. That covers only the planning step, not running the activities.
Taskade offers a customizable agent that builds children's activity plans from a child's age, interests and learning style. A caregiver still has to carry out the plan.

Nanny work means caring for children in person and without supervision, which is why it needs vetting (for example a UK Enhanced DBS check). Running games, sports, walks and play dates needs a physically present, trusted caregiver.

Camera and IoT baby monitors (for example CuboAi, and research prototypes such as ThermoCam) can watch a child and send fever or temperature alerts. They support observation, but they do not take a reading by hand, drive a child to the doctor or give medicine.

Under Texas HB 1615 (Nathan's Law), child-care staff need a parent's signed, electronic or phoned-in authorization before giving a child medication. The rule covers medication given through a parent's authorization; it does not require a licensed professional, so a lay caregiver can do it with consent.
Utah's child-care rules require parental consent each time over-the-counter medication is given. Giving medication is a physical, hands-on job done by the caregiver who is present.

Ohai.ai's AI connects to Google, Outlook and Apple calendars. It finds free time, schedules events, avoids overlaps and pulls dates and deadlines out of forwarded emails. A third-party reviewer says it also helps coordinate drop-off and pickup, with reminders.

Skylight syncs several family calendars, and its paid Sidekick AI turns forwarded school emails and paper handouts into events. A reviewer notes that such tools do not answer the coach or set up the carpool, so human coordination is still needed.
Ohai.ai is described as an AI household assistant for family scheduling and household logistics.

The chore and reward apps I found (FamilyPoints, NeatKid and others) only let parents assign chores and track points or stars. A human still has to watch the child and give the praise; none of these apps does it on its own.

NeatKid includes positive-reinforcement features, but the praise is digital and gated by parents. Software can support the task (chore lists, tracking), while praising a child at the moment of the behavior requires a person who is physically present.

Nanny licensing rules differ by jurisdiction and usually cover the care setting and background checks. None of the sources I found requires a licensed human to assign chores or praise behavior, so legal accountability is not the main barrier.

AI companions such as ElliQ can provide conversation and reminders to older adults. New York's state pilot with the maker reached more than 800 people, and 95% of users said it reduced their loneliness. That figure is self-reported, not from a controlled study. This covers only the companionship part of the task, which a device can supplement, not replace.

State rules define personal care as hands-on work: bathing, dressing, grooming, toileting, transfers, positioning in bed, feeding and help with walking. All of it requires a person to be physically there.

States such as New York require at least 40 hours of training plus demonstrated skills, which shows the role depends on a trained human being present in person. These rules set competency standards; they do not require anyone to sign off on the care.

In nursing-home rules, the interdisciplinary team that reviews and revises the care plan must include the nurse aide responsible for the resident. The aide's role is to report firsthand observations from contact with the resident, not to write the plan.

Vendor AI tools (StoriiCare) draft care plans from assessments and progress notes, and staff review the drafts before finalizing them. This shows AI can help with the documentation and summary parts of a review.
Home-care platforms predict AI agents will handle documentation, risk detection and information routing for care teams in 2026. Clinical judgement and the team discussion stay with people.

Park and recreation departments already use AI to draft social media posts and program descriptions, and to suggest new programs from national trend data and local data. This covers the promote and organize sub-steps.

Rec Technologies sells recreation management software it calls AI-powered, with email and SMS program marketing and help with registration and administration. Its feature claims come from its own vendor pages.
Recreation workers plan and lead activities in person, supervise participants and keep them safe. Some employers require CPR or first aid certification, so the leading part needs physical presence.
BLS says recreation workers do hands-on work such as setting up equipment, helping participants during activities, and cleaning and maintaining equipment or facilities.
O*NET lists 'Provide for entertainment and set up related decorations and equipment' as one of the occupation's tasks.

AI tools can suggest themes, decor concepts, checklists and shopping lists, which covers only the planning part. Hanging decorations, setting up equipment and running the entertainment still need a person on site.
Recyclers, which are cash-handling machines rather than software agents, can prepare tills at the start of a shift. Someone still has to handle the physical drawer and the cash.
