In patented cash-handling devices, a cashier or manager physically puts the drawer into the machine. The device then counts the cash and checks it against the expected amount, so the counting is done by hardware.

Brink's recyclers automate till dispensing and counting at shift start and close. A software-only AI agent can at most read the device's reports or the POS expected-float figures to help reconcile, and cannot count physical cash itself.
Vendor says its storefront AI assistant learns a store's products, policies and FAQs, and handles shipping, order-tracking and return questions on its own.

Microsoft's Store Operations Agent helps store staff find answers on store procedures, order status and inventory. This supports in-store question answering, but a human still deals with the customer face to face.
Retail AI phone assistants answer questions about store hours, orders and return policies, and pass complex cases to staff. Edge cases still need a human.
Computer-vision produce recognition is sold for self-checkout (Toshiba ELERA, Diebold Nixdorf pilot at Aldi Süd). It identifies the item, but a person still has to put the produce on the scale.
Vision systems recognize produce and price it from the measured weight. The price calculation is already automated by the scale and POS system, so AI adds very little to it.
Checkout scales used for direct sale to consumers must be NTEP-approved and legal for trade. This rule covers the device, not a requirement for a human operator.

Conversational AI agents can already sell event tickets end to end in chat. They recommend events, handle seat selection and run checkout for venues and ticketing platforms. This covers remote or digital sales channels only, not the counter.

AI agents are expected to automate ticket-buying steps such as queueing for ticket releases, comparing prices and making the purchase. The digital transaction side of selling tickets can be automated.

2026 AI customer-service agents can understand what the customer wants, pull account data and carry out actions such as payments and refunds within the conversation. At a cashier's counter, a person still has to take cash, hand over printed tickets or goods and scan items, which needs a physical presence.

Cash-recycler and smart-safe software tracks cash and coin levels in real time for each till and clerk, and alerts managers when levels need attention. This automates the cash-monitoring step, but someone still has to carry cash to the till.
Avivatech's XpressControl dashboard shows cash on hand by cashier, till and location, and automatically alerts users to issues that need fixing.

Computer-vision queue systems count customers at checkout lanes and alert managers to open lanes when lines pass a set limit. This automates spotting staffing gaps, but a person still has to staff the lane. These claims come from vendors and have not been independently checked.

Vendor pages say AI property-inquiry assistants answer buyer questions around the clock. They cover property details, HOA fees, taxes and mortgage estimates, and they qualify buyers on financing. These are marketing claims with no independent accuracy data.
A mortgage AI tool (Roof AI from Mortgageable) answers routine financing questions 24/7 and sends complex cases to human advisers. This supports partial delegation, not full delegation.

Agents who answer outside their expertise, such as repair costs, construction or inspections, face negligence claims and discipline. That gives a reason to have a human review answers, though no law says a human must give them. These sources are secondary.

According to vendor descriptions, AI agents extract unit price, tooling, MOQ, lead time and freight terms from quotes in any format and convert them to a common delivered cost basis. These are product claims, not independent evaluations.
One vendor guide describes an agent that checks current supplier pricing for a materials list and applies the firm's markup, overhead allocation and profit rules.
Quote-extraction tools such as Procumi have the user review and confirm extracted data before it is saved. Scanned PDFs and inconsistent item descriptions are known weak points.

Cassidy's vendor page describes a payroll reconciliation agent. Before funds go out, it compares current payroll against prior periods at the employee and aggregate levels. It also matches outbound payroll debits against bank statements and journal postings.

Spendflo's bank reconciliation agent pairs payment and ledger records, flags unmatched items with likely causes, and produces a period summary for sign-off. Accountants still accept the matches and make adjusting entries, and controllers sign off.
Oracle Fusion Cash Management reconciles payroll bank accounts automatically using matching and tolerance rules. Exceptions still need human resolution.

Benevity says its certified Workday integration automates payroll giving and cuts internal admin work. Third-party listings say it handles payroll-deduction donations and automatic corporate matching.
In January 2026 ADP launched Assist Agents that plan and act across HR and payroll workflows, with humans keeping oversight.
QuickBooks' Payroll Agent drafts pay runs and journal entries for wages, taxes and benefits for a human to approve. It does not run payroll by itself.

Riff describes an agent that finds open purchase orders with no supplier confirmation, sends follow-ups to suppliers on its own, updates the ERP (SAP S/4HANA, Oracle, Dynamics 365) and escalates to a buyer when a supplier doesn't respond. This is the vendor's own claim and has not been tested independently.

Fellowmind describes a Supplier Communication Agent that sorts incoming supplier emails into confirmations, change requests and rejections, then shows the proposed ERP changes to a person for review before applying them. So changes still need a human step. This is the vendor's own claim and has not been tested independently.

SAP says Lemvigh-Müller's agents read supplier responses and compare quantities, dates and prices against purchase orders in SAP Cloud ERP. Mismatches are sent to follow-up workflows or flagged for a buyer to review. This is a customer story published by the vendor, with no independent measured results.

Teller-platform software such as CheckPartner Enterprise and TROY AssurePay Teller takes the teller's request, sends the official check to a secure MICR printer and emails larger amounts to a manager for approval. That digitizes the data entry, funds and debit posting, and approval steps, but someone still has to handle the check stock, sign or endorse the check, and give it to the customer.

Cloud official-check software integrates with the core banking system and uses multi-factor authentication. An agent would only have access to these issuance and verification systems if the bank granted it credentials.

Remote official-check issuance with secure printing is already offered, so preparation can be centralized. Under bank internal-control policies, an authorized human signer or approver is still accountable for official checks, especially high-value ones.
Stayntouch says its PMS sends a room's 'dirty' status to housekeepers' mobile devices when the folio closes at checkout, and then assigns cleaning tasks automatically. This is a vendor claim.
Oracle OPERA's documentation describes a setting that changes a room's housekeeping status automatically at checkout, so front desk staff don't have to set it by hand.

Mews MakeUpMyRoom reorders the housekeeping queue as soon as a checkout is logged in Mews. This is a vendor claim. Remaining cases, such as guests who leave without checking out, may still need a staff member to confirm the room is empty.

Libraries now automate returns sorting with robotic materials handling: conveyors read each item's RFID tag and route it to bins. That is physical robotics, which is outside the reference agent's abilities.
Even with automated sorters, staff still carry materials to the shelves on carts and place them by hand. Shelving remains physical work.
Sorting is driven by RFID lookups in the library management system (SIP2). That digital step is small and already automated, and no law requires a human to do or sign this task.

Libraries already run chatbots that point users to databases, help them search the catalog and answer questions about library services. Examples are Ask ALEX at the University of Oklahoma and ELIZA at Mahasarakham University. They are available around the clock, but no independent study has checked how accurate they are.

Job specifications say library assistants greet and help patrons at a front counter or public desk and show them where library services and materials are. Much of this instruction happens in person, on site.
No licence or certification is needed. Postings ask for a high school diploma plus experience, so no law requires a human to do or sign off on the task.

Librarians already use AI chatbots and design tools for the digital parts of display work: picking themes, building themed booklists and read-alikes, finding quotes and making signage. These tools help with the work but do not set up the display.

State library guidance treats AI as an optional tool that sparks ideas and speeds up tasks, not a replacement for staff. Editable bookmark reading lists and poster templates in Canva support display signage.

Library assistant job descriptions combine arranging and maintaining displays with physical work: pulling books from shelves, lifting and carrying materials, pushing trolleys and reaching above shoulder height. This part is physical and needs a person on site.
Order-intake agents built on Dynamics 365 use MCP to match customers, items and quantities against ERP records. Items they cannot match go to a review screen where a person corrects them.
Workist's Order Agent processes more than half of Primavera's orders fully automatically. When order data conflicts with master data, a salesperson reviews the order before it goes to the ERP.
A multi-agent system with a customer-validation agent uses business rules and fuzzy matching to find the right ERP customer IDs. The vendor reports that 85% of order workflows are fully automated.

Vendor material says AI cash-application agents can take payment details from lockbox PDFs, bank files and remittance emails, match them, and post payments to the ERP with little manual data entry. This covers the recording step. These are vendor claims and have not been checked independently.
HighRadius describes specialized agents that download bank statements and lockbox files and post payments to the ERP. That means software already does the recording and reconciliation sub-steps.

Paper checks and money orders still have to be physically received and scanned by staff, or sent to a mail-in or lockbox service, before they can be deposited. So the 'send items for processing' step needs a person or physical equipment.
Monitor ERP's Agent automatically sends regular reports, such as order inflow and sales statistics, to the right employees in Excel or PDF format.
The OutSystems Sales Reporting Agent answers sales questions in plain language using the Customer, Order, Product and Supplier data stored in OutSystems.
The Infosys order management app on SAP uses agentic AI to give insights on order status, fulfillment performance, exceptions and reconciliation.

Vendor buyer's guides from 2026 describe AI recruiting agents that run hiring workflows from a goal, including screening applications against criteria and changing the criteria when too few candidates match, with little human input. These are vendor claims and have not been independently checked.

NYC Local Law 144 covers tools that substantially assist or replace discretionary hiring decisions. Employers must get an independent bias audit within the past year, publish a summary of it and notify candidates. It does not ban automated screening, and the sources found do not show it requires human review.

Commentary from 2026 says the EU AI Act and NYC LL144 put compliance duties on hiring AI. I did not confirm from a primary source that the EU AI Act classes recruitment AI as high-risk with human-oversight duties, so this rests on background knowledge. That is why barrier_accountability is set to true and the work is rated partial rather than full delegation.

Superunit says its agent 'Ava' runs employment verification end to end by phone, email and fax. The company reports 200k verifications across 17 countries, about 70% completed, most within a day. These are the vendor's own figures.
Bright Horizons uses Phenom's AI voice screening agent to run reference checks at scale. Concerning responses are flagged for a recruiter to review, so a human still checks the output.

Under the FCRA, the applicant must receive a written disclosure and give authorization before a consumer report is obtained. The law does not require a human staff member to make the request, and these rules generally don't apply when the employer calls references itself.

Motorola Solutions' Assist AI for 911 (expanded June 2026) streams live 911 audio, call summaries and transcripts to field units through CAD and mobile apps, and adds real-time translation. This automates passing information from callers to responders, but dispatchers still run it.

AI call takers handle non-emergency calls in Minnesota PSAPs. In Dakota County, AI redirected about 33% of calls in 2025. Emergency radio traffic and inter-agency relay are still done by human telecommunicators.

Some states require each PSAP calltaker or dispatcher position to be staffed by a person who has completed approved telecommunicator training (e.g., New Jersey, Florida, North Carolina). That implies a human must perform the work, though there is no single national standard.

Aurelian's AI voice assistant is used by more than a dozen 911 centers, including Snohomish County WA, Chattanooga and Kalamazoo. It handles non-emergency calls such as noise and parking complaints and transfers real emergencies to a human dispatcher.
In 2025 Dakota County, MN's AI attendant redirected about 33% of calls to the dispatch center and answered common questions. Anoka County, MN is launching an AI non-emergency call taker.

AI only rarely answers 911 calls directly. NENA's operations and standards VP said a caller reporting an emergency should hear a human voice. State rules such as Utah's require at least two telecommunicators answering 911 at all times.

Motorola Solutions' Dispatcher Assist Suite produces real-time transcripts of radio traffic. Its Assist product prepares incidents from transcribed radio traffic, but a dispatcher must confirm them before they count.

Hobbyist tools such as Scanner Command transcribe live scanner audio with Whisper, use AI to pull out what happened and where, and map incidents automatically. The core monitoring sub-steps can be automated.

AI transcription of radio feeds makes mistakes that matter. In Bend, Oregon, 'Shop with a Cop' was transcribed as 'shot with a cop' and set off false alerts. A human still needs to review the output before acting on it.

A FEMA posting for a mobile communications vehicle job lists movement planning, operating and maintaining the vehicle, pre-trip inspections, and setting up and maintaining communications equipment. It asks for the ability to safely operate large commercial-size vehicles under federal and state rules. This is hands-on physical work, and only the planning, record-keeping and IT troubleshooting can be done in software.
A county telecommunicator posting says some duties are done outdoors in a communications trailer, so the worker has to be there in person.

Canadian Job Bank descriptions of emergency communications officers include operating radio and telecommunication equipment and coordinating vehicles and personnel. These are tasks done at a console, which software can help with but not physically carry out.

Salesforce says Agentforce for Field Service lets customers schedule, reschedule or cancel service appointments around the clock in natural language, with the booking finalized without human involvement. This is a vendor claim, not an independent evaluation.
Fieldcode presents AI voice agents that take field-service requests, check them and pass them directly into scheduling workflows. This is also vendor material.

Fieldproxy's marketing says its AI voice agents answer inbound calls, qualify requests and book jobs, and that it assigns work by technician skills, availability and location. These claims are not independently verified, and no source covering trucking or freight dispatch turned up.

The carrier Hirschbach uses Augment's AI agent, Augie, for outbound driver outreach: information requests and pickup and delivery arrivals. That is about 40% of its track-and-trace contacts. Humans still handle the rest.

Vendor voice AI agents (Bubba AI, Bland, Telnyx) say they handle check calls, status updates, dispatch instructions and rescheduling. They connect to TMS and ELD systems and pass exceptions to human dispatchers. These are the vendors' own unverified claims.

A third-party guide summarizing FCC rules says business and industrial two-way land mobile radio needs no commercial operator licence. I did not confirm this against current 47 CFR Part 90, so no legal rule appears to require a human operator.

AI scheduling engines use real-time location, skill match, traffic and parts availability to build and rebuild schedules automatically. One guide cites Geotab's 2025 report saying 76% of field-service leaders already use AI scheduling and dispatch.
Agentic AI dispatch connects to telematics and IoT sensors to monitor locations and coordinate assignments. Vendors say fully autonomous loops are only in pilots, and they name no customers.

Adaptive scheduling keeps recalculating assignments as technician availability, job priority and traffic change. This is a software-only task that needs no physical presence and no licensed human sign-off.

The Weather Company's Operations Dashboard for Ground Transportation (2017 coverage) combines weather, road conditions and live traffic and incident data. It sends drivers real-time hazard alerts for their current and upcoming locations, and dispatchers can push custom alerts to drivers through an API.

WeatherOptics, sold through the Motive and Samsara marketplaces, can automatically alert drivers in real time to weather hazards and suggest actions such as slowing down, pulling over or taking another route.
Lytx Weather Hazard Alerts uses AI-powered geospatial technology and NOAA data, and fleet managers can set alerts by place, time window and weather type. It covers weather, not traffic.

Vendors describe AI receptionists that answer calls, work out why the person is calling, apply routing rules and connect them to the right person, team or queue. They hand the call to a human when the caller asks or when the AI can't help. These sources are vendor marketing, and no independent accuracy benchmarks were found.

Virtual reception systems check visitors in and alert the host by SMS, email or chat. When a case is more complex, they connect the visitor to a live receptionist by video. This means walk-in visitors still partly need a human or physical kiosk hardware.
AI front-desk products say they welcome and verify visitors and notify hosts automatically at check-in, while sources note that AI still struggles to show empathy to stressed or confused visitors.

OpenAI's Deep Research agent plans and carries out multi-step web research by itself. It backtracks when needed and returns a report with citations in 5 to 30 minutes. This is the core of the task. The coverage found dates from the 2025 launch, so current limits may differ.
ChatGPT agent combines Deep Research with Operator. It can navigate websites, filter results, ask the user to log in when needed, run code, and produce editable documents or spreadsheets.

Agents that search and synthesize hundreds of online sources into research-level reports were commercially available well before October 2026. The task needs no physical presence and no licence or signature. These two points are a judgement from the task's nature; I did not search them separately.

Adobe's InDesign AI Assistant takes plain-language requests and carries out multi-step layout changes. It is still in beta, so it can make modifications from instructions, but the documentation does not show it judging rendered pages visually.

Computer-use agents work in a loop: take a screenshot, decide what to do, act, then check the result and correct it. This matches viewing the work in progress on screen and fixing it. The source describes the general pattern and does not mention InDesign.

Design agents in Figma and Framer build layouts from components and accept screenshots as references. The work is done entirely in software, so no physical presence is needed. Final aesthetic judgment and acting on client feedback usually still go through a human.

Prepress systems such as Enfocus PitStop Server already ingest files without a person: they watch hot folders, check incoming PDFs against preflight profiles and sort them into pass and fail folders with reports. Switch can also pull jobs from email, FTP and cloud services.
Kodak Prinergy ships Smart Hot Folder setups that are fully or semi-automatic for bringing jobs into the prepress workflow.

In 2026, computer-use agents can operate desktop apps with mouse and keyboard to enter and move data. This covers the keyboard and mouse part of the task, but someone still has to place physical originals on the scanner or in front of the camera.

Canva Magic Design creates layout options from a text prompt or an uploaded image. A 2026 update reportedly lets its AI resize, recolor and adjust layouts on its own, so agents can draft sample layouts from start to finish. A person still reviews the result for brand fit and typography.
Canva Magic Layers (March 2026) turns flat designs into editable layered layouts, which supports automated layout revision.
Desktop publishing operators are not a regulated occupation in Canada, and no professional licence is needed to prepare layouts. The work is done entirely in software, with no physical step.

In InDesign, the Separations Preview panel and Ink Manager let a user turn spot colors into CMYK, decide which inks get their own plate, and check ink-coverage limits, all in software. An agent that can operate a desktop could run these steps. Adobe still advises checking with the printer before converting brand inks.

Esko Equinox, a prepress tool, converts spot colors into a fixed process ink set (CMYK plus up to three extra inks). The vendor says this makes the choice of ink count and separations predictable. These claims come from Esko, not independent tests.

Choosing how many colors to use is a trade-off between budget, brand accuracy and the press. Results depend on the printer's own press setup and need proofing. In practice a human usually confirms the choice with the client or printer, but no licence or legal sign-off is required.

Flooring estimating software such as Measure Square can automatically create carpet cut sheets. It optimizes seam placement, layout direction, waste, roll width and pattern-repeat allowances, so the planning that follows the floor sketch can be done digitally.
Users still adjust the software's cuts by hand, and reviewers say moving cuts is clunky and some calculations are unreliable. A human has to check the plan before carpet is cut.

The main work is physical: rolling out the carpet, measuring and marking it on site, and cutting it with a carpet knife. An agent with no body or robotics cannot do these steps, so it can only help with the cut plan. No licence or sign-off requirement applies to this step.

Vendor material says procurement agents can draft purchase orders from approved requests and check them against budget and contract terms, but a human buyer still releases each order. Other vendors describe spending caps and limits as guardrails. These are vendor claims.
A practitioner source says agentic AI in procurement is mostly used in pilots and narrow cases. Unusual price variances are typically handed off to a human.

A CMMS vendor says AI analytics can forecast maintenance costs 12 to 24 months ahead from historical spend, PM schedules and asset age. This supports automated spend monitoring and budget input, but the claim comes from the vendor.

Repair-shop estimating software already automates labor and parts calculations using labor guides and pricing matrices, and vendors claim AI can generate estimates from historical repair orders. These are vendor claims, not independent results.
Estimating tools pull parts availability and supplier pricing straight into estimates, work orders and invoices, so collecting cost data is a software job.

CMMS tools record planned against actual labor hours and material costs and produce variance reports, but they depend on technicians entering accurate time and materials, which is often guessed after the job. A human still has to judge the scope of the job and verify contractor invoices.

A Morgan Lewis analysis from 2026 says AI agents are coming into labor relations work but will not replace labor negotiators or employee relations professionals. Unions are also pushing back on algorithmic management and bargaining over its use.
UK legal guidance in 2026 says AI can support HR and management decisions on grievances but should not replace human judgement. Acas is consulting on whether its grievance code should cover AI use.

Under the NLRA, meetings with employees and union representatives come with legal representation rights (Weingarten). These are person-to-person dealings between management and labor, not document processing.

Pactum's AI agents negotiate with hundreds of suppliers at once over chat, following policies set by humans. This is vendor marketing, and it covers routine commercial terms, not technical discussions about products.
NEC's automated negotiation AI is a Gartner-cited use case. It automates adjusting delivery schedules with suppliers, a narrow, rule-bound sub-step.

Procurement sources say AI agents work well for transactional negotiations with clear parameters, but strategic supplier discussions still need human judgment and relationship skills. No source showed agents running vendor product meetings, which often include in-person demos and handling samples.
AI maintenance copilots search manuals, work-order history and procedures to give troubleshooting guidance to technicians. The technician still does the physical repair.
Vendor AI assistants are sold as technician aids, claiming faster issue resolution and shorter mean time to repair. They do not carry out repairs on their own.
Some states, such as Hawaii, require at least a maintenance electrician's licence for electrical maintenance work and a journey worker or master plumber licence for plumbing work.

The vendors that automate weld-path generation (Path Robotics, TetraGen, ABAGY, CENIT FastSuite) all rely on robot cells with 3D vision. A software agent without a body cannot hold a torch or join metal; at most it can look up procedures or settings, which is a small share of the time.
Even the AI-driven robotic welding systems listed in 2026 are described as not yet fully autonomous, and they need dedicated robot hardware. They do not fit varied general repair work done on site.

OSHA 1910.252 requires on-site safety work for hot work: moving combustibles within 35 ft, having extinguishers ready, and posting fire watchers for at least 30 minutes afterward. All of this needs physical presence. It covers hot-work safety; the searches found no welder licence requirement for general maintenance.

O*NET (49-9044.00) lists this as a core millwright task, rated 73/100 in importance. Millwrights install, take apart and move heavy machinery, which involves hands-on rigging, alignment, shimming and shrink-fitting.

Employer job postings describe the duty as taking equipment apart for transport and sharing installation and upkeep with a crew. The work uses hoists, lift trucks, rigging, leveling and foundation building, so it needs physical presence.

The available digital tools give AR step-by-step instructions to guide human technicians through disassembly and reassembly. A software agent can help with documentation and sequence planning, but it cannot do the physical work.

O*NET says helpers work hands-on, assisting with maintenance, parts replacement and repair of vehicles, industrial machinery and electrical equipment, and lists examining and testing machinery and parts for defects among their tasks.
AI vibration-analysis tools flag obvious defects from collected sensor data so analysts can focus on harder cases. The vendor presents the tool as helping analysts rather than replacing them.
Cloud ML platforms find anomalies in sensor data, but experienced analysts review the results. The sensors have to be physically installed on the machines first.

O*NET lists this as a core task for Helpers--Installation, Maintenance, and Repair Workers (49-9098.00). It is hands-on work: cleaning and lubricating vehicles, machinery, tools and work areas with hand tools, power tools and cleaning equipment.

The other core tasks in this occupation are physical too, such as installing or replacing parts with hand or power tools, moving tools and supplies between work stations, and applying protective coatings against corrosion. This leaves almost nothing a software-only agent with no body could do. At most it could look up lubrication schedules or specs, which is a small share of the time.
No licence or sign-off rule requires a human for routine cleaning and lubrication. The barrier is entirely physical.
O*NET lists this as a Machinists (51-4041.00) task. The neighbouring tasks are taking machines apart with hand or power tools and replacing defective parts, which is hands-on mechanical work.

Job postings describe installing machined replacement or repaired parts in mechanisms, machines and equipment, then running the unit to check that it works. All of this needs someone physically there. An agent with no body can only help at the edges, for example by finding manuals, torque specs or installation steps.
Machinists generally do not need a licence or sign-off for this work, so the main barrier is physical, not legal.

Camera-based AI occupancy software can find occupied and free bays, including in unmarked areas, using standard IP cameras. That covers only the monitoring side of space use, not the cleaning or tidying itself.

Parking AI platforms offer live dashboards showing available, occupied and reserved spaces by zone, plus APIs that feed signage. An agent could watch these and flag problems, but a person still has to sweep, remove debris and move cones or vehicles on site.
Bosch AI cameras can monitor parking bays without sensors fitted to each bay, which helps with space-use analytics. They do no physical cleaning or rearranging.

Parking guidance systems already direct drivers to free spaces without an attendant. Sensors in each space detect occupancy and feed LED indicators and directional signs. These are fixed sensor and signage systems, not AI agents, and they only work in garages that have them installed.

Guidance signage at major intersections inside a garage sends drivers only down rows with free spaces. This does the wayfinding part of the job through installed infrastructure rather than a software agent.

The task as described means a person standing in the lot and directing cars with hand signals or a flashlight. An agent with no body cannot do that. Searches found no licence requirement for this work, though I did not run a search aimed specifically at licensing law.

Driverless parking at SAE Level 4 depends on specially equipped vehicles and garage infrastructure, such as the Bosch/Mercedes system approved for Stuttgart Airport's P6 garage. That is robotics and vehicle automation, not a software-only AI agent.
Parking and retrieving cars means physically driving customers' vehicles, and an agent without a body cannot do this.
City codes such as Baltimore's require each valet attendant to hold a valid driver's license and be at least 18.
Valet job descriptions list greeting arriving guests and opening the passenger doors as core duties. Both are done in person, by hand, at the curb.
A state job description has attendants greet guests, open vehicle doors, explain valet procedures and tag keys at the vehicle. These steps happen face to face.
Valet setups without attendants use kiosks and robots to handle check-in and parking. They do away with the human greeting and door service. No software-only AI agent opens car doors.
O*NET lists this as a core hand-packer task: mark and label containers, container tags, or products using marking tools, alongside physical handling duties such as forklifts and pallet jacks.

Label printing software already designs labels, fills in their data from WMS, ERP or e-commerce systems, and prints them automatically from triggers or APIs. A software agent could therefore handle the digital part (label content and printing), but a person or a print-and-apply machine still has to put the label on the item.
SHRM's hand packer job description treats marking and labeling as manual physical work. Standard sources mention no licence or sign-off requirement for this task.

Measuring, weighing and counting on packing lines is automated by dedicated machines, not software agents. Examples are combined checkweigher and vision systems (±0.5 g at 150 packs/min) and line-scan counters. A hand packer still has to put items on scales and count them by hand. A software-only agent can only help with record-keeping, tally arithmetic and checking tolerances.
Vision counting machines can count products into boxes at high speed (vendor claims up to 100,000 per hour at more than 99% accuracy). This is robotics and machinery, not the reference agent.

NIST Handbook 133 sets the rules for testing net contents of packaged goods. It mainly governs compliance testing by officials and does not require a licensed human to weigh or count during routine packing.

O*NET lists 'Load materials and products into package processing equipment' as a task for Packers and Packagers, Hand (53-7064.00). The occupation is defined as packing or packaging a wide variety of products and materials by hand, which is physical manipulation work.

The occupation's related tasks are also physical (examining, weighing, sealing and labeling containers). The reference agent has no robotics, so it can do at most minor digital support like looking up loading specs, not a substantial part of the task.

In O*NET, Packers and Packagers, Hand (53-7064.00) is manual work. Related tasks include moving products and orders by hand and placing them on conveyors or loading docks. My search found no O*NET task with the exact wording 'transport packages to customers' vehicles', so the task was rated as given.

The task means physically carrying or wheeling packages to a customer's vehicle. The reference AI agents have no body or robotics, so they could at most help with small digital steps like order lookup or pickup notifications. Not checked by search; inferred from the task and the agent definition.
Saleo launched an AI Demo Agent in January 2026. Saleo describes it as a fully conversational agent that runs product demos on its own, in several languages, 24/7, with live co-browsing for buyers.

In 2026 there are several AI demo agent tools that build demos or present them to buyers, including Consensus, Storylane, Navattic, Naoma and Saleo. Setup takes days to weeks and needs a human to configure and approve the content.
Sales reps worry that AI demo agents will botch demos or pass along cold leads. This suggests that live, high-stakes demos to field staff and key customers still need human delivery and review.

Instantly says its AI SDR agent finds leads, writes and sends personalized outreach emails, follows up and books meetings to a rep's calendar without a person. This is the vendor's own marketing claim.
Relevance AI's marketplace lists AI agents for outbound email and meeting booking. They contact organizations, explain what is offered and book qualified meetings directly. The page is promotional.

Independent reviews of AI SDR tools say autonomy varies. Some tools only run sequences that humans design, and the reviewers point to a big gap between sending emails in bulk and getting qualified meetings. That supports keeping a human to review the messaging and to build the relationship.

Vendor sources describe AI-moderated and synthetic-audience concept testing that can run many consumer interviews at once and finish in hours instead of weeks. These are marketing claims and have not been independently verified.
By 2026, agentic project-management tools such as ClickUp, Wrike, Notion and Linear handle triage, spec drafting, tracking and reporting, but they hand key decisions back to humans at defined points.
A 2026 systematic review found that AI agents can simulate project-manager roles for planning and progress tracking, while humans keep the final decisions.

AI benefits decision-support products are on the market in 2026. HealthJoy's tool estimates each plan's annual cost and recommends one. Alight's generative AI assistant helps employees compare plans and set HSA/FSA contributions. A published 2026 blueprint for an AI enrollment agent still keeps confirmation steps and hands judgment calls to HR, so humans stay in the loop.

Pave, Decusoft, MangoApps and Salary.com sell AI compensation tools. They generate merit recommendations within budget, flag pay-equity risks and explain their reasoning to managers. Pave's agent is described as an AI compensation analyst. This means an agent could prototype and configure guidance tools. Managing the design work still involves human steps: getting stakeholders and the pay philosophy aligned, choosing a vendor, and approving the result.

The research found that employers are expected to provide an easy path to a human counselor and to review AI recommendations before use. No licence or signature requirement applies to the work of designing these tools, and none of it needs physical presence.

Bridgit's construction workforce-planning AI agents put together project teams, find available workers and suggest assignments, but planners review and approve the suggestions before any change is made.

Sir Robert McAlpine is rolling out AI workforce-planning software across its UK operations to replace spreadsheet processes. The software checks workers' availability, certifications, location and project experience, and forecasts labour needs.
Lumber's SmartPlanner automatically picks crews by availability, skills and proximity for construction scheduling and dispatch.

Batesville's Family Choices Digital Showroom is an online tool that guides families through choosing burial and cremation products. It suggests products based on information gathered in conversation, shows choices in real-time 3D and links to ordering. Software can therefore present product information without a person, but it does not maintain the physical casket display.

Funeral home software such as Passare and the tools listed on Capterra includes product catalogs that can be shared online and online arrangement features. One funeral director said these tools are not easy to use for showing caskets in the arrangement room, which suggests in-person showing is still the norm.

The FTC Funeral Rule requires funeral homes to give a General Price List to anyone who asks about goods, services or prices in person. They must also offer a casket price list before showing caskets, and give accurate prices to people who ask by phone. The rule sets how the information must be disclosed, but it does not require a licensed person to give it.

Funeral homes usually notify the Social Security Administration (SSA) of the death and help with SSA and VA burial paperwork. Survivors must apply themselves for the $255 lump-sum payment and for monthly survivor benefits. The work is mostly finding out who is eligible and explaining the rules, which is document and information work an agent can do from the case details.

The VA cannot pay DIC, survivor pension or burial allowance until the death is recorded in its system, and families need the DD-214. These are clear, rule-based eligibility checks that an agent could build into a personalized benefits summary.

Funeral software already offers aftercare and case-management modules, and some store burial claims and Social Security forms. The talk itself usually happens face to face with grieving families during the arrangement conference, so a person still delivers the information and checks it.

The funeral director normally gathers pallbearers 10–20 minutes before the service for an in-person rehearsal. During the service the director cues them aloud or by gesture and shows them where to place their hands when loading the casket. This on-site part needs a physical presence that an AI agent can't provide.

Funeral home case-management and family-portal software, such as Passare, Procession and Tukios, already handles scheduling and sends arrangement updates and notifications. An agent could use these tools to recruit and confirm pallbearers and send them written instructions. I found no feature built specifically for pallbearers.
Funeral-home guides describe the director as the person who instructs pallbearers. None of the sources say a licence or law requires a licensed person to arrange or brief them.

A paid funeral usher job posting lists in-person duties: greeting families and guests, directing them to the service area and restrooms, handing out memorial folders, moving flowers and setting up extra chairs. All of these require physical presence.
Funeral directors discreetly guide immediate family to the front rows. This seating is done in person, with tact, for grieving people.

Ushers are often the first point of contact. They help guests find their designated seats and get around the venue, which is face-to-face hospitality that a software-only agent cannot do. An agent could at most draft a seating chart or digital signage.

Affirmative action plan software already handles the data collection, analysis and reporting for equal-opportunity compliance, such as flagging underrepresentation and tracking progress toward goals. These analytic and drafting sub-steps can be done digitally. The source is a low-authority page.

Under 41 CFR 60-2, as of the 2022 legal alerts, covered US federal contractors had to certify through OFCCP's registration portal that they had developed and maintained their affirmative action programs. The results do not name the signatory, but the certification is an organizational legal representation, which points to a human accountability step. Whether the requirement still applies in 2026 was not confirmed; it was not verified here, but EO 11246 was reportedly revoked in January 2025, which would reduce this barrier.
The EEOC has warned that using AI does not excuse employers from liability for employment decisions. That makes human review of AI-generated appraisal and equity programs necessary before use.

ServiceNow says its AI agent resolves 90% of inbound IT tickets at its own employee help desk. It handles password resets, account unlocks, software access requests and connectivity issues end to end. This figure is reported by the vendor and has not been independently audited.
Ivanti's April 2026 release put an agentic AI service-desk agent into commercial use for autonomous ticket resolution.

A 2026 industry roundup says the best platforms resolve 40% or more of incoming tickets without a human. Routine Level 1 requests get automated first, and humans still handle escalations and complex or hardware-related malfunctions.
AI interviewer tools run parallel one-on-one stakeholder interviews and synthesize where stakeholders agree and disagree. This supports delegating question design, conversation and synthesis.

BA practice guidance in 2026 says AI can draft requirements, but a skilled analyst is still needed to tell whether the real problem matches what the stakeholder described. The human keeps final ownership of the requirements.
In the US, no licence is needed to work as a computer systems analyst, so no legal sign-off barrier applies.

Vendor and analyst comparison guides for software platforms are widely published online in 2026, so an agent that can browse can gather and synthesize this material end to end. These guides note vendor bias and the need to verify pricing and vendor viability, which supports keeping a human review step.

Structured product assessments profile enterprise vendors (AWS, Microsoft, Google, Salesforce, ServiceNow and others) on features and roadmap. This is the kind of evidence an agent can collect and compare to draft a recommendation without a human doing each step.

Procurement guidance says to judge vendors on performance, governance, ROI and roadmap fit rather than feature checklists. That depends on internal requirements, budgets and existing systems, which usually sit with people and internal systems an agent may not reach. No licence or legal sign-off is typically required, but a human usually approves the purchase.

Commercial survey software (Carlson Survey, MicroSurvey CAD, Geo-plus VisionCogo) already handles COGO, traverse and least-squares adjustment, and lot closure checks. Leica Cyclone II TOPO and VisionLidar find ground points and classify point clouds automatically. An agent that can operate these tools could do most of the number-crunching.

An industry article says AI handles numeric data well but struggles with historical, vague or contradictory boundary descriptions, and that automated output must be checked against known benchmarks. That means a human still has to review the work, especially for property lines.
In states such as Oregon, Maryland and Oklahoma, surveying documents have to be signed and sealed by a licensed surveyor who is in responsible charge of the work.

Automated decline-curve analysis already exists. It combines Arps empirical models with AI models such as gradient boosting and LSTM, then extends production to an economic limit. That covers the main sub-steps of forecasting production and value.

An SPE session in 2026 says engineers use generative AI such as Claude, Gemini and ChatGPT for decline-curve, type-curve and economic modeling. It warns that a working prototype is not a production-ready analysis, so a human still has to review the result.

Manual decline-curve analysis depends on the engineer's judgement and is subjective. This supports partial delegation: an agent can do much of the work, but an expert still needs to validate the forecasts. A formal sign-off by a qualified reserves estimator mainly applies to booked reserves, not to internal screening of drilling sites.

SLB says its AI-enabled digital tools automated workover candidate screening and ranking at PGN Saka. It reports an 89% cut in selection time, with review moving from yearly to weekly across 196 completions. These figures come from the vendor.
A commercial AI tool is marketed as ranking every well in a portfolio by expected intervention ROI. This is vendor marketing, not independent evidence of performance.

In these BLM sundry examples, workover and plugging work needs prior regulator approval of a sundry notice that the operator's representative signs. The search found no rule requiring a PE stamp on a workover program, though the sources are scattered office-level examples rather than a statewide rule. In practice, operators keep an engineer accountable for the final rework design and spending.

Vendors describe AI agents that run the maintenance paperwork from start to finish. They flag equipment anomalies, open CMMS work orders, order parts through the ERP, schedule technicians and draft service reports. These claims are self-reported, and no independently verified oilfield deployment was found.

Oil and gas work-order creation and maintenance scheduling are being automated. Manual creation reportedly takes 15–45 minutes per order, and the same pipeline is used in refinery and oilfield settings.

Under OSHA 1910.119(i), the employer must carry out a pre-startup safety review for new or modified facilities. A multi-disciplinary team of engineers, operations, maintenance and safety staff checks physically that installed equipment matches the design. This means humans have to be on site and accountable for installation and startup.

Electronic field-data and logbook tools such as MonitorPro MP-Field, SUEZ eRIS-LOG and Ambisis already handle digital entry, validation, audit trails and AI extraction of data from documents. An agent could do the record-keeping and file-maintenance steps end to end.

EPA Region 4 logbook procedure: entries must be contemporaneous, objective and legible. Hardcopy logbooks are bound and handwritten, and electronic entries need an audit trail. The observations come from the person in the field, so a human must supply or check the content.

Field logbooks are treated as accountable documents in enforcement proceedings, and the person responsible signs, dates and initials the entries. This comes from SOPs and QA plans, not from a licence requirement.

Commercial SPC software, including Minitab Real-Time SPC, already monitors production data and flags process variation. AI tools (from vendors whose claims are unverified) say they can turn raw files and logs into control charts on their own.
No US license is specifically required for quality control technicians. Certification such as ASQ CQT is voluntary, so no legal sign-off barrier applies to the statistical analysis itself.
QA sign-off and review of production documentation are duties set by the employer. In practice, a human still checks the data's provenance and the reliability conclusions before acting on them.

Client-facing benefit chatbots already exist, such as Connecticut DSS's 'Laurel'. It answers common questions, checks benefit status, pre-screens eligibility and gives guided help with applications. Code for America and Anthropic are also building a Claude-based SNAP Policy Navigator that answers caseworkers' policy questions.

On a public-benefits SNAP benchmark (September 2026), the best model scored about 77%, so roughly a quarter of its answers were still wrong. Its advice needs to be grounded in state-specific policy and checked by a human.

Job specs for this role list home visits, hands-on teaching of budgeting, meal prep and housecleaning, and escorting clients. The work is done under a supervising professional, but the assistant does not need a licence.

Nava's open-source form-filling assistant is being piloted with caseworkers in Riverside County, California. It moves through benefit portals and databases and fills in application forms on its own. Caseworkers still review the forms, add missing information and submit them.

In a March 2026 report on the California pilot, frontline staff said they spend about half their time getting through benefit applications. The AI fills in the forms, but a human checks them before submission.

Agents that guide clients through assistance applications in plain language, including in Spanish and other languages, already exist, such as Link Health. Coverage of AI tax filing says most current work automates only part of tax preparation rather than handling the whole job.

NPS Conserve O Gram 17/3 describes cavity-packing objects in boxes that float inside a shipping crate, and marking foam with directions for removal and placement. This is hands-on work with the object and the packing materials.

Gallery Systems' TMS Collections has a Shipping module that groups objects into crates and produces shipping reports, crate lists and valuation documents. The paperwork side of the task can be done in software, but the physical packing cannot.

An NPS/Harpers Ferry registrar guide says that before packing, staff should assess each object's surface and structure and note weak points and earlier repairs. That is a physical inspection, though building the master list of catalog numbers, sizes and weights is clerical work an agent could support.

XTEN-AV's own product pages say its AI-assisted X-DRAW tool generates signal-flow diagrams, rack layouts, speaker layouts, bills of materials and cable schedules. This is the vendor's claim and was not independently verified, but it suggests an agent can draft the layout-design part of the task.

O*NET lists this task as a core duty of Audio and Video Technicians, next to setting up, maintaining and taking down physical equipment such as microphones, speakers, cables, mixing boards and cameras.

Employer job descriptions require hands-on work, such as using 16 ft ladders to reach projectors, speakers and wiring in ceilings. This makes the upgrade and maintenance part physical work that an agent cannot do.

O*NET lists 'Perform minor repairs and routine cleaning of audio and video equipment' as a core task for Audio and Video Technicians. Next to it is 'Notify supervisors when major equipment repairs are needed', so the work is hands-on upkeep of physical gear.
AI-assisted AV monitoring platforms analyze incidents and logs, suggest fixes and automate approved remote workflows. They help with diagnosis but cannot clean equipment or make physical repairs.

Remote AV monitoring gives per-device telemetry (lamp hours, power state, input errors) and remote commands. The vendor claims this cuts unnecessary on-site visits, but a technician still has to go on site to fix physical faults.

Broadcast automation systems commonly have a traffic or scheduling layer that builds program logs and feeds a playout layer that produces as-run logs. This means scheduling and reading logs is already digital, structured work done in software.
Aiir Scheduler can generate and export up to 30 days of music logs automatically, so log scheduling is already largely automated.

Playout vendors sell AI-driven scheduling that recommends the order of content. This is vendor marketing, but it shows the sub-steps are machine-executable. Final on-air and recording decisions and handling last-minute changes still usually need a technician in the control room to review them.

Vendor and FDA-cleared software already automates much of the image processing and quantification. Examples are Cedars-Sinai Cardiac Suite (QPS/QGS with motion correction), AutoQUANT, Siemens xSPECT Quant and GE's MIM portfolio. The technologist still checks and corrects the output, for example ROI and contour placement and motion artifacts.
GE HealthCare showed AI-driven nuclear medicine imaging and quantification software at SNMMI 2026, so these tools are current and on the market.

The SNMMI scope of practice includes operating imaging and computer instrumentation and documenting procedures. Technologists must follow federal, state and institutional rules, and state licensure governs who may perform these duties. The interpretation is signed by the physician, not the technologist.

Under NRC rule 10 CFR 35.25, a licensee that lets supervised people use radioactive (byproduct) material must teach them radiation safety and periodically review their work. Supervision must come from an authorized user or licensee, so a human remains responsible.

In accredited imaging programs, a qualified technologist must directly supervise students until they reach competency. That technologist reviews the procedure, checks the patient's condition, is physically present and approves the procedure or images. This is the general imaging-education pattern (JRCERT); I did not find the nuclear-medicine-specific JRCNMT text.

Hospital clinical-education policies require certified technologists to supervise student patient care, and to be present for some procedures regardless of the student's competency. An AI agent can only help with teaching materials, quizzes, scheduling and record-keeping.

Computrition's AMPS add-on builds menus from a master menu, handling therapeutic diets and recipe substitutions. Vendors such as MealSuite and Menutech advertise automated or AI menu and nutrition planning for healthcare.

Nutrition and dietetics technicians plan menus with registered dietitian nutritionists for people with special nutritional needs. In clinical care they typically work under RDN supervision, so a human professional reviews the work.
A Brazilian school-menu tool generates weekly menus that meet nutritional references, but a nutritionist still chooses the final menu, so a human stays in the loop.

A global survey of practice found that contact lens application and removal training sessions took a median of 30 minutes. Lenses were usually dispensed only after the instructor watched the patient apply and remove them successfully three times. This is hands-on, in-person supervision.

Nevada requires dispensing optician applicants to log 15 hours of insertion and removal training on a record signed by a supervisor. The UK College of Optometrists requires a witness to confirm that a trainee can insert and remove a lens on a patient's eye safely. Both make this a licensed, physical competency.

Some AI tools already cover parts of the task. J&J Vision's 'Andy' chatbot answers questions about insertion, removal and lens care. The 'Lensie' app says it uses camera tracking to give real-time coaching on insertion. That claim comes from the developer and has not been validated.

Exercise-prescription platforms like Physitrack, MedBridge and Wibbi use AI to speed up building and personalizing rehab programs. Clinicians still choose and approve each exercise and stay responsible for treatment planning and red-flag screening.

Alaska's statute lets athletic trainers practice only under a licensed physician's direction, given through verbal or written orders, treatment plans, protocols or standing orders. Trainers must refer athletes to another licensed professional when athletic training is contraindicated.

Illinois bills describe athletic trainers providing rehabilitation on the direction or prescription of a physician, or in collaboration with one. Putting a program into practice means hands-on physical medicine and rehabilitation techniques with the athlete in person.

FDA-cleared home wearables such as Current Health and Mindray mWear automatically measure pulse, respiration and temperature and use software to flag changes. Software can then read, log and flag the data, but a person still has to put on, apply or operate the sensor at the patient's side.

In an Oxford hospital-at-home study, patients' own manual temperature readings were logged on only 51-58% of days, while the chest patch captured pulse and breathing rate much more consistently. Measurement still depends on someone being physically there.

Taking temperature, pulse and respiration is a standard aide skill, done non-invasively under RN supervision and reported to the supervisor. No licence requires a human to sign it, but it is a hands-on bedside task.

AOTA guidance and state OT rules say an OTA may administer standardized assessments only after service competency is established, under a supervising OT who directs the evaluation and interprets the results. A licensed human therefore stays accountable for the testing.

Tablet-based tests and AI or computer-vision scoring of cognitive and motor skills exist but are still being validated against standard tests given by human examiners (for example TGMD-3, NEPSY-II and ATEC). Agents can help with scoring, recording and drafting reports, but not with the hands-on situational testing.

The OT supervision guidelines describe OTA services as delivered in person and in a supervised partnership. Situational testing means setting up materials, physically guarding and cueing the client, and observing the client directly.

O*NET lists 'Clean and organize work area and disinfect equipment after treatment' as a core task for Physical Therapist Aides (31-2022.00). Related tasks include changing linens and setting up equipment, which are also hands-on physical work.

APTA guidance says to clean all equipment, devices and surfaces between patients, following CDC disinfection recommendations. This means wiping physical surfaces at the point of care, which a software-only agent cannot do. An agent could at most look up the disinfection steps or keep the cleaning log.

Under infection-control manuals, shared equipment is disinfected at the point of care between each use, following the manufacturer's instructions. No law requires a licensed person to do this work, but it must be done in person.
O*NET lists 'Arrange treatment supplies to keep them in order' as a physical therapist aide task, done next to hands-on work like cleaning the work area and disinfecting equipment after treatment.
Aides keep linen and supplies stocked and tell a manager when more stock needs ordering. Supplies are physically handled in the clinic under PT/PTA supervision.
Clinic inventory software (low-stock alerts, vendor and order tracking) can handle only the digital tracking and reordering side. It cannot physically arrange supplies.

O*NET lists the task as 'Assist patients to dress, undress, or put on and remove supportive devices, such as braces, splints, or slings.' Aides do it under close supervision of a physical therapist or physical therapy assistant, which means hands-on physical help with patients who may be injured.
A state job specification lists 'assist patients with dressing and undressing; apply and remove braces and splints' among the aide's in-person patient-care duties.

An employer job posting describes aides removing and replacing braces, splints and slings on patients' bodies before and after treatment. This is direct physical work that a software-only agent cannot do.
O*NET lists fitting orthopedic braces, prostheses and supportive devices as a task for physical therapist aides, who work under close supervision of a PT or PTA and do only delegated, routine tasks.
An Illinois state position description requires aides to work under direct supervision of a PT or PTA. This shows the work is supervised, hands-on clinical care.

Phone-based 3D scanning apps such as SnugFit, Thuasne3D and SpinalTech3D take body scans for designing custom orthoses. A human still holds the device, and none of the apps do the physical fitting or adjust the fit on the patient.

Job postings for sterile processing and medical equipment preparers describe hands-on work: handling instruments, assembling trays, and moving supplies to hospital units and the operating room. Moving patients and setting up traction are physical bedside duties of the same kind. An AI agent with no body can do none of this. At most it could handle a small piece of transport-request logistics.
The role sends clean and sterile supplies to inpatient units and collects contaminated items. That means being on the floor in person, alongside patients and staff.

Vendors sell AI video analytics for casino surveillance. They say it flags dealer errors, odd hand movements, chip placement problems and suspicious betting, links play data with dealer rosters to spot collusion, and checks thousands of cameras automatically for scene compliance with regulations. These are vendor claims and have not been independently verified.

Nevada's surveillance standards set required camera coverage for games, the cage and count rooms. Only surveillance personnel and key employees may enter the surveillance room. The work is done through camera systems from a separate room rather than by handling things on the floor.

Surveillance agents must know the department's procedures, Gaming Commission regulations and minimum internal control standards. Under these rules, surveillance personnel are regulated staff with restricted access. The searches did not confirm the exact licensing requirements for these staff.

The payout math is easy to automate. Payout calculators and casino management systems that reconcile expected table results with chip-bank changes already exist. But at a live table the dealer must first see the physical chips bet on the layout, and then pay out in physical chips, which an agent without a body cannot do.
Patents for winning-bet payout calculators show that live-table payouts are computed by the dealer from bets on the physical table. The tools only assist with that calculation.
Card game dealers must hold a licence. For example, Montana requires an annual dealer licence from the state Department of Justice. Casino payouts are handled only by licensed staff.

RFID uniform and linen systems such as InvoTech GIMS track items as they move, count laundry carts and storerooms with fixed and handheld readers, and keep a running uniform count in a central database. This automates record-keeping but still needs staff to tag, scan and handle items.
A vendor case study from Ocean Resort Casino reports about 50% lower labor costs from automating uniform and linen inventory. Physical handling and issuing of items still happens on site.

LinenTech advertises RFID inventory counts with automatic reordering, the digital part an agent could take over (reconciling records, reordering). Counting, sorting and storing the items themselves needs a person on site.

FoundFastApp can turn one photo of several items into separate records with description, brand and category. It also matches found items to lost-item reports and alerts owners by SMS or email. The digital record-keeping and owner-contact steps can be automated, but a person still has to collect, photograph and store each item.
Traista offers AI matching on description, date and location, with image recognition and automatic categorization. Staff still have to log found items and upload photos themselves.
AI image-matching systems are used for lost luggage at airports. Physical handling and returning items to owners remain human jobs.

Mortuary cosmetic work means hands-on restorative art on the body, such as styling hair, applying makeup, covering bruises and rebuilding features. Several sources say a cosmetologist, funeral director or embalmer license is required, but these are career guides, not official licensing boards.

Funeral-industry AI tools found, such as the Tukios AI Photo Engine (launched February 2026), only edit tribute photos digitally. No software or agent was found that applies cosmetics to the deceased.
Embalmer licensing usually requires a mortuary science program, the NBFSE board exam and often an apprenticeship. An older (2005) California code lists restorative art among the exam subjects.

Michigan requires a case report for every body. It must list the personal effects that come with the decedent, the embalming details, and the name, license number and signature of each licensee who did the embalming. It must be kept at least 7 years.
Virginia requires a separate report for each embalming, with the embalmer's name, signature and license number, plus the supervisor's signature if an intern did the work.

Funeral home software already handles case management from first call to disposition, regulatory paperwork tracking and inventory. An agent could automate record entry and upkeep, but a person still has to look at and handle the clothing and valuables to list them.
O*NET lists packing body orifices with cotton soaked in embalming fluid as a hands-on embalmer task done directly on the body.
In Wisconsin, only a licensed, registered embalmer may embalm a body, and only in approved places such as licensed funeral establishments or hospitals.
Hawaii's rules let an apprentice embalm only in the presence of, and under the direction of, a licensed embalmer.

Funeral home software such as MorTrack and Last Rites handles dispatch, vehicle tracking and allocating staff and vehicles. That covers only the planning paperwork around a procession, not the physical work.

State procession laws (Delaware, Kansas, New Hampshire) govern escort or lead vehicles driven by funeral home staff or police. Organizing a procession means a person on site driving and directing traffic.

The Tribute Technology 'Procession' product supports case and task management, so an agent could help with scheduling and notifying families. Placing the casket and leading the cortege still need a person there.

O*NET lists offering assistance to mourners as they enter or exit limousines as a Funeral Attendant task. The same profile includes other hands-on duties such as driving funeral vehicles and supervising processions.
SHRM's sample job description says attendants help mourners into and out of limousines, funeral vehicles and other transportation. This is done in person, physically and with compassion.
Alberta's occupational profile says the role has physical demands, including heavy lifting of over 50 kg.
In Louisiana, funeral homes enter death records in the LEERS online system and can get and print burial transit permits there at any hour. This is browser work an agent could do.

In Massachusetts' default opt-out setup, a local burial agent must review the record and assign permit information before the permit can be printed. That means a human checkpoint outside the agent's control.

Passare's funeral software connects directly to Pennsylvania's death registration system through an API. Software already handles the filing step, but a credentialed funeral director still has to sign the record.
A pallbearer is one of several people who physically carry the casket at a funeral, usually in a team of four to six, depending on how heavy the coffin is.
Pallbearers move the casket from the hearse into the service and back, then from the hearse to the grave, following the funeral director's instructions in person.
The role is a solemn, ceremonial one: bearers hold the casket at their sides and arrive early to coordinate with the funeral director. This needs a physical body and a human presence before mourners.

AI cameras at fixed sites can flag visitors who get too close to exhibits or cross set lines and alert a control room. Operators can then speak to visitors through two-way audio. This only covers fixed, camera-equipped venues, not moving tour groups, and the source is a vendor case study.
Tour guides are responsible for the group's safety and for keeping the group together. They watch visitors on the spot to make sure tour rules and safety practices are followed.

South Africa's Tourism Act requires registered tourist guides to take all reasonable steps to ensure the safety of the tourists they accompany. This puts a duty of care on a human guide in at least some jurisdictions. Australian training material says no licence applies to the guiding unit, so this varies by country.

LLM-based museum guides and chatbots already answer visitor questions, recommend routes and support wayfinding in many languages on kiosks and phones. Physically leading visitors still needs a robot or a person.
An LLM-based guide system maps visitor requests to answers or to location and navigation codes. Research prototypes that physically lead visitors around museums rely on robots.
Cities that license tour guides attach the licence to giving guided tours. Simply giving directions or information to visitors does not require a human by law.

Off-the-shelf tour operator software such as TourOperation already takes payments in several currencies, issues QR-coded tickets, sends WhatsApp and SMS notices and produces reconciliation reports. An agent could run these steps: payment links, reminders, tracking who has paid and reconciliation.

Viagilize offers online payment by PIX and credit card, QR check-in for boarding and attendance, and a portal for guides. This automates collecting fees ahead of time, but someone still has to scan or check tickets on site.
UltimaTour Operator supports offline payments, mobile check-in and taking attendance in person. Collecting cash and paper tickets from group members on site still needs a person there.

Consumer AI climbing apps such as Climbah, Bouldering AI: Coach and MoveCl say they analyze uploaded videos for body position, foot placement and technique, and give feedback and training plans. That helps with coaching. Showing a skill in person, checking harnesses and knots, and spotting a climber still need a human on site. These capabilities come from app store listings and have not been independently verified.

MoveCl's listing says it detects 28 climbing techniques with pose estimation and scores them against ideal form. This shows AI can help with feedback on technique, but it cannot give hands-on instruction or demonstrate equipment.

Forum posts (not authoritative) say AMGA certification is not legally required in the US. They also say insurers and land permits in practice expect certified or vouched-for guides, so liability for the safety of people being taught sits with a human guide. I did not confirm any statute.

Vendor AI BDR and cold-call script tools pull CRM data, buying signals and web research to write a tailored opener, talking points and objection prep for each prospect before the call. These capabilities are vendor-claimed, not independently verified.
Several products say they follow the conversation and suggest talking points live, or adjust scripts based on how the prospect reacts. There is little independent evidence on how reliable this is.

Off-the-shelf tools such as EasyCallScript are sold as giving live call scripts tailored to each lead. I found no licensing or sign-off rule requiring a human to write or adjust sales scripts (not separately searched). Rules such as the TCPA govern consent and disclosures on the call, not who writes the script.

Vendors describe AI voice agents that place outbound calls, hold full conversations, handle basic objections, book meetings and log results to the CRM without a human. Follow-up of leads who have already shown interest is described as the strongest use; these figures come from vendors.

Vendor benchmarks say 28-34% of mid-market and enterprise B2B sales teams used AI voice agents for outbound calling as of Q1 2026. They also report that AI voice follow-up got prospects to act more often than email.

In a February 2024 ruling, the FCC said AI-generated voices count as 'artificial or prerecorded voice' under the TCPA. Marketing calls using them need prior express written consent, which closes the 'live human' exception for AI callers. Calls without that consent effectively have to be made by a human.

Commercial AI voice agents (e.g., Aloware) qualify prospects, run campaign- or CRM-triggered outbound calls, and book appointments directly into Google Calendar, Cal.com or Calendly using real-time availability, so the whole scheduling task can run end to end.

Documented builds on Vapi/n8n show an agent calling a lead list, explaining services, booking meetings on a sales lead's calendar and sending confirmations with meeting links, all without a human in the loop.

The FCC's February 2024 Declaratory Ruling puts AI-generated voices under TCPA 'artificial or prerecorded voice' rules. Marketing calls need prior express (written) consent, so cold outreach without consent in practice still needs a human caller. The task itself requires no physical presence.
Vendors say their AI answering-service agents answer every call, record messages and send urgent inquiries to the right person. These are marketing claims, not independent tests.

Vendors say AI voice agents route calls based on what the caller says, transfer or escalate urgent issues, and take detailed messages for follow-up. They also say emergencies, complaints and sensitive calls still need a human.
A guide says caller details are transcribed and sent to email, CRM or help desk automatically, and warns the AI only works as well as the business information it is given.

Commercial systems already send automated text-to-voice alerts from video analytics and access-control alarms to security staff's two-way radios, and staff can acknowledge them from the radio. This means the contact step can be done in software without a human keying the radio.

BearCom AlwaysOn turns standard two-way radio systems into an interface between people and machines. Machines and software can talk on the same radio network as human operators, so an agent could reach security staff if it is connected to such a gateway.

A patented speech-based two-way radio assistant uses a computer to control a radio base station, hear speech on the channel and speak replies back. This shows two-way voice exchanges over radio can be automated. Without such a radio-over-IP or push-to-talk-over-cellular gateway, though, an ordinary handheld or desk radio is out of an agent's reach.
HashMicro's AI agent records order requests, checks the details and creates sales orders with no manual admin work. It can also pull order data out of POs, PDFs and voice messages.
Jotform's AI Order Taker answers phone calls around the clock, collects order details and checks them in real time against existing form systems, so no staff member is needed.
Some AI ordering setups still have a human confirm orders or step in on complex or unclear cases. Accuracy depends on audio quality and how complex the menu or catalog is.

State internal control standards require physical cage protections that people carry out and answer for: restricted keys kept in locked boxes with access logs reviewed before each shift ends, cage doors and windows secured against unauthorized access, and surveillance verification of each cashier's transactions.

Indiana regulators disciplined a casino after cashiers made even exchanges without notifying surveillance and a cage supervisor moved $10,000 without requesting surveillance coverage. The required procedure is that the cage requests a security escort and security requests surveillance coverage, so these steps are in-person and coordinated by staff.

AI in casinos is mostly used for transaction and video anomaly detection that sends alerts to security staff. This helps with monitoring but does not physically secure the cage or replace cashier control of cash and keys.

Banks already let customers order foreign cash themselves online, with shipping or branch pickup. That automates the order, rate quote and payment steps. A clerk is still needed to physically hand over cash at the counter.

US Bank Secrecy Act rules require the bank to verify the customer's identity and keep a log for sales of monetary instruments such as traveler's checks paid in cash between $3,000 and $10,000. Cash transactions over $10,000 need a Currency Transaction Report. Checking the ID document usually happens in person at the counter.

Rules for foreign exchange and traveler's cheque transactions require identity checks above set thresholds. That means looking at physical ID documents, while the cash itself must be counted, checked and handed over.

AI masonry takeoff tools (e.g., Civils.ai, Oncenter Takeoff Boost) measure block/brick wall runs, deduct openings and count units directly from PDF drawings; vendor claims cut takeoff time by up to 95%.

A 2026 independent study of Togal AI on a live commercial project found near-perfect count accuracy but consistent underestimation of area quantities, especially on exterior finishes, and concluded that estimator oversight remains essential.
