Togal's own help documentation recommends treating automated takeoff results as a starting point to review before finalizing.
Crafco's Model 30 pavement router is a walk-behind machine. A worker on site steers it by an adjustable handle, and an electric clutch starts and stops the cutter-head.
A Cimline patent says the router operator has to keep raising and lowering the cutting bits when moving between random cracks. Doing this task means handling the machine by hand in real time.

Marathon's CR250KL crack router is a 20-25 hp engine-driven machine with carbide router blades. It is field equipment run by a person on the pavement and has no software interface that an agent could operate remotely.

O*NET lists this as a core task for Helpers–Electricians (importance 77). The related tasks are all hands-on: stripping and terminating wire, cutting and bending conduit, carrying materials to the job site, taking apart defective equipment and cleaning the work area. A software-only agent cannot do any of these. At most it can look up procedures or specs, which is a very small share of the work.

In Maine, licensed helper electricians may do installations only under the direct supervision of a master, journeyman or limited electrician who employs them. So a licensed human carries responsibility for the work.

Hawaii lets helpers and other unlicensed people do electrical work only under a licensed journey worker or supervising electrician, who must be physically present at the project site the whole time the work is done.

Under Maine law, a licensed helper electrician may do electrical installations only under the direct supervision of a master, journeyman or limited electrician, and the master electrician is responsible for the work of the people they supervise.
A city job description for an electrician helper lists hands-on maintenance and repair work that a journey-level electrician inspects. The work happens on site.

The search found no software or AI agent that inspects or tightens connections. The task means seeing, touching and turning screws on the equipment itself, which a software-only agent with no body cannot do. This point is a judgment, not a cited finding.

Employer and O*NET-style task descriptions say helpers thread conduit ends with a pipe threader, connect couplings and fittings with a wrench, and fabricate support brackets from strap iron with a hacksaw, shaping dies, hammer and punch, then bolt or screw the brackets in place. This is entirely physical manipulation on site.
In Maine, helper electricians are licensed and may make electrical installations only under the direct supervision of a master, journeyman or limited electrician.
In Hawaii, unlicensed helpers may do electrical work only under a licensed journey worker or supervising electrician, who must be physically present at the project site.

The O*NET task list for Helpers--Electricians (47-3013.00) describes this duty as physically raising, lowering or positioning equipment, tools and materials with a hoist, hand line or block and tackle. It sits alongside related physical duties such as rigging scaffolds, hoists and shoring.

OSHA requires a qualified rigger, meaning a person the employer judges qualified, when workers in the fall zone hook, unhook or guide a load (29 CFR 1926.1425(c)). It also requires one for hoisting during crane assembly and disassembly work (1926.1404(r)(1)).
Under OSHA, the employer decides whether a rigger is qualified, based on their knowledge, training and experience. For hoisting equipment rated at 2,000 lbs or less, a separate exception applies.

O*NET lists this as a core hands-on task for Helpers--Electricians (47-3013.00): operating cutting torches and welding equipment on conduit and metal components. The occupation is described as using, supplying or holding materials and tools.

Related task entries are also manual conduit work: threading conduit ends, connecting couplings, making support brackets with hand tools, and measuring, cutting and bending wire and conduit. A software-only agent with no body cannot do any of this. At most it could look up weld settings or read drawings, which is a small share of the time.

O*NET lists Helpers--Electricians (47-3013.00) as hands-on support work: stripping insulation, attaching wires to terminals and helping electricians on site. Soldering with an iron means physically handling wires, solder and a heated tool.

The task 'Solder electrical connections, using soldering iron' shows up on job-board copies of the O*NET helpers-electricians profile. It is a physical step on the job, and a software-only agent has no way to do it.

O*NET lists this as a core helper task. Related duties are cutting and threading pipe, setting pipe in hangers, drilling openings in walls and floors, and supplying or holding materials and tools. All of these are hands-on work.
A plumber-helper job posting says the work is about 70% standing and 25% walking. It also requires climbing, kneeling, crouching, crawling, reaching and handling, so it needs a person on site.

Rule-based software already generates piping isometrics, dimensions and bills of materials from 3D models. That covers design-office layout work, not the helper's physical help with layout, assembly and installation in the field.
Plumber helpers cut and thread pipe with pipe cutters, cutting torches and threading machines, and help lift and position objects on site.
A posting requires helpers to carry up to 75 lbs and lift up to 100 lbs, mostly while standing or walking.
Canadian guidance lists manual material handling, bending and repetitive motion as the core physical demands of the helper job.

O*NET lists 'Clean shop, work area, and machines, using solvent and rags' as a core task for Helpers--Pipelayers, Plumbers, Pipefitters, and Steamfitters. It is a hands-on cleaning duty done in the shop or on the job site.

O*NET says workers in this occupation help plumbers, pipefitters, steamfitters and pipelayers by doing less-skilled manual work, such as supplying or holding materials and tools and cleaning the work area and equipment. All of this requires being there in person.

The MUTCD's automated flagger assistance devices (AFADs) still need a human flagger to run them remotely, either at one end of the work zone or from a central location. Flagging is not done autonomously by software.
Iowa's AFAD guidance requires trained flaggers on site who can switch to manual flagging if a device fails. Physical presence is needed.

State specifications require AFAD units to be linked and controlled by wireless communications with fail-safe behaviour. The devices are physical roadside hardware operated by people, not something a software agent would normally reach.

O*NET lists this task for Highway Maintenance Workers (47-4051.00). Related duties include driving heavy equipment and vehicles with attachments to sweep debris from paved surfaces, and setting out signs and cones to divert traffic. The work is physical, done on site and with equipment.

The occupation's core duties are hands-on field work: clearing debris from culverts, ditches and drains, hauling material to fill washouts, and driving trucks to work sites. A software-only agent with no body cannot do any of these.

The typical entry route is a high school diploma plus moderate-term on-the-job training. No professional licence requires a human to sign off on debris removal itself, though heavy vehicles may need a CDL.

Robots that mark roads, such as Civ Robotics' CivDash, exist, but they are dedicated hardware run remotely from a safety truck. A software-only AI agent cannot do this work. It could only help with minor planning or record-keeping.

Most robots so far only do layout and pre-marking. Final thermoplastic marking, heated to about 400°F, still uses crews with truck-mounted or hand equipment. Systems like RoadPrintz still need an operator in the truck.

Under the MUTCD, pavement marking happens on site in work zones. The work has to be staged with temporary traffic control, and workers with traffic-control duties must be trained. All of this needs people physically present on the road.

Wisconsin DOT's maintenance manual says crews set snow-fence posts in the field before the ground freezes, then hang the fencing taut after it freezes, 35 times the fence height from the shoulder edge. This is hands-on fieldwork.
In a Utah DOT case study, a crew of three trained workers placed about 1,000 ft of fence in an 8-hour shift. The work is manual labour on site, and an agent without a body cannot do it.
MnDOT employees built a permanent 1,500-ft woven snow fence by hand after an agreement with the landowners. Only the planning and coordination around it is digital.

The only automation found for changing drill bits and loading bolts on roof bolters is mechanical: carousels and manipulators described in patents and controlled by machine controllers. That is robotics hardware, not a software agent, and on conventional machines operators still reload by hand.

Patents for autonomous roof bolters describe drilling and bolting sequences run by controllers and physical loading arms on the machine. A software-only AI with no body cannot do the physical work of pulling a bit from a chuck and seating a bolt underground.

A newer patent describes a controller that rotates the carousel to swap consumables such as drill bits, resin cartridges and bolts. This confirms the task is manual handling at the drill head in an underground mine.

Ross mixers can come with a PLC control panel and a touchscreen HMI/SCADA package that handle recipe selection, mixing, heating and vacuum control, and log data. Some adjustments can therefore be made through software, but an operator still works the touchscreen and controls on site.

In a retrofit, a manually run food mixer was given an HMI+PLC that stores up to 99 recipes and has manual and automatic modes. It still pauses for manual ingredient additions, which shows the equipment is run by hand on the plant floor.

Food-processing automation runs on plant PLCs and local control systems. These are operational networks that a general-purpose AI agent normally cannot reach, so pressing switches and turning knobs remains a physical, on-site task.

Bühler's Finer S Edition 26 five-roll refiner uses digital sensors to watch the process in real time and adjusts roll speed, pressure and temperature on its own. So the machine's built-in controls already handle the parameter tuning, not an outside AI agent.

HDM/MacIntyre refiner/conches save process recipes in plant PLC software that runs on Siemens or Allen-Bradley interfaces. These are plant-floor control systems that a software agent would not normally be able to reach. The operator still has to load the batches, take samples and run the machine on site.

Commercial refiner/conche units of 500 to 2000 kg are run from a touchscreen PLC, and the target particle size changes with the type of product. The work is physical machine operation on the production floor, and no licence or sign-off rule requires a particular person to do it.

Manufacturing execution system (MES) recipe-management software stores recipe steps and parameter values, such as oven temperature settings, and flags when operators depart from them. This means pulling cook parameters from recipes and work orders can be done digitally.
Recipes are often stored on, or editable only through, the equipment controller on the plant floor. An agent may therefore not be able to reach those systems or paper work orders.

Under 21 CFR 113/114, thermal-processing operators must work under the supervision of a supervisor certified through the Better Process Control School, and scheduled processes must be set by a qualified person. Human oversight stays in place, but no one has to sign for the act of reading the recipe itself.

Clean-in-place (CIP) systems automate washing of pipes, vessels, tanks and fittings. They run on PLC/HMI controllers, not software AI agents, and people still have to clean the outside of equipment and the cooking area.

Automated CIP cycles push a pre-rinse, a caustic or acid wash and a post-rinse through equipment that is already in place. Hosing down, scrubbing and sanitizing the cooking area are still physical jobs done by hand.

CIP replaces a slow, hands-on routine of taking equipment apart and cleaning it by hand. That routine is physical work an agent with no body cannot do. At most it could start a CIP cycle that is already set up or log sanitation records.
O*NET lists this as a task for furnace, kiln and oven operators: cleaning and oiling equipment with scrapers, solvents and air hoses. It is hands-on maintenance work done in person.
Related tasks for this job include clearing jams with hand tools, replacing worn parts and removing ash with shovels and buckets. These all need someone physically at the equipment.
Furnace-wall cleaning equipment is a hand-operated pneumatic tool run by one person, not a software system. An AI agent without robotics could at most look up maintenance schedules or manuals.

O*NET lists this as a core task for Cleaners of Vehicles and Equipment (53-7061.00). The work is done by hand: sweeping, shoveling or vacuuming debris and scrap into containers, then carrying the containers out of work areas. A software-only agent with no body cannot do any of it.

The occupation's other tasks use physical tools and materials such as water, cleaning agents, brushes, cloths, hoses and vacuums. This confirms the job requires being on site and handling things physically.

AI drowning-detection systems such as Lynxight and AngelEye watch pool camera feeds and send alerts to lifeguards' smartwatches. They are presented as an extra layer of safety, not a replacement for lifeguards, and they only work at pools that already have the cameras installed.
Industry bodies treat AI drowning detection as a supplement to lifeguard supervision and are still working out how to fit it into existing supervision frameworks.
Florida law requires anyone working as a lifeguard at a public pool to hold a certificate from the American Red Cross, the YMCA, or another nationally recognized aquatic training program.

Existing AI CPR tools, such as purpose-built chatbots and apps like CPR AI, only coach a human through compressions and AED use with voice or visual prompts and feedback. The person still does the physical rescue.
Most US states require lifeguards to hold Red Cross or equivalent lifeguard, CPR and first-aid certification. Massachusetts requires annual CPR/BLS for Professional Rescuers certification.
AI CPR-guidance apps can improve bystander performance, but someone physically present still has to act, and calling emergency services stays essential.

Lifeguards already log weather, tides, water conditions, equipment checks and first-aid or rescue records on digital forms and apps such as SafetyCulture, SLSQ's LIMSOC and the SLSA Operations App. An agent could pre-fill the conditions data and turn a lifeguard's notes into structured reports.

Some regulators and governing bodies require signed and dated incident reports filed within set deadlines, for example Vermont's tramway incident form and New Hampshire's 5-day injury report. This makes a human who saw the event responsible for the content.

Alpine Canada's incident form must have all applicable sections completed and carries a signature and date block. Those details come from someone who was there and observed the injury and the treatment.

Vision AI products such as Tiliter Cleensight and FieldProxy score cleanliness from photos taken by staff or from fixed cameras. A person or installed hardware still has to capture the scene, so an AI agent can help with the inspection but cannot carry it out alone.

Oregon's daily aquatic facility checklist is an on-site walk-through before opening. It checks that decks and walkways are clean and free of debris and that drains and skimmers are clear. This needs someone physically present.

Health-department self-inspection checklists require decks to be free of algae, biofilm and dirt. Facility staff do these checks by sight and touch, and no license is required for a human to sign the routine cleanliness check.

Restaurant inventory software such as Restaurant365 can set par levels, send low-stock alerts and build suggested purchase orders. This covers only the digital tracking around restocking. The actual wiping, sanitizing and carrying stock to the line still needs a person's hands.

Food-code-based state rules require food-contact surfaces to be cleaned and sanitized at set intervals, about every 4 hours for TCS food, and whenever contamination may have occurred. These rules set when the work happens but do not require a licensed person to do it.
Digital cleaning-schedule and checklist tools exist for food safety operations. They schedule and log the cleaning but do not perform it.

Dough is automated with dedicated robots and machines (Pazzi's robotic pizzerias, Zume's Doughbot press), not with software-only AI agents. The task needs physical mixing, kneading, dividing and shaping.
Industrial dough lines use a vacuum filler and a tray-loading robot to divide and handle dough balls, which shows the core work is physical handling.
Zume Pizza used an automated dough press to make crusts faster. This is physical automation, not an AI agent working through software.
Robots that stir and pour pancake batter exist only as research prototypes that need robot hardware. A software-only AI agent cannot do this physical work.

Automated pancake makers are dedicated machines that dispense and cook batter, and the patent says pancake production is still mostly manual and labor-intensive. Physical handling is central to the task.
Commercial units like POPCAKE use pre-mixed batter bags in dedicated appliances. That is not something an AI agent working through software, documents or messages can do.

Zoo Atlanta used an AI Animal Assistant from Satisfi Labs. It answered visitors' questions about species, where exhibits are, and daily feeding schedules and activities, using facts from the zoo's own database.

At Madrid Zoo, a virtual keeper called IrenIA appears on a screen beside the panda enclosure. It answers visitors' questions about the animals and the facility in Spanish and English. That puts on-site question answering in AI hands, but the question is still answered at the exhibit.

A Mysuru Zoo assistant answers in five languages and bases its replies on the zoo's own information about animals, timings, facilities and rules. The vendor reports a large rise in handled queries, but nobody outside the vendor has checked that figure.

Calf milk calculators and ration-formulation software already do the calculation part of the task: amounts, concentrations and adjusting feeding for calf weight, age and ingredient supply. A human still has to measure and mix the food or formula.

Veterinary compounding rules tie drug preparation and use to a veterinarian's prescription and supervision. The caretaker follows existing instructions and does not sign for them, so the main barrier is physical work, not licensing.

Kentucky allows a veterinarian or a licensed veterinary technician to administer compounded veterinary drugs. In this task, medication is prepared from a veterinarian's prescription rather than prescribed by the caretaker.

Commercial vivarium systems such as Setra and Rewire Neuroscience's Degrees of Freedom offer networked temperature and humidity monitoring with remote dashboards, mobile alerts and some control features. An agent with access could read data and possibly change setpoints, but these systems mostly monitor rather than adjust room conditions.

Remote control of vivarium devices through a web browser or phone app exists only in patents and research or hobbyist prototypes. Most caretakers in kennels, zoos, nurseries and farms adjust thermostats, heaters, humidifiers and vents by hand on site.

The Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and institutional policies require species-appropriate ranges, daily recorded checks and calibrated devices. They also note that conditions inside cages can differ from room readings, so on-site checking matters, but no law says a licensed human must make the adjustment.

Zoos move animals between enclosures and into transport crates through hands-on shift and crate training led by keepers in person: targeting, positive reinforcement and handling the doors. That is physical work an agent without a body cannot do.
Moving an animal depends on keepers reading its behaviour on the spot and dealing with social or environmental problems, for example separating individuals or adding visual barriers.
Software such as Species360 ZIMS covers only the paperwork side: recording transfers and visits. An agent could help there, but that is a small part of the time the task takes.

Ticketing software can track exits and re-entries: scanning a ticket on the way out makes it valid again for coming back in, so the system does the record-keeping part of a door check. Staff still operate the scanner at the door.
For multi-day or high-volume events, vendors recommend physical credentials such as wristbands or hand stamps that staff check by eye at the door. That means a person has to be physically present.
At large venues, guests ask staff for a re-entry wristband when they leave and must show it with their ticket when they return.
Usher job postings describe this task as physically placing event and venue signage, putting up or taking down posters, and setting up and staffing information tables or kiosks in the lobby.
Washington State's usher job specification lists staffing kiosks or stations and doing set-up and tear-down, all on-site duties.

Venue digital-signage software such as CultureSuite pulls event data and updates screens automatically when events change. This covers only the digital-display part of the task, which is a small share of what ushers do here.
Beach equipment rental software such as Booqable already runs online booking, live availability, deposits and e-signed waivers, so the transaction side of renting can be done without a person.
Bookyt treats each numbered beach chair as its own rental item, so the system can allocate and track chairs automatically. A person still has to set up and hand over the chair.

Self-service kiosks linked to the Lightspeed point-of-sale system handle scheduling and rentals in store, but handing over the physical items (shoes, balls, chairs, suits) still needs someone on site.

Disney California Adventure tested automated entry gates where guests tap MagicBand+ or tickets themselves and the gate opens after the ticket is scanned and a photo is taken or checked. This replaces an attendant's handheld scanner, but it is fixed gate hardware, not a software AI agent.
Theme park turnstile vendors sell sensor-based speed gates tied to ticketing systems. The digital checking step is automated, but the gates and readers are physical equipment at the entrance.

Walt Disney World entrances have used RFID ticket readers with a fingerprint scanner. Ticket checking can be automated through on-site devices, yet collecting or punching tickets and admitting or stopping patrons still happens in person.

AI tools such as Beam AI and Civils.ai already read HVAC blueprints and schedules to pull out duct sizes, lengths and fittings. Vendors say a human still has to check the results, and the tools do not do 3D coordination or clash detection. No 2026 tool was found that turns blueprints into finished shop drawings without a human checking them.
CAD add-ins such as Design Master HVAC already lay out ductwork automatically and size ducts inside AutoCAD or BricsCAD. An agent with computer use could run these tools to draft much of the work.

Standard HVAC duct specifications require scaled fabrication drawings showing fittings, reinforcement, seams and hangers. They are submitted to the engineer of record for review, and no PE seal by the drafter is generally required.

Job postings list installing pipes, HVAC ducts, flashing, rain gutters and furnace casings as a core hands-on task. The work also includes reading blueprints and fastening seams on site, which needs a person physically there.
Installation work includes laying out and installing gutters, downspouts, ducts and flashing. Only small paperwork steps, such as estimating materials and labour hours, could be done in software.
Some employers and jurisdictions require a journeyman sheet metal worker licence or a trade certificate to do this work.

Building a new bike from the box means handling the parts by hand: mounting wheels, seatpost, bar and stem, aligning the derailleur and brake calipers, and tightening bolts to spec with a torque wrench. An AI agent with no robot body can't do this. At most it can look up the manufacturer's instructions and torque specs.
Brake setup means holding the lever in while tightening the caliper bolts to 8 Nm, then spinning the wheel to check for rotor drag. These are hands-on adjust-and-check steps.

Under 16 CFR 1512.3, a bike sold partly assembled must meet federal safety requirements once it is put together according to the manufacturer's instructions. The rule sets a product standard and does not require a licensed or certified person to assemble it.

Servicing a hub axle is hands-on work. The mechanic holds the cone with a cone wrench, loosens the locknut, unscrews the cone, catches the loose bearings, regreases and reassembles the hub, then sets bearing play by feel. An agent without a body can do none of this, and its only help would be to look up procedures or specs.
The work uses physical tools such as cone wrenches, locknut wrenches, an axle vise, tweezers, degreaser and grease.
No government license is generally required for bicycle mechanics. Certification is voluntary, through bodies such as UBI and BBI, so accountability is not a barrier.

Published rubrics already define how K-12 tools and programs are judged for teaching fit and for federal privacy law (FERPA, COPPA). An agent can apply them and draft the analysis and reports, but administrators still have to do the review.
Vendor guides for evaluating programs call for structured pilots and real-world checks in schools, which humans have to carry out and interpret, before a district adopts a program.

State law (for example Ohio and Michigan) and district contracts require in-person formal classroom observations and walkthroughs by administrators. Judging teaching methods therefore needs someone physically in the classroom.

A RAND survey covered by District Administration found nearly 60% of K-12 principals use AI tools for work. Drafting communications such as newsletters, emails and staff memos is the most common use, and administrators still review the output.

Apptegy's school newsletter builder has a 'Write with AI' drafting feature and sends newsletters digitally under district-level control. This automates both writing and distribution of promotional material.
An ESD 112 school communications guide recommends using AI to draft newsletters while keeping the district's voice, so human review is still expected before publishing.

Workday Adaptive Planning, a common higher-education planning platform, lists an AI Planning Agent and uses machine learning for predictive forecasts. This means much of the forecasting, modeling and report production can be automated.
University boards delegate to the CFO the authority and responsibility to set up and manage the budget and accounting system. Accountability stays with named human officers.
The Comptroller prepares the annual financial statements under GAAP, an independent CPA audits them, and the Trustees must approve them. Human sign-off and review are required before use.

HR AI agents in 2026 handle recruiting (screening, scheduling), onboarding (provisioning, document tracking, FAQs) and performance (data aggregation, coaching nudges), with claimed cuts in HR admin time of up to 40% (vendor-reported).
About one in three organizations uses AI for first-round video or voice screening interviews, and AI scheduling tools reportedly cut coordinator time by 36%.

Postmasters recruit, interview, select, hire, train, supervise and evaluate post office staff, and select and train postmasters of associate units. This includes on-site on-the-job training and a final hiring decision made by an accountable manager.

Since 2022 the IRS has used AI voice bots for collection calls. Taxpayers who received notices can confirm their identity with a PIN and set up or change payment plans, and the bots also explain notices and answer common questions.
The IRS reported that its voice bots handled over 4.8 million calls, with about 40% resolved without a human. Callers who wanted a person could still ask to reach a live assistor.

Calls from mailed collection notices went to the ACS voice bot, which set up payment plans for balances under $25,000. Early on, the share of calls resolved without a human was about 30%, below the 40% target.

The BLUPF90 suite is standard software for mixed-model analysis in animal breeding. It estimates variance components and heritability by REML, including standard errors, and it can be run from scripts, so an agent with code execution can do the core estimation.
UNE lab handouts show that AI-REML in blupf90+ reports standard errors for heritability and genetic correlations. This is a routine computational workflow.

bpf90tools is a Python wrapper built to automate breeding-value pipelines (renumf90, remlf90, airemlf90). The search found no turnkey end-to-end system, so a human still needs to choose the model and check the results.

Sakana AI's 'The AI Scientist' (Nature, March 2026) runs a pipeline that analyses data, drafts the full manuscript and reviews its own work. One of its papers passed first-round peer review at a workshop, which shows that drafting a write-up of findings can be delegated end to end.
A May 2026 survey found that frontier LLMs still make up results, miss hidden errors and judge novelty poorly, so a human still has to review and correct the work before it is published.
ICMJE, COPE and major publishers do not allow AI tools to be listed as authors. Human authors must approve the final manuscript and take responsibility for its integrity.

A March 2026 paper describes agents that read files, run code, query databases and work across the research pipeline from literature review through analysis to drafting. They are strong on speed, coverage and method, but weaker on theoretical originality and tacit field knowledge, so a human still has to interpret and review.

Brookings says agents can now carry out social-science research steps on their own, but output quality can drop the longer an agent works on one task in a single session, so humans still need to review the work.
No US state licenses sociologists. The available certification (AACS) is voluntary, so the law does not require a human to do or sign this analysis.

NWCG Crew Boss (CRWB) qualification requires prior Firefighter Type 1 experience, a certified Position Task Book, specific courses (RT-130, S-230, S-290, ICS-200) and an arduous fitness level, so a qualified human must lead fire crews.
The CRWB role involves running, climbing and lifting over 50 lb, plus real-time decisions in the field, such as judging changing fire conditions and deciding when to withdraw a crew.

Digital tools such as VR forest-worker training and AI wildfire-planning platforms support training and planning, but they do not lead crews in the field. AI can only help with training materials, scheduling and briefings.

Commercial AI tools (TherapyFuel in TherapyNotes, Twofold, Mentalyc) draft treatment-plan goals, measurable objectives and interventions from diagnoses and chart data. An independent review says clinicians still have to review and adjust the drafts for diagnostic nuance, risk and medical necessity.
In the MedicsCloud SUD EHR, AI generates ASAM assessments and builds problem lists that flow into treatment plans, so clinicians can move straight to goal setting.
Minnesota Stat. 245G.06 requires the individual treatment plan to be signed by the client and the alcohol and drug counselor, and to document the client's involvement in developing it.

As of 2026, agentic tools can find funding opportunities, draft proposals and check them against funder rules (for example GRAIL and the SciSpace NSF agent). Guidance and testing still recommend that people write the core scientific narrative, because reviewers notice generic AI prose.

NIH notice NOT-OD-25-132 says NIH will not treat applications substantially developed by AI as the applicant's original ideas. This is reported by a secondary comparison site and was not checked against the notice itself.

NSF asks proposers to disclose generative-AI use and holds authors responsible for the accuracy of AI-assisted content. An Authorized Organizational Representative must certify the proposal when it is submitted.

A 2025 study of AI grading on a handwritten general chemistry exam found high agreement between AI and human graders on text and reaction questions. Agreement was lower on numerical and graphical items, so the authors recommend human review of partially correct or ambiguous answers.
Gradescope's AI groups similar handwritten answers, including chemistry diagrams, so they can be marked in batches. It gave no help with grading paragraph-type answers.

University of Utah policy says AI may not be the sole or final grading authority. The instructor of record has to review AI-assisted output before grades are finalized, and student work counts as a FERPA-protected record.

Commercial AI chatbots and agents for higher education already handle program information for prospective students, application guidance, eligibility checks, course selection and enrollment changes. These are the main digital sub-steps of recruitment and registration.

Agent templates such as StackAI's Advising Assistant connect to student information systems to pull student records and match them against requirements. They support placement and registration advising, but a human advisor stays in the loop.

A 2026 academic comparison finds current advising chatbots mostly reactive. Students and advisors still have to build the academic plans themselves, so humans remain essential for personalized placement decisions.

Current AI use for supervising teaching assistants is limited to pilots and human-in-the-loop tools. Examples are AI-built onboarding modules for TAs and 'shadow grading' agents that work alongside instructors. Mentoring and research guidance stay with the human supervisor.
University policy makes the faculty supervisor the instructor of record for an internship, and that person assigns the grade.
The faculty supervisor has the ultimate responsibility for evaluating students' internship or practicum work, even when a sponsor's representative oversees the student day to day.

Korinek's NBER Working Paper 34202 (2025) shows AI agents helping at every stage of economic research, from background research to coding and analysis. These are sub-steps an agent can prepare before or after meetings with colleagues.

Agentic co-scientist systems such as Google's generate, critique and refine hypotheses, but they support research that humans lead. They do not stand in for the interpersonal back-and-forth between colleagues.
Academic forums in 2026 warn against relying on agents for every decision, so collaborative judgement and agreement stay with the faculty members.

Commercial AI course-design tools available in 2026 (ibl.ai Course AI, Coursebox, Taskade) produce syllabi, weekly plans, learning objectives, rubrics and assignments from a course description, map content to accreditation outcomes and export to LMSs. These sources are vendor marketing with no independent quality data, and all of them assume a human reviews the output.

A 2025 case study describes a graduate course built quickly with generative AI to meet an accreditation deadline, including AI-generated syllabus, lecture and homework files. Faculty still had to direct and refine the work.

University governance gives faculty responsibility for curriculum. Course proposals start with a faculty member and pass through department, college and university committee approval. This is institutional governance, not a legal licence or signature requirement.

Scite, Elicit, Consensus and Scopus AI pull real citations from scholarly databases (Semantic Scholar, Scopus) and summarize them, so the search-and-compile sub-steps of a bibliography can already be automated.

These tools do not show journal quality metrics, and coverage varies (Scopus AI defaults to post-2013 studies). A human still has to check source credibility and whether each item suits the course, so the output needs instructor review before use.

Library guides present AI tools as aids for literature discovery that need human checking. Neither guide mentions any legal or licensing rule that a human must compile or sign a reading list. The task is fully digital, though some full texts sit behind subscriptions.

Vendor pages (not checked against Instructure's own documentation) say AI agents can write scores into the Canvas gradebook through LTI Assignment and Grade Services, within the permission scopes set up for them, while Canvas remains the official record for grades. Integration platforms describe automatic enrollment sync and scheduled gradebook-to-SIS pushes. My search found nothing on automating attendance or roll call.

The instructor of record is responsible for making sure final grades are submitted for every enrolled student by the deadline. FERPA limits posting grades by name or identifiable number. This responsibility comes from university policy, not from a FERPA clause.
At WSU, submitting grades requires a current FERPA certification and the department listing you as instructor of record, so access is tied to a named, credentialed person.

Campus bookstore adoption portals such as Barnes & Noble's Adoption & Insight Portal let faculty search by ISBN, re-adopt materials in one click, and compare options across price ranges, including OER. These are all digital steps that a computer-use agent could carry out.
The Akademos Adoption & Analytics Portal includes a recommendation engine that suggests other high-quality, low-cost options. That means software already handles part of the selection work.

Adoption systems such as Follett Discover sit behind campus single sign-on and Canvas or Blackboard, and have adoption deadlines. An agent therefore needs the instructor's credentials, and the instructor still has to make the final decision about which texts fit the course.

Students in qualitative methods courses used custom GPTs, including an interview simulator, to get quick feedback on interview questions and field notes. This counts as assisting supervision, not replacing the supervisor.
Cogniti lets educators set up AI agents that act as a qualitative methods mentor and give students feedback on how they code their data. The educator still controls the agent and stays in the loop.
University IRB rules make the faculty advisor responsible for how student human-subjects research is carried out, and require the advisor to sign protocols. A human must keep oversight.

Vendor AI tools for medical education say they draft syllabi, learning objectives, curriculum maps, modular course content, review questions and accreditation paperwork from goal specifications. These claims are the vendors' own and have not been checked independently.

Lecturio says its AI syllabus and lesson plan generator drafts competency-aligned syllabi and session plans for health sciences faculty. Its workload-reduction figures are self-reported. AAMC warns against relying too much on AI without enough human oversight.

Accreditation criteria require faculty to take part. In this AACN crosswalk of CCNE standards and NTF criteria, faculty must take part in program governance and quality improvement, and NP faculty must give input into developing, evaluating and revising the curriculum. That means human faculty judgment and sign-off stay essential.

AI agent add-ons for Canvas can send scores straight to the Canvas gradebook through LTI grade passback. Canvas stays the official record for enrollment and grades, and other platforms already send session attendance to the gradebook automatically.
A news report says Instructure is rolling out an agentic AI assistant in Canvas that automates routine teaching work such as basic grading and rubric creation.

Nursing programs treat clinical evaluations and competency records as FERPA-protected education records. Access is limited to the course instructor and coordinators, so a human instructor stays responsible for certifying and controlling these records.

A May 2026 study found that coding-assistant AI tools such as Claude Code could turn instructor-written course notes into lecture slides that were accurate, complete and pedagogically sound. A separate study found that students rated AI-generated slides about as highly as slides made by instructors.

At Acadia Divinity College, an AI avatar wrote the syllabus, scripted and gave lectures to graduate students, and graded their work. Students said they felt 'duped' and preferred a human professor, which suggests that live, trusted delivery still depends on a human.

The University of Newcastle used short lecture videos delivered by an AI avatar but kept in-person labs and live Q&A. Some students worried about losing engagement, so universities are adding avatars alongside human teaching rather than replacing it.

OpenAI Academy runs sessions on building workspace agents for higher-ed faculty and researchers. These agents help with prep work such as drafting, research synthesis and admin, not with the faculty collaboration itself.

Agents in higher education are said to speed up research workflows: literature work, simulated research teams like Stanford's Virtual Lab, and lower per-paper costs at Johns Hopkins' Agent Laboratory. These are vendor-reported claims, but they suggest AI can help with research tasks while colleagues still make the decisions.
Faculty teaching collaboratives are still run as human peer-learning communities. AI shows up as the topic and as a shared resource, not as the participant.

Agent layers that connect to Canvas through its APIs say they can write scores straight into the gradebook (LTI grade passback). Integration tools can push gradebook and completion data on to the SIS or a reporting system. This shows that entering, calculating and syncing records can be automated. These are vendor claims and have not been checked independently.

In March 2026 Instructure released the IgniteAI Agent for Canvas, which runs educator workflows. It is still at the early-adopter stage, and its announced features do not mention gradebook or attendance tasks.

Under institutional policy, the instructor of record is responsible for making sure final grades are submitted for each enrolled student. Faculty must also follow FERPA when recording grades. So a human still has to review and certify the grade records.

Some education platforms such as KUNSTMATRIX.EDU, Artsteps and Artsonia let users build and publish 3D or online exhibitions of student work in a browser, with role-based access. An agent could upload the work, lay out the gallery and write the labels without a human doing each step.
Schools commonly use online galleries such as Artsonia, ART.SPACES and website exhibition pages to show student art. This supports digital delegation of the display and promotion sub-steps.

Physical shows in schools and galleries require handling, hanging, lighting and installing artworks on site. No law or licence requires a human to sign off, but the physical installation and the curatorial choices are still human steps.

2026 researcher tooling already does the main sub-steps: Semantic Scholar AI and Elicit find and group literature, and Zotero MCP and paper-search MCP servers let agents search for and manage references.

Reading lists made by AI still need human checking: the Chicago Sun-Times printed a summer list where 10 of 15 books were invented, and librarians report many hallucinated citations. A faculty member still has to review the list before assigning it.

Studies report high rates of invented or wrong references in AI-assisted literature work (about two-thirds in one GPT-4o study), so checking each item against library catalogs is an essential step, along with the instructor's judgment on whether a work suits the course.
Commercial AI chat agents run prospective-student engagement around the clock, answer program questions and sync leads to a CRM. These are the main digital recruitment sub-steps.
Agentic recruitment workflows can find students who left an application unfinished, send follow-ups on their own and pass cases to staff only when needed.

AI-agent advising chatbots help students build degree plans and give registration and placement guidance from catalogue rules. Faculty still handle in-person open houses, recruitment events and persuading students to choose a major or program.

Vendors such as ibl.ai, Coursebox and Edvisor sell tools that generate syllabi, course content and outcome-aligned course structures. These are their own marketing claims and were not independently verified.
A 2025 IEEE study found that no LLM produced a complete curriculum as good as human-built ones, but LLMs helped a lot when humans worked closely with them.

Kinesiology curriculum changes go through votes by department faculty and approval by the chair, college committees, the dean and the curriculum committee. This is institutional faculty governance, not a legal or licensing requirement.

NIH notice NOT-OD-25-132 says NIH will not treat applications substantially developed by AI as the applicant's original work. It also says NIH will use AI-detection tools and caps PIs at six applications per year. Because of this, the PI has to write and own the core of the proposal.
Limited AI help with grant applications is not banned. Applicants must check AI-assisted text themselves for plagiarism, made-up content and invented citations, so a human still has to review it.
NSF encourages applicants to disclose AI use rather than restricting it. This shows that AI drafting of proposals is already common and is accepted when the applicant is open about it.

University of Duisburg-Essen tested Claude Opus 4.6 as an assistive grader on 18 written IHK vocational exams in summer 2025. It matched the human grade exactly in 14 cases, was one grade off in the other 4, and never changed a pass/fail result. The researchers say high-stakes use still needs validation and recommend combining digital tests with in-person exams. No 2026 study was found of AI scoring hands-on vocational performance tests.

NYU Stern's voice-AI system ran personalized oral exams for two undergraduate cohorts of 36 and 37 students, and LLMs graded the transcripts for under $1 per exam. It had flaws: it sometimes asked several questions at once, did not randomize topics, and its cloned professor voice sounded harsh.

Gradescope's AI groups similar answers on handwritten or digital exams, with OCR handling handwriting, so instructors can grade in batches. Instructors still review the groups and apply the rubrics, so the human stays in the loop.

Teacher license renewal requires the educator to complete professional learning personally. For example, Colorado requires 90 contact hours every 7 years and North Carolina requires 15 renewal units per 5-year cycle. An agent cannot earn the teacher's own competence or credit.

AI note-takers such as Read AI, Leexi and Zoom AI Companion can record, transcribe and summarize virtual professional-development sessions and conference talks. This helps the teacher, but the teacher still has to take part and absorb the learning.
Vendor case studies show AI summaries being used to track conference sessions and pick out key content. This speeds up the review and follow-up steps of attending, not the learning itself.

Gemini in Google Classroom can draft rubrics from the assignment context and suggest personalized feedback on written work. Teachers review and edit this output before using it. AI agents can therefore create assignments, score objective and written work, and draft feedback, but the AI's work is still checked by the teacher.

District policy in Dorchester District Two (South Carolina) says AI cannot be the sole basis for a grade. Teachers must review the work and make the final call, so a human keeps the essential sign-off step.

Illinois Senate Bill 416 would bar teachers from using AI to grade student work. This shows legal and accountability pressure to keep grading with the teacher of record. Note: the bill's final status was not confirmed.

Vendor AI tools available in 2026 cover the side work around parent conferences: drafting talking points from student data, adjusting the tone of messages, writing emails on sensitive topics, booking conference slots and collecting parent intake information. The search found no source showing an AI running the conferences or settling behavioral or academic problems itself. The time savings come from the vendors and were not measured independently.

Scheduling and intake agents for parent-teacher conferences exist, so logistics can be handed off. The conference conversation and the decisions still involve the teacher, parents, counselors and administrators.

District guidance says FERPA covers student records, including those held by AI vendors. A vendor may receive the data only if it qualifies as a 'school official' and the school keeps direct control over it. Teachers are told to keep identifiable data such as grades and IEP or 504 information out of unapproved AI tools. This limits what an agent can work with but does not require a human to sign off on the conference.

AI teacher tools such as MagicSchool's lesson planner produce full standards-aligned lesson plans, with objectives, activities, assessments and differentiation, from a short goal description. This covers the planning sub-step end to end, though a teacher still reviews and adapts the plan.
Oklahoma's law effective July 1, 2026 keeps classroom AI use educator-directed. This shows K-12 policy keeps a human teacher in charge of instruction.

A Pennsylvania bill would require certified human teachers, not AI, as the primary instructor in charter schools. California AB 2370 already bars AI from replacing community-college instructors of record. Both point to a human-in-charge rule for instruction.

In 2026, AI grading tools generate quizzes and grade multiple-choice, essay and STEM work against teacher rubrics, and they connect to the school's learning management system (the online course system). Examples include CoGrader, which pulls work from Google Classroom, Canvas and Schoology. That covers the test-writing step and the grading of written work.

Some vendor designs, such as OpenEduCat, keep a human in the loop: the AI suggests scores and feedback, and the teacher approves each grade before it counts. That points to partial delegation rather than full delegation.

Career and technical education is often assessed through hands-on performance tests. Students complete real jobs with the tools, materials and equipment of the trade while a skilled evaluator watches in person. An agent with no physical body cannot run or score this part.

MagicSchool offers an IEP Generator and an Accommodation Suggestion Generator for special education teachers. The vendor says to review the output closely before using it and to treat it as suggestions only. So an agent can draft strategies end to end, but a teacher still has to review them.

Guides for educators warn that AI does not know the individual student. They say its strategy and accommodation drafts need the teacher to add baseline data, context and professional judgment. This depends on observing the student and on student records that districts often restrict.

Under IDEA, special education teachers need a bachelor's degree and full state special education certification. Emergency or provisional credentials do not qualify. A licensed human is therefore responsible for carrying out the strategies with students in the classroom.

MagicSchool AI's Lesson Plan Generator builds a plan from grade, subject, topic and state or Common Core standards. It also has tools for differentiation and IEP accommodations, so it can produce written lesson-prep documents.
A review of EduAide.AI says complex IEP differentiation for students with severe learning needs still needs a human specialist, which supports keeping a teacher review step.
A university guide on AI in education advises checking AI-generated material before using it with students because the output can be biased or incorrect.

A library has tried to automate end-to-end cataloguing with an AI system to reduce administrative load. Cataloguers still oversee the workflow, which means the cataloguing sub-step can be partly delegated but a human still reviews it.
Commercial AI agents already automate inventory tracking, reorder triggers and anomaly flagging. These are the digital parts of maintaining and distributing materials and equipment.

Scheduling agents organize staff schedules and track inventory, with a person reviewing the output. This covers the routine coordination sub-steps, but supervising workers in person in libraries and labs stays with a human.
Vital signs monitors can send readings straight into the EHR through HL7/FHIR middleware. This automates the recording step, but someone still has to physically take each measurement.

In a vendor-published case study, Welch Allyn monitors with Accelero Connect integration are used on a hospital's psychiatric unit. Staff say the main gain is no longer having to type readings in by hand.
Vendor material describes GE Carescape VitalsLink as sending readings wirelessly to the EHR, with nurses doing this at the bedside. The measuring itself is still done by a person with the patient.

Mediation between roommates is run in person by trained Resident Assistants. Each roommate states the issues, they discuss each other's side and propose compromises. Sessions usually take under an hour and sometimes need a second meeting.

RAs hold in-person conversations with roommates to draft and document roommate agreements. Unresolved conflicts go to Resident Directors. This means the agent's digital share is mainly drafting agreements and documentation.

Roompact and similar software only support the process. They send check-ins, flag conflicts early and alert residence life staff, and they do not replace a human mediator. No purpose-built AI mediator was found in use at residence life offices.
Residence hall package software like Notifii Track lets staff log packages and automatically sends email and text alerts, with signature capture at pickup. A human still handles the items.
Parcel Tracker reviewers describe scanning a parcel and the resident being notified automatically. The scanning and delivery are done by hand by staff.

Student-housing mailroom software reads courier labels through a mobile camera to pull out recipient names and sends notifications across several channels. Only the data and notification sub-steps can be automated.

Jackpot handpays have traditionally needed an attendant to walk to the machine. Vendors such as JCM Global and CasinoSoft are building systems that pay jackpots by TITO ticket and handle the W-2G at the machine. That is fixed casino-floor equipment, not something a general AI agent does.

An IRS document describes the handpay steps: a casino employee verifies the jackpot at the machine and collects the winner's details for the W-2G. The IRS requires winners to show two forms of ID, one with a photo.
State regulators such as Pennsylvania's gaming board set internal controls that require employees to verify and sign off on jackpot payouts in certain dollar ranges.

In a traditional hand pay, the slot machine locks and a casino employee pays the jackpot by hand, usually with a W-2G copy, then unlocks the machine. Software can fill in the form, but the payout and the signature are physical, face-to-face steps.

Louisiana rules require the slot attendant to get a valid ID, the patron's name, address and SSN, and the jackpot amount before paying out jackpots of $1,200 or more. This means the regulation puts responsibility for the step on a human attendant.

Hard Rock's Self-Pay Jackpot system keeps a stored electronic signature for W-2G forms and moves the jackpot to the machine's credit meter, so no attendant is needed for that payout. Software can replace parts of the process, but only through casino system redesign, not through an AI agent acting for the cashier.
AI dispatch and routing software plans the order of stops, re-plans routes during the day and assigns jobs to drivers. That only supports the human courier, who still carries every item to the door.
Courier platforms offer smart dispatch that assigns the nearest available driver based on location, load capacity and availability. The physical delivery is still done by a person.
Autonomous delivery robots are a separate robotics technology studied in research. They fall outside a software-only AI agent with no physical body.

Making a rubbed finish means wetting hardened concrete by hand and grinding it with a carborundum brick or similar abrasive until the color and texture are even, usually within 24 hours of removing the forms. The work is entirely manual and has to be done on site.

The worker moves coarse and then fine rubbing stones in circular strokes and has to control the pressure to avoid gouging the surface. A software-only agent with no robotic body cannot do any of this.

Industry commentary from an ACI-affiliated source treats rubbed finishes as a manual craft step whose feasibility depends on curing time and how strong the concrete mix is. The step is not linked to licensing or sign-off.
Terrazzo workers partly press metal divider strips into the wet sandy concrete underbed before it sets. This is hands-on manual work done on site.
NTMA guidance says strips must be anchored well into the cement/sand underbed so they cannot move. This calls for physical setting and judging on the floor.

Federal specs require strips set with tight butt joints, true and square, held with cement mortar, and laid out following the drawing pattern. An AI could at most help interpret the layout from the drawings.

Echometer's wireless Base Station records liquid level, dynamometer and pressure data. A user runs it through TAM software on a laptop or at the sensor, and the software can analyze the acoustic liquid-level data automatically. An agent could do the interpretation if it can reach the digital traces.

Echometer's 2024 equipment comparison says a laptop running TAM software must be present for data acquisition. This means the gun still has to be attached to the wellhead and the shot run on site, so the task is not fully remote.

Automatic echometers such as the SUDOS-automat 2 measure liquid level without an operator and send the data by GSM to a remote database. This shows that monitoring can be digitized and done remotely where such equipment is installed.

Palm Beach County bridges use edge video analytics that watch safety zones and automatically alert operators to breaches. At the Jupiter US 1 bridge, tenders watch AI thermal camera screens that pick out people, cyclists and cars before opening, and a LiDAR interlock blocks the opening if it senses motion. The human tender still makes the final check.

The Caltrans bridge operations manual says the drawbridge operator shall thoroughly check that all pedestrians and vehicles are safely behind the barriers and that the movable parts of the bridge are clear. This makes the human operator responsible for the check.
Some remotely operated drawbridges depend on a human remote operator watching CCTV and infrared sensors. Coast Guard rules for these bridges assume a human operator does this surveillance.

Most movable bridges are worked from a local control console with physical switches, signals and gates. Remote operation exists at a few sites (WisDOT Sturgeon Bay since 2011, Canal & River Trust). Even there, a human operator watches CCTV, checks the deck is clear and starts the sequence. Lasers block the barriers from lowering if people or vehicles are on the deck, which shows how much depends on safety checks.

The federal traffic manual (MUTCD) Standard says signals, gates and movable spans shall be controlled by the bridge tender through an interlocked control. Responsibility therefore sits with a human tender.

Remote setups depend on site cameras, PLCs, safety-rated (SIL2) control systems and dedicated fiber links. These are closed industrial control networks that a general AI agent would not normally be able to reach. Early remote trials also had trouble judging distance and dealing with headlight glare on camera at night.

Under 49 CFR 396.11, the driver must complete a written or electronic inspection report that lists defects affecting safety. The next driver must review it and sign off that repairs were made. The finding and the signature have to come from a human driver.

Vendors sell voice-enabled and app-based electronic DVIRs that turn a driver's spoken or photo input into a structured defect report. This lets software handle the form-filling and paperwork side of the task.

Vendors say refuse-fleet telematics (J1939 fault codes, PTO hours) and yard-exit camera scanning can find some defects and create work orders automatically. These claims are unverified. Many defects on packers, hydraulics and lifts still need a person to inspect the truck and the equipment.

The only real example of a driverless refuse truck is Volvo's trial with Renova in Sweden around 2016–2017, which used lidar and GPS on a purpose-built vehicle. That is robotics, not a software-only agent. The search found no 2026 deployment of a fully driverless garbage truck; the 2026 'automated collection' programs use mechanical arms, and a human still drives.
Automated side-loading trucks being piloted in 2026, such as Casella's work for Concord, NH, still have human drivers. Only the cart lifting is automated.
Municipal refuse truck driver jobs usually require a commercial driver's licence (CDL Class B) for the vehicle being operated, so the law expects a licensed human driver.
OptimoRoute sells automated route planning for garbage and waste collection that takes driver skills, breaks and vehicle limits into account.
Wastehero's Route AI turns collection schedules into routes automatically, using vehicle capacity, time windows and road limits, and syncs them with the office in real time.

Dayjob AI pulls data from waste ERP systems to build next-day schedules and has an in-day planner for changes. A human still has to set the rules and approve the plan, and the work depends on access to company dispatch systems.

Agentic AI recruiting tools already handle sourcing, screening, outreach, scheduling and structured or conversational screening interviews end to end. Vendors still advise keeping a human in the loop for final hiring decisions.
Vendors say AI agents can run structured, role-specific interviews without live scheduling and can score candidates.

Gaming regulators license casino employees and key employees, including HR managers in Ohio. Licensing covers the hire's suitability, not who conducts the interview. The final hiring decision and the check that new hires are licensed are still done by accountable managers.

A 2025 survey of LLM-based scientific agents describes planner modules that break broad research aims into ordered steps (hypotheses, experiment design, analysis, validation), with replanning when results are uncertain. This is the detailed-planning sub-step that agents can draft end to end.

Project2Task (arXiv, August 2026) proposes graph-guided project-level planning that turns a project brief into candidate contributions and ordered tasks for autonomous research. This shows that turning broad goals into plans is a current agent capability, but it is research-stage work, not a proven replacement for a manager's judgement.

Commercial agents such as ClickUp's research roadmap planner break research goals into tasks with roles and deadlines. Setting the goals themselves within management's outline still requires organizational judgement, choices about resources, and agreement from stakeholders, and no licence or law requires a human to sign the plan.

Vendors sell FP&A AI agents that track budget against actual spending on their own, look into variances and draft financial commentary. The figures they publish (for example, 60-70% less time spent) come from the vendors themselves and have not been independently checked.
Vendors also claim AI agents can analyse all budget-to-actual variances in real time, which suggests budget administration and report preparation can be handed off end to end.

Under 2 CFR 200.415, the fiscal reports and payment requests for a federal award must carry a certification signed by an official who can legally bind the recipient. That means a human has to approve and sign the expenditures and financial reports.

Vendor tools describe AI agents that read a client brief, pull comparable past proposals and draft scope, timelines and pricing. They claim this cuts scoping time by 40-60%, but these figures are unverified vendor claims.

Planning agents (Taskade's three-agent team, Microsoft Planner Agent) generate scope, timeline and resource plans from briefs or meeting notes. Guidance still stresses that a human applies judgment to the plan.
The CMC is a voluntary professional designation, not a government licence. Only use of the title is regulated, for example in Alberta, so no law requires a human to plan or sign a study.

FDIC examination procedures include on-site checks such as surprise counts of vault cash and dual control over the vault and cash shipments. An agent with no body cannot do these physical inspections.

Vendors offer AI agents that check collateral eligibility, haircuts and concentration limits, and verify borrowing-base calculations with custodians. These are vendor claims, not independently verified deployments.

Reconciliation agents can investigate and propose fixes for securities and settlement breaks, but typical designs leave a human to approve the result. This fits a partial-delegation rating with human review.

The free Rangeland Analysis Platform estimates vegetation cover and herbaceous biomass from satellite imagery going back to 1986, refreshed every 16 days. Its Production Explorer shows how forage changes affect AUMs, grazing days and carrying capacity, which is analysis an agent can run from a browser.

The satellite models are calibrated against plots collected by hand. Stocking-rate tools such as StockSmart also need site inputs like distance to water, slope and how animals use the land, so someone still has to check grazing patterns in the field.

BLM rangeland management specialist postings ask for education and experience, such as monitoring livestock grazing. The excerpts reviewed did not require SRM certification or a licensed signature, though SRM offers voluntary certifications that NRCS recognizes.

Distributors such as Wurl already send each channel's schedule to Gracenote automatically. The feed covers tomorrow plus six days and includes episode IDs, titles, descriptions, original air dates and start times, so the step of passing schedule information to outlets is largely done by software today.

A patented EPG provisioning system takes broadcast traffic data, reformats it for each guide provider and sends it out in real time. This is a system design, not proof of a deployed product, but it shows that both the checking-and-formatting and the delivery sub-steps can be automated.

Clipsource says it can automate the distribution of linear and TV/VOD listings straight from planning sources. That covers the main sub-steps through software alone, with no physical presence needed. My one search found nothing saying a licensed human must sign off on listings, though I did not check this point directly.

Under CMS medical-direction rules, the anesthesiologist must personally do all seven required activities for each of 2 to 4 concurrent cases, including staying physically present and available for emergencies. Missing even one activity disqualifies the claim.

AI platforms such as Qventus, which connect to the EHR, automate operating-room scheduling. Vendors like ScheduleForward say they coordinate anesthesia coverage and rotations, though these claims come from the vendors and are unverified. These tools cover the planning and logistics part of coordinating staff.

Staffing software claims it can coordinate anesthesia coverage and fair rotations, but this is marketing. Directing nurses and technicians in real time during a case, at the bedside, remains a human job.

Game wardens describe public speaking as a large part of their outreach work. They prefer bringing physical visual aids, such as wildlife items, to slideshows, so the officer has to be there in person.

Conservation officers run in-person education and outreach, such as hunter education classes and school and community programs. The value of these programs depends on the uniformed officer being present and trusted.
AI presentation agents in 2026 can produce whole slide decks from a prompt and can even narrate them. That covers the preparation step, but an officer still has to give the talk or interview live.

Agency staff justify proposed regulation changes with harvest data and population models. In Alaska, a moose model projected harvest by age class to test proposed hunting rules. This kind of data analysis and model-based drafting is work an AI agent can do.

Biologists and field staff submit regulation proposals, a board or commission votes on them after public comment, and the final decision belongs to the commission. Field staff recommend, so their recommendations need no licensed human signature, but they draw on firsthand field observation.
Agencies already use AI tools to summarize public comments that feed into staff regulation recommendations.

Wardens collect wildlife data on the ground and from the air to estimate distribution and abundance, and they investigate water pollution and habitat damage. This fieldwork requires being physically present.
AI tools such as SpeciesNet can automatically detect and classify animals in camera-trap images. This speeds up the processing of survey data.
Camera-trap AI handles common species well but struggles with rare, small or similar-looking species and with changes in location. Workflows still rely on humans to validate the results.

Parks already use AI assistants to answer visitor questions about routes, permits, hours and safety, usually in several languages. Examples include Gran Paradiso's Sibilla, the Mysuru Zoo assistant and Frisco's park avatar. Most of these accounts are written by the vendors, and I found no confirmed chatbot run by a US state wildlife agency.

State job descriptions say wardens give information and education to the public on statutes and regulations while doing field enforcement on patrol. That means they mostly advise visitors face to face, on site, during patrols.

Warden duties include patrolling by car, boat, plane, horse or on foot and making daily contact with many outside groups. In that setting, advice is given in person, in the moment, and with the authority of the badge.

O*NET's profile for Fish and Game Wardens (33-3031.00) describes fieldwork such as patrolling on foot, by vehicle, boat or aircraft, and protecting wildlife and habitat. The search summary did not show this maintenance task in O*NET's list, so the claim that the job is physical rests mainly on the task wording itself.

A New Mexico state job description says wardens spend much of their time writing reports and keeping records. Software can only touch side jobs like that (for example planning, ordering supplies or logging), not the hands-on building, repair, or weed and pest control.

Motorola Solutions' Assist tools transcribe field radio traffic and suggest incidents to dispatchers. This speeds up the communication and logging part of the task, but a human dispatcher still confirms the incident.

In 2026, police agencies such as San Diego County Sheriff, La Mesa and El Cajon use AI voice agents (Hyper, Aurelian Ava) to take and route non-emergency complaints. These calls include parking issues, and humans review the intake or receive the hand-off.

Motorola bought Hyper in April 2026 and sells agentic AI for public-safety call handling. This automates the dispatcher side of the exchange, not the field officer who answers the radio call and goes to the scene.

Local codes (e.g., Dayton and Fort Mitchell, KY) let a hearing board consider a written report made under oath by the issuing officer in place of personal testimony. The sworn witness must still be the human officer, though an AI could draft or assemble the report.
In Fort Worth the issuing officer is not required to attend the hearing. When the officer does appear, they testify as a fact witness about what they personally saw, which an AI agent cannot do.
A contestant can require the officer who wrote the ticket to attend the hearing. Live witness testimony in court needs a human to be present and under oath.

The Passport immobilization API works with tow processors such as AutoReturn. An officer can request a tow from a handheld device, get the fees calculated in real time, and follow the tow's status in a central back-end system. This means the arranging step is already digital and could be scripted by an agent.
Tow-dispatch software sends requests straight to drivers' phones in place of manual rotation, with automatic assignment and timestamps. The dispatch and rotation sub-steps can be automated.

Department policies require an officer to tag or sticker the vehicle on site, wait 24 to 72 hours, and re-check before towing. Some also require a consent form from the private property owner. This confirms that physical presence and the officer's legal authorization are needed for the parts an agent cannot do, such as verifying the vehicle and pointing the driver to it on scene.

Coin collection is hands-on work. Collectors pick up vault keys and sealed canisters, sign custody logs, physically open each meter and empty its coin can into a canister. Software cannot do any of this.

Software only handles the planning side. Vendor tools watch canister fill levels, send low/warning/critical alerts, plan just-in-time collection routes and reconcile cash totals by route, which shortens the work but does not remove the physical collection.
NYC DOT uses alerts from its Parkfolio software to set collection schedules, targeting meters at about 900 coins. Software sets the timing, and crews still collect the coins in person.

Multnomah County's job profile says animal control officers examine animals to judge how severe a sickness or injury is, then arrange medical care and take the animal to a veterinarian. That means hands-on handling and transport in the field.

Long Beach's job classification says officers give routine care and preventive treatment under a veterinarian's direction. The officer does the triage, and a licensed vet decides on and provides the medical treatment.

The AI pet-health apps I found screen photos for skin, weight and wellness problems and send users to a vet. They say they are not diagnostic tools, and none of them does validated injury triage. So AI can help from photos, but it can't do the physical exam.

The Salem, VA animal control SOP says the officer must unload every animal before doing paperwork. Each animal has to stay restrained by leash, snare pole, carrier or trap until it is placed in a cage or kennel run. Dangerous animals need a second officer present. The whole task is hands-on physical handling.
The Texas DSHS animal control officer training covers transport in cage-equipped trucks and careful handling to calm the animal. It describes this as manual work.
In the Salem SOP, the officer also has to clean and disinfect any body waste spilled in the unloading area. That step is physical too and no software agent can do it.

A vendor case study says a county animal services chatbot answers questions about lost and found pets, licensing, adoptions and welfare programs, and uses map data to give answers for the resident's own area. The results are self-reported.
Maricopa County's 24/7 AI assistant handles resident questions about county programs. Early data shows strong interest in pet services.
A shelter chatbot vendor claims, in its own marketing, that 80% of routine questions were resolved instantly. Harder cases still go to staff.

Camera traps with AI (Microshare EverSmart, BrightAI/Pelsis) can identify species and counts and send alerts. This only supports monitoring at fixed devices; the worker still has to walk the premises, find the source and judge structural damage and entry points.
In Washington State, inspecting for pests, their signs or conducive conditions requires a WSDA licence. WDO reports for property transfers must carry state-issued inspection control numbers.
Florida Stat. 482.226 requires the licensee or a qualified representative to produce wood-destroying organism inspection reports on a state-prescribed form.

Several AI breed-matching tools, including PawMatch, which is built on Gemini, ask about the owner's lifestyle, living situation and preferences and score them against databases of about 170–195 breeds to recommend specific breeds. That covers the research and matching part of purchase advice.

Expert buying advice often means seeing the individual animal in person: watching how it is caught, led, groomed, tacked and tied, and spotting signs that it was worked beforehand to calm it down. An agent without a body can't do this.

Extension guidance recommends taking along a trainer who knows the buyer's riding level and goals. The buyer handles and rides the horse in person, and a vet exam follows. No licence is needed to give purchase advice; only the vet exam is a separate professional act.

AI tools for horses only analyse gait from phone video or sensors (Sleip, TrojanTrack, Horscan, HorseCare DR). The trainer still handles, rides and conditions the horse, and Sleip's output is not diagnostic: vets interpret it.
Kentucky does not let a horse race unless its trainer holds a current commission licence. To get one, the trainer must show experience and pass a standard exam given by the stewards.

Minnesota requires racing trainers to have 2 years of horsemanship experience and to pass a written exam and a practical horsemanship test. The practical test shows that the core of the work is hands-on handling of live animals.

Starting a horse means training it to accept a saddle, bridle and rider and to respond to rein and voice cues. A trainer has to be physically with the horse, handling it on the ground and riding it, to do this; software cannot.

Starting a horse to harness also means hands-on work with the horse and the equipment, step by step. An AI agent without a body could at most suggest a training plan, which is a tiny share of the working time.
