AI treat dispensers like CompanionPro and a Jetson Nano prototype can recognize and reward simple behaviors. Their makers describe them as aids to a trainer, not stand-alone trainers. They cannot teach assistance or protection tasks, which need hands-on handling, so the agent's role is limited to planning, logging and analyzing video.
Service dog training is typically at least 120 hours of hands-on schooling over six months or more, including 30 hours in public places. This requires a person to be physically present with the dog.
The ADA does not require service dogs to be certified or professionally trained. No law requires a licensed human to perform or sign off on the training.

Dallmeier's AI camera system recognizes cards and chips at baccarat and blackjack tables, and the vendor reports more than 1,000 tables in Macau. That figure comes from the vendor and was not independently checked. This shows that machines can do the hand-reading and comparison step when the table is fitted with these cameras.

Patented card-reading shoes and monitoring systems read card ranks and apply the game rules (for example in baccarat) to decide which hand wins. The judgment itself is easy to automate, but only on tables with this special hardware, which an AI agent would not normally be able to reach.

Dealers at live tables must hold a gaming license from their state. Examples include the Nevada Gaming Control Board, the Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board and the Indiana Gaming Commission. Dealers also work in person, revealing cards and settling hands at the table.

Keno writer and runner jobs include scanning winning tickets, working out winnings, paying customers in cash and keeping a personal cash bank balanced. These steps are physical and need someone present at the window or on the floor.

The rule lets a human writer or a self-service kiosk redeem winning tickets once the sports wagering system has checked them. So checking tickets and working out payouts is already automated in fixed systems, not done by a general AI agent.
Sportsbooks have not widely adopted full self-service cash-out machines because of technical, regulatory and risk concerns. Mobile accounts pay winnings out digitally, so no paper ticket is needed.

Inspecting a physical film print means winding the reels by hand on a rewind bench, feeling for splices and torn edges, looking closely with a loupe, checking reel flanges and remaking bad splices. All of this is hands-on work that an agent without a body cannot do.

For digital cinema packages (the digital equivalent of a print), software can check completeness and integrity automatically. ClairMeta and DCP-o-matic check file hashes, sizes, schemas and signatures, and can spot an incomplete transfer or corrupted files. Only this digital portion of the work could be handed off to an agent.
A DCP workflow guide says automated checks do not replace human playback review. Ingest and screening checks still take place on the cinema server inside the projection booth.

Barco Insights is a cloud platform for projectors. It shows live usage and environmental data, health history and log-file review, and sends health-issue alerts through email and an API. An agent could run this digital part of the pre-show check from start to finish.

Barco's NOC already monitors networked cinema projectors, servers, theatre management systems and UPS units remotely, and can analyse and upgrade them remotely. One exhibitor has more than 160 projectors monitored this way across 12 sites.

Christie's NOCs monitor projectors, players and theatre management systems around the clock, and use predictive maintenance tools to spot problems early. Physical checks such as lens and port-glass cleanliness, focus, film path and mechanical condition still need a person on site.

Replacing a projector sprocket is hands-on mechanical work. Taper pins are pressed in hard and take real effort to drive out, and the shaft must be supported so it does not bend or damage the sprocket. An agent with no body cannot do any of this.

The sprocket must fit the shaft with no play and without being too tight, or the picture will weave. Some swaps take about two minutes on the machine, but intermittent sprockets need precision tools and are often sent to a service station. The judgment and fitting are physical work.

Projection manuals describe spotting worn sprockets by checking the machine in person and seeing unsteady pictures or torn perforations. An AI could only help with the paperwork: looking up the manual, ordering parts, or writing a maintenance ticket.

O*NET lists 'Install and connect auxiliary equipment, such as microphones, amplifiers, disc playback machines, and lights' as a supplemental task for Motion Picture Projectionists (39-3021.00). The work means physically mounting, cabling and connecting hardware. An agent without a body cannot do that. It can only help with wiring diagrams, manuals, signal-flow planning and troubleshooting advice.
O*NET describes the occupation as setting up and operating projection and related sound reproduction equipment, which is hands-on work in the booth and auditorium.

Virginia's rules say multiuse tools such as clippers, scissors and combs must be washed with hot soapy water, rinsed and fully immersed in disinfectant for at least 10 minutes before use on a client. This is hands-on physical work that a software-only agent cannot do.

California requires removing visible debris from clippers and other electrical tools and then disinfecting them before each use with an EPA-registered spray or wipe. Every step involves handling the tools by hand.

Arkansas requires cleaning by physically removing debris, then disinfecting with an EPA-registered product that kills bacteria, viruses and fungi, before any tool touches a client. The board's sanitation rules hold the licensee responsible but do not require a human signature. The real barrier is physical.

Consumer AI apps already handle intake: HairHunt uses a short quiz to build a personalised shortlist of styles, and other apps offer an AI stylist chat and photo try-ons that clients can share with their barber. An agent could run the service-and-style questioning before the visit.

Barber-facing tools such as StyleForge offer 3D hair and beard try-ons to show customers in the shop. They support the consultation, but the barber still runs it at the chair and checks hair texture, growth patterns and head shape in person.
State law requires a licence to practise barbering, meaning the physical services. Nothing found shows that law requires a licensed human to do the consultation or questioning itself.

Consumer and salon tools already analyse photos of a person's scalp and hair, identify conditions such as dryness, oiliness or hair loss, and recommend matching products or in-salon treatments. Examples are HairCoSys, L'Oréal Professionnel My Scalp ID and iHairium. These are vendor claims; I found no independent accuracy testing.

A start-up's app uses photos of the head to identify hair and scalp conditions and suggest ways to treat them. This covers the analysis-and-recommendation step from start to finish, but someone still has to take good images. In a barbershop, the barber normally checks the client's hair and scalp in person by looking and touching.

Barber licences include scalp treatments, but barbers may not practise medicine. California's board rules require licensees to stay within the areas they are licensed for, and I found no rule saying a licensed human must sign off on cosmetic product suggestions. Medical scalp conditions have to be referred to a doctor, whoever is giving the advice.
Georgia law defines barbering to include giving facial or scalp massages and treatments with oils or creams. This is a licensed, hands-on service.
Delaware law defines a barber as someone who, for pay, gives facial or scalp massages. That ties the service to a licensed human practitioner.

New Mexico barber rules cover facial and scalp massage and applying products to the scalp, face and neck. All of this is physical manipulation, which an AI agent that works only through software cannot do.

Current consumer AI apps such as Glamify and roboMUA work out a person's skin shade from a selfie or live camera. They then recommend shade-matched foundation, lip and eye products and give step-by-step routines and tutorials. This covers the color- and type-advice part of the task.

Brand and enterprise tools, including Maybelline's Virtual Beauty Studio and Perfect Corp's YouCam tutorial and shade-finder SDKs, offer virtual try-on and guided makeup tutorials from a camera feed. Accuracy depends on lighting and photo conditions, and a person still has to demonstrate on the client's face and correct their technique in person.

Esthetician licensing, for example in California, covers applying makeup for pay. Advising clients and teaching techniques is not shown to need a licensed person's signature, and many states do not license makeup artistry at all.

AI shade-matching, virtual try-on and personalized product recommendation tools (Perfect Corp/MAKE UP FOR EVER, ModiFace) already handle advisory sub-steps of makeup selling, but they support the in-person sale rather than complete it.
Retailers have deployed virtual makeup try-on at scale (L'Oréal ModiFace on Amazon; Watsons offering try-on for 300 products), so the digital part of recommending and selling makeup can be automated.

Selling makeup at a counter generally needs no esthetician license, but applying makeup on clients for pay can count as licensed esthetics practice. Salon selling usually involves hands-on demonstration and in-person persuasion.

O*NET says this occupation loads, operates, and sometimes adjusts and repairs mail processing, sorting and canceling machinery, and clears jams in sorting equipment. All of this is hands-on work on the equipment.
A private mail-sorting job posting describes sorter operators doing hourly hands-on barcode quality checks against a physical USPS template while running the machines.

The automated parts of the work, such as optical character reading and barcode sorting, are already done by the machines themselves. What the human operator adds is feeding mail, sweeping bins and clearing jams, all physical tasks a software-only agent cannot do. It could at most help with console or sort-plan software it would not normally have access to.

USPS buys driverless tow tractors and pallet trucks to move mail containers around processing plants. This is robotic hardware, not a software AI agent. A software agent could at most send moves through a fleet-management system it would not normally have access to.
Moving mail containers means physically driving, hitching and staging carts, OTR containers and powered industrial trucks on the workroom floor.
Similar autonomous tugs in parcel hubs, such as UPS Tacoma, depend on physical robots that navigate with lasers. A software-only agent has no body and cannot do this.

Barn feeding and cleaning are automated by dedicated robots and mechanical systems (feeding robots, manure scrapers), not by software-only AI agents. Without those robots, the work needs someone physically present to handle feed, water and disinfection.
Robots for cleaning pig barns and cattle feeders are still in research or development, so cleaning and disinfecting pens and cages remains largely manual work.

Automated feeding and watering systems are physical installations that run on their own control logic. A software agent could at most adjust schedules on a connected controller, which is a small part of the task.

Commercial camera-and-AI systems already score lameness and body condition automatically. CattleEye says its system monitors more than 150,000 cattle using a camera at the milking parlour exit. These systems need fixed farm hardware and cover only some signs of illness, not a full hands-on exam.

Research systems detect cattle lameness from a single side-view camera in real time using Mask-RCNN and YOLOv8. A software agent could analyse such video feeds, but palpation, taking temperatures and handling the animal still need a person on site.
Nedap's SmartSight computer-vision product monitors livestock health with farm cameras. This supports AI help with spotting symptoms, but the breeder still does the physical examination.

Vaccinating through drinking water or by spray is hands-on work. Someone has to prepare the water lines, make the birds thirsty, mix and dose the vaccine, finish giving it within 1.5 to 3 hours, and spray from about 50 cm away. An agent without a body can only help with the dose and dilution maths and with the timing plan.

Product labels set the reconstitution and dosing rules, for example 1,000 doses per litre per day of age. An agent could look these up and do the calculations, but a person still has to give the vaccine.

Automated vaccination for livestock exists only as robotics, such as RFID or vision-guided needle-free injectors, and is mostly at prototype or early-deployment stage. That falls outside a software-only agent.

STgenetics' web-based Chromosomal Mating program uses linear programming to assign sires to females. It controls inbreeding and lethal haplotypes while maximizing the predicted producing value of offspring, so the semen-selection sub-step is already done by software.
Viking Genetics' VikMate mating plan tracks inbreeding back six generations and builds a sire list from the semen doses held in storage. It covers the pedigree and trait-matching work in this task.

In BoviSync, mating recommendations are produced by genetic advisors using mating software and then imported into herd-management systems. A human advisor or breeder still sets the breeding goals and accepts the plan, and choosing which animals to breed still relies on on-farm observation of the animals.

Livestock AI tools like Betty and VetWiz suggest likely diseases from symptoms the farmer enters, and Betty can point farmers to a local vet. But the breeder still has to examine the animal, and none of these tools combines AI triage with direct vet telehealth for livestock.

State veterinary practice acts, such as Florida's, let owners and their regular employees treat their own animals. So a licence is not required for minor treatment, though diseases of public-health significance need a licensed vet.
California's owner exemption (B&P Code 4827) lets bona fide owners give veterinary care to their own animals, except for certain specified procedures.

Commercial heat-detection systems (Heatime, ai24, SelectDetect, Afimilk) use neck-collar or pedometer activity sensors to flag estrus. An agent can read and interpret these dashboards, but only on farms that already have the sensors installed.

A neck-mounted accelerometer collar (RUMI) detected estrus with 90.9% sensitivity and 100% specificity in 47 Holstein cows and suggested insemination timing windows. This supports the monitoring/data side of the task, not physically handling the animals.

On pasture, neck collars work less well, so rump-mounted standing-behavior sensors such as Heat Switch were developed. Detection still depends on physical hardware on the animals, and exercising animals to induce estrus has to be done in person.

EID readers and scale indicators store each weight against the animal's tag and sync it to software automatically. The software then calculates average daily gain and growth trends without anyone typing the numbers in.

Farmbrite says (vendor claim) its software links EID scans to automated weighing scales and feed stations, and tracks daily weight gain, feed consumption and feed efficiency per animal. Someone still has to handle the animals physically and keep the hardware running.

The iLivestock app logs weights and medicines, monitors growth, and exports weighing sessions as CSV files. These are digital records that an agent could consolidate and analyse, but the measurements themselves are taken on the farm.
Shows take entries online during set windows and accept no late entries (Milam County, TX; Kent County, DE uses the Showman system). An agent could handle this paperwork and deadline work.
Entry forms need each animal's name, birth date, breed and registration number, which is document work an AI can prepare. Showing the animal itself still happens in person in the ring.
Showmanship must be done with the same animal entered in that species' market class, so a person has to handle that animal physically in the ring.

Free online fence configurators already take animal species, area size, fence type and power supply and produce a material list you can export. An AI agent could also do this planning and quantity work, but that is a small part of the job.

Building a hutch means using a saw, drill, impact driver, staple gun, tin snips and hog-ring pliers to cut lumber, put up framing, fit wire mesh, hang doors and lay roofing. This is hands-on work that a software-only agent with no robot body cannot do.

University extension guidance on building farm fences covers post spacing, bracing and gates as on-site construction work. It does not mention any licence or sign-off needed for typical small animal pens.

Fully automated wool harvesting is still at the proof-of-concept stage. AWI funded Ranken Research and Robo Shear to build a prototype machine, which would be dedicated robotic hardware, not a software agent.

Research on semi-autonomous shearing treats it as a physical job: restraining the animal and guiding the cutter over it. Even the most advanced robot work still needs hand clipping for the head and tail areas.
Later automation work moved to handling wool after shearing, such as trimming dirty wool, classing and baling, using physical robots. None of it can be done through software alone.

Machines fill, seal and print semen straws in one step at about 14,000 straws per hour. A person still has to set up and run them. Print data can be loaded from customer databases and linked to lab-management software such as Prism10 Bull. This means an agent could prepare the label data and keep the records, but the physical packaging cannot be done through software.
ICAR guidelines set the minimum straw identification: centre code, breed, bull ID and a collection code in yyddd date format. These are fixed data fields that software can generate.

CSS certification (a NAAB subsidiary monitored by USDA) sets standards for producing the semen and for what goes on the straw label. The search did not show any rule that a licensed person must personally label the straws.

CattleMax and other herd-management software already track semen inventory (owned and non-owned bulls, tank location, collection codes) and connect breeding and pregnancy records. The logging and record-keeping steps are already digital, so an agent could run them.

Digital Beef has a semen module that records AI breeding data, semen usage and tank or canister location. An agent could fill in and reconcile these records once it has the breeding-event data, which is created in the barn when someone inseminates an animal and reads its ID.

Form-based apps let breeders and vets record semen use on mobile devices on site. Someone physically present still has to capture the event (which straw went into which animal), so a human supplies or checks the source data.

Online livestock marketplaces like LivestockMarket.com already handle for-sale listings, inventory and sales management, and buyer messaging. An agent could post listings and answer inquiries through them.
Marketplaces such as Farmia let buyers search by location, category and price, and the platform also coordinates vet checks and transport. These logistics steps are digital and can be automated.

Under the USDA Animal Welfare Act, breeders who sell to research facilities need a USDA license (Class A or B). This applies to the business, not to a human signing each sale. Search results were mostly 2004 to 2017, so current rules were not confirmed. Final contract terms and relationship-based negotiation with institutional buyers still usually need human sign-off.

Loading an insemination gun is hands-on lab work. The worker takes the straw out of liquid nitrogen with forceps, thaws it in a 35°C water bath, wipes it dry, puts it into the gun, cuts it about 7 mm below the crimp, and then warms or protects the loaded gun. A software-only agent can't do any of these steps.

The setup also needs physical adjustment. The plunger is pushed until it touches the cotton plug, a protective sheath is fitted over the gun, and semen is pushed forward until it just shows at the tip. Automated straw-filling machines exist, but they are mechanical equipment and not AI agents.

The steps differ by species. One source says to cut the straw at the sealed end and not the cotton end. An AI could only help by looking up the right protocol, which is a very small share of the work.

Australia's national competency unit AHCAIS303 is assessed through observed workplace practice. It requires the inseminator to restrain the animal, thaw the semen and perform the insemination by hand, which an agent with no body cannot do.

In Tyrol, Austria, insemination technicians must hold a certificate based on veterinary or inseminator training and declare the activity to the Chamber of Agriculture. People without the certificate can be banned from practising.
UK equine guidance (BEVA) says AI technicians must complete an approved AI technician course before inseminating mares, so a trained human has to do the procedure.

VES DairyBOS is a cloud-based barn controller. It lets producers adjust ventilation, cooling and lighting and watch near real-time barn temperature and humidity from a phone or tablet. Software can therefore change setpoints when the barn is connected.

With AP Connect and Agri-Alert, swine producers can monitor and change temperature, humidity and static pressure settings from a smartphone. One producer changed a barn's temperature remotely after an alarm, so the adjustment step can be done digitally.

BarnTalk and Little Giant BARN-IQ sense conditions and send alerts when they go out of range, and BARN-IQ can switch smart-plug fans and heaters. Many barns still use local thermostats, heat lamps, curtains and inlets that a person has to set by hand, so physical presence and system access limit how much an agent can delegate.

Computer-assisted semen analysis (CASA) systems already measure sperm motility, kinematics and concentration automatically. Someone still has to collect the sample, load the slide and work the microscope and analyzer.

Concentration and motility (total and progressive) are the values used to work out how many doses an ejaculate can yield. That calculation is the part of the job an agent could do in software, along with recording the results.

CASA accuracy depends on methodological factors and microscopy limits, and the slide prep and extender mixing are hands-on work in the lab. Because of this, an AI agent with no body cannot do the core steps of the task.

Animals are identified with physical ear tags (840 RFID, NUES metal or plastic button tags), brands and tattoos. Someone has to restrain each animal and apply the tag or mark by hand. The software-friendly part of the job is getting a premises ID and keeping records.

USDA's proposal to require RFID tags for interstate cattle movement by 2023 was withdrawn. Brands and tattoos can still count as official ID if the shipping and receiving states agree. The rules set which ID methods are accepted, not who may apply them, so no licence is needed to do the tagging.

To get official tags, a producer needs a premises identification number (PIN) from the state. This registration and tag-record step is the only part an AI agent could do; branding, tattooing and tagging the animal itself needs a body and hands.

O*NET lists this task for Helpers--Carpenters as cleaning work areas, machines or equipment by hand on the job site. It is manual work. An agent can only add minor digital help, such as checklists or scheduling dumpster pickups.

OSHA 29 CFR 1926.25 requires that scrap lumber with protruding nails and other debris be physically cleared from work areas, passageways and stairs, and that waste be put in containers and removed at regular intervals. This needs someone on site. The rule is a duty on the employer and does not require a licensed person to do or sign the cleanup.
A DOL-listed carpenter helper posting describes the work as physical: building wood forms so they are aligned and plumb, then helping lift them to the required height.
Helpers build rough wooden structures such as concrete forms, gang forms and column forms from sketches, blueprints or verbal instructions, with a carpenter directing the work.

Software such as Tekla Structures automates formwork layout and planning in BIM. That planning is done by engineers and foremen; the helper's own work of building and raising forms is hands-on and cannot be done through software.
O*NET lists 'Cut and install insulating or sound-absorbing material' as a task for Helpers--Carpenters (47-3012.00), an occupation that helps carpenters with lower-skill hands-on duties
DOL job postings for carpenter helpers list this task next to other on-site physical work such as cutting lumber and holding materials for fastening
Occupation profile confirms the work is manual and done on construction sites, so a software-only agent with no body cannot cut or install material

Hot vulcanizing is hands-on work: the worker places the patch over the puncture, protects the tube, clamps the press arm, switches on the heater, then waits about ten minutes for the tube to cool before taking it out. An agent with no robotic body cannot do any of this.

Hot patches are cured by heat and pressure from a heated plate that presses the tube onto the patch, with a controlled rise and fall in temperature. The work is done with a physical tool and the rubber itself, not through software.

Before patching, the tube is scuffed and the patch clamped onto it by hand, so every main step needs physical handling. AI could only help a little, such as looking up cure times in the manufacturer's instructions. I found no licence requirement for this work.
Cleaning whitewalls is hands-on work: put a whitewall-safe cleaner on the tire, scrub the sidewall with a brush or pad, then rinse. A software agent with no body can't do any of these steps.
For stubborn yellowing, sources suggest scrubbing with a Scotch-Brite pad or sanding with fine-grit paper. Both need a person (or robot) handling the tire.
The guidance is about picking a safe product, such as avoiding bleach and ammonia. An AI could only help a little by looking up which product to use, which isn't a substantial part of the task.
Track brackets are fastened to jambs and headers with lag screws driven through brackets into the wood structure. The installer has to find the framing and drive the screws into it by hand on site.
The steps are hands-on: install wood bucks on masonry jambs, drill pilot holes and drive 3/8 in. lag screws with minimum edge distances. An agent can only help by looking up these specifications.
Fastening the track involves loosely attaching lag bolts, checking the track for level, then tightening them. Each step needs a person physically working on the track.

Job postings for underground linemen describe the work as physical field labor. Crews dig trenches, pull cable by hand from truck-mounted reels or with winches, rod and rope through conduit, and run trenchers, backhoes and bucket trucks. A software-only AI agent can't do any of this.

Underground lineman roles require splicing and terminating URD cable, setting up work zones, wearing PPE and lifting about 50 lb. These steps happen on site, and the paperwork or mapping reports that an agent could help with are a small part of the job.
Utility contractor postings list laying cable in trenches or pulling it through conduit, then backfilling and restoring the site, as core field duties for the line crew.

O*NET lists hands-on work as the core of this job: adjusting shutters, light meters and lens systems with hand tools, taking equipment apart to find defects, testing with precision gauges, and reading engineering drawings. Advising on equipment design draws on what the repairer sees during this physical work, which an agent cannot do itself.

Industry AI reasoning agents already go through past work orders and failure events and produce recommendations with cost and risk tradeoffs, which engineers then test before acting. That covers the analysis and write-up steps of a design-change recommendation, but humans still review the result.

Generative AI reliability assistants are described as adding to maintenance practice while keeping human expertise and oversight, so human review of engineering recommendations is still expected. I found no licensing or sign-off rule that applies to camera repairers.

HR case-management and AI-agent products (for example ServiceNow Now Assist and Newgen) handle grievance intake, documentation, case summaries and suggested resolutions. A human still validates the findings and resolves the case.

In a typical union grievance procedure, the first step is an informal meeting between the employee, a steward and the immediate supervisor to resolve the matter. The step depends on face-to-face discussion and negotiation.
Grievance steps carry contractual deadlines and require written management responses, which an AI can draft. The decisions belong to designated management representatives.

Dedicated PLC-controlled autowinders already switch reels and cut at a preset length. Setting them up, threading the product, and handling and weighing the reels are still done by hand on the shop floor. A software-only AI agent cannot do any of that physical work.

Conair's ATC coilers change spindles automatically once the programmed footage is reached and save recipes. The only digital part an AI agent could help with is choosing or entering recipe parameters, and that depends on access to the machine's HMI.

Under 10 CFR 50.54(i) and 55.3, only NRC-licensed operators or senior operators may manipulate controls that directly affect reactivity or power level. Licensed operators must be at the controls at all times (50.54(k)), and a person who directs another to manipulate the controls counts as manipulating them.

In July 2026, INL, UIUC and Purdue used a reinforcement-learning digital twin to remotely and autonomously move an auxiliary control rod on the low-power PUR-1 research reactor. This was an expert-supervised experiment with the reactor's own safety systems keeping the final say. It was not a general AI agent running a commercial power reactor.

Researchers describe the work as an early step toward letting AI eventually assist in reactor operation, which means autonomous control of commercial plant rods, flux and coolant temperature is not deployed in October 2026.

Under 10 CFR 50.54(k), an operator licensed under Part 55 must be present at the controls at all times while the facility operates. Under 50.54(i), only licensed operators may manipulate controls that affect reactivity or power.

Current AI tools for nuclear plants are decision-support and document assistants that inform plant staff, not systems with control authority. Examples are Argonne's PRO-AID for monitoring and diagnostics and Atomic Canyon's NIVA.

AI agents that suggest control-rod adjustments exist only as research prototypes (Texas A&M). Developers still have to solve sensor and controller latency, and the agents are not deployed in plant control loops.
AI tools for warehouses are sold as 'digital co-pilots' for supervisors. They flag exceptions and help troubleshoot, but they support human expertise rather than replace it.

AutoScheduler.AI's Warehouse Decision Agent answers voice questions from the floor about late shipments and labor decisions and gives recommendations, so it helps with analysis inside problem-solving that humans still lead.

O*NET lists collaboration with workers and managers alongside floor-based duties such as monitoring safety and reviewing work as it happens. These are in-person roles under job titles like Floor Supervisor and Warehouse Supervisor.

Dedicated computer-vision systems at the dock (e.g., Accella Dock Check) can count cases, read barcodes and flag pallet discrepancies before shipment. These are fixed-camera installations that sit on site, not something a general software agent can reach.
Vision AI can detect broken boards, leaning stacks and loaded vs. empty pallets, but only if cameras and models have been set up for that site. This covers a small part of what a supervisor checks.

Reviewing hand-labor work as it happens and once it is finished mostly means walking the site and checking stacking, cleanup, loading and safety in person. An agent with no body can only help by reviewing photos, scanner logs or WMS records the supervisor is able to share.

As of September 2026, SmartBOL's inbound module uses AI to classify and extract data from shipping documents and check each line against the purchase order. This covers the document side of checking loads against work orders.

Camera systems at dock doors count cases, read labels and compare them with expected order data. They need cameras installed on site, and staff still handle the flagged exceptions, so a software-only agent depends on that hardware or on a person doing the physical inspection.

PackageX says it matches 95% of blind receipts and sends low-confidence items to a person for review. These figures come from the vendor, which supports rating this as partial rather than full delegation.

A patented load-confirmation tool runs the final load manifest accuracy check electronically, a check once done by hand. It starts when loading staff send a 'load complete' notification, so a human still triggers it from the floor.
Dock management systems spot deviations such as delays, documentation problems or busy docks and raise them as automatic alerts, so people only handle the exceptions.

In Infor WMS receiving, the system creates expected-load records and staff note discrepancies at the dock; EDI and RF devices remove most of the paper. Problems are still found physically and entered by people.

Load-planning software (e.g., SAP TM, ORTEC, Cargo-Planner) calculates load arrangement and sequence from freight dimensions, weights, and stop order. It applies LIFO, stackability, fragility, and axle-weight rules and produces 3D load plans, so the sequencing part of the task can be automated end to end.

Load-planning tools need structured inputs such as pallet and carton sizes, weights, and handling rules. A supervisor physically checking freight at the dock still supplies or verifies these inputs, including the condition, fragility, and actual dimensions of the freight.

Carrier and FMCSA guidance treats safe loading as something checked on site through physical inspection or supervised loading. No law or license requires a human to sign the sequencing decision itself.

Project44's AI Freight Procurement Agent, part of its Intelligent TMS, compares carriers on cost, transit time and reliability. Depending on configurable rules, it either recommends an award or makes it, and customers can start in recommendation-only mode.
Agentic TMS platforms re-plan continuously and handle routine dispatch and allocation decisions automatically, but material decisions still go to a human for approval.

In 2026, most freight workflows run in copilot mode, where a human approves quotes above a threshold. AI is used for mode selection and load consolidation, but there is little sign of fully autonomous mode selection in production.

AutoScheduler.AI says its decision agents automate warehouse task sequencing, labor scheduling and dock management, and reorder tasks when trucks are late. It adds these agents to an existing WMS rather than replacing it. These are vendor claims.

A trade article says agents need WMS, TMS and ERP data to be connected to see the full picture. The supervisor normally works in these systems, so an agent can reach the same orders, schedules and shipping notices.

A 2026 post from Opendock, itself a vendor, says agentic dock and yard scheduling can reprioritize doors and trucks, but door assignments and exceptions still need human judgment. That supports a human review step before the plan is used.

Vendor guides describe AI agents that check every timesheet entry against dispatch records and job codes, flag overtime anomalies, cross-check GPS data, and send only the exceptions to a person for a decision. That covers the main record-keeping and verification steps, but a human still reviews the flagged exceptions and approves the result.

Agentic reconciliation tools compare time logs with badge or access data, schedules, project plans and budgets, and send suspect entries to managers. This automates checking time and expense records against each other.

For driver hours-of-service records (ELD), the driver certifies each 24-hour record and the driver and carrier share responsibility for accuracy. I found no rule requiring a supervisor to personally sign these records, so the legal barrier to delegation is low. Some records still depend on human attestation, and physically checking materials or observing crews on site stays with people.

OSHA's forklift training rule (1910.178(l)) has three parts: formal instruction, practical training (demonstrations by the trainer and exercises by the trainee), and an evaluation of the operator's performance in the workplace. A person with hands-on knowledge, training and experience must do the training and evaluation, and the records name that trainer or evaluator.

Under the standard, operators must run the equipment while someone watches and evaluates them before they count as trained. The first evaluation should be done in a safe area under close supervision, so the hands-on demonstration needs a person on site.

VR forklift simulators from Raymond and Jungheinrich provide graded training levels and progress reports for instructors. These tools support digital parts of the job, such as tracking progress, choosing training tasks and preparing materials, but a human still demonstrates on real equipment.

EMS inventory software can track par levels and usage for each vehicle, raise restock alerts and send digital orders to suppliers. That covers the planning and ordering side, but not putting supplies on the ambulance.
ESO's inventory tools use min/max par levels and usage data to decide what to reorder. Restocking the truck itself is still done by crew members by hand.
AngelTrack's supply-room software tracks stock moving between stations and checks that each ambulance is stocked before it leaves. People still have to load the vehicle.

Vendor material (not independently verified) describes predictive ETA tools that use GPS, hours-of-service and traffic data to flag loads that may be late. The vendor says these delay alerts go to dispatchers and customers automatically by email, SMS or EDI, so the routine delay-reporting part of the task can already be automated.

Telematics crash detection can send real-time crash alerts to fleets and pass data to emergency services. Still, in serious crashes a human often has to call and give details, and judging the scene, such as injuries or hazards, depends on the driver being there.

FMCSA rules allow commercial drivers to use hands-free phones and one-touch dialing. Push-to-talk phones that must be held are banned while driving, but CB and two-way radios are not covered. This supports voice-assistant relaying and does not create a requirement that a human perform the report.

Econolite's Centracs MMS is a maintenance module that runs alone or with the Centracs ATMS. It supports user-defined preventive maintenance plans and schedules, mobile reporting of work activities, and a map of active work orders, so writing the work order is already a software task.

Trimble AgileAssets Signal/ITS has configurable workflows for work requests and creates work orders. It turns annual plans and problem reports into actual work orders, which shows the main sub-steps can be automated without anyone on site.

OxMaint says its product connects to traffic management systems and controller cabinet data feeds and opens priority work orders when a controller faults. This is an unverified vendor claim. It still means the remaining human work is mostly judging site conditions and approving changes to signal timing or devices, not writing the order.

Agency job descriptions say supervisors watch field work, train staff in MUTCD/ATSSA rules and inspect crews installing signs, signals, barricades and markings. This happens in person at the work site.

An AI assistant based on the MUTCD answers questions about where to place signs and flaggers and about temporary speed limits. It can help a supervisor with guidance, but it cannot direct crews on its own.

A research project (NCHRP IDEA 264) is building inspection software that uses vision-language models on dashcam video to check work-zone traffic control. It is still at the research stage, which points to partial help with inspection rather than full supervision.

Current AI tools such as Chalkie, Brisk and LessonCrafts generate slide decks, differentiated worksheets, flashcards and handouts from a topic, with export to Docs, Slides or PDF. So the digital part of preparing materials can be delegated end to end, though the instructor still checks it.

AI worksheet generators take a topic or pasted text and produce worksheets that can be printed or exported as PDFs. The agent cannot do the physical work of printing, gathering supplies, or arranging the room and equipment for hands-on classes like art, cooking, dance or music.

Several vendors offer lesson-material generators that export to PDF, Docs or Slides. No licence or sign-off is needed to prepare non-credit enrichment class materials, but setting up the classroom still needs someone there in person.

Machines that paint nails automatically do exist, such as Clockwork's MiNiCURE. They use 3D cameras and AI to steer a robotic nozzle, so the job needs dedicated robotic hardware. The reference AI agents have no body or robotics, so they cannot do this.
Clockwork's robot paints nails in about 10 minutes but is only in a few locations and does not cut or shape nails. Painting nails is a physical manipulation task.
Most US states require a cosmetology board license to do nails professionally. That means school hours plus written and practical exams, for example 300 hours in New Hampshire and South Carolina.
Perfect Corp's YouCam AI/AR nail tools let users and retailers virtually try on nail colors, styles, shapes and press-ons in real time, which covers product and color advice in software.

State manicurist licenses (e.g. Texas TDLR) cover hands-on nail services such as trimming, polishing and attaching false nails. They do not require a licensed human to give general nail care or product advice.

Boards such as California's keep conditions like calluses outside the manicurist's scope. Advice therefore depends on looking at the client's hands or feet, which usually happens in person during the service.

Nail robots such as Nimble and Clockwork only apply liquid polish using cameras and a nozzle. None of them gives a full salon manicure with shaping or buffing, and none works with powdered polish and a buffer. They are robots in any case, which the reference AI agent is not.
Clockwork's robot paints nails with 3D cameras and AI in about 10 minutes. It is limited to polish cartridges, so it still needs physical hardware and cannot buff with powdered polish.
US state cosmetology boards generally require a license, with training hours and practical exams, to perform manicure services on clients.

Stone chip repair is hands-on work: cleaning the surface, mixing and tinting polyester mastic with catalyst (100:2–3), applying it with a knife and polishing it. A digital-only agent can't do any of these steps.

A repair guide says to warm the stone with a small propane torch and work filler in while the surface is hot, then remove the excess with a razor blade. Handling the torch and judging the result by eye are both manual.

Chipped-marble repair means taping off the area, cleaning it with acetone and bonding with epoxy or marble cement. AI can only help with information such as product choice or color matching, which is a small share of the time.

An OSHA interpretation letter describes the work: a crane lifts monuments of about 100 to 1,700 lb from the delivery truck bed onto a pre-installed foundation or a heavy-duty cart. It is hands-on rigging and equipment operation at the grave site, which a software-only agent cannot do.

OSHA's crane rules (29 CFR 1926.1427) require operators of larger cranes to be certified through written and practical tests, and some states add stricter licensing. A qualified human has to run the hoist or crane.

Truck crane operation requires a practical test showing safe hands-on operation. Small cranes rated at about 2,000 lb or less are exempt from certification, but someone still has to operate them physically.

Hobart's automatic wrapping system has a built-in scale and label applier; it weighs, wraps, computes the price and labels up to 30 packages per minute. It is a physical machine, not a software agent.
Mettler Toledo sells weigh-price labelers and the 880 Auto Wrapper for fresh meat in back rooms. The pricing and labelling are automated in hardware, but a person still handles the product.
Digi's AW-5600ATII and LI-700 II weigh, wrap and label meat automatically. The only parts software can reach are the label and price data settings.

Vendor 'Executive Recruiter Agent' products research senior candidates and deliver market analysis and curated shortlists, leaving relationship-building and negotiation to humans. This is a vendor claim, not independent evidence.
Executive search practice uses AI for sourcing speed but keeps selection and judgment human, and hiring outcomes depend on human oversight and governance.

Under Delaware DGCL §142, officers are chosen as the bylaws or the board determine. Appointment authority is a corporate act vested in accountable humans, not something that can be handed to an agent.

Lattice's agent (2026) drafts performance reviews from months of performance data that is already in the system. By design, it never picks a rating and never submits a review on its own, so the manager stays accountable.

Lattice MCP, released July 2026, lets managers draft, edit and submit reviews from inside Claude, ChatGPT or Slack. An agent can reach the performance data and handle the drafting sub-steps from start to finish.
The EU AI Act treats AI used for promotion or termination decisions as high-risk and requires qualified human oversight. Compliance may be delayed to December 2027, but the classification stays.

This is vendor marketing, not independent evidence. ChatFin says its FP&A agents watch general-ledger actuals against the budget and flag variances. It also says they trace each variance down to the transaction and write first-draft commentary and monthly business review decks.

This is vendor marketing, not independent evidence. The source says agents refresh rolling forecasts and automate much of the data gathering and analysis in FP&A. It does not say they replace human judgement on strategic development opportunities.

Another vendor, Tellius, sells agentic AI for finance that does automated root-cause and trend analysis on financial data. This supports L2-level delegation of the analysis sub-steps, though a human still prioritises the strategic opportunities.

Vendors such as Board, Prophix and Lucanet released FP&A, controller and treasury AI agents in 2026. These agents keep rolling forecasts and scenario plans up to date and build models from prompts. Human-in-the-loop controls on significant decisions are still the norm.

Directors' and officers' duty of care, which includes acting on an informed basis, means AI is unlikely to replace human judgment on financial decisions. Courts may expect fiduciaries to test AI outputs against their own judgment.
Practitioner guidance says AI can produce forecasts, spot trends and suggest actions, but should not have the final say on financial recommendations to leadership.

Claude in PowerPoint launched in February 2026 and reached Pro plans on February 20, 2026. It can build slides and make targeted edits to existing decks, so an agent can produce the presentation materials itself.
Claude Cowork can read a folder of files, plan a multi-step task and produce a finished .pptx. That lets an agent turn analysis files into a proposal deck end to end.

Vendors sell AI agents that write logistics proposals from templates and client data, though these are marketing claims rather than independent case studies. Delivering the proposal orally, answering questions and persuading stakeholders is still done by people.

Sanoma in Finland uses GPT-4o to write local forecasts for 26 regions from Finnish Meteorological Institute data, and a synthetic voice reads them on radio. Separately, a former US TV meteorologist runs AI avatars that produce 27 forecasts a day across nine markets.

The Weather Company's ReelSphere makes near real-time weather video clips for broadcast and social media, with an AI voice or a meteorologist's voice. Humans still write the scripts and correct errors.

The National Weather Service uses AI to translate its warnings and forecasts, which cut translation time from 1 hour to under 10 minutes. Forecasters still review the translations before release, and official warnings remain the responsibility of human forecasters.

Aircraft whole-air samplers such as NOAA's PFP and the Medusa sampler on ATom fill flasks automatically on a preprogrammed schedule, so software can trigger and log samples. Installing the hardware, handling the flasks and running the flight operations still has to be done in person.

NCAR's Advanced Whole Air Sampler (AWAS) is a certified instrument installed on the HIAPER aircraft. It collects samples into stainless steel canisters that are taken off the plane and analyzed later, which requires physical installation, retrieval and transport.

In UC Irvine's proposed SEAC4RS whole-air sampling on the NASA DC-8, scientists on board would collect up to 168 canister samples per flight. Researchers on the aircraft do the sampling, while an AI agent's help would be limited to planning, the sampling schedule and data logging.

A developer reports that Claude Code, running an agent interface for MODFLOW 6, built a groundwater model on its own: data import, grid, boundary conditions, wells, model runs and result checks. Human judgment is still needed for assumptions and for checking that results make sense. This is a vendor claim, the tool is in private beta, and the claim is not independently checked.
The AQUAH hydrology agent can run cold-start simulations and write documentation without manual steps, but its authors say calibration and validation are still needed before operational use.
In Washington State, a licensed geologist or hydrogeologist must stamp or seal, sign and date every final hydrogeologic report. Other states have similar rules.

AI scribes for therapy record the session, draft progress notes in formats such as SOAP, and place them in the EHR. Vendors also say clinicians must review, edit and approve each note before it is submitted.

Under California law, failing to keep records consistent with sound clinical judgment and professional standards is unprofessional conduct. This makes the licensed therapist responsible for the record.
Ontario's regulator requires every clinical record entry to show who made it and when, so the professional stays accountable for its contents.

Legal-aid chatbots such as Lone Star Legal Aid's Navi and Legal Aid of North Carolina's LIA already give people information, referrals and possible next steps around the clock. This shows an AI can handle the research-and-referral part of the task.

Illinois's WOPR Act (HB 1806, 2025) bars AI from directly interacting with therapy clients or making therapeutic decisions without review by a licensed clinician. Nevada has a similar restriction, so a licensed therapist has to review and deliver anything client-facing.

Under the same law, licensed professionals may still use AI for administrative and supplementary support with the client's written consent. Drafting a resource list for the therapist to review fits that, and the task needs no physical presence.
Commercial AI tools such as Krea's Sketch to Concept Design turn rough sketches and text prompts into several clean, presentation-ready concept design variations.
Pencil is a commercial AI tool for 3D jewelry design, sold by subscription and used by brands for customer customization. AI can generate the design drawings for a craft object.

A 2025 study tested an AI image-generation tool for ceramic-craft design and found clearer design communication and better feedback. The students and instructors still made the design decisions, which suggests partial rather than full delegation.

Museum guidance says objects chosen for an exhibit must be surveyed in person for condition and display vulnerability. The designer, conservator and curator then work together on display methods, so the hands-on examination is a step a human has to do.

Each object's condition assessment sets its display requirements, including light, humidity and case protection. If an agent is given the condition reports, photos and dimensions, it can turn them into a placement and mounting plan.

Using AI to plan museum layouts is still mostly at the research-prototype stage, such as generated floor plans for exhibition halls. A digital agent can still draft layout options and display plans from digitised object data.

2026 research systems use LLMs to compare source and translation, mark span-level MQM errors and post-edit them. Their error annotations agree strongly with human MQM judgments, so the agent can run the check of the original against the translation end to end.

A large production study (EAMT 2026) of AI post-editing across 10 languages still relied on 60 professional translators to judge quality. Human review is still used to confirm meaning and tone before the work is used.
ISO 17100 requires a second person to revise translations. This is a voluntary quality standard, not a legal licence, but it keeps a human reviser in the workflow under common industry practice.
Aftershoot automatically finds duplicates, blurry shots, closed eyes and other technical flaws. It then picks the best image from each group of similar shots, and the user can set how strict it is.

Narrative Select groups similar shots into scenes and ranks them by focus and whether eyes are open, but the photographer still makes the final rating and selection. FilterPixel can aim for a target number of final images.

Imagen's culling tool groups similar images so the photographer can choose the best one. In practice the human still reviews the AI's picks for artistic quality and fit with the client before delivery.

OT aides work under close supervision of a licensed OT or OTA. They only do delegated routine tasks: helping patients carry out the regimens the therapist sets, moving patients to and from the treatment area, and setting up, cleaning and storing equipment.
O*NET describes the occupation as hands-on patient support and equipment preparation inside therapy programs that a therapist directs.

2026 AI tools draft OT treatment plans, SOAP notes and home exercise programs, but their own marketing says the output is only a starting point that the clinician must review and edit. That helps with the planning paperwork, not with delivering in-person therapy.

Correction sergeant job specs say the role enforces rules on security, conduct, discipline and safety in person. That means supervising inmates at meals, recreation and in cells, searching for contraband and taking direct charge of disturbances, which needs a physical presence and command authority.

Policy-management platforms such as Lexipol supply legally vetted corrections policies and track acknowledgments, training and compliance reporting. This supports the 'maintain knowledge' part (looking up policies, summaries, updates), but I found no confirmed AI agent that enforces policy.
Sergeants investigate and report rule infractions to superior officers and may take command of the facility. These are sworn, accountable supervisory acts that a human must perform.

Job descriptions for correctional sergeants say they directly supervise officers, do rounds, check logbooks, run head counts and shakedowns, and respond to emergencies, including using force and chemical agents. All of this happens on site in the facility.

A Michigan sergeant position description puts about 40% of the job into directing custody and housing officers, including checking work-area rounds and logbooks. Virginia's class description defines the sergeant as the first-line supervisor of officers who also reviews logs and reports and evaluates staff.

Industry and county reports from 2026 describe AI in jails as a support tool for scheduling, movement tracking, documentation and monitoring alerts, freeing staff for direct supervision rather than replacing it.

Under prison use-of-force policies, the on-site supervisor approves planned force and decides what type and how much. Staff physically apply restraints and chemical agents, and the use is recorded on video.

In North Carolina, chemical agents may only be used with authorization from the facility head or a designee. They are handled by trained chemical officers who are sergeants or above, so a human with that rank has to authorize and carry out the use.
Prison AI tools such as Leo Technologies' Verus Vision AI only analyze video feeds and alert staff to incidents. They do not restrain or control anyone.

In policing, AI tools such as Truleo and Polis turn body-worn-camera audio into text and flag unprofessional language or interactions. A preliminary randomized trial found that AI-led auditing changed officer conduct. This covers one sub-step: reviewing recorded footage.

Correctional sergeants supervise their officers in person. They make rounds of housing units, inspect units to confirm officers are doing their duties, and monitor staff morale. These rounds are logged and required at least once per shift.

Agency post orders require the area supervisor to make rounds and log them in person. The facility's chain of command holds the supervisor accountable for staff conduct and for any discipline that follows.
Correctional sergeants run roll call at the start of each shift. They check who is present, assign officers to posts, and inspect their appearance, equipment and any contraband in person.
Philadelphia's job spec says the sergeant inspects guards for appearance, equipment and contraband, which has to be done physically.

Corrections scheduling software such as UKG TeleStaff already handles post rosters, staffing levels and attendance tracking. That covers the clerical parts of roll call, but the in-person muster, inspection and briefing still need a human.
Inmate transport means putting restraints on prisoners, counting heads before departure and on arrival, and keeping them in sight for the whole escort. These are physical, in-person duties.
Agency policy requires two trained, weapons-qualified detention deputies on transports. Using only one deputy needs a supervisor's approval, so sworn humans are required by rule.
Software only helps with the surrounding steps, such as scheduling transports, checking the routing and doing paperwork. Making the actual transfer or driving the vehicle cannot be automated.

School nutrition inventory tools such as PrimeroEdge with IntelliScan, Nutrikids and Meals Plus already track product usage, purchases, variance and costs. Staff still scan receipts and count stock physically using UPC codes.

Invoice-scanning tools such as ShelfCount capture receipt data automatically and hold price changes for approval before records are updated. This automates the expenditure side of record-keeping, but a human still checks it.

Institutional foodservice suites such as CBORD handle cafeteria inventory, purchasing and cost records. Once usage and invoice data are entered, an agent with system access could compile and maintain them.

Food-service costing platforms such as Galley work out the cost per portion and the food-cost percentage of a recipe from its ingredient prices. When a supplier price changes, they recalculate the plate cost automatically and flag dishes that have fallen below the target margin.

Some restaurant systems read invoices to update ingredient prices and quantities automatically, and they save unit conversions such as cases to pounds. This covers the main data-entry and calculation steps with no physical presence needed.

Some recipe-costing apps suggest menu prices based on target food-cost percentages. The final price still depends on institutional policy, such as subsidies and fixed cafeteria or school price rules, so a manager typically reviews and approves it.

O*NET lists directing kitchen operations, including the presentation and serving of food, as a task of private household cooks. Their main tasks are cooking, shopping and serving meals to the family and guests in the home.

The work involves standing for long periods, working at hot stoves, cleaning work areas, knife skills and hand-eye coordination. Similar cook postings add plating, garnishing and portion control, so the role depends on hands-on work in the kitchen.

AI kitchen tools such as Chefpilot, AIKA and KitchenCommand handle inventory, recipe generation, meal planning, scaling and shopping lists. These are planning and admin steps that an agent can speed up, but none of these tools runs the physical kitchen or serves food.

Hospital cleaning platforms such as MyCleaning, HealthClean and SmartView already handle the digital parts of the work: logging and prioritising cleaning requests, dispatching staff, verifying finished cleans and flagging hygiene risks. An agent could run these coordination steps.

In a 2026 trial, a computer-vision AI checked cleaning staff on-site against a nine-step procedure. This shows that checking how cleaning is done depends on physical, on-site observation, not on a software-only agent.

EVS supervisor duties include disinfecting contaminated areas, taking surface samples, setting cleaning methods and choosing disinfectants, and coaching staff on how infections spread. CMS assigns overall responsibility for the infection control program to the facility and its infection preventionists. It does not require the EVS supervisor personally to perform or sign this task.

AI tools such as Taskade, Creately, Guidde and Process Street already produce housekeeping and room-cleaning SOPs, checklists and workflows, and can add approvals and task assignment. An agent can therefore draft the standards and procedures from start to finish.

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1200 requires the employer to keep a written hazard communication program covering labels, SDSs, a chemical inventory and training. An agent can draft it, but the employer is responsible for it, and on-site checks of the chemical inventory are needed.

OSHA guidance tells employers to name a coordinator who assigns staff to tasks such as training. Putting procedures into practice means in-person training, inspection and enforcement with cleaning crews, which a human supervisor still has to do.

Vendor material describes AI agents in maintenance software that rank the work backlog, schedule work, create purchase requisitions and choose a vendor by lead time and cost. The requisition still goes to a human for approval. These are marketing claims and have not been checked independently.

Vendor management software for property maintenance teams handles contractor scheduling and work-order dispatch digitally. This covers the 'arrange' part of the task. This is a vendor product page, not an independent evaluation.

Not shown by either source above (inference): the recommendation part depends on someone physically inspecting worn furnishings, damage and paint condition on site, plus local judgment on budget. Spending approval normally stays with a human manager. No licence or legal requirement applies to the supervisor's recommendation.

Velosi's housekeeping software covers supervisor inspection workflows, reporting of maintenance defects, and inventory of linen and amenities. These are digital supervisory sub-steps that software can run end to end.

OXmaint's AI takes work orders from the front desk, housekeeping, the guest app, IoT sensors and scheduled preventive maintenance, then classifies and prioritises them automatically. That covers the coordination side of supervising maintenance and repair.

AI scheduling tools assign and sequence staff using occupancy, check-out patterns and staff availability. The in-person parts of supervising laundry, valet and repair staff stay with the human: directing people on site, physical quality checks and handling problems. These figures come from vendor marketing and are not verified.
Housekeeping apps send each room status change to the property management system (PMS) in real time, so the front desk can see which rooms are ready without phoning a supervisor.
Housekeeping software can mark a room as ready automatically once it passes inspection, so no one has to re-enter the status in a second system. That covers most of the communication step.

Maestro PMS automatically texts guests when their room is ready, as soon as the front office receives the new status from housekeeping. A person still has to inspect the room and enter that status, and that step needs someone on site.
Smart restroom systems such as Gojo Onvation only monitor dispenser levels and traffic. They send alerts and track response times, and a human attendant still has to service the restroom.

CMMS software such as OxMaint creates cleaning work orders when usage passes a set threshold and sends them to the nearest attendant. This automates scheduling only, not the cleaning or restocking itself.
Patents for washroom maintenance systems describe sensors that report usage data to staff, who then do the physical maintenance.

OSHA training material for housekeeping staff covers handling, diluting, storing and spilling cleaning chemicals, and wearing protective gear. These are hands-on steps a worker does on site. An AI agent can only help by looking up labels and safety data sheets or explaining the steps.

Some robot scrubbers and dispensing systems already measure and mix cleaning chemicals automatically. That is robot hardware, though, not a software-only AI agent, which is the technology being rated here.

OSHA's 1991 guidance letter applies its hazard communication rule to janitorial work. The rule puts the duty to train on the employer and does not require a licensed person to sign off on routine use of cleaning chemicals.

Stripping and refinishing a floor is hands-on work. A worker applies stripper, removes the old finish with a floor machine, a razor scraper and pads, picks up the slurry with a wet/dry vacuum, neutral-mops and puts down several coats of finish. A software-only agent can do none of these steps; at most it could look up procedures or chemical dilutions.

Even the floor machines themselves have limits here. Autoscrubbers cannot reach edges, corners or alcoves, so those areas need manual work. Stripping solution should also not be run through a scrubber's solution dispensing system.

A university custodial procedure has crews dust-mop and neutral-mop after stripping, then apply two finish layers with drying time between them. All of it is physical, on-site labour over several hours.
Venue software such as Tripleseat Floorplans can draw room layouts and count tables, chairs and linens. That covers only the small planning part of the job; it does not physically set anything up.
Planur can count tables, chairs and linens automatically and share the layout with the crew, but people still have to carry out the setup by hand.
The main work is physical: moving and arranging tables, chairs, decorations, ladders and scaffolding. The reference agents have no body or robotics, so they can't do this part.

Search results only covered robot vacuums, which have height-clearance limits (bodies about 97mm tall) and get stuck under furniture. None addressed dusting furniture, walls or machines, which takes hand and arm work. The rated agent has no body at all, so dusting has to be done in person.

Floor robots skip areas behind thresholds or furniture over about 2cm high and avoid narrow gaps. This shows that even physical cleaning robots can't do above-floor dusting, and a software-only agent can't do any of it.

An industry report says furniture specifications prevent robots from reaching 100% floor coverage, and that loose fibres and cables tangle them. This confirms the task depends on physical work. No law or licence requires a human to do the dusting.
O*NET lists 'Move heavy furniture, equipment, or supplies, either manually or with hand trucks' as a core task for Janitors and Cleaners (37-2011.00). The work is all physical lifting and pushing.

Janitorial job postings include moving furniture and handling heavy loads. That takes a person on site, which a software-only AI agent without robotics can't provide. At most it could help plan the move or schedule it.
Janitors spend most of their time on their feet and sometimes lift or push heavy furniture or equipment. I found no licence or legal sign-off rule for this task.

Chimney sweeping is hands-on work. CSIA certification covers chimney construction, NFPA 211 and cleaning technique, all done on site with brushes and tools. A software agent with no robotics cannot do any of it.
Sweeps generally do not need certification. It is recommended but optional, so the law does not require a human to perform or sign off on routine cleaning.
O*NET lists a Certified Chimney Sweep credential (exam plus renewal every 3 years). It is a voluntary professional credential, not a legal licence for cleaning.

To dust blinds you physically tilt the slats, vacuum them with a brush attachment from top to bottom, and wipe both sides with a microfiber cloth. That is hands-on work an agent with no body cannot do.
Hanging window coverings means measuring, marking bracket spots, drilling pilot holes and fastening hardware on site. All of it is physical manipulation.
Before taking draperies down you have to free hooks and rod hardware from the fabric, and you shake them out before washing. The only part software could help with is looking up care instructions.

Polishing silver is hands-on work. You apply polish with a cloth using small circular motions, use a toothbrush or cotton swab for tight spots, then wipe and dry the piece by hand. A software agent with no robotics can't do any of this.

Housekeeping guides describe silver care as a physical, in-person process (prep, clean, polish, buff). The only part an AI could help with is advice on the method, such as which polish to use or whether to avoid dips, and that is a tiny share of the time spent.

Cvent Event Diagramming (formerly Social Tables) has an AI assistant that builds room layouts from text prompts and can import event details from uploaded event orders (BEOs). This covers the planning step, but the room setup itself is still done by hand.

EventDiagram makes to-scale floor plans, seating charts and 3D views for hotels and venues, and shares them for approval. It produces a plan only: staff still have to move the furniture, set up the AV equipment and put up the decorations.

ChatDiagram generates scaled 2D event floor plans from a text description. This could speed up the layout sub-step for housekeeping staff, but most of the working time goes to physically arranging the room, which a software-only agent cannot do.
Housekeeper job postings list moving and arranging furniture and turning or flipping mattresses as duties. These need someone physically present to lift and carry objects up to 40–50 lbs.
Postings require the worker to move dressers and flip mattresses without help, and to bend, squat, kneel and twist continuously. A software-only agent cannot do any of this.
Some employers send furniture moves to maintenance staff, so this is purely physical labor. No licence or sign-off is involved.

The task consists of hands-on work with hand tools and power equipment: string trimmers where mowers can't reach, aerating, dethatching, removing debris and spreading mulch. A software-only agent cannot do any of this physically.

The robotic mowers with edge-trimming arms shown in 2026 (Anthbot R7, Eufy S2 Max, Segway Navimow) are robots, which the reference technology excludes. Reviewers also say edge trimming is still largely unsolved for robot mowers.
O*NET describes this as routine field labor that also includes sod laying, mowing, digging and raking. None of these tasks needs a licence or a human sign-off; the barrier is purely physical.

Lawn care software can calculate application rates, spray mixes and treatment schedules, and can identify pests from photos. This covers only the planning sub-steps. Mixing chemicals and spraying or spreading them on site is physical work that a software-only agent cannot do.
Remote AI measurement of a property can supply the square footage used to work out fertilizer and herbicide quantities and application rates.
Anyone applying pesticides for pay on another person's property must hold a state commercial pesticide applicator license, earned by passing a core exam and a category exam such as lawn care.

Current AI landscape tools mostly produce designs and visualizations: planting schemes, layouts and plant suggestions based on site data. They help a worker read and understand a plan but do nothing on the ground.

Consumer AI landscaping apps are mainly photo-based idea generators or planners that set placement on screen. None of the material found describes an agent that marks or stakes out real planting locations on site.

AI tools aimed at landscape architects generate planting and grading proposals, which covers the design step the task starts from. Carrying out that design on the ground still takes a person working on site.

Machines that plant automatically (Milrem's planter robot, the Continental/Land Life seeding robot) are robotics for reforestation fields. A software-only AI agent cannot run them, and they do not do landscape planting or mulching.
Planting robots that can dig holes, plant saplings and cover the soil are still mostly research prototypes. This shows the task is physical manipulation work.

Autonomous tree planting depends on robots with LiDAR and GPS working on site, which confirms the core work needs a physical body. A software agent could only help with small side steps like looking up planting guidance or scheduling.

Smart controllers such as Rachio can be put into standby and have their schedules switched off from an app. A contractor can also be given limited access to run zones remotely during a blowout. This means software can handle only the controller and scheduling parts of winterizing and spring start-up.

Winterizing means physical work on site: closing the backflow preventer's ball valves, connecting an air compressor downstream of the device and blowing out the lines. The utility recommends a qualified licensed contractor for the blowout method.
The local plumbing code requires a certified tester to test the backflow preventer each season when it is reinstalled at spring start-up.

Making a poured concrete border is hands-on work done on site: digging and compacting the trench, driving stakes, fastening hardboard or plywood forms, mixing and pouring concrete, troweling, cutting control joints, sealing and stripping the forms.
The manufacturer's method is also physical: compacted gravel base, forms with spacers, bagged crack-resistant mix poured and finished in place, with no software-run step an AI could do.

The only automation is mechanical curbing machines that push concrete through a mold. A person still has to steer them and control their speed and material flow, so there is no software or AI substitute. An agent could at most help with planning or working out how much concrete is needed.

In airline and union checklists, preparing for landing means physical walkthroughs. Flight attendants check that passengers are seated with belts fastened and that seatbacks and tray tables are up. They also latch bins and closets, check lavatories, and stow galley and service items. An agent with no body cannot do any of this.

Part 121 rules give these duties to certificated flight attendants. They must secure the cabin and galley for landing, then stay belted in their assigned jumpseats from landing until the aircraft parks at the gate. A human crewmember is legally accountable for this.

The only part that is automated so far is announcements. A patent describes pre-recorded announcements triggered by flight phase, and Pegasus uses AI-synthesised voices for some languages. Crew still make the main announcements and do all physical cabin checks.

Pre-recorded announcements are stored on the Flight Attendant Panel (FAP), and newer units can be loaded from USB sticks. Crew can power down a misbehaving IFE at the flight attendant panel or cabin management terminal, which means using onboard hardware in person.
When IFE malfunctions, crew reset the system at the individual seat or, on older aircraft, for whole blocks of seats. PA announcements pause or override IFE.

The system already automates some of this: it can store and replay standard safety, boarding and arrival messages in several languages at the touch of a button. Regulations require a working interphone/PA system on commercial transport aircraft.

AI recruiting agents available in 2026 handle sourcing, screening, outreach and scheduling end to end. Adoption is still partial: Bullhorn found 30% of firms using some agentic AI, and guides recommend that a human sign off on final hiring decisions.

NYC Local Law 144 requires annual independent bias audits and candidate notices for automated employment decision tools. The EU AI Act classes employment AI as high-risk, with risk-management, transparency and documentation duties, which keeps a human accountable for hiring and evaluation decisions.

Sources warn that automated screening with no human review before the offer stage is where bias and compliance risk concentrate. They recommend human sign-off and audit logs, so final hiring and evaluation judgments stay with the supervisor.

Agent templates for sales engineers already analyze client usage patterns and technical requirements, find upsell opportunities and produce tailored presentations on the ROI of recommended solutions. These are the main drafting and analysis sub-steps of this task.

Sales engineer roles involve regular customer site visits to learn about installed equipment and operating conditions, and to recommend equipment that improves productivity and profitability. That on-site understanding and persuasion is the input an agent cannot gather by itself.
