A case study of a sales proposal agent reports that the time humans spent editing technical proposal drafts outweighed the time saved, so humans still had to review the work before use.
Seismic's Aura Role-play Agent acts out live buyer scenarios, scores how reps perform, and gives coaching feedback on the spot. Its presentation agent puts together branded decks automatically.
Letter.ai says it builds interactive training modules in minutes and tailors coaching to the company's own products, customers and frameworks.

SalesHood's AI role-play builds simulations for sellers, sales engineers and customer success managers, including discovery and demo practice. Expert human judgment on how customers actually apply the technology still has to check the content and the coaching.

Vendor sources (self-reported marketing, not independently checked) say AI recruiting agents handle sourcing, screening, outreach and interview scheduling with little human input. They describe only preliminary AI-run assessments, not complete interviews or final hiring decisions done end to end.

The EU AI Act classes AI used in recruitment as high-risk. Employers must keep monitoring it and must have humans able to spot and correct errors, including discriminatory patterns, so a human has to stay in the loop on selection. According to a secondary source, these obligations may be postponed from 2 August 2026 to December 2027.
Commentary on the Act says that under Article 14 a policy document alone does not count as human oversight. Real people must be able to detect and correct errors.

Agentic procurement platforms advertised for 2025–2026 claim to create requisitions, turn them into purchase orders, source vendors and buy low-risk, high-volume items on their own. These are vendor claims and have not been independently checked.
ServiceNow has announced autonomous procurement workflows that can run equipment and supply buying from start to finish inside enterprise systems.

Disposing of IT assets requires physical work: removing drives, keeping a chain of custody, and getting destruction certificates from certified vendors. An agent can arrange and document this, but people have to do the physical handling and check it on site. No law requires a supervisor to sign it personally.

USDA FNS lists New Mexico using robotic process automation to move client-portal data into the eligibility system, add case notes and create caseworker tasks. Code for America and Anthropic are building Claude-based tools for SNAP caseworkers that review documents and draft communications.

Code for America and Anthropic's SNAP Policy Navigator helps caseworkers look up policy, review eligibility documents and draft plain-language messages to recipients, with the caseworker still in the loop.

Under 7 CFR 272.4(a), SNAP certification work, including interviews and eligibility and benefit determinations, must be done by state merit-system staff. Nonmerit personnel cannot enter data into eligibility-affecting fields, so a human must review and own those records. The task needs no physical presence.

Sabre offers agentic APIs and an MCP translator. A vendor integration says AI agents can read live reservation and itinerary data in Sabre and handle booking changes, cancellations and rebookings across air, hotel and car travel.

Amadeus's 2026 report with Microsoft describes agentic AI working on airline transactions. In one trial, an airline AI agent found a booking, understood a change request, offered new options, explained the fare difference and started payment. This is reported as vendor-adjacent coverage.
Computer-use agents such as OpenAI Operator check availability and make reservations on their own through web interfaces. They hand control to a human for login, payment or CAPTCHA steps.

Self-service bag drop is kiosk and conveyor hardware: the passenger scans a boarding pass, prints and attaches the tag, and puts the bag on the belt. Bulky bags still go to staffed counters, so the core work is physical and is automated by machines, not by software agents.

Under 49 CFR 1544.203, checked baggage must be received by an authorized representative of the aircraft operator and handled under the TSA-approved security program. The rules also cover firearm declarations and refusing bags when the passenger will not consent to a search.

Kiosks can match bags to boarding passes, and LAX trialled self-service bag check with optional biometrics. Weighing, tagging and handling odd-size or cargo items, and directing passengers to loading points, still need people or physical machines on site.

Commercial software can turn flight data from an airport operational database (AODB) or other external systems into voice announcements. Vendors say it works with common PA systems such as Q-sys, Bosch and Honeywell, so routine arrival and departure announcements can run end to end without a person.

Text-to-speech is used for announcements at rail, metro and bus stations and at airport gates, and can be updated for schedule changes, delays and emergency alerts. Gate agents still make unscheduled live announcements that depend on what is happening at the gate, so a human stays involved there. The source is vendor marketing.

One search found no FAA or ADA rule saying a human must make PA boarding announcements. A DOT notice says carriers do not have to make a general preboarding announcement at the gate, and the Air Carrier Access Act deals with accessible information rather than who delivers it. The regulation text itself was not checked, so treat this as a likely finding.

SITA's WorldTracer Bag Mate is a managed service that runs the mishandled-baggage process from the passenger's report to the bag's return or compensation. It uses a hybrid of AI agents and SITA-trained human agents, so humans are still part of the process (vendor claim).
With WorldTracer Baggage Self-Service, passengers report and track delayed bags digitally. In Lufthansa Group trials, two-thirds of passengers chose it over the baggage counter.
Aeromexico's Aerobot chatbot pulls a missing bag's status from WorldTracer through its API without a human agent, so automated status lookup has been in use since 2019.

Julius AI is reported to choose suitable statistical methods (regression, clustering, ARIMA) on its own, write and run Python/R code in a sandbox, and explain the results. It also runs t-tests, chi-square, ANOVA and regression, though complex multi-stage custom analyses are beyond what it handles well.

An academic study found that ChatGPT's statistical test recommendations depend heavily on how the prompt is written. This means a human must still specify the study design and research question and check the choice.
A 2026 review of AI statistics tools warns that ChatGPT sometimes makes calculation errors on complex problems and that critical results need checking. This supports keeping a human review step.

Log scanners already detect defects and assign quality grades automatically, for example MiCROTEC Logeye (laser, color imaging and X-ray with deep-learning AI) and SMARTI iLog. These are fixed sawmill machines with their own sensors, not software agents that only reach digital systems. A human grader in a log yard or landing still has to look at the logs in person: knots, sweep, rot and end defects.

SMARTI's iLog X-ray scanner builds 3D models of logs, detects surface and internal defects, and sorts logs into quality grades. It shows that grading done by sensors depends on dedicated physical hardware.

Idaho law makes it unlawful to scale logs for commercial purposes without a license from the Board of Scaling Practices, or to work as an apprentice except under a licensed scaler. Getting a license requires passing written and practical exams.

Dedicated scanning hardware now does much of the data capture. LoadMon 3D truck scanners measure load volume, diameter and skew in under two minutes, and Woodtech LogMeter scales logs from photos of the log ends. Both need sensors at the mill or yard, not just a software agent.

Scalers type tally data into handheld computers or write it on tickets while standing at the logs, then send it to the main office. The data comes from in-person measurement, so recording it is tied to being on site.
In Idaho it is illegal to scale logs for commercial use unless you hold a licence or are an apprentice supervised by a licensed scaler, so a human scaler is accountable for the recorded scale.

Paint marks go on logs with handheld spray cans or with compressed-air sprayers mounted on processors. Either way, someone or something has to physically act on each log in the yard or on the line. A software-only agent can't do that.
When log marking is automated, it's done by sprayers built into harvesting or processing machinery. That's robotics and mill equipment, not an AI agent working through software.
Log scanners in mills, such as MiCROTEC Logeye, can grade logs. But they're fixed mill hardware, so they cover the grading decision, not the act of painting marks or calling out grades on site.

Commercial log-scanning and computer-vision products exist. LoadMon 3D-scans log trucks to get volume and diameter, and Roboflow measures log diameters and length and calculates Scribner, Doyle or International 1/4 volume. Both depend on cameras or scanners mounted at the site, so a software-only agent cannot take the measurements itself.
LoadMon scans log or bulk-wood trucks with more than 70 million points per scan and calculates volume, diameter and load skew in under 2 minutes. This hardware is installed at the site.
In Idaho it is illegal to scale logs for commercial use without a state licence, which requires written and practical exams, or without working as an apprentice under a licensed scaler.

Onboard harvester systems like Ponsse Opti and Log Max LogMate measure stems and optimize bucking in real time. They are machine control systems on physical harvesters, not software agents working without a body.

Waratah TimberRite handles real-time bucking optimization, stem measurement and production data logging on the harvesting machine itself. This shows that the measuring step depends on physical sensors at the log.

Skogforsk's 2025 wood value trial found that even automated harvester bucking loses value mainly through length and diameter measurement errors, so physical measurement at the stem is still the deciding step.

Camera-based and 3D log scanning systems for measuring logs and detecting defects exist, but they are still at the research or preliminary stage and need dedicated scanning hardware at the mill. Certified scalers are still used to check the results.
A USDA laser-scan system found 53 of 64 severe surface defects on hardwood logs and flagged 9 sound areas as defects. That is specialized hardware, not something a general software agent can operate.
In Idaho, anyone doing commercial log scaling must hold a license, which requires passing written and practical exams. Licensed scalers also face unannounced check scales.

Log-load measurement is being automated with fixed hardware such as Woodtech LogMeter's camera portals and LoadMon's 3D truck scanners at mill intake. These are sensors installed on site, not software agents, and they do not replace a person driving to sawmills, wharfs or skids to inspect logs.
Idaho law requires anyone scaling logs commercially to be licensed by the Board of Scaling Practices, and getting the licence means passing written and practical exams.
Idaho's Board of Scaling Practices requires a practical exam for the licence and a re-examination every two years at renewal.

Oregon logging rules require hand signals or audible contact when noise, distance or poor visibility make voice unclear. Operators must not move loads unless the signal is clear, and all workers must be clear before a signal to move a log.

Idaho rules say that if the loading machine operator does not have an unobstructed view, a signalman must be properly placed in the loading area and their signal followed. Signals are standard hand signals, whistles or similar.
BC safe work procedures say all landing workers must be in view or in the clear, or their whereabouts known, before logs or equipment are moved. This is a real-time, line-of-sight, on-site judgement.

Vendor material describes unattended truck-scale systems that use RFID cards, licence-plate readers and automated gates to identify vehicles and drivers and record weighments without an operator. This covers the sub-steps of capturing weights and supplier identities.

Weighbridge software connects to weight indicators, RFID readers, ANPR cameras and barriers, and keeps an audit trail. Once a vehicle is recognised, a weighment can start without anyone keying it in, so an agent could log and reconcile records through software. The truck still has to be physically on the scale, and exceptions need handling.

Several US states require a licensed public weighmaster or deputy to issue certified weight tickets. In Arizona, for example, nobody may act as a public weighmaster without a state licence, which keeps a human accountable for certified weights.

On harvester machines, the onboard computer decides where to cut using taper predictions and price lists ('bucking to value'). This runs as embedded machine control, not as a software agent, and an operator still has to be present.
Commercial bucking optimizers like Waratah TimberRite are onboard harvester control systems. They are tied to the physical machine.
In manual chainsaw bucking, the cutter makes the decisions out in the woods. The only digital help is simple tools like an Excel value matrix.

Construction firms already use AI assistants such as Skanska's Safety Sidekick, which combine company EHS manuals with OSHA construction standards to answer workers' safety questions. These tools help the worker; they do not do the learning or the compliance for the worker.

Research and commercial RAG chatbots, such as Turner's SafeT Coach and academic prototypes, find and explain OSHA clauses with high factual accuracy. They speed up the learning part of the task but leave a human in the loop.

OSHA 1926.1427 requires the operator personally to be certified through written and practical tests, and to be trained and evaluated as competent on the equipment. Safe operation on the jobsite is a physical duty the operator must carry out in person.

To run excavators and bulldozers on their own, Built Robotics fits each machine with an aftermarket hardware kit (Exosystem) that includes an enclosure, radar, 360° cameras and GPS. This is robotic hardware on the machine, which a software-only AI agent does not have.

Bedrock Robotics' autonomous excavation also relies on retrofitted machines. It streams video and machine data to a cloud platform where human supervisors step in when needed, so even purpose-built autonomy keeps people in the loop.
Built Robotics' autonomy is used mainly in narrow niches such as solar piling and trenching. Ordinary bulldozers, graders and backhoes still need an operator in the cab working the levers and pedals.

Elevat's AI Technician Assistant (Feb 2026) turns machine telemetry, fault codes, service manuals and repair history into prioritized repair steps. It advises the technician but does not do the repair itself.
Cummins Connected Diagnostics lets off-highway equipment send engine fault alerts wirelessly for remote diagnosis. That is software help with diagnosis only, not the physical maintenance work.
A practitioner guide notes that AI cannot disassemble, repair or reassemble heavy mechanical components. That hands-on work makes up most of this task.

Confined-space testing means a trained person takes a calibrated direct-reading meter to the space and samples it in a set order: oxygen first, then flammable gases, then toxic gases. An entry supervisor has to confirm the tests were done before signing the entry permit.

Cloud-connected detectors with pump cartridges, such as the Blackline G7, still need a worker on site to lower the probe and sample the space. The software only streams the readings and stores the record, which an agent could watch and use to fill in the paperwork.
Sample programs require monitoring for O2, LEL, H2S and CO, and require protecting the tester from the space's atmosphere while sampling. This is physical work done at the space.

Blast design software such as Strayos and Orica SHOTPlus/BlastIQ can produce pattern layouts and charge designs from drone survey and drilling data, and can calculate the charge needed for a desired outcome. That covers the calculation part of the task, but someone still has to collect the field data.
Orica's SHOTPlus does 3-D blast design and timing simulation to flag problem areas before firing. It works as a decision aid for the engineer or blaster.

OSHA Subpart U allows only authorized, qualified blasters (as defined in 1926.901) to use explosives. The blaster must make sure everyone is out of the blast area before firing and must inspect the area after the blast. This is personal, on-site responsibility that a licensed human holds.

Electronic blasting systems such as Austin Powder's E*STAR check detonators before the blast and let firing data be downloaded and exported to a PC afterward. That digital record could help an AI confirm detonation, but it does not replace the blaster's own observation at the firing point.

MSHA rules require faces and muck piles to be checked for misfires after each blast. They also set waiting periods before anyone re-enters a blast area where a misfire is suspected. This makes confirming detonation a physical, on-site safety duty.
For surface coal mines, the rules say blasting must be under the direct control of authorized persons, and blasted areas must be examined for undetonated explosives after each blast.

MSHA guidance says shot-firers carry radios close to electric blasting circuits. Each radio has a set minimum distance it must be kept from detonators. That makes setting up and placing the radio a physical, hazard-sensitive job at the blast site.

Wireless remote firing systems such as Austin Powder E*Star, Dyno Nobel SmartShot and Daveytronic send coded radio messages from a tablet or console. However, a certified blaster on site still runs them, and they rely on field hardware that an AI agent cannot reach.

MSHA blasting rules (30 CFR Part 75 Subpart E) put shot-firing and circuit-check duties on qualified people at the site. This leaves an AI agent only minor help, such as drafting message scripts or logs.

Under FRA rules, railroads must designate qualified persons to inspect freight cars and decide whether they can safely move. Those people must show the railroad they have the knowledge and ability to do so, and the railroad must keep records of each designation.

AI and CMMS tools for rail fleets predict when components such as wheelsets will wear out and turn those predictions into prioritized work orders and maintenance schedules. They support planning, but they do not do the hands-on maintenance or cleaning.
Railcar wheelset analytics, such as Railinc/TransmetriQ, help owners set the mileage between repairs. The repair work itself is still physical work done by people in the shop.
Accenture/Avanade/Microsoft's 'agentic factory' agents give operators and supervisors guided troubleshooting, suggest likely causes and draft maintenance tickets, but people keep the final decisions.

Manufacturing quality-control agents pull together sensor, inspection and maintenance data and send summaries with evidence to engineers and operators, but much operator knowledge sits in silos that the agent cannot reach.
CausalTrace is an academic agent that does root-cause analysis with real-time operator interaction on an assembly testbed. It supports human problem-solving rather than replacing the operator.

Vendor AI support agents run step-by-step troubleshooting for electronics products (printers, laptops, peripherals). They ask diagnostic questions, give targeted fixes and automate warranty and RMA intake. These are vendor claims.

When electrical equipment needs hands-on guidance, a remote human expert directs the on-site operator over live video with AR annotations. The instruction can be given remotely, but complex or safety-critical cases still rely on expert human judgment.
AR 'see-what-I-see' tools let a remote party guide customers through repairs, so instructing does not require being there in person. It is mostly human-led today.

Line-side replenishment depends on a warehouse system that reads consumption signals from the line and issues replenishment tasks. The software handles the planning and triggering, while people or vehicles carry the materials.

In electronics assembly, SMD reel replenishment software works out real-time demand from consumption and sends requests to the reel warehouse. That covers the digital planning sub-step, but the reels still have to be delivered to the line physically.
Moving materials to the line is physical work. It is done by operators, or by robots, tuggers and AMRs triggered by the warehouse system. A software-only agent with no robotics cannot do it.

O*NET lists this as a core task for Structural Metal Fabricators and Fitters: aligning and fitting parts with jacks, turnbuckles, wedges, drift pins, pry bars and hammers. That is hands-on work with tools on heavy steel.

Automated fit-up systems such as the PeddiAssembler (robotic tacking, parts scanning, laser measurement) do exist. They are dedicated robotic hardware, though, not software AI agents, so they fall outside the reference technology, which has no physical body.
Robotics has been less common in structural steel shops because steel framing projects are highly customized, so most fit-up is still done by hand.

Steel Genie by ALLPLAN, launched in April 2026, uses AI to read structural drawings. It picks out member sizes, lengths, weights and connection details, then produces quantities and a 3D model that can be exported to fabrication tools.

Ferra and LIFT (SketchDeck.ai) take PDF drawing sets, detect beams, columns, braces and trusses, and output bills of materials and tonnage. The output is meant for a human estimator to review, not for use without checking.

ConstruSteel builds cut lists, nesting and CNC files from model data, which automates the material-preparation step. It does not interpret drawings directly, so the work sequence still depends on a person who knows the shop.

Parts are physically fitted and positioned by dedicated robotic hardware such as Voortman's fitting and welding machines, which align parts using hole-based positioning and laser scanning. A software-only AI agent cannot do this.

OSHA crane rules (29 CFR 1926 Subpart CC) require qualified riggers when workers hook, unhook or guide loads, and qualified signal persons when hoisting. A human must physically carry out the lift and take responsibility for it.
Signal persons must be qualified through a third-party or employer evaluator before they give any signals during crane operations.

Product is levelled on dryer belts by machines such as oscillating spouts and spreaders, set up mechanically for each product. This is equipment automation, not something a software agent does, and when it's done by hand it is physical raking or shovelling.
Inline dryer and roaster lines use mechanical spreaders (ramshorn, vibratory, oscillating belt or rake spreaders) to spread product on the band. All of these are physical machines.
Uneven bed depth across the belt leads to under- or over-dried product, so the task is physical handling of material on the line.
OSHA 1910.218 requires that before dies are changed on forging presses, the pumps and power equipment are locked out and the ram is blocked. A person has to do this hands-on at the machine.
California Title 8 §4242 requires lockout, a flywheel at rest and ram blocking with rated material when dies are changed on forging and hot trimming presses.
Removing dies means unclamping them and moving heavy dies with hoists and slings. This is physical rigging work that a software-only agent cannot do.

Speed regulation in rolling mills is already handled by closed-loop automatic speed controllers and control computers that send speed presets. The operator watches the line and makes manual corrections for problems such as worn rolls or poor threading. This control is built into the plant's own automation, not done by a general AI agent.

Mill speed control is done through the plant's Level 1 PLC/HMI systems and operator desks. These are closed industrial control systems on the shop floor, and a software agent would not normally have access to them.
Automated rolling mill data is monitored continuously from operator desks and HMI systems in the control room, and operators are physically present at the line.

Automating die and tool setup takes dedicated machine hardware: automatic tool changers built into the press brake with robotic manipulators. Software alone does not do it. Without that hardware, setup means placing, aligning, shimming and clamping tooling by hand, which can take more than 30 minutes for complex layouts.

OSHA 1910.217(d) sets physical safety procedures for diesetters on mechanical power presses: lockout of power, inch mode, and moving the slide by hand. Die setting is in-person work at the machine. The rule sets safety requirements but does not require a license or signature.

Offline software such as DiamondBend can write tool setup programs. That is the only digital part a software agent could help with: looking up setup sheets or tooling layouts. A machine or a person still has to install and lock the tools physically.

Press-brake control software can store tool and gauge-finger libraries and work out ram positions and backgauge settings automatically. That supports the planning side of setup, but a person still has to mount the dies and adjust the machine by hand.

When a die is replaced by hand, the operator works out the new die's interference region and limits the backgauge to stay clear of it. Patent US5211045 notes that a manual die change can lead to selecting the wrong die, so the work is hands-on at the machine.

OSHA 1910.217 covers die setters during die setting and requires the employer to train them and keep them competent. During die changes, lockout/tagout must be done by authorized employees in person. These are workplace-safety duties, not a licence or sign-off rule.

To take nicks out of a cutter with an oilstone, a person holds the edge on a coarse stone, presses firmly until the nicks are gone, then finishes on a finer stone. It is skilled work done by hand, so an agent with no physical body cannot do it. At most it could look up instructions.
Before honing, the worker looks at the edge to find nicks and check that it is straight. Oil on the stone carries away the metal filings. Every step means handling the tool and the stone directly.
Oilstones are sold as ordinary hand tools for shop use. No law or licence requires a person to do or sign off this work, so physical handling is the only thing stopping an agent.

Furnace AI and advanced process control products, such as SMS group's EAFXpert and patented AI arc-furnace control, recommend or set power and electrode moves, and the patent also covers gas and oxygen supply. These are specialised control systems built into the plant, not general AI agents. Their public materials do not describe a general agent controlling burners or fuel on its own.

A patent describes AI that could recommend or apply moves such as electrode position, voltage and current, natural gas and oxygen supply, while avoiding hazards like water ingress. This shows the setpoints can be reached through software, but only via the plant's own control systems.

NFPA 86 says people who run furnaces must be trained by a qualified person, show they understand the equipment, and take regular refreshers covering startup, shutdown and lockout. Safe furnace work assumes trained staff are on site, checking the equipment hands-on.

MTConnect is an open, read-only standard. Its agents expose machine data items such as spindle speed and feed rate over HTTP, so software can log these values from networked machine tools without manual entry.
Commercial collectors poll the MTConnect /current stream at set intervals and save the values to a database automatically. This is the core 'record operational data' step for connected CNC equipment.

Data coverage depends on the controller: no single adapter exposes every NC data item, and FOCAS is used for Fanuc. On older or non-networked presses and gauges, someone still has to read the values physically at the machine.

Existing CAD add-ons such as BlankWorks, NESTINGWorks and Solid Edge's sheet-metal and nesting tools already turn 3D designs into flat patterns and nested layouts, accounting for stretch, bend radii and thickness. So the trigonometry and pattern-development steps can be done in software an agent can operate.

O*NET shows the role is tied to physical workpieces: workers mark lines and holes with scribes, soapstones and punches, check templates with measuring instruments, and fit parts before welding. Planning the layout depends on physical stock and templates that an agent cannot handle or check.

Automatic nesting tools for sheet metal, such as NestIt released for IronCAD in 2026, organize flat patterns by material and quantity. This supports delegating the digital layout-planning steps, while shop-floor judgment about heat distortion and the material still needs a human to review it.

Vendors sell dedicated vision systems: cameras with lighting fixtures and deep-learning models mounted on finishing lines that pass, reject or send plated parts for rework. They detect blistering, peeling and skip plating. This is fixed hardware, not a general software agent, and each line must be set up and calibrated in person.

A vendor says AI vision can flag air bubbles, dewetting and thin or missing coverage on coatings, but only with specialised lighting such as low-angle darkfield. Someone has to arrange the lighting and handle the part, which a bodiless agent can't do.
How well the model works depends on inspectors agreeing on defect labels before training. Humans still set the acceptance standard and judge borderline parts.

Plating-line production logs record bath chemistry, temperature, current density, voltage, rinse checks and corrective actions, with one entry and a sign-off per shift. The source readings come from the shop floor, by hand or from instruments.

Plating ERP and maintenance tools can track amp-hours, titration logs and lot traceability, and link rectifier logs to timestamped records. But reviews say automated shop-floor data capture is weak in some tools, and many still rely on manual entry.

EPA Subpart N requires chromium electroplating facilities to keep monitoring, inspection and maintenance records for 5 years, with dates and times. The rule requires the records to exist but does not say a licensed person must prepare them.
Wire brushing is a hands-on surface-prep step done before plating. The worker has to remove rust, dirt and grease from the actual workpiece, because any spot left uncleaned will not plate.
Wire brush cleaning means physically scrubbing the material's surface, and the brush hardness and pressure have to be controlled by hand. A software agent with no body cannot do this.

Community-built MCP servers (adobe-mcp-indesign, lucdesign/indesign-mcp-server, NilasA indesign-mcp) let AI agents control InDesign directly: placing text, applying styles, laying out pages and exporting. Several describe themselves as experimental or proof-of-concept, and their stated tool counts are inconsistent.
Vendors connect AI workflows to InDesign Server to build complex documents and layouts automatically, which supports headless, template-driven page make-up. This is the vendor's own marketing claim.

Practitioners mainly use AI to write InDesign scripts. Forum experts report that AI-written scripts are often broken and that AI cannot yet do real page layout on its own (a 2025 opinion), so a human still needs to review typographic and layout quality.

Printing proofs from plates is still mostly done by hand. Operators pull sheets from the delivery and check them under standard lighting or with an optical instrument, and many printshops depend on experienced operators to judge makeready results.

Built-in inspection systems such as Fujifilm's Revoria PIS scan sheets and compare them with RIP data to find streaks, registration errors and density changes. This automates the quality-checking step, but only on equipped presses and through the press's own systems.

Press-integrated systems like RYOBI MHI's PQS-D catch plate-mounting mistakes and missing characters. These are machine functions, not something a software-only agent can do. Plate mounting, inking and running the proof press still need hands on the machine.

AI layers on top of CO2-based demand-controlled ventilation can set CO2 limits matched to ASHRAE 62.1 ventilation rates for each space type, learn occupancy patterns and adjust ventilation automatically. These are vendor claims, not certified compliance.

ASHRAE 62.1 sets accuracy and calibration rules for the CO2 sensors used in DCV. Sensors that are inaccurate or badly placed can cause under-ventilation, so someone still has to place, check and calibrate the hardware on site.

In Maryland, licensed stationary engineers oversee boilers and machinery including air-conditioning equipment, and every license grade requires a state exam. NYC requires a licensed engineer who works in boiler and ventilating rooms.

Fuel-logging software such as Fluidyne FuelLog and AW Company's fuel monitor reads boiler fuel flow meters and produces consumption reports on its own. Spirax Sarco's B850 boilerhouse monitor tracks fuel use from historical trend data. So on metered plants an agent could pull, check and log the data without a person doing each step.

Job descriptions say boiler operators read meters and gauges and log the fuel consumed at set intervals. Where meters aren't connected, that means walking the plant, dipping tanks and weighing coal, which needs someone physically there.

Most US states require a licence to operate a boiler, but no source found requires a licensed person to sign the fuel-use records themselves. Licensing covers operating the boiler, not keeping the log.

O*NET lists this as a task for Stationary Engineers and Boiler Operators: helping plumbers repair or replace water, sewer or waste lines, and with daily maintenance. It is hands-on physical support work.
The occupation's repair duties include overhauls and replacing defective valves, gaskets or bearings. These are physical jobs on equipment and piping.
Other job-profile sources describe helping plumbers with line repairs as an occasional, on-site helper role.

Orthotics and prosthetics CAD/CAM tools (Canfit, OMEGA, Rodin4D) use reusable digital templates, trimlines and rule-based shape changes. These can produce the dimensions and patterns ahead of time, but a person still has to put the marks on the physical part.
Wrapstyler creates pattern templates from 3D surfaces and replaces hand-drawn pattern making. This is digital help that comes before the hands-on layout work.
Scanning and design software builds 3D models that serve as templates for carving positive molds. The measuring and marking itself is still done by hand on real materials with precision instruments.

O*NET 51-9082.00: medical appliance technicians build and repair orthotic and prosthetic devices with hand and power tools, and one of their listed tasks is repairing production equipment or tools. The work is hands-on shop-floor repair.

Current agentic maintenance AI predicts faults, checks parts availability, drafts work orders and searches manuals to help technicians troubleshoot. People still approve the work and do the physical repair.
Generative AI's main near-term value in maintenance is helping technicians troubleshoot complex machines by searching large PDF manuals. Robotic repair is a separate, longer-term trend.

AI tools such as Air Space Intelligence's Flyways at Alaska Airlines already study weather, winds, turbulence, airspace and traffic, and suggest optimised routes and fuel changes to dispatchers and pilots. The suggestions are advisory. Dispatchers take them only about 30% of the time, and the final decision stays with people.

Jeppesen Dispatch automates checking routes and recalculating flight plans that balance cost, time and fuel. This means the computing part of a change to route, fuel or load can be done by software from start to finish.

Under 14 CFR 91.3 the pilot in command is directly responsible for the flight and is its final authority. Under 121.533 the PIC and a licensed dispatcher share responsibility for preflight planning and the dispatch release, and in flight the PIC is responsible for safety. So a human has to make and own the decision to order the change.

Under 14 CFR 43.3, maintenance is limited to authorised people. Pilots may do preventive maintenance only on aircraft they own or operate, and not on aircraft used under Part 121/135. The person who does the work signs the return to service (43.7), so a certificated human has to perform and sign it.

Electronic tech logs such as Thales Aviobook Techlog send pilots' defect entries straight to the airline's maintenance information system. This digitises the 'arrange for maintenance' part, but a pilot still makes and signs the entry.

Vendors advertise AI-assisted CMMS that move a pilot squawk through deferral triage to release to service. This speeds up arranging the work, but the hands-on minor maintenance still has to be done physically.

Truck-specific routing tools, such as NextBillion.ai's routing API, are marketed as building routes from vehicle height, weight and cargo type. They also claim to apply hazmat tunnel codes and bridge weight limits. This is vendor marketing and has not been independently verified.

Commercial truck navigation products also say they check every route against bridge heights, weight limits and hazmat restrictions. The pre-trip map reading and route choice can therefore be largely automated in software, though accuracy is unverified.

Under 49 CFR 397.67, hazmat routing duties fall on the motor carrier, and for some explosives a written route plan must be given to the driver. The rule does not require a human to personally read the map, but the driver remains responsible for checking the route against real conditions and adjusting it.

Load-optimization software such as ORTEC uses AI-driven logic for dimensions, weight, stacking rules and load stability. It produces 3D plans that serve as loading instructions and can connect to TMS, WMS and SAP systems.

ContainerMath uses AI to read packing lists and produce phone-friendly 2D dock views with weight distribution. This automates the planning part of the directions, but people on the dock still carry out the loading and supervise it.
Load planning systems produce labeled loading maps and loading sequences for drivers and dock workers to follow. The real-time verbal direction and checking at the trailer stay with a person on site.

Under 49 CFR 232.103(n), unattended equipment must be secured by applying hand brakes, and railroads must have procedures to verify securement. FRA guidance defines unattended equipment by whether a qualified person can readily control its brakes.

Remote electrically driven hand brakes are still FRA prototypes and are not standard in the fleet. The FRA describes hand brakes as requiring workers to climb ladders or go between cars to operate them by hand.
Under 49 CFR 232.105(b), a locomotive's hand or parking brake must be applied and released by hand and be able to hold the unit on a 3% grade.

Yard software such as GE RailConnect TMS and PST SwitchPro already automates car-movement tracking, switching sequences and work orders. An agent could parse switch lists and car schedules into a move plan, but the certified engineer still has to take in the plan and act on it in the cab.
Vendor yard-automation platforms cover hump, flat, receiving and departure yards, which shows that the planning and scheduling side can already be done in software.

Under FRA rules (49 CFR 240), anyone who moves a locomotive, including a remote-control operator, must be a certified engineer. The certified person who carries out the conductor's radio or in-person orders is accountable for understanding them.

Norfolk Southern's AI inspection portals use trackside cameras and deep-learning models, but only on trains moving past them. They do not cover stationary equipment, and experts in the operations center review what the AI flags.
Under 49 CFR 215.13, freight cars must get a pre-departure inspection by a person the railroad designates under 215.11, who must have shown the knowledge and ability to inspect cars.
Canada's rules require a 'qualified person' with the right knowledge, training and experience to do pre-departure inspections.

Yard management systems already record railcar arrival and departure times, dwell and track status automatically from AEI tag reads, wheel sensors and cameras. Crew apps such as Wabtec mCrew let crews report arrivals, departures, pickups and set-outs digitally.

Electronic hours-of-service records are allowed under 49 CFR Part 228, but the employee or reporting crew member must certify them, and each record is stamped with the certifier's name and the certification time. A human still has to sign off on time on duty.

FRA requires electronic hours-of-service recordkeeping systems to meet set technical rules and to give inspectors access. The data sits in railroad-controlled systems that an outside agent would not normally reach.

Installing and repairing rails and ties is heavy manual work. Workers remove and replace crossties, lift and carry track material of 50 to 70 lb, shovel ballast, and use hand tools and maintenance-of-way machines outdoors in all weather. A software-only agent cannot do any of this.
Tie gangs work with on-site machinery such as tampers, spike inserters and pullers, tie cranes, and tie extractors and inserters. People must be physically present to run these machines.

Under FRA Roadway Worker Protection rules (49 CFR 214 Subpart C), roadway workers need annual training, and roadway maintenance machine operators must prove they can run the machines. This means trained humans have to be on the track.

Under federal rules (49 CFR 218.37), when a train stops on main track, a crew member with flagman's signals must walk back a set distance, place torpedoes on the rail and show a lighted fusee. The crew does this on site and is responsible for it under the regulation.

In practice, after an unplanned stop the conductor takes the flagging kit and walks back to protect the train unless the dispatcher (RTC) relieves the crew of flagging. Meanwhile the engineer radios the dispatcher. Directing and coordinating this happens on the spot, by voice and radio, during the emergency.

Flag protection is a GCOR operating rule (around Rules 6.19/6.20) that certified train crews carry out. Software could at most help by looking up the rules or drafting radio messages. No product was found that gives these instructions by itself.

Card payment at fuel dispensers is already automated by EMV/PCI-certified outdoor payment terminals and card readers built into the pump. These are fixed devices on the forecourt that the customer uses directly. They are not AI agents.

At some marinas, fuel is sold through apps or tag-on-account systems with no staff on site. This makes the payment digital. It replaces the attendant with self-service rather than with an agent that does the attendant's work.

On staffed fuel docks, attendants still run a mobile POS app to tender card sales and put purchases on account. An agent could process the digital parts (account charges, receipts), but taking cash and making change needs a person on site.

Robotic refuelling systems such as Autofuel and a Russian pilot at Oillab rely on physical robot arms. They need vehicles to be pre-registered and fitted with special fuel caps the arm can grip. That is robotics, not a software agent, so an AI agent without a body cannot insert the nozzle or fill the tank.
A robot arm finds the fuel cap, inserts the nozzle and removes it when fuelling is done. This shows the core of the task is physical handling.

New Jersey's 1949 Retail Gasoline Dispensing Safety Act says only a trained attendant may dispense fuel. Sources from 2022–2023 say it was then the only US state with this rule. Most jurisdictions allow self-service, so there is no general licensing barrier. I did not confirm whether New Jersey's law has changed since 2023.

Gemini in Google Maps, rolling out to Android and iOS in 2026, answers spoken questions about traffic on specific roads and alerts drivers to congestion and road closures. That covers the main information-gathering part of the task.
State 511 systems publish closures, detours and restrictions such as weight and width limits, and some share feeds with third parties on request. An agent can query current road information this way.
511 is the FCC-designated national traveler-information number. Road and highway information is a public service that needs no licence or human sign-off.

Petrosoft's CStoreOffice back-office software for convenience stores and gas stations forecasts demand from past sales and builds suggested orders. An operator reviews and approves them. This is vendor marketing and has not been independently checked.
Petrosoft says AI back-office tools can analyze sales data, predict demand, suggest orders and set prices based on competitors and demand. These are also vendor claims.

Industry writing says AI can adjust gas station prices in real time from market and competitor data. Unpacking, checking, labeling and shelving incoming goods is still physical work that a software-only agent cannot do.

Battery testing requires a person to clean the terminals by hand, attach the red and black clamps to the right posts, and rock them until they make solid contact. Each of these steps is physical manipulation.
A dedicated tester runs the test and interprets the result (good / charge and retest / replace). An AI agent would add little beyond looking up specs or explaining the reading.

The procedure involves hands-on safety controls: switching the engine and ignition off, working with ventilation, keeping sparks and metal tools away from the terminals, and not reversing the clamps. None of these can be done through software alone.

Vendor tools such as Veryon Guided Troubleshooting and Pratt & Whitney's AI borescope software already produce fix and replacement recommendations from fault and inspection data, but qualified engineers or inspectors review, correct and give final approval of the result.
AI predictive maintenance in airline MRO flags component wear such as cooling units early so a replacement can be scheduled, but people make the maintenance decisions.

Under 14 CFR 43.9, a maintenance or alteration record must carry the signature, certificate number and certificate type of the person approving the work, so a certificated human stays legally accountable.

Belt-scale integrators such as Thermo Scientific Ramsey work out belt loading, flow rate and total tonnage automatically. They can be monitored from a networked PC or a web interface, and some, like Belt-Way Plant Connect, report through cloud or mobile apps. So the 'read conveyor scales' part can be done in software if the scale is networked. Putting materials on scales or measuring them by hand still needs a person on site.

NIST Handbook 44 Section 2.21 requires every belt-conveyor scale to have a built-in audio or visual alarm when flow reaches 100% or more of rated capacity, or falls to 20% or less. The overload check is therefore already done by the equipment, so the human or agent only monitors it and responds.

Scales used for buying and selling (legal for trade) need NTEP certification and sealing by weights-and-measures officials. That rule covers the device, not the person reading it. No licence is needed for an operator to read a scale.
Tools like CraneTime already handle tower crane scheduling digitally, aiming to remove booking conflicts and keep teams coordinated, so this mostly digital task can be automated in part.
Delivery scheduling software for construction, such as Canary Wharf's Zone Manager, matches deliveries to crane and hoist slots. That covers the 'determine sequence of deliveries' step of the task.

HeviLift, used by PCL, simulates thousands of possible lift sequences and their cost and schedule effects. The operator still has to turn special loading instructions into how the crane is actually run on site.

Tool crib software (ToolWatch, CribMaster, ShareMyToolbox) only logs who checked a tool out and when it is due back, using barcode, RFID or badge scans. A person still has to carry the tools physically, so software only handles the small record-keeping part of the task.

Bluetooth tags can find tools and send an alert when a tool leaves the crib. That helps someone locate a tool but does nothing to move it, which needs a body or a robot. The reference agent has neither.

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.176 says storage areas must be kept clear of materials that create tripping, fire, explosion or pest hazards, and that stacked goods must be stabilized. Meeting this means physically cleaning, stacking and securing things on site. No human sign-off is required.

Commercial IoT sensor systems already watch warehouse temperature, humidity, flooding, smoke and entry, and send alerts. The task's digital part (watching conditions, flagging problems, writing checklists) can be supported or automated by software, but a person still has to act on each alert.
Industry guides describe warehouse monitoring as sensors, IoT and RFID tracking conditions and materials. They support inventory protection but do not replace the hands-on upkeep of storage areas.

Rigging consists of physical sub-steps: padding wire-rope slings against sharp load edges, keeping sling legs from kinking, and inspecting slings and removing damaged ones by hand. An AI agent with no body or robotics cannot do any of these. At most it could look up load or sling-capacity reference information, which is a very small part of the task.

OSHA rules for slings and rigging equipment are 29 CFR 1910.184 for general industry and 1926.251 for construction. They apply to the people who rig loads, and in construction rigging work is assigned to qualified riggers whom the employer judges competent.

A qualified rigger is defined as a qualified person who has shown the ability to solve rigging problems, and the employer decides who qualifies. The definition quoted is the construction-side one, taken from a secondary source and not checked against the eCFR text.

O*NET lists this as a task for Laborers and Freight, Stock, and Material Movers, Hand (53-7062.00): connect electrical equipment to power sources so that it can be tested before use. The work is hands-on handling of equipment, plugs and cables at a site, and an agent with no body cannot do it.

OSHA 1910.303 requires listed equipment to be installed and used according to its listing instructions. OSHA safety-related work-practice rules apply to the physical connection, and some live electrical work needs a 'qualified person'. Plugging equipment in to test it generally needs no licence or professional sign-off, which is why the accountability barrier is set to false.

The OSHA qualified-person training described here covers recognizing exposed live parts, choosing PPE and keeping clearance distances. All of these are physical, on-site skills. Software could at most look up equipment specs or a checklist, which saves very little of the task's time.

Agents can already be connected to Canvas through its API and MCP integrations. Through those they can read gradebook data and grading activity, so they can pull together grade summaries and prepare paperwork before a meeting.
In current AI-assisted grading setups, a human reviews grades before they are posted to the LMS. Grade decisions still get a person's approval.
University policy makes the instructor of record responsible for submitting final grades, so a human must sign off on grade paperwork.

Commercial AI tools already maintain watchlists, run ongoing monitoring of art-market and art-press news, generate recurring reports and send alerts when a tracked artist moves. This covers the monitoring and reading sub-steps, though the claims come from vendor marketing.

Artprice News, launched in late 2025, pairs art-market databases with Perplexity AI real-time search to cover museum exhibitions, art fairs, institutional appointments and market news, so an agent can produce automated digests of art-world activity.

Galleries, fairs and museums offer online viewing rooms and 360-degree virtual tours, which give an agent partial digital access to exhibitions. Going to shows in person still needs a physical visit, and the artist has to take in the material personally to develop their own ideas.

Off-the-shelf tools (Scenario, 3D AI Studio using GPT Image 2, Nano Banana Pro, Flux Kontext turnaround LoRA) generate multi-view character turnaround and model sheets from one prompt or reference image, keeping the character consistent across views.

Character sheet generators turn a single image into a four-view grid. Vendors still advise checking consistency on your own characters, so a human still has to review and correct the sheet before production use.

The US Copyright Office won't register purely AI-generated images, and prompts alone don't count as human authorship. This affects who owns the character, not whether an agent can draw it, so no licence or signature is needed to do the task.

Commercial exercise-management platforms, such as 4C Strategies Exercise Manager, use AI to generate realistic emergency and continuity scenarios and exercise reports. They base these on an organization's own plans, dependencies and risk profiles.

Innovation Labs' Scenario Builder uses AI to design, run and evaluate tabletop emergency-management exercises for authorities and organizations. This shows that scenario design and evaluation sub-steps can already be automated.

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.38 requires employers to keep a written emergency action plan. OSHA guidance recommends evacuation drills, with the employer choosing how often. No licensed signatory is required for drill plans, but site-specific details such as exits, assembly areas and coordination with responders still need a human to check them.

FHWA's interim approval describes automated flagger assistance devices (AFADs) as remote-controlled STOP/SLOW signs or signal-and-gate-arm units. A human flagger runs them, either at the work zone or from a central location. They are physical roadside hardware, not software an AI agent could operate on its own.

A Roads & Bridges item quotes the MUTCD: an AFAD shall be operated only by a flagger trained on it and must never be left unattended while in use. This came from a trade publication's quote, and I did not check it against the current MUTCD text myself.
Iowa DOT's AFAD specifications require trained staff on site who can switch to manual flagging if a device fails, so a human has to be physically present.

Existing software and patents can generate traffic control plans: they pull location-specific rules and lay signs, tapers and lane closures onto a map. This covers drafting the plan, not the flagger's discussion with superiors.

Under MUTCD, flagger stations must sit far enough ahead of the work space for drivers to stop, with sight distance, shoulder position and escape routes taken into account. These depend on site conditions that the flagger reports from the field.
States require trained or certified human flaggers to provide temporary traffic control. The flagger's role in planning discussions comes from being the person stationed on site.
Agentic AI inventory tools forecast demand from POS sales and stock data and generate purchase orders. The setup vendors recommend has a manager review orders before they are sent.
BlueCart's predictive ordering uses depletion rates, real-time inventory and seasonal trends to suggest reorder quantities, which staff then approve.
Restaurants spend about 8 to 12 hours a week on manual stock counting and ordering. The physical count is still done by people unless sensors are installed.

Commercial tray-tracking software (Computrition Tray InMotion Elite) checks patient identity and diet orders automatically, tracks trays from ticket creation to delivery and alerts staff when diet orders change. The vendor says this helps prevent delivery mistakes, but this claim comes from marketing and has not been independently checked.

In a real hospital deployment, a staff member still scans the tray barcode and the patient's wristband with an iPad at the bedside before handing over the meal. The final match is still done in person.
Under a manual hospital policy, staff compare the diet order with the tray slip on the spot and ask the nurse to confirm when unsure. This is physical, on-site checking with no licence requirement.

evidence.fact: O*NET lists stocking service stations with ice, napkins and straws as a task for Food Servers, Nonrestaurant (35-3041.00). The work is physically carrying supplies and refilling them on site.
Server sidework checklists treat restocking stations with napkins, straws, silverware, ice and glasses as hands-on side work. Software can only help by tracking checklists or inventory.
Toast's server job description includes restocking server stations and refilling ice at the soda station, which takes a physical presence.

Bedside tablet and app ordering systems in hospitals, such as CBORD Patient App and menuPick, let patients pick meals and set diet and allergy preferences digitally. The order is then delivered to the bedside, but staff still have to carry it out in person.
At UCSF Mission Bay, every bed has a bedside tablet for meal ordering, but only about half of patients use it. The rest still order by phone, so the order capture part is only partly automated.

Some vendor systems have staff take orders at the bedside on touchscreens and support either traditional or room service delivery. Settling patients in to eat, such as positioning them, the tray and the table, still requires a physical presence.
Pizza Ranch leased bussing robots to carry dirty dishes so human bussers could spend more time cleaning tables. Wiping tables stays a manual human job, and these are robots, not software agents.
Smile Robotics' ACUR-C bussing robot with an arm clears tables much more slowly than a human. Physical table work needs robotics, which the reference AI agents do not have.
Automatic table wipers were still only a student prototype meant to replace the rag. I found no results from its planned trial.

Food-carrying in restaurants is being automated, but by physical delivery robots such as PuduBot, not by software-only AI agents. Even with these robots, staff place the dishes on the robot by hand and enter the table numbers.

Moving dishes from the kitchen to a table or counter takes a body or a robot with a gripping arm, as with the Pudu A1. That is robotics, which falls outside the reference technology of software-only agents.

Autonomous floor scrubbers are sold for restaurants and kitchens, for example the Cenobots L50/SP50 sold through Martin Bros. These are robots, and the reference agents have no robotics. The agents also can't polish counters, shelves, walls or equipment.

The Keenon KleenBot C40, marketed for restaurants and priced at $19,600, is physical robotic hardware. A software-only agent could at most schedule or monitor a robot like this, which is not the cleaning work itself.
A vendor recommends running robotic scrubbers in kitchens after hours. That confirms floor cleaning is physical work done on site.
Most steam-table tools only log hot-holding temperatures and water levels; staff still enter the checks by hand. I found no software agent that refills food or equipment.
Steam-table automation hardware such as Eagle AutoFill senses and refills water in the wells, not food. Physical restocking of pans, utensils and bar supplies stays manual.
Restaurant sensors can flag when storage inventory is running low. This helps with deciding when to restock but does not do the physical replenishment.

Mashgin's countertop checkout uses several cameras and computer-vision AI to identify packaged items and plated food in cafeterias without a cashier. This is dedicated kiosk hardware, not a software-only agent.

Autocanteen's vendor page claims its AI checkout identifies meal plates in about 10 seconds per transaction, with one assistant overseeing several checkout points. Supervision and cash handling still fall to a person, and these figures are marketing claims that have not been independently verified.

An Intel brief describes camera-based self-checkout systems that take over item recognition and billing in food service. Taking cash, making change and handling the trays are still physical work that a bodiless software agent cannot do.

Bars use commercial underbar glasswashers that a person has to load, unload and run by hand, using either high-temperature (185°F rinse) or chemical sanitizing. These machines are physical equipment, not software an AI agent can operate.
Health rules for bars describe hands-on steps, such as fully immersing glassware in sanitizer of at least 25 ppm for at least two minutes. This document is an older local code from Albany, Oregon.
One spec sheet shows a unit that runs a 185°F sanitizing rinse every cycle. A person still has to collect, load and put away the glasses, which an agent without a body cannot do.
Bars slice citrus garnish by hand or with manual pull-handle and lever wedgers (Nemco Easy Wedger, Prince Castle CW-6). This is physical knife or tool work that a software-only agent cannot do.
Automated fruit wedge-cutting machines appear in patents, but these are hardware, not AI agents. The task is about manipulating fruit, and no law or licence requires a specific person to do it.
Commercial lemon slicers range from handheld cutters to countertop units. All of them need a person to load and operate them.
O*NET lists this as a Dishwasher task. It means washing, peeling and cutting produce and other foods by hand in a kitchen.
In employer job postings, dishwasher food prep is hands-on work done in the kitchen, such as cleaning and peeling vegetables.

The O*NET duty list puts food prep (washing and cutting produce) next to physical kitchen work like running dish machines and storing items. A software-only agent can at most look up a recipe or prep list.

OSHA's restaurant guidance describes delivery and storage work as lifting and carrying heavy supplies by hand, with back and strain injuries as the main hazard. This is physical handling of goods that a software-only agent cannot do.

OSHA's trucking guidance treats loading and unloading as physical work done by hand or with forklifts and pallet jacks. It requires training, and powered industrial truck rules apply to the equipment. There is no licence or sign-off rule that applies only to humans, beyond age limits on young workers.
NIOSH guidance on grocery truck unloading recommends mechanical aids such as conveyors and powered pallet movers. Automation for this task is physical equipment, not AI software.

Ready-made landscaping safety documents already exist, such as Safe Work Method Statements, safe operating procedures for mowers and excavators, and OSHA-oriented checklists. An AI agent could draft and adapt this kind of written material from start to finish.

A landscaping supervisor is generally expected to enforce OSHA guidelines and company safety rules, including PPE use and safe chemical handling. They also train crews and record infractions. Much of this is done in person at job sites, which an agent without a body cannot do.

OSHA puts the duty to provide a safe workplace on the employer. One training vendor notes that only an employer can designate an employee as certified. However, no licence requires a human to personally write or sign the work standards themselves.

SiteRecon sells landscaping site-audit software with mobile scoring templates, geotagged photos and notes, automated alerts for poorly scored sites, and client audit reports. The person on site still does the inspecting; the software records and reports it.
OrangeQC offers groundskeeper inspection forms with photos, scores and GPS tags, including templates for turf, irrigation and tree inspections. A field user has to fill them in on site.

Jotform offers a landscape maintenance site-audit AI agent template that collects conditions and photos through a chat interface. It structures what a human reports and does not observe the site itself.

Landscape software such as Aspire already handles crew scheduling, route optimization, sending work orders to crew phones and geofenced time tracking. These are the digital sub-steps an agent could run.
Foreman job postings describe on-site work: setting the day's work list, working alongside crews pruning shrubs, coaching pruning technique and inspecting finished work in person.
Foremen must make sure crews follow safety procedures, wear protective equipment and use machinery safely, which takes in-person supervision.

Vendor pages say AI scheduling agents for landscaping plan crew routes by zip code and crew skill, send reminders and handle weather-driven reschedules across the customer base. This is marketing material, not an independent benchmark.

FieldProxy says its tool plans crew routes using traffic, how long each property takes, crew skills, equipment needs and time-of-day limits, and that on rain days it finds the affected jobs and suggests new times. These are vendor claims.

A competitor comparison says some field-service tools such as ServiceM8 still make dispatchers move weather-affected jobs by hand. That suggests a supervisor still checks and adjusts the schedule using what they know about the sites and crews. This is one vendor writing about a rival.

Smart irrigation controllers (Rachio, Rain Bird ARC, Hunter Hydrawise) already set watering schedules automatically from weather data. Only this small digital part of watering could go to software that an agent might configure; mulching, mowing, pruning, planting and fertilizing all need hands-on work on site.

In Florida, a landscape maintenance operator cannot apply pesticides without proper certification, and for-hire lawn fertilizer application needs a state license (GI-BMP training plus an exam). The person applying it must be licensed or work under a licensed operator's supervision.
Some cities add their own license for businesses that apply lawn fertilizer or pesticide, and the application lists each employee's state commercial applicator license number.

Landscaping field-service software such as RootControl offers GPS-geofenced crew tracking, AI scheduling and real-time dispatch sync. An agent could use these to track schedules, deadlines and job status.

Fieldproxy's blog describes AI scheduling for landscaping crews that weighs location, skills, equipment and weather, plus automated crew management. These are vendor marketing claims and have not been checked.

Landscape site-supervisor job postings say the role means checking site quality in person every day, doing walk-throughs, coaching crews hands-on and making sure deficiencies get fixed. Checking that instructions are followed needs someone physically on site. No license or legal sign-off is mentioned.

Landscape training platforms such as Greenius deliver course content on safe work and equipment operation, supply 110 weekly tailgate talks and track who has completed courses. They cover the digital materials and record-keeping side of training. A related OSHA-aligned course says the practical proficiency check is done hands-on by the employer.

An OSHA-aligned online landscaping course covers equipment use, chemical handling and PPE in theory. Practical evaluation is a separate in-person step, and only the employer can designate an employee as certified.

In states such as North Carolina, the licensed supervisor must make sure a non-certified pesticide applicator has recent training and has been taught to operate the equipment in the past year. Training is required by law for some sub-tasks, but the law does not say an AI cannot take part in it.

O*NET lists 'Provide workers with assistance in performing duties as necessary to meet deadlines' as a task for this occupation. The occupation's core role is directly overseeing and coordinating crews that do the landscaping or groundskeeping work.

Job postings for this supervisor role describe hands-on field duties: planting or maintaining vegetation by mulching, fertilizing, watering, mowing or pruning. That needs a physical body, which a software-only agent does not have.

Related tasks in the same occupation also involve physical help, such as directing or assisting workers who maintain or repair power tools and motorized equipment. No license or legal sign-off is needed to do this help.

Landscaping equipment apps such as SafetyCulture link each machine to its maintenance and usage history through QR codes or asset tags. Crews scan the codes on site to run inspections and report problems. That means a person has to handle and look at the equipment, while the software holds the records.

Asset Panda's guidance for landscaping inventory uses barcodes as unique IDs, pulls up each item's lifecycle details when scanned, and can import existing spreadsheet records. This is the digital record-keeping and reconciliation work that an agent could take over.

A trade article on keeping maintenance trailers organized says supervisors must check tools and materials in person ('inspect what you expect'). Counting stock and judging whether items still work requires being there physically.

AI add-ons for maintenance work-order systems read requests from email, text, calls, Slack and forms, then create or route work orders as a 24/7 digital coordinator. This covers the routine information-passing between units.

Facilities AI assistants can be trained on a team's own procedures to sort and route requests across departments and show request trends to facilities leaders. Agreeing on priorities and committing crews still falls to the human supervisor.

Agentic AI for facilities is described as ranking urgency, scheduling against staff availability and resource limits, and grouping related tasks. These are sub-steps of coordinating work between units, but the negotiation between supervisors is still done by people, often face to face.

Vendors sell AI phone screening for seasonal landscaping crews. They say it calls applicants soon after they apply, runs structured interviews and supports Spanish. These are the vendor's own claims, not independently checked.

In 2019 U.S. Lawns rolled out JobBot.Ai's bilingual chatbots across its franchises to contact and screen hourly applicants and schedule interviews. The case is old, so it does not show how well the tool performs now.

Employers stay liable for discrimination caused by AI hiring tools, including vendor tools acting for them. This is a liability exposure, not a rule that a human must make or sign the decision. Commentary is from 2023, and the EEOC guidance was reportedly withdrawn in 2025.

Turf apps such as TurfPath include spray and tank-mix calculators, application logs and AI extraction of spray sheets and soil tests. These cover the planning and record-keeping steps, but mixing and spraying are still done by hand.

In Connecticut, a commercial supervisory certificate is required for the person who decides what pesticide to use, how it is mixed, the dose, timing and method. Operators must work under a certified supervisor's written instructions.

In Louisiana, no one may apply or supervise the application of a restricted-use pesticide as a commercial applicator without certification. Supervising uncertified workers on ground applications requires direct supervision by a certified applicator.

SingleOps' property measurement tool uses aerial photos to measure square footage. It feeds production rates and custom inputs such as labor rates, chemical usage and equipment usage into estimates. That covers the main sub-steps of working out labor and machine needs.

LMN, which merged with SingleOps, partnered with Attentive.ai on AI mapping and measurement to cut takeoff time. I found no product that turns a contract directly into crew and equipment assignments, so a supervisor still adds site and crew knowledge and checks the plan.

Aspire's commercial landscaping software includes estimating templates, scheduling and routing, and takeoff integrations. The task is document review and planning work done in systems an agent can reach, with no licence or sign-off required.

Landscaping platforms such as LMN, Jobber and Aspire already digitize crew timesheets, GPS time tracking, job costing and scheduling records. That makes it feasible for an agent to compile and update records through the software. However, no vendor clearly offers end-to-end AI automation of record upkeep.

The source data comes from field work done by the applicator and crew. Federal rules require pesticide application records that list the product, EPA registration number, amount applied and treated site. A human has to supply or confirm these field facts, but filling in the record itself is documentation, not a licensed sign-off.

Commercial applicators must keep records of all applications, available for inspection for at least two years. States often set stricter deadlines, for example completing records within three business days. This is a structured, rule-based task that an agent can track and enforce.

Landscape field-service platforms such as Jobber, Aspire and RootControl already record crew hours by GPS and produce timesheets, proof-of-work records and automated reports. General tools like ClickUp Brain flag missing entries and summarize tracked time, so most of the compiling and formatting can be automated.

Pesticide application records are required, but any format is accepted as long as it contains the required data, such as product, site and date. The rules require keeping the records, not that a human writes them. The facts recorded still come from what the crew did in the field, so a supervisor must supply or check them.

Under EPA rules for commercial applicators, records must be kept and made available for inspection for at least 2 years. The applicator or supervisor stays responsible for their accuracy, so a human review step remains.

FieldProxy's landscaping blueprint, a vendor workflow, describes AI scoring of photos from completed jobs. It flags defects such as missed mowing strips or uneven edges, sends low-scoring jobs to a supervisor's mobile dashboard, and turns rejected items into follow-up tasks for the crew. This automates issuing corrective work orders, but a person still has to take the photos on site.

OrangeQC's groundskeeper inspection software captures inspection checklists with photos and GPS tags, plus corrective-action tickets that can be assigned and tracked. The ordering and tracking are digital, but the inspection depends on someone being physically at the site.

None of the sources found shows a law or licence requiring a human to order corrective landscape work or recommend procedural changes. The physical fix is done by crews, and the supervisor has to judge problems at the site and convince crews to change how they work.

Many AI apps already diagnose plant diseases and pests from a single photo or a text description of symptoms and suggest organic, biological or chemical treatments. Their accuracy has not been independently checked, and someone on site still has to scout the area and take the photos.

In Texas, applying any pesticide to lawns, trees or ornamentals for pay requires a state license held by a person, so a licensed human stays accountable for which treatment is chosen and how it is used.
Commercial applicators who use restricted-use pesticides must hold certification or licensing, which they get by passing exams and must renew.

Complaint management software for commercial landscaping firms already takes client requests and complaints through web forms with photo attachments and routes them to crews. An agent could handle intake, triage, records review and drafting the response.

Vendors market AI agents for landscaping work orders that cover scheduling, GPS crew tracking and customer chatbots. These data sources let a first check of a complaint (was the crew on site, was the work logged) happen in software. The performance figures in these posts are marketing claims and were not verified.

No source found shows AI doing the on-site check of landscaping complaints. Software covers intake and tracking with photos, but confirming problems such as turf damage, missed areas or plant loss still needs someone on the grounds. This is an inference from what the tools document, not a sourced finding.

Fleet maintenance AI such as Fleetio's AI Service Advisor sorts repairs by priority, drafts service requests, approves low-risk work within set policies and handles routine follow-up. That covers the paperwork side of repairs, not the hands-on fixing or coaching of workers.

Landscaping fleet software can pull diagnostic data from telematics and track parts like oil filters and blade belts. Small equipment without telematics, such as walk-behind mowers and trimmers, is a gap, and the actual repair work stays physical.

OSHA rule 29 CFR 1910.147 requires a written lockout/tagout program, a procedure for each machine and worker training. A supervisor has to coordinate this on site, but no licence or sign-off is required for small-engine repair.

The machines that clear sidewalk snow on their own, such as the SnowBot Pro, are robots with GPS navigation and brushes. The reference AI agent has no physical body, so it cannot do this work. Vendor claims about labor savings are unverified and some are dated.
Even consumer snow-clearing robots like Yarbo need a person to set them up on site, so physical presence is still required.

The search found no software or robots for pouring cement curbs or repairing sidewalks. These are hands-on construction work, and a software agent could help only with small side jobs like scheduling or ordering materials.

Field-service time tools such as QuickBooks Time and Hubstaff record crew clock-ins with GPS and geofences, send clock-in reminders and send time cards to managers to approve before payroll. An agent could compile timesheets, reconcile them and flag errors, but a manager still approves them.

ClickUp's AI marketing page for landscapers says its assistant can chase missing time logs, flag overtime and summarize labor hours. Workstatus says it tracks time-off requests. This is vendor marketing, not independent proof, but it suggests the processing sub-steps can run on their own.
