Under the FMLA, the employer must send eligibility and designation notices within 5 business days and handle medical certifications. Management makes the decision, and mistakes create legal risk, so leave approvals need a human judgment and review. No law says a human must personally sign them.

Landscaping route-optimization software takes a list of service addresses and produces efficient crew routes automatically. Vendors claim it cuts in-field travel time by up to 25-30%, but these figures are not independently verified.

Landscaping fleet software combines GPS data with maintenance scheduling and cost tracking, which supports data-driven decisions about equipment and vehicles. An agent with access to these systems could analyze the data and draft recommendations.

GPS and time-tracking apps record crew arrival and departure times automatically. This gives productivity data an agent could analyze, but seeing on-site working conditions and how equipment performs still needs a person in the field.

Vendor AI agents for landscaping (e.g., Fieldproxy) say they build weekly maintenance plans and crew schedules on their own, using weather, property size, seasonal needs, crew skills and equipment availability. This covers the work of drafting the plan or schedule, though these are the vendor's own marketing claims.

Landscaping software needs to combine recurring maintenance contracts with one-time improvement projects. AI scheduling tools can draft these combined schedules, but a human still has to agree priorities and budget with managers and architects.

State law says landscape architecture design and sealed plans must be done by a licensee. A supervisor talking through maintenance or improvement schedules is not doing licensed work, so no licensed human signature is needed for this task.

Vendors say their AI phone agents for lawn care collect the address, lawn size and mowing frequency, then quote from the business's rate card and book the job. This is vendor marketing, not independent testing.
Avoca says its lawn-care AI agent answers calls, handles customer objections and books jobs into the CRM. This is a vendor claim that suggests partial automation of price talks.

AI estimating tools such as SiteRecon, QuoteIQ and BayQuote measure properties from maps or satellite images and price them. A human still adjusts margins and rates and approves the quote before it goes out. The search found no source on AI handling discounting or price pushback by itself.

Vendors sell AI receptionists for landscapers that answer service questions and give ballpark price ranges. Final pricing waits for an on-site estimate, and commercial or HOA inquiries go to a human sales rep.
AI answering services for landscaping companies handle calls, answer service questions and capture leads around the clock.

Landscape contractor licensing rules vary by state and apply to the business doing or bidding the work. None of the sources found require a licensed human to answer customer questions about methods, materials or price ranges.

Attentive.ai Automeasure measures landscape maintenance, snow and paving sites from aerial imagery for estimates and bids. The vendor claims over 98% accuracy, and a headline announces a partnership with LMN, an estimating and job-costing platform (only the headline was seen).

SiteRecon's AI maps turf, planting beds and paved areas from aerial imagery for takeoffs and says it offers open APIs and works with common CRMs and estimating software. So the measuring and costing steps can run without a site visit, though crew productivity rates, local pricing and the final bid still need a supervisor's judgment and review.

Landscaping business systems like Aspire (a ServiceTitan company) and LMN hold the estimating, job-costing and budget data. An agent can track budgets only if it is given access to these company accounts.

Commercial platforms such as GreenSight TurfCloud and AerialData Turf Health Explorer use drone multispectral and thermal imagery with NDVI analytics to map turf stress. That lets software help with remote condition assessment, but a person still has to fly the drones or capture the imagery on site.

AerialData drone surveys find turf stress that cannot be seen from the ground and show it as hotspot maps. The analysis is useful, but the walk-through inspection of plants and soil (touch, soil probing, pests, close looks) is still done in person.

Dronifi and Pix4D/TerraView tools use computer vision to flag encroachment, irrigation problems and moisture issues from aerial data. An AI agent could interpret these outputs, but it cannot physically tour the grounds.

Irrigation design software, including CAD plugins and web planners, already automates zone layout, sprinkler placement, pipe sizing and pressure-loss calculations. Vendors still advise checking the results with engineering judgment.
In Texas, San Antonio's water utility requires a licensed person to be present and supervise each new irrigation installation, and a city permit must be issued for the work.
Connecticut says it is illegal to install an irrigation system without a license. Controller low-voltage wiring must be done by a licensed contractor, and local permits are required.

Under 40 CFR Part 171, anyone who uses or supervises restricted-use pesticides must be a certified applicator. A noncertified worker may apply them only under the direct supervision of a certified applicator.

Herbicide spraying is being automated with drones and robots, not software agents. Spray drones are used on ditches and roadsides, but their performance depends heavily on flight height, speed and weather. That automation needs a robotic body, which the reference technology does not have.

Utility vegetation management is testing autonomous drone spraying as a replacement for labour-intensive manual work. The manual job itself is physical: lifting, pushing and swinging nozzles and hoses.

Free tools like TeeJet SpraySelect already suggest nozzle tips, target pressure and flow rate from speed, spacing, application rate and droplet size. This covers the selection step, which an AI agent can also do. The hoses and nozzles still have to be fitted by hand.
A smartphone calibration write-up shows the app gives a per-nozzle flow target. The operator then checks output with a timed catch test on the sprayer itself, which is physical work.

Federal rules say non-certified people may use restricted-use pesticides only under a certified applicator's direct supervision. For some products this means the supervisor must be physically present. The rules govern handling, not specifically connecting equipment, so the main barrier to this task is physical rather than legal.
Vendors sell email triage agents that classify incoming mail by intent, urgency and topic, then send it to the right department or person for reply.

A 2026 vendor blog describes AI triage that classifies, routes and prioritizes inbound email, with routing rules and escalation of unclear threads to a human. Figures such as about 70% of mail auto-routed are vendor claims and have not been checked independently.

In shared inboxes such as Front, AI triage runs on top of a rules engine that routes by sender, keyword or tag. Routing is a software step: no physical presence and no licensed sign-off is needed for digital correspondence. Paper mail would first have to be scanned.

Online certified-mail services let a user upload a document, enter addresses, choose USPS Certified Mail and an electronic return receipt, then review and pay. The provider prints, assembles and mails the item, so records that are already digital can be sent without anyone handling them.

Commercial platforms such as Quadient ConnectSuite e-Certify and SimpleCertifiedMail through Endicia automate certified-mail preparation, tracking and electronic return receipts, and say they connect to existing systems or APIs.

When the records are paper files, someone still has to gather, copy and put them in envelopes, attach PS Form 3800 and the green card, and drop them off for mailing. An agent without a body cannot do these steps, so a human is still needed for that part.

Vestris says its platform takes a ratified contract from a shared inbox, parses it, assembles the title commitment, reconciles the settlement statement and prepares the lender package. This is the vendor's own marketing claim.
Rocket Close uses Amazon Bedrock and Textract to process about 2,000 title abstract packages a day, averaging 75 pages each. It reports the process is 15 times faster.

V7 Go's loan-closer agent checks conditions precedent, including insurance certificates and title policies, and produces an auditable checklist. Closing packages are still reviewed and signed off by people, and some documents come from outside parties or as paper.

Vendors say their agentic intake tools read borrower documents like pay stubs and tax forms, extract and check the data, and push it into the loan origination system (LOS), CRM or internal databases. Exceptions go to a person.
Layerup says its intake agent takes in 1003 loan applications, extracts and indexes the documents, and verifies income and assets inside existing mortgage workflows.

UiPath's lending automation connects to major LOS platforms (Encompass, nCino, Empower) and works alongside them. Vesta, an AI-native LOS, says about 40% of tasks run on its platform are handled by AI agents, and issues needing human review are escalated. Both figures are the vendors' own claims.

Route management software such as Sensus AutoRead already moves reads from handhelds into billing systems without retyping, by passing ASCII files back and forth. That covers the upload step in software.
Gurnee's route management system downloads reading data from handheld interrogators and writes the billing transfer files. The reader still has to physically bring back or connect the device.

Oracle CC&B's meter-read cycle sends route download files to handheld software, and reads return to billing only after field readers finish their routes. The process is software-driven and needs no licensed human sign-off.

Customers give utilities keys to reach meters, or leave them with a neighbor or on the premises. Meter readers keep and use these keys in the field, so a person has to physically find that a key is lost or broken before anything can be reported.

Utility procedures send access problems, including key or combination fixes, to case handling by customer contact staff and meter reading staff. That handling happens in internal systems, where an agent could write and file the report.
Field-service apps for utilities already record site-access blocks, such as a locked access door, as structured digital entries. This shows the reporting step can be done in software.
USPS self-service kiosks handle some counter sales, such as stamps and postage labels, paid by card. Kiosks are dedicated hardware, not a software agent acting for the clerk.
Postal money orders are bought at Post Office locations with cash, a debit card or a traveler's check, not a credit card. That means handling cash and physical instruments at the counter.
Retail associates also help customers use the kiosks in person during business hours, so counter sales are still largely physical, face-to-face transactions.

USPS Automated Package Verification (APV) checks parcel postage from scanned weight and dimensions. USPS still says detection is imperfect and that staff find many discrepancies by hand during acceptance and processing. Software handles postage calculation and checking, but a person or physical equipment has to capture the inputs.

Under Publication 52, acceptance staff must look closely at every side of each mailpiece for hazmat markings and old labels, and must ask the customer about hazardous contents. This is physical, face-to-face handling and inspection at the counter.

Retail guidance says associates must ask any follow-up questions needed to accept each package safely, and must reject it if the contents are unknown. Unclear cases go to the postmaster or the PCSC for a ruling.
Customers can already pick a PO box size and location, reserve it and pay for it online through USPS's reservation system. That covers the selection, application and payment sub-steps.
Renters must show two current forms of ID in person, one a photo ID and one proving their address, together with PS Form 1093 at the Post Office where the box is located.
A Post Office employee checks the IDs during business hours and then hands over the keys or the combination number. This step needs someone physically present.

In 2022 USPS tested Rapid Dropoff Station kiosks that print return labels and give acceptance scans. The customer still drops the parcel in a physical drum, so the automation is hardware plus self-service, not a software agent.

USPS Automated Parcel Drop machines, piloted at five California Post Offices, take prepaid parcels by physical deposit, with a maximum size of 24x16x12 in. Receiving and bagging the mail is still physical handling done by people or machines.
UPS Store self-service kiosks follow the same model for prepaid drop-offs. Taking in the item still depends on physical hardware, not on what a digital agent can do.

MES systems already log production data, material usage, operator activity and process history automatically, and that record serves as the audit trail. Most of the transcription and compilation work in this task can therefore be done in software.
Infor MES documentation says automatic data collection cuts errors and improves timing accuracy compared with manual entry.

Vendors sell AI agents for manufacturing data entry, inspection logging and quality-record upkeep. These are marketing claims, not independent proof. Counts, gauge readings and checks on the shop floor still need someone there in person when sensors or PLC feeds are missing.
Vendor-reported: AI agents for manufacturing planning feed demand forecasts into MRP and calculate material needs such as safety stock and consolidated purchase orders inside ERP systems.
Vendor-reported: QAD describes agents that check inventory and capacity across ERP systems and propose schedule and material changes for a human to approve.

Vendor-reported: SAP cloud ERP offers real-time MRP, demand-driven replenishment and AI-agent production order release. The task is calculation on software and data the clerk already uses, and no licence or physical step is needed.

Sage Intacct's 2026 R2 release includes AI-driven line-level matching of purchase orders, receivers and vendor invoices. It flags differences in quantity and price automatically and uses tolerance thresholds, so the document-to-document comparison step can be automated.

Vendors such as Veryfi offer AI that extracts and matches data from bills of lading, purchase orders and invoices, which reduces manual intervention. These sources are vendor marketing and do not include independent accuracy data.

O*NET 43-5111.00 describes the work as largely clerical but tied to physical goods. Workers weigh, measure and check materials, and they remove loads that fail standards. Reading the actual labels, tags and tickets on shipments requires someone on site or scanning equipment there.

Google Document AI's human-in-the-loop feature uses confidence thresholds to send only uncertain extractions to human reviewers, who check and correct values before the data reaches business systems. Software already does most of the comparison, and people handle the exceptions.

RapidAutomation's verify_me block shows AI-extracted data next to the original source file. A reviewer accepts, rejects or edits the values, and the validated result is logged with a timestamp. This automates the side-by-side check with a human approving the output.

ABBYY markets human-in-the-loop verification for AI document processing to get higher precision. Vendors still keep a person reviewing low-confidence or exception fields, so full unattended verification is not yet standard.

O*NET lists 'Select materials needed to complete work assignments' as a core task for Data Entry Keyers (importance 85). The neighboring tasks involve source documents such as canceled checks and bills, and storing completed documents in the right locations, which points to paper-based work in many settings.

Commercial document-classification agents take in email, fax, scans and uploads, identify document types and route files to the right workflow. Their accuracy figures are self-reported by the vendor and unverified. This covers selecting digital source material for a work batch, but low-confidence items usually still go to a human.

A typical agent pipeline runs OCR, then LLM classification, then RPA data entry, and it works only on documents that are already digital. Gathering physical forms, paper batches or supplies needs a person on site, and I found no licensing or legal rule requiring a human to do this task.

Bridgit's AI workforce-planning platform, rolled out at Sir Robert McAlpine (May 2026), matches workers to jobs using availability, certifications, location and project experience, replacing spreadsheets

Corfix's planned AI scheduling feature suggests crew allocations from co-assignment history, availability, fatigue signals and distance to site, and schedulers can adjust or override each suggestion, so a human stays in the loop
AI crew-matching depends on verified skills data, since title-and-tenure records can't tell apart workers' task-level skill, and most scheduling tools don't connect to safety and compliance records

OSHA 29 CFR 1926.25 requires physical housekeeping: clearing scrap lumber with protruding nails and other debris from work areas, passageways and stairs, removing combustible scrap at regular intervals, and providing and emptying waste containers. All of this means handling material on site.

AI vision tools for construction housekeeping (vision-transformer classifiers, CCTV/drone dashboards, photo-analysis apps) only detect and flag poor housekeeping. None of them does the physical cleaning or preparation.
Research systems such as the NUS project detect hazards like loose rebar, pipes and water ponding from camera feeds and send alerts to site teams, who still remove the hazards by hand.

Commercial AI tools in 2026 (for example Handoff H1, launched July 2026, and Attentive.ai) read blueprints and produce material takeoffs end to end. This shows that agents can already interpret construction drawings. The accuracy figures come from the vendors, not from independent tests.

On-Screen Takeoff and Bluebeam are established plan-reading platforms with AI-assisted features for extracting quantities and scope from PDF plans. Coverage of how well AI reads specifications, as opposed to drawings, is thinner.

Attentive.ai claims its automated tracing finds exact material quantities across trades. This would cover the part of the task about working out activities and quantities from plans. The laborer still has to match the plan against conditions on site and receive the foreman's instructions, often verbally or on paper plans in the field.

This task is manual earthwork done on site with picks, shovels, pneumatic tampers and rakes. A software-only agent with no body or robotics cannot dig, backfill or compact soil. At most it could look up grade specs or compaction guidance, which saves very little of the working time.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1926.651(k), a competent person must inspect the excavation, adjacent areas and protective systems every day. The inspections happen before work starts, as needed during the shift and after every rainstorm. The competent person must have authority to correct hazards on site.
OSHA's interpretation letter says 1926.651(k) is cited when no competent person is available to do the daily inspections. That means a human with on-site authority is required by law.

O*NET lists Construction Laborers (47-2061.00) as workers who do physical labor at construction sites. Their tasks include installing sewer, water or storm drain pipes with pipe-laying machinery or laser guidance equipment. That work needs a person on site, and a software-only agent cannot do it.
DOL seasonal job postings describe laborers carrying, positioning, holding and supporting pipe materials, backfilling trenches, and helping join components. All of this is hands-on manual handling.

The O*NET summary describes the occupation as physical labor that helps other craft workers on site. Software can only play a small side role, such as looking up specs or alignment tolerances, and a person still has to do the positioning, joining and sealing.

Automated layout marking exists, but it depends on physical robots. HP SitePrint is an autonomous robot that prints layouts on site floors and comes with cloud job-management tools and a tablet controller. That puts it outside a software-only agent.

Dusty's FieldPrinter robot prints layouts on site floors from building models, with workers supervising it on site. An agent without a body could only prepare the digital layout data, not measure or mark the site.

A field study on an eight-floor building found robotic layout cut total labor hours by 68% compared with manual layout. The savings come from robot hardware working physically on site, not from a software agent.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1926.451(f)(7), scaffolds may be erected, moved, dismantled or altered only under the supervision of a competent person who is on site. The work itself must be done by trained, experienced employees that this person selects.

OSHA interpretations say the competent person must be on site to spot hazards and correct them, and that erectors face the physical hazards of working on a partly built structure. This makes the task hands-on physical work.

Scaffold software such as Avontus Scaffold Designer, scaffmax and Layher LayPLAN automates layout design and material lists. It only covers planning, which is a small side part of a laborer's erecting and dismantling work, not the physical assembly.

AI and telematics tools can monitor engine hours, oil pressure, and hydraulic fluid temperatures to schedule or predict maintenance. They only flag the work. Humans still do the greasing, cleaning, and repairs.
Equipment must be de-energized and locked out before anyone cleans, maintains, or repairs it (29 CFR 1926.417), and the work itself is done by hand with hand and power tools on site.
Job postings for repair and maintenance laborers list hands-on preventive maintenance, hand and power tool use, welding and grinding, and following lockout/tagout procedures.
O*NET describes finishing poured concrete as hands-on work: spreading, leveling and smoothing it with trowels, screeds and floats, and watching how wind, heat and cold affect curing on site.

The automated troweling that exists is done by physical robots and machines (for example Bright Dream's BDR-1 troweling robot and patented autonomous power trowels). A software-only AI agent without a body cannot do this work.
Even autonomous trowel robots have needed per-job reprogramming and may not reach the required finish quality, so automation of this task relies on robots and is still limited.

Pipe laying is done in the trench with physical equipment: a pipe laser projects a beam along the trench to set the gradient, and each pipe section is placed and aligned by hand against targets. A software-only agent cannot do any of this.
To line up the laser and pipe, someone in the trench has to place and move physical targets on the pipe and read the beam against them.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, a competent person named by the employer must inspect the trench on site every day and after events like rainstorms, and must have authority to fix hazards. This keeps the work tied to a human on site.

O*NET lists 'Provide assistance to craft workers, such as carpenters, plasterers, or masons' as a Construction Laborers task (importance 68). The neighbouring tasks are hands-on: erecting scaffolding and tending pumps for concrete and plaster.

Helper duties include supplying materials to masons, mixing mortar, plaster and grout by hand or machine, holding tools and materials, and cleaning work areas. All of this requires being on site and handling things physically.

A state job classification describes the work as helping carpenters erect scaffolding and helping drywall plasterers apply finishes. This is physical labor on construction sites, which a software-only agent cannot do.

In job postings, laborers handle the pump hose, spread concrete with rakes and shovels, consolidate it with hand-held or walk-behind vibrators and must be able to lift and carry 75 lb. All of this is physical work an agent without a body cannot do.

Software only helps with a small part of the job. Maturity sensors with AI or cloud analytics (Giatec SmartRock/Roxi, Maturix) estimate curing strength and suggest when forms can come off. They do not place, consolidate or physically protect concrete.
Vendor products like CEVO Digital use sensors and AI to plan when to strip formwork. They help with scheduling, not with the manual placing or curing protection a laborer does.

Operator competency standards for this work are all hands-on site work: checking floor machines, removing debris and adhesives, choosing machine speed, rotation and diamond tools, and running overlapping, staggered passes while watching motor load. A software-only agent with no robotics cannot do any of these steps.
Manual grinders are still common, and the quality of the finish depends heavily on the operator's skill. Riding multi-head machines also need an operator on site.

OSHA's silica standard (29 CFR 1926.1153, Table 1) treats concrete grinding as an on-site, high-exposure task that needs dust controls and sometimes respirators. It regulates worker safety but does not require a licensed human to perform or sign off the work.

Construction laborer job postings and the O*NET-based task lists describe this work as hands-on: mixing cement, sand, grout or cleaning solutions with tools such as a margin trowel, then spreading or mopping them onto surfaces. An agent with no body can't do this. At most it can look up mix ratios or read product data sheets, which is a small part of the time.
Minnesota's rule for laborer classifications treats mixing cement, plaster or stucco as physical support work done at a craft worker's direction. It doesn't require a licence or a sign-off.
OSHA guidance says mixing mortar or concrete exposes the worker to silica dust on site and calls for controls there. This confirms the task is done in person with the materials.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1926.850, a competent person must do an engineering survey on site before workers start demolition. They must also check adjacent structures, shore or brace weakened walls and shut off utilities. All of this means being physically present.

AI tools for deconstruction planning mostly do research- or pilot-stage material assessment from scans, thermal imaging or drone data. The actual removal is still done by manual crews or future robots, not software agents.
Mattersite turns 3D scans and point clouds into pre-demolition material reports. Digital help is limited to inventory and estimates, not the work of tearing down buildings or salvaging materials.

Glazier software's AI-assisted takeoff reads uploaded floor plans, finds the glazing scope, applies default glass and edgework templates, and exports to estimates or purchase orders. The user still makes selections and reviews the result before exporting.

Ruh AI says (vendor marketing, not verified) its glazing takeoff measures curtain wall by system from elevations, measures storefront in linear feet, counts openings and separates glass area using the elevations and schedules.

General AI takeoff tools such as Bobyard and Attentive automatically extract quantities from construction drawings. The search found no tool that produces a full lite-by-lite glass makeup straight from drawings, and no tool that plans staging or scaffolding from site conditions. Those steps still rely on human judgment and field checks.

To secure a mirror, a worker screws a J-channel into the wall studs, applies beads of mastic to the back of the glass, sets the heavy glass in place and clips it while the adhesive cures. All of this is hands-on work that an agent with no physical body cannot do.

The guidance on which mastic to use, where to support the mirror and how long it cures is already in manufacturer documents, so software can only help with looking up information. It cannot do the act of securing the mirror.

Mounting guides describe hand steps: leveling the clips or channels, placing the adhesive and getting the screws into studs. None of them mention a licence or sign-off needed to install a mirror. This was checked against DIY and trade guides only, not legal sources.

Manufacturer glass configurators such as AGC's can configure single, insulating and laminated glazing and find products by optical, thermal, acoustic and safety performance. This is the part of the task that turns a specification into a glass type, and an agent can do it in software.
Vitro Construct, which is built on LBNL's WINDOW software, lets users choose pane count, thickness, coatings and laminates from tables. An agent operating a browser could run these tools.

Building codes such as IRC R308 set rules for safety glazing in hazardous locations and require permanent marks on the glass. These rules are written down and an agent can check them. No licence or sign-off by the glazier is required to select the glass. The physical work is still done by a person: picking the actual sheet or mirror from stock, checking its color by eye and matching existing glass on site.

In the US, the EPA's Renovation, Repair and Painting (RRP) rule covers paid work that disturbs paint in homes, schools and child-care facilities built before 1978. It requires a certified firm and a certified renovator, and the training includes hands-on practice. This means a person must physically do and oversee the paint removal.

Robots that remove paint by blasting or water jet do exist, but they are physical machines. Some are steered by a human with a joystick, and most are built for ship hulls, tanks, aircraft and factory parts. An AI agent that only works through software cannot do this kind of work.

Companies that sell AI-guided robots for surface preparation say the biggest obstacle is how much surfaces vary. Stripping, sanding, wire brushing, burning and blasting on a job site are all hands-on work.

Faux finishing is hands-on work done at the wall. The painter puts on a base coat, then dabs glaze with a sea sponge, bunched rag, stippling brush or comb, and has to work wet glaze across a whole wall in one session. An agent with no body can't do any of these steps.

Rag rolling means applying glaze with a roller and lifting it off with a rag by hand. Software can only help at the edges, for example by looking up glaze ratios or mocking up colors. It can't do the core work.
Guides recommend testing the technique on scrap board or a hidden area first and choosing the base coat sheen on site. These are physical judgment steps that need someone present.
Pipe-zone backfill goes in lifts of 8 inches or less, and each lift is compacted by hand tamping or mechanical means without damaging the pipe. This is physical work done in the trench.
Bedding and backfill must meet required compaction levels (for example 6-inch bedding at 90% relative compaction), which crews achieve on site with equipment.
Heavy compaction or vibratory equipment has to be kept about 0.9 to 1.2 m from the pipe, so the work relies on hands-on handling of equipment and material in the field.

Pipelayer duties are hands-on work in the trench: laying and joining sanitary and storm sewer pipe, installing manholes and catch basins, setting grade with lasers or grade rods, and backfilling and compacting.
The job means digging to the required depth, moving trench boxes, and running compaction equipment. Workers must follow OSHA trenching safety rules, and all of this needs a person on site.
Postings describe the job as manual pipe installation and repair in excavations. An agent with no body or robotics could help only at the edges, for example by looking up specs or reading plans.

KONE 24/7 Connected Services uses cloud-based AI analytics on sensor data to flag elevator and escalator faults and to judge whether each one is critical. Technicians get alerts and diagnoses before they reach the site. A human still confirms and fixes the fault on site, so the AI helps with fault-finding but does not do it.

Otis ONE sends equipment sensor data to the cloud so engineers can spot and diagnose faults before arriving on site. The physical checks of brakes, motors, switches and controllers with meters and other test equipment are still done by hand.
In Illinois, a person needs an elevator mechanic license to maintain, alter or repair a conveyance. This puts troubleshooting work on the equipment in the hands of licensed people.
Employer postings for septic and vacuum truck drivers require a commercial driver's license (Class A or B), often with a tanker endorsement. That means a licensed human must drive the vehicle.

Sewage truck operator postings ask for a Class B CDL at minimum, with endorsements depending on the truck's weight and waste capacity. The job is physically operating heavy vehicles, which a software-only AI agent can't do; it could only help with side work like route planning.
In septic pumper technician roles the same person drives the truck, carries equipment and crew, and does the on-site work, so the driving can't be split off to software.

Matching cable and cutter size to pipe diameter is a simple lookup in published charts (for example, 3/8-inch cable for 2-3 inch lines, 5/8-inch for 3-6 inch mains). The real work is fitting the cutter onto the cable by hand, which an AI agent cannot do.
Commercial drain machines come with physical cutter sets that a person mounts on the cable at the drum or reel. No software or AI product does this step.

To find an excavation point, a worker puts a camera or sonde into the pipe, sweeps the ground with a receiver, and marks the spot using a measuring wheel. All of these steps are physical work done on site.

In some states, excavators must physically mark the dig area with white paint, flags or stakes before requesting a utility locate. Arizona's new rule says electronic mapping alone does not meet this requirement.

Washington, Oregon and Iowa all require white-lining (marking the dig area in white) before calling 811, so marking is a physical field act. These sources do not require a licensed person to sign the marking.

O*NET lists 'Dig out sewer lines manually, using shovels' as a Core task (importance 63) for Septic Tank Servicers and Sewer Pipe Cleaners (47-4071.00). The task is manual excavation, so it needs a person on site using hand tools.
The occupation is about cleaning and repairing septic tanks, sewer lines and drains in person, including fixing breaks in underground piping. A software-only agent cannot do any of this.

Field-service software used by trades such as septic pumping lets users create purchase orders by choosing a vendor, job and items. Orders above a set limit need an approver's sign-off, and receiving is tracked by truck or warehouse location. A human approval step is still part of the normal process.

A septic-specific vendor says its automation tracks stock of pumps, filters and risers and creates purchase orders when items reach a reorder point. This shows that the ordering steps can be automated, but it is the vendor's own marketing claim.

Procurement agents in 2026 can spot a shortfall, shortlist approved vendors, write and send purchase orders, and log them. People still handle exceptions and approvals. In this job, the need for a tool often comes from damage or wear that a worker finds on site.
ATM field service work means hands-on repair and swapping parts at the module level on site. Postings ask for the mechanical skill to take components apart and put them back together.

Technicians use smartphones to get work orders and open support documents. That is the only digital part an AI agent could help with, such as finding reassembly steps; the reassembly itself is physical.
ATM technician jobs are on-site roles for repair, maintenance and replacement, with no licence requirement for reassembly. Physical presence is the only thing stopping an AI agent from doing it.

O*NET lists this task for occupation 49-2011.00. It involves taking machines apart by hand and inspecting wires, gears and bearings with hand or power tools and measuring devices, which is physical manipulation.

A posting for an ATM cassette repair technician describes the job as hands-on: troubleshooting with hand tools, replacing worn parts, cleaning mechanisms and calibrating to the manufacturer's specifications.
O*NET says the occupation includes travel to customer sites for service or emergency repairs, so the technician has to be there in person.

AI-native test frameworks such as GlobalLogic TAK and HCLTech Turbo, along with LLM multi-agent systems like NeTestLLM, can generate, run and analyse validation tests for telecom equipment and protocols from software. This covers the remote, software-side checks of updated equipment.

Patent filings and products describe remote autonomous testing of telecom and wireless networks without a site visit. That supports delegating post-update functional checks, but on-site physical test hookups and visual observation still need a human.

Some states license low-voltage and telecom technicians. For example, Rhode Island's TST licence covers installing, servicing and testing systems. These licences govern who works on the equipment, but they generally do not require a licensed person to sign off on each test.

Nokia's Gemini-powered Assurance Center agents (router agent and event triage agent) are already running and do network fault triage and diagnosis. Operators keep the final say over critical actions, and only low-risk cases are closed-loop automated.
TM Forum's Agentic NOC catalyst says current AIOps stops at recommendation and leaves humans to drive each step. Its goal of autonomous closed-loop remediation is still at project stage.

Remote testing is done in software: switches are reached over telnet or a remote maintenance system to run card and line diagnostics. Remote testing can isolate faults and avoid sending a technician, although some faults still need someone on site.

O*NET lists this as a core task for SOC 49-2092.00: taking apart faulty equipment with hand tools so it can be repaired. That means physical manipulation of motors and power tools, which a software-only agent with no robotics cannot do. At most it can look up service manuals or exploded-view diagrams, which is a small share of the time.
Related core tasks in this occupation, such as testing, reassembling and rebuilding parts, also rely on hand tools, power tools and electrical meters. The work is hands-on at the workbench.

The occupation is described as repairing, maintaining or installing electric motors, wiring or switches. Taking equipment apart does not typically require a licence or a human signature; the physical work itself is what keeps an agent out.

O*NET lists this occupation's work as hands-on: inspecting, testing, rebuilding and reassembling motors with hand tools, power tools and electrical meters. Making a joint is physical work, and the only part an AI could help with is looking up procedures or specs.
The IPC J-STD-001 hand-soldering credential certifies a person's manual soldering skill. Job postings usually list it as preferred, not as a legal licence requirement.
J-STD-001 training is aimed at operators who already have hands-on soldering experience, which shows the core of the task is manual dexterity.

Battery terminal cleaning is hands-on physical work: disconnecting terminals, scrubbing with a wire brush and baking-soda paste, rinsing, drying and reconnecting, while wearing gloves and eye protection.
Corrosive battery acid makes PPE and physical handling necessary. Software can do no more than give guidance, such as safety steps or which cleaner to use for heavy buildup.

AMETEK Insight is a cloud tool that lets operators monitor battery performance, adjust charge settings and update charger firmware remotely. This covers the digital part of operating a charger, but not repairing one.

ACTview is a browser-based platform that collects data from Quantum chargers and BATTview battery monitors to help diagnose charger and battery problems. An agent could analyze this data, but a person still has to do the physical repair: replacing components, rewiring, connecting batteries.

Saft Intelli-Connect monitors temperature, current, voltage and electrolyte level remotely so maintenance can be scheduled by condition. This helps with diagnosis and planning, but the hands-on maintenance stays physical.

OSHA's construction asbestos standard (29 CFR 1926.1101) requires training by class of work for any worker who handles or disturbs asbestos-containing material. Class I/II work needs EPA Model Accreditation Plan-equivalent training, Class III needs 16-hour O&M-equivalent training, and the work needs a competent person on site. A trained human has to do it.
OSHA says asbestos competent persons must be able to identify hazards and choose control strategies on site. That is in-person supervision of hands-on work.

Asbestos training under 1926.1101(k)(9) covers recognizing damage and deterioration of ACM at the actual work location. Sealing joints with putty extruders and knives is manual work that an AI without a body cannot do. Software can only help with side lookups such as material specs or safety procedures.

Fleet maintenance software (Fullbay) builds repair estimates from labor time guides, parts data, PM history and live parts pricing and availability, so most of the estimating work is already automated.
ShopView's heavy-duty truck labor guide advertises VIN-specific labor times and AI-generated estimates and work orders from a repair prompt. These are vendor claims, not independent tests.

ARI offers AI labor guides that find parts and labor line items and move them into quotes or invoices, which covers the main pricing sub-steps. A technician still has to diagnose the fault and confirm the scope before the estimate is used.

The Megger DELTA4000 12-kV tan delta test set runs automatic tip-up tests and uses PowerDB software for automated testing and reporting. Software already handles the measurement and calculation, but a technician still has to set up and connect the equipment in the field.
Analysts still read bushing power factor voltage and frequency sweeps visually by plotting them. An agent could help with this interpretation and with reports from exported data.

DELTA-series test sets send high test voltages to substation apparatus and their stored results can be exported to a PC. The core work is physically hooking leads to de-energized and grounded equipment, which an agent without a body cannot do.
Substations are restricted to qualified persons, so supervising splicing on site needs a qualified human who is physically there.

Splicing and termination supervision is a field role held by a sub-foreman who splices and terminates XLPE, PILC and PR cables. An agent could only help with scheduling, color-code schedules and records.
Checking that the color-code sequence was followed is done by visual inspection of the physical termination. Wiring color schedules follow ICEA E-1 and E-2, which software can document.
Dielectric breakdown testing (ASTM D1816/D877) means drawing oil samples on site from breakers or transformers and running them through a high-voltage test cell, which is physical, hands-on work.
Software only helps with the digital side: it turns oil and DGA test results into trends, diagnostics and maintenance work orders. It does not do the sampling, testing or refilling.

Vendor tools claim to turn oil lab reports into prioritized work orders automatically. These claims are promotional and not independently confirmed, and they cover only recordkeeping and interpretation.

AI predictive-maintenance tools already use FFT-based vibration analysis from installed sensors to flag faults such as misalignment, unbalance, loose foot, bearing defects and worn belts. This covers only the monitoring and analysis part of the task, and it depends on sensors and data that are already in place.

Most of the task happens on the machine itself: watching and listening to it run and placing test leads on circuits. Using test instruments on energized equipment is limited to qualified persons wearing arc-flash PPE.

Vendor and practitioner sources say poor data is the most common reason AI diagnostics fail. A human still has to observe the machine and take the measurements, while the AI helps by interpreting readings and suggesting troubleshooting steps.

Modern CMMS platforms already support reorder points, safety stock calculations and automated purchase requests. AI adds dynamic reorder thresholds. The source is a vendor blog, so treat it as vendor-reported.

Technicians log the parts they use against a work order from a mobile device, which updates inventory. Purchase orders are created automatically when stock falls to its minimum. The ground truth about what was actually used still comes from the technician who did the repair. This is a vendor claim and has not been independently checked.
AI systems can pull parts lists into generated work orders and send them on for action. This is vendor marketing, so treat it as vendor-reported.

Line installers dig the ground open for underground cable with trenchers, cable plows, borers and digger derricks, and then lay cable in the trench or in conduit. This is physical, on-site work with heavy equipment.

State dig laws (for example Washington RCW 19.122 and Colorado) require a locate request through 811 two to three business days before digging. An agent could file this request online, but it is only a small part of the task's time.
Under Idaho law the person who actually does the digging is responsible for making sure the locate request was made and pays for any damage. That puts the liability on the human excavator on site.
O*NET lists polishing instruments with rags and polishing compounds, buffing wheels or burnishing tools as a hands-on task for musical instrument repairers.

Professional polishing is physical work: a buffing wheel is used first with Tripoli compound to cut out scratches, then with red rouge to bring up the color. A software-only agent with no robotics cannot do this.
Before re-buffing, the instrument usually has to be taken apart and the old lacquer stripped with solvents, which are more hands-on steps. No licence or sign-off rule applies to this task.

Repair shops strip lacquer by physically dipping instruments in chemical tanks such as methylene chloride, then brite-dip them and scratch-brush them by hand. This is hands-on chemical handling that a software-only agent cannot do.

Removing tarnish and corrosion from brass is an industrial bright-dip process that needs physical immersion, PPE and ventilation. An AI agent could at most look up process settings or safety data sheets.
O*NET lists the task as attaching, altering and trimming wire, insulation and coils with hand tools. This is hands-on work at the bench.

Related tasks are also physical: cutting, stripping and bending wire leads with pliers and wire scrapers, and lining slots with sheet insulation. Software agents without robotics cannot do any of this.
This is a production job and needs no licence. The only barrier is physical manipulation, and the reference AI agents have no body.

Vendor says its bakery vision systems could signal oven controls to change zone temperatures, belt speed or steam injection when bake color drifts, in near real time. The wording is conditional and comes from the vendor.
Camera inspection links pale or dark crust to oven temperature drift, conveyor speed changes and steam-injection timing errors.

Vision platforms can send rejects and alarms through PLC/MES, the plant-control link that automatic adjustment depends on. Without camera feeds and networked oven controls, observing and adjusting stays physical and on-site.

Dedicated sensor-based adaptive control systems such as Caron TMAC track spindle load, adjust feed rate in real time through the CNC control and detect wear or breakage. This shows the main sub-steps can be automated, but only with special sensors and a direct link to the machine control, which a general software agent would not normally have.

AI tool-wear monitoring platforms combine spindle power, vibration and acoustic signals, but each spindle needs its own sensors and signal processing. Without that hardware, a software agent cannot 'listen' to a machine on the shop floor.

In TMAC case studies, a backup tool is called automatically when wear goes over the limit. Without that setup, an operator has to change dull tools or fix vibration by hand at the machine, so a human must be there.

Caron TMAC 3.0 is a commercial adaptive control system. It reads power, vibration or strain sensors, raises or lowers feed as tools wear, marks worn tools as expired and stops the machine and retracts the tool if it breaks. This is dedicated controller hardware, not a general software agent, and the physical tool change still happens at the machine.

Heidenhain iTNC 530 Adaptive Feed Control changes feed based on spindle power against limits set in a teach-in cut. Feed adjustment is built into the control on the shop floor, not reachable by a remote AI agent.

A 2026 research system adjusts CNC milling feed automatically from tool wear measured by vibration sensors. This shows that sensor-driven feed changes are possible, while diagnosing malfunctions and changing tools stay hands-on work.

Research in 2025-2026 shows LLMs can edit and optimize existing CAM-generated G-code. In one small test on a single Haas machine, ChatGPT-revised code cut cycle time by about 37%. Commercial CAM agents, such as Cimatron's shown at IMTS 2026, generate toolpaths automatically. So the editing step itself can largely be done in software.

LLM G-code generation still needs syntax and geometry checks plus correction from user feedback (GLLM self-corrective approach). A human or simulator therefore has to check the code before it runs on the machine.

Operators usually change programs in Edit mode on the machine's own control panel and save them there. They also adjust feed overrides and tool offsets, and confirm changes with test cuts. Spotting problems like chatter, tool wear or out-of-tolerance parts, and checking the fix, takes physical presence at a control that is often not networked.

Vendor tools such as Workerbase's Troubleshooting Agent pull machine error history, SOPs and OEM manuals together to suggest fixes for alarms at the machine. The operator still asks the questions and does the work, so this helps the human rather than replacing them.

Shop-floor monitoring agents can spot anomalies and send information to the right person. That covers the routing and drafting parts of escalating a problem, but someone at the machine still has to observe and report the fault.

Customer contract clauses hold further fabrication until the first article is accepted. The approval comes from authorized people in the quality system, not from the operator, and no law requires a human operator to perform this step.
O*NET lists cleaning machines, tooling or parts with solvents or solutions and rags as a task for CNC tool operators. This is hands-on physical work.
In shop practice, operators sweep, mop and use degreaser and shop rags on the machine, the work area and the inspection table. A software-only agent cannot do any of this.

The other option is automated parts washers, which are physical equipment, not AI agents. Manual solvent cleaning also requires PPE and disposing of used rags as hazardous waste. This source is a vendor selling parts washers.

CAM vendors offer agentic AI that builds toolpaths and creates or updates operations and parameters. Examples are the Cimatron CAM Agent shown at IMTS 2026 and the ENCY AI Superagent, in closed beta from April 2026. These are vendor claims, and I found no independent check that the output is ready to run on a machine.
The SprutCAM X assistant writes G-code from a text description and explains existing G-code line by line, so editing program text is something software can already do.

Competency standards have the operator enter tool offsets in the machine controller, run first-off samples, check them against the specification and then edit speeds, feeds and operation sequence. This means hands-on work at the machine control and a physical prove-out that an agent cannot do.

Shot peen operators read blueprints and work orders, then lay out and mark peen areas by measuring and marking or by fitting templates and peeling maskant. They also fill hoppers with the specified shot size and type. All of this is hands-on work.
Specifications require no-peen areas to be physically masked with maskant, tape or rubber/metal masks. An AI agent could only help by reading drawings and specs or suggesting a layout.
O*NET lists this task for CNC Tool Operators (51-9161.00).
Tool-life management systems (usage counters, wear prediction from sensors) only signal when a tool is worn. Removing and installing the tool is still a physical job on the machine.
Patents describe manual drill changes as machine downtime done by hand. Automatic tool changers and robotic bit changers are mechanical or robotic hardware, not software agents.
Industry sources say manual bit replacement limits full automation and carries safety risks, which confirms the task is hands-on.

With manual edge finding, the operator jogs the edge finder at the machine in very small steps until it pops off center. The operator then stores that position in the work offset and adjusts for the tool radius. All of this is hands-on work at the machine.

Siemens separates manual edge-finder touching, where the operator confirms contact and the CNC saves the zero, from switching-probe cycles that find and save the zero automatically. The automatic cycles still need a probe installed, the part fixtured and the cycle called correctly in the NC program.

Probing G-code routines and vendor wizards can find a workpiece corner and set X, Y and Z to zero. Software, including AI that drafts these routines, can cover only the programming part. Installing the probe and placing it at the part stay physical work.
Setting up lathe work means physically clamping stock in a chuck, sometimes changing chucks, and loosening locking rings with a spanner. All of this is hands-on work with hand tools at the machine.

Shop procedures require the operator to physically check that the chuck is tight and the workpiece is rigidly secured, support long stock with a tailstock, and remove the chuck key before starting. The hazards include fingers caught by slipping jaws and long workpieces bending and striking the operator.

OSHA 1910.212 places machine-guarding duties on employers and says hand tools for loading may supplement guarding but not replace it. It does not require a licensed person to load the lathe, so the barrier here is physical rather than legal.
Melt-shop molten-metal sampling is automated with dedicated robots, such as the SMS X-Pact Sampler built on ABB or COMAU arms. That is physical robotics. A software-only AI agent cannot do it.

Polytec's PolySAMPLE robot takes molten-metal samples and temperature readings with little human involvement. Its stated purpose is keeping workers out of the hazardous area next to the melt, which shows the task needs a physical presence there.

Robots handling sublance sampling probes at voestalpine Linz replaced manual work at the furnace. The automation is in the hardware. A software agent could at most send the sampling signal or log the request, which is a small part of the task.
SST Temperature AI at Marienhütte Graz uses neural networks to estimate arc-furnace melt temperature and give recommendations 24/7. It supports operators and does not replace them.
ABP FoundryCloud, built with Zorc, sends AI-based suggestions for melting parameters to foundry workers. It is advisory, and people still carry out the adjustments.

Inductotherm's Melt-Manager Plus works out the energy needed to reach pouring temperature on induction furnaces. It is an embedded control system, not a general-purpose agent, and torch or flame furnaces still need someone on site to watch the melt color and adjust them by hand.

LevelField-1 is an open-source vision-language model that reads 2D drawings, pulls out dimensions and tolerances, and proposes process routes across 18 machining types. Its developer reports that process engineers still review the output and that drafting time fell by about 60% in pilots. These figures are the developer's own and have not been independently checked.
An academic pipeline for reading engineering drawings retrieved dimensions with about 81% end-to-end accuracy. That is good enough to speed up the work, but a human still has to check the results.

An informal test found that frontier language models can only sometimes plan how to machine simple parts. This suggests a human is still needed to confirm the operation sequence and the equipment choice.
O*NET lists marking identification numbers or symbols onto patterns or templates as a core task for metal and plastic patternmakers. The work is done by hand on physical patterns.

Foundries put numbers on patterns, using prefix letters for the intended metal (B for bronze, C for cast iron) and paint colours for features like machined surfaces. An agent could help pick or look up the right code, but someone has to apply it physically.

Pattern labels support process control and quality tracking, and foundries use equipment that embosses date codes and heat numbers onto patterns. The marking itself is physical, so software can only help with the codes and the label design.

Furnace loading is automated only with dedicated industrial robots, such as 6-axis or FANUC arms with grippers and vision that place parts in baskets, fixtures or on furnace belts. A software-only AI agent has no such physical capability.
Robotic furnace loaders for conveyor and sinter furnaces are custom hardware cells, for example the Adaptec Model 100A with a magnetic gripper. This confirms the task means physically handling parts.

Heat treat operations have traditionally relied on manual loading and batch transfer, and placing parts correctly in baskets affects how evenly they heat and how much they distort. This is physical handling work that is done in person.

Shafts and similar parts are mounted for induction hardening by hand: the operator places the workpiece on the lower center and pushes the upper end between the holding blocks of a fixture. This is physical handling that needs no software.
Where loading is automated, it is done by machine hardware such as escapements and indexing spiders with spindle centers, not by software agents. A system with no body cannot mount parts.
In crankshaft hardening, the part is clamped between a chuck and a lower center. This is mechanical work on the shop floor with no licensing or sign-off requirement.

Spotting means handling the garment by hand on a spotting board. The worker positions the stain over the board's vacuum nose, applies steam and detergent, and tamps the fabric on the solid part of the board.
Spotting boards have glass, marble or stainless-steel tops, and the worker tamps garments on that surface. This is physical manipulation of the textile, which an agent limited to software cannot do.

The patented spotting systems treat, inspect and track articles with steam and vacuum stations, but a person still places the garment on the station. Software only handles the tracking and inspection data, not spreading or positioning the article.

Colour-matching software such as X-Rite Color iMatch suggests dye formulas and searches past recipes. It still needs spectrophotometer measurements and a physical lab dip made and checked by the dyer, so a human does the physical matching and the AI only assists.

Datacolor Match Textile handles dye compatibility and colour shifts after dyeing when building a formula. It helps with knowing dye properties, but it relies on measurement hardware that small dry cleaners usually don't have.

Commercial colour matching starts by measuring a physical sample with a spectrophotometer, followed by dyeing fabric lab dips by hand. Both steps need someone physically present to handle the garment, dyes and bleaching agents.

Automated sewing of this kind needs dedicated robotic hardware. SoftWear Automation's Sewbot uses vision plus vacuum grippers to steer fabric through the needle. A software-only AI agent has no body and cannot do this.

The task is physical by nature: the fabric has to be fed under the needle stitch by stitch, with corrections for how the cloth stretches and turns. The agent cannot reach this through any digital channel.
Robotic sewing exists only in a few niches, such as T-shirts, towels and denim. Even there, it is robots doing the work, not software agents, so it falls outside the reference technology.

Folding and stretching fabric edges while sewing is done by hand at the machine. The automated alternatives are specialised robot hardware such as F-FOLD end-effectors and dual-roller stretch systems, not software agents.

Robotic sewing uses grippers, suction devices and vision-guided hardware to hold and tension fabric. Many complex operations are still hard to automate cost-effectively, and a software agent with no body cannot do any of it.
Research on stretching fabric during automated sewing relies on physical roller mechanisms that match fabric tension to sewing speed, which confirms this is a manual or mechanical task.
Marker-making and nesting software (e.g., Tukatech SMARTmark) automates the digital planning of cut layouts, but this is upstream of the operator's manual cutting.
Cut-room software plans cuts and nests pieces. The physical cutting itself is done by people with knives or scissors, or by dedicated CNC cutting hardware, not by a software-only agent.
Automatic fabric cutting needs a physical gantry and oscillating knife. Nesting tools like Deepnest only supply the layout.

The task is cutting fabric by hand on the garment itself: trimming, grading and notching seam allowances with shears so seams lie flat. A software-only agent with no body cannot do this physical work.
It is done with hand tools such as notching scissors, which trim excess fabric and cut V-notches in one stroke.
One shortcut is to angle the shears and grade both seam allowances in a single cut. That kind of tactile skill can't be handed to a digital agent.

Automation of buttonholing and button attachment is done by dedicated industrial sewing machines such as Yuho's buttonhole feeders and button-sewing indexers, which still need operators to load and handle garments. Software AI agents have no part in it.
Button-attaching machines physically handle the fabric and buttons, and manual loading and unloading by operators is a recognized labor cost. The task is hands-on.
Operating a button-attach machine is taught as a hands-on skill in sewing-machine-operator training, which shows the task is physical manipulation.

For CNC equipment, cabinet and CAM software (Mozaik, Cabinet Vision, Fusion, EnRoute, PartNester) can already nest parts and write toolpaths and G-code. An agent could prepare these programs. Someone still has to load the stock, fit the tooling and run the machine by hand.

Vendor and user material on CNC cabinet production describes a workflow from design export through nesting to per-sheet G-code. Software only automates the programming step. Material handling and machine setup remain physical work.

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.213 sets point-of-operation guarding rules for saws, jointers, shapers and similar machines. This confirms the task means hands-on operation of dangerous machinery. It does not require a licensed person to sign off.

Cabinet design packages such as Cabinet Vision, KCD, SketchList 3D and Mozaik build cut lists and CNC-ready output from a 3D design. KCD checks that measurements and machining instructions are consistent. These tools cover much of the work of setting specifications and planning operations, but a human still enters the design.

A 2026 roundup lists AI-assisted cabinet design tools. One of them, WoodWright, claims to cover design, cut lists and CNC output, but its listing is a third-party review. I found no confirmed product that turns scanned 2D drawings straight into a buildable model, so a human still has to review and correct the output.

Cabinetmaker trade certification is voluntary in every Canadian province and territory. Australian licensing applies to on-site installation, not to reading drawings or planning work, so no licence requires a human to sign this task.

O*NET lists reading blueprints, drawings or written specifications to work out pattern sizes, shapes and machine setups as a core task for wood patternmakers. The other core duties are physical: laying out stock, running bandsaws and lathes, assembling and measuring.

AI tools and research systems can already pull dimensions and tolerances from engineering drawings automatically. Reported accuracy is about 81% for a research pipeline and 90-95% in vendor claims, so a human still needs to check the output. The search found no tool built for foundry pattern allowances such as shrinkage, draft or core prints.
None of the career sources mention a license or certification requirement for wood patternmakers. Training is a high school diploma or a post-secondary certificate, plus apprenticeship.

Foundry ERP software such as iCast ERP lists pattern management features, including lifecycle tracking, maintenance schedules and history. An agent with computer use could enter, update and cross-reference these records in software like this.
FOMIS foundry software covers pattern and tool administration together with traceability and certificate records. This shows pattern record-keeping is already digitised in commercial systems.

In general ERPs like Epicor, patterns are tracked as inventory items through standard transaction reports. That makes record upkeep a software job, but a human on the shop floor still has to check the physical pattern's condition, measurements, tags and storage location.
Algorithms and CAD methods exist that automatically choose the parting direction and parting line for cast and molded parts, so an agent can help with planning where to divide a pattern.
Split patterns are made by cutting the wooden pattern into pieces and adding dowels and guide holes. This is physical shop work done with saws, planes and drills.
O*NET lists dividing patterns into sections as a core task for wood patternmakers, alongside shaping and joining the parts with hand tools.

Mills automate board measurement and cut marking with dedicated scanners and optimizers built into the production line. These are physical sensors and machinery, not software agents. An agent with no body cannot handle a ruler, square or caliper on a workpiece.

Optimization software and the cut markers or projectors it drives (for example VAB's Pointer Projector) need scanning and marking hardware installed in the mill. An AI agent could at most do the small calculation part, such as cut lists and tolerance checks.
Vision systems that check cuts and grades are scanning hardware fixed on the production line, which shows that checking cut accuracy depends on physical sensing rather than on digital documents.

Dedicated sawmill scanners such as Lucidyne, Weinig CombiScan and FinScan use deep learning with cameras, lasers and x-ray to find defects and grade lumber. They are fixed industrial machines with sensors, not general software AI agents. In one study they were more accurate than human line graders.

A Microtec Goldeneye scanner with the GradeView algorithm graded 9,454 hardwood boards with 92% grade accuracy. Most of its errors came from board geometry, which means the board has to be physically measured and handled.

Accredited agencies own the grade stamps and run spot checks on mills. Certified graders or machine grading apply the stamps, but this applies to official grade stamping, not to an operator's routine inspection of stock at the saw.

Automatic lubrication pumps (e.g., Graco G3) can be programmed to deliver lubricant to bandsaw guides and bearings, but these are physical machine systems that humans still have to install, refill and clean. They are not AI agents. A sawmill has 300-500 lubrication points.
In sawmills, lubrication programs mean hands-on work at each lubrication point. Software can only help with scheduling and tracking.
In a hardwood mill, the shift from manual to automatic lubrication was a hardware change. It still needed physical maintenance and a choice of lubricant.

Machines that scan for defects and optimize cuts already find flaws, work out the best cuts from a cut list and send them to a CNC crosscut saw. These are dedicated mill machines, not software agents, and the work still happens at the physical stock.
The TigerSaw1000 reads cut lists, but someone still marks defects on the board in crayon. This shows that measuring and marking stock is hands-on work at the board.

The software step, matching order data against flaw locations to produce cut lines, is the only part a software-only agent could help with. The physical measuring and marking stays with a person or a machine.

Setting knives means unplugging the machine, placing a jig on the cutterhead, loosening the set screws, raising or lowering each knife to the right height and tightening it again. Every step is done by hand at the machine.

Automatic tool changers on CNC routers swap bits on their own, but people still load and preset the tool holders by hand. That is automation built into the machine, not a software agent doing the job.
Workers must use safe practices such as isolation and lock-outs while setting up the machine. This is a workplace safety rule, not a licence or sign-off requirement.

In plants with a DCS (distributed control system), open/close commands for motor-operated valves and drives come from the DCS and run through interposing relays. Every drive still has a local emergency stop pushbutton, so manual field operation remains part of the job.

Automated unit start-up sequences already exist, but they stop at breakpoints where the operator checks the stage and presses a permission button to continue. Many plants still start units in a very manual way.
NERC Reliability Standard PER-003 requires operators in real-time positions that control the Bulk Electric System to hold NERC certification. Licensed humans are expected to be in the control loop.

AI computer-vision and gas-monitoring tools for chemical plants flag unsafe conditions and suspend permits automatically. Vendors such as Intenseye present them as an addition to gas detection and process-safety instruments, not a replacement. This is support for the human operator.

Industry guidance (AIChE CCPS) calls for continuous monitoring on site, stopping work when combustible gas is found, and gas testing by certified testers. These are physical steps done in the field that only a qualified person can carry out.

Under OSHA PSM 29 CFR 1910.119, employers must train process operators and run a hot work permit program. Training providers and site policies say permits must be approved and signed by authorized people, so a human stays accountable for the safety precautions.

Vendors say agentic systems already watch chemical-plant process data and flag anomalies before normal alarms go off, and claim deployments at over 30 plants. These are press-release claims, not independent results. Celanese's JO.AI reportedly uses an anomaly-flagging agent across 50 plants (secondary source citing Forbes). Yokogawa says its FKDPP AI controlled a chemical plant on its own for 35 days.

In PSM-covered processes, operator rounds still include physical field checks: local pressure and temperature gauges, tell-tale gauges, tank levels, heat tracing and taking samples. An agent with no body cannot do these.

Vendors sell wireless instrumentation to digitize manual gauge rounds because charting gauges by hand is time-consuming and error-prone. This suggests the digital share of monitoring is growing but many plants still do it manually. OSHA PSM (29 CFR 1910.119) requires trained operators and management procedures, but I found no rule that only a human may read instruments.

PLC-controlled CIP systems already automate the rinse, chemical and final-rinse phases. They switch between acid, alkali and hot-water phases and control flow and temperature, but this is dedicated plant automation that has to be pre-installed. A software agent cannot do this on its own.
Mobile CIP units run on a Siemens S7-1200 PLC with pneumatic valves. Someone still has to bring the unit to the equipment and connect it physically, which needs on-site manual work.
Plants without CIP clean tanks manually, and operators handle hoses, valves and chemicals by hand. Automating this needs a physical retrofit that an agent with no body cannot carry out.

O*NET lists this as a core task for SOC 51-9012.00, with an importance rating of 82. It covers installing, maintaining or repairing hoses, pumps, filters and screens on processing equipment by hand with hand tools, so it needs a person physically present.

In this occupation, workers set up and tend filter presses, shaker screens, centrifuges and stills on the shop floor. A related task is clearing clogs from machines and screens, which is also physical work done on the equipment.

An AI agent without a body or robotics cannot use hand tools. Its only possible help is minor: looking up part specifications or repair manuals, or logging maintenance work orders. That is a small share of the time spent on the task, which is why share_delegable is 5.

One patented chain-wear monitor uses a proximity sensor and a camera mounted along the conveyor to measure chain pitch and estimate wear. This kind of tool needs dedicated hardware installed on the machine, so a software-only agent cannot do the inspection alone.

Vendors describe AI vision systems that flag belt tears, edge wear and splice wear and send alerts to maintenance software. These need fixed cameras on site. Without them, someone has to look at and handle the chains, belts or scrolls in person, and an agent could only help with interpreting images or keeping records.
Vendor pages claim AI vision cameras can detect belt tears and estimate remaining belt life, but the accuracy figures they give have not been checked independently.

Minor ingredients, about 5–10% of a batch, are traditionally scooped, weighed and carried to the mixer by hand, then added through a hatch. This is physical handling that a software-only agent cannot do.

Where ingredient addition is automated, it is done by dedicated dosing hardware such as loss-in-weight feeders and barcode-verified pre-mix stations under PLC or MES control, not by AI agents. At most, software guides the operator through weighing steps.
Vendors sell operator-guided micro-ingredient weighing alongside fully automated dosing equipment. In both cases the human or the machine does the physical addition.

Electronic batch record and MES products already log material moves, parameter readings and equipment data automatically. They time-stamp each entry against the master record and flag out-of-tolerance values for review by exception. This means an agent connected to these systems could fill in most of the forms.

Vendors say batch records combine automatic equipment and automation data with operator entries. Manual inputs are still needed for observations that are not instrumented, and a person has to physically read those at the mixer.

21 CFR 211.188(b)(11) requires batch records in regulated industries to name the person who performed, supervised or checked each significant step. If equipment did the step automatically, the record must name the person who checked it. So a human still has to sign or verify.

Manufacturing job postings describe this work as loading, unloading, stacking and staging materials with forklifts and pallet jacks, moving raw materials to production lines, and lifting up to 50 lb. All of it is physical handling that an agent without a body cannot do.
OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(l) says that only trained and authorized operators may run powered industrial trucks. Employers must certify each operator's training and evaluation.
Some forklift roles include inventory tracking and recording shipping and receiving. That paperwork is the only digital part of the job an agent could do, and it is a small share of the work time.

Cutting CAD/CAM software such as ESAB Columbus Job Wizard can generate NC programs from customer orders automatically, nest parts on plates and assign a machine. An agent could do the program-preparation part of 'typing instructions'.

SigmaNEST automates programming for profile cutting machines (laser, plasma, waterjet, router, punch) and batch-processes BOMs and work orders. The software side can be automated, but the operator still loads, starts and sets up the machine.

Hypertherm ProNest Production Manager connects to EDGE Connect CNCs for automatic data capture and remote access. Only some networked machines can be reached this way; manually setting guides, clamps and knives at the machine needs a person there.

Older cutting machines were run by hand, with operators working close to moving parts. PLC-based control systems are built to replace that manual operation, but they are fixed machine controllers, not software agents.

On a PLC/HMI panel-cutting line, the operator enters the panel count and size and starts the cycle at a control screen on the machine. The controller then secures the panel, makes the cut and returns. Starting the machine still happens at the machine.
Recent retrofits of cutting machines add safety door bars and safety switches on the protective shields, so starting and running the machine depends on a person at the guarded machine.

Knife positioning on slitters is automated by PLC and touch-screen systems that use machine actuators and stored job recipes. This is factory hardware, not something an AI agent controls. Fitting the blades still takes physical work: knife holders are usually repositioned and clamped by hand.

In the Computaslit system, the operator enters slit widths or recalls a saved recipe, and an electric actuator moves the knives into position. Software can help choose settings from the specifications, but a person still mounts the blades, rollers and templates.
The knife holders mount on a dovetail support bar and are normally moved and clamped by hand. Installing components with hand tools needs a physical presence that a software-only agent does not have.
MES application servers are set up to print production labels on Zebra printers, so the ticket content can be generated from system data without anyone filling it in by hand.
