In this production-operator posting, the operator prints pallet tickets, applies them and checks that the information is correct. Putting the ticket on the product is physical work.
On an extrusion line, the operator checks that the labels match the shift schedule's lot, color and denier, and applies a stamped label to each finished package by hand.

Test-data platforms already run analysis on measurement data inside the test context. Werum HyperTest Boost connects to JupyterLab, and ZEISS INSPECT automates metrology analysis. Frontier agents with code execution can do the computations and pass/fail checks against a spec end to end.

Under ISO/IEC 17025 and 17020, management must name specific people to authorize and sign test and inspection reports, and accreditation bodies keep lists of these signatories. The analysis can be automated, but a human still has to authorize the result in accredited settings.
The standard requires a review and authorization before results are released, but it does not say how the work behind them is done. That makes the rest of the task digital and open to delegation.

Size, color and weight grading is already automated, but by dedicated conveyor sorters with built-in cameras (ENSCO PROSORT, Key Technology Optyx, Robovision). These are hardware lines, not software agents. A software-only agent could at most classify items from camera images it can reach, while picking up, weighing, moving and sorting the items still has to be done by hand or by the sorting machine.
AI vision is now used for ripeness, color and cluster-size grading, with weight estimated from images. This again runs as purpose-built sorting equipment on the production line.

Official USDA grading certificates need a licensed grader (7 CFR 58.33; for eggs, plant-employee grading is check-graded by a licensed grader). The routine sorting this task describes generally does not need a license, so the accountability barrier is marked false.

O*NET 51-9124.00 lists 'Operate auxiliary machines or equipment used in coating or painting processes' as a supplemental task. The occupation's core tasks are hands-on: positioning spray guns, adjusting dials and valves, and disposing of hazardous waste.

Paint-line auxiliaries such as conveyors, ovens, pumps and paint circuits are run by on-site PLC/HMI control systems with recipe management and diagnostics. These systems are operated by shop-floor staff, not by general-purpose AI agents, and an alert goes to a human supervisor when a correction limit is reached.

Even where remote assistance is possible over an Ethernet-connected HMI, the work is still done at the machine: loading, starting, adjusting and clearing it. Plant control networks are normally closed to outside software agents.

Run-to-run control takes metrology results after each wafer step and automatically calculates parameter changes for the next wafer. Software already does much of the routine monitoring and adjustment.

AI/ML run-to-run control has been shown in closed-loop deposition and can outperform classic APC for some processes. Its effectiveness still depends on model quality and measurement latency, so engineers and technicians handle exceptions and retune.
A typical fab has about 2500 on-line SPC charts, and manual over-adjustment can make processes oscillate. Fabs therefore depend on automated factory-wide control systems.

AVEVA's MES documentation says production employees use its Operator app to claim quantities produced and report consumption. It also says many of these transactions can be automated by linking the MES directly to shop-floor PLCs.

Infor's MES documentation describes barcode scanning at each operation and automatic data collection. Planned and actual quantities are recorded and tied to the production order, which reduces manual entry and errors.

Laminating equipment includes inline thickness-measuring devices and automated batch counting, so some dimension and quantity data can come from sensors. Measurements that are not instrumented still need a person at the machine, and no law requires a human to sign these records.

One case study I found describes a camera-based system that checks 100% of products at up to 10 items per second. Operators teach it using labeled good and bad sample images. These systems are dedicated hardware installed on the line, not general software agents.

On packaging lines, sensors detect each item and a camera photographs it. Software then compares the image with preset quality specs. This only works with cameras and sensors physically on the line. A remote AI agent cannot handle the product or adjust machine settings by hand.

A patent for detecting defective bags from a packaging machine says these bags are mostly still checked by eye. It also says manual inspection cannot keep up with high-volume lines. This shows the inspection step is still largely done on the line itself.

O*NET lists 'Examine products to verify conformance to quality standards' as a core task of production helpers. It describes the role as hands-on, lower-skill work alongside loading machines, moving stock and packing goods.

Employer postings for production helpers combine watching for defects and checking finished goods for width and length with heavy lifting (up to 75 lbs) on the plant floor. The inspection is done in person by handling and measuring products.

AI visual inspection systems such as Siemens' end-of-line defect detection can automate defect checks, but they need cameras and sensors installed on the line. That is purpose-built hardware, not something a software-only agent can reach by default.

One vendor describes an AI loop where sensor signals such as vibration, temperature and cycle data feed an anomaly detector, which sends early-warning alerts to maintenance staff. On instrumented equipment, software can do the detect-and-notify step. This is a vendor workflow template, not an independent study.

Predictive-maintenance products and research systems use machine-learning anomaly detection on machine data to flag malfunctions and cut unplanned downtime. They only work where machines are fitted with sensors and connected to software. The figure of up to 50% less downtime is a vendor citing a McKinsey survey, and I could not confirm it.

Retrieval-augmented generation (AI that looks up stored records before answering) can pull up equipment performance data when an anomaly is detected, which helps diagnose the problem and notify operators. Intel presents this as an illustrative design, not a deployed product. A production helper's task is mostly watching machines in person on the plant floor (sight, sound, smell), and an agent with no body and no connection to plant sensors or cameras cannot do that.
Automated part labeling relies on software that generates label data and sends it to peripheral label devices, so the agent's piece is digital: preparing label content and print jobs.
Automated part marking for traceability is done by robotic or fixed laser and dot-peen hardware, which is industrial automation, not a software-only AI agent.
Marking data can be pulled straight from ERP/SAP/MES systems, which is the sub-step an AI agent could speed up. Physically marking, tagging and handling the parts still needs a person or a machine.

PHMSA's glossary separates valves run remotely from a control room through SCADA from manually controlled valves, which are operated by sending company personnel to the valve site. The helper's task is the manual kind, so someone has to be there in person.

An Emerson white paper says many plant valves are still manual and have no monitoring, so plant staff have to operate them by hand. Software can only reach these valves after the plant installs wireless or electric actuators, which is a hardware change, not an AI capability.

Industrial practice separates Manual mode, meaning local physical control at the actuator, from Remote mode, meaning control from an operator interface. Even remote valve control runs through operator or PLC systems, which a production helper does not normally have access to.

O*NET lists 'Remove products, machine attachments, or waste material from machines' as a core task (importance 69) for Helpers--Production Workers. It sits alongside other hands-on duties such as loading and unloading machines and moving materials.

Helpers support production workers by doing less-skilled manual work on the plant floor. Removing parts, attachments and scrap means physically handling them at the machine, which a software-only agent with no robotics cannot do.

Bundles are tied by people or by dedicated strapping machines on conveyor lines (e.g., Signode SGP 3330, which detects, positions and straps bundles). This is mechanical automation, not something a software-only AI agent can do.
In-line squarer-bundlers such as the Mosca MCB-2 align and strap stacks physically. The task means handling products and strapping material by hand or machine, so a physical presence is required.
Automatic bundle strapping systems feed, compress, strap and eject bundles mechanically. The only digital part an AI agent could help with is looking up the prescribed procedure or bundle specs.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(l), the employer must certify each powered lift truck operator after formal instruction, hands-on practical training and an in-person evaluation in the workplace. The forklift part of the task is done by a trained, certified human operator, and federal law bars anyone under 18 from operating these trucks in non-agricultural jobs.

Moving material around warehouses without a human is done by physical robots (AMRs) run by fleet orchestration software. A software-only agent with no body cannot carry, push or drive loads. At most it could help with digital side steps such as reading a move ticket in the WMS or planning a route.

Warehouse robotics software assigns tasks, plans paths and manages charging for physical robots that connect to WMS/ERP systems. The movement itself still needs physical hardware, not just a language-model agent.

In the O*NET profile for Helpers--Production Workers (51-9198.00), the role is less-skilled support for production workers. Listed duties include loading and unloading machines and moving materials between storage and work areas. This is physical, on-site work that a software-only agent cannot do.
The ASU mirror of the O*NET profile describes the occupation as hands-on production support, with a median wage of $38,890 and a projected change of -2.8% from 2025 to 2035.

The task 'Prepare raw materials for processing' appears in O*NET task comparisons for production occupations. The work is handling materials: cutting, mixing, sorting and staging them. An agent could only help with a small slice, such as looking up specs or recipes.

O*NET lists 'Wash work areas, machines, equipment, vehicles, or products' as a supplemental task for Helpers--Production Workers (51-9198.00). The occupation is described as lower-skill help duties, including cleaning work areas and equipment. All of this is hands-on physical work.

Related O*NET tasks for this occupation, such as cleaning and lubricating equipment and doing minor machine repairs, also need someone physically present to handle tools and machines. A software-only agent with no body cannot do any of it.

O*NET lists 'Break up defective products for reprocessing' as a task for Helpers--Production Workers (51-9198.00). It is manual work on the factory floor: breaking, crushing or taking apart rejected goods by hand or with hand tools so they can be reprocessed.
Several other hands-on production jobs list the same task, such as 51-9111.00, 51-4071.00 and 51-9161.00. This confirms it is shop-floor physical work and not a digital or information task.
Software alone can't do this task. An agent with no robotics could at most help with minor paperwork, such as logging scrap or reprocessing records, which is not a substantial part of the task.
Removing flash by hand still means cutting it off with a knife or hammer and finishing it with a scraper, which is physical, labor-intensive work.
When flash removal is automated, it is done by physical equipment such as cryogenic tumbling drums, not by software agents.
Robotic deflashing uses physical cutters that follow the part. That needs robotics, which the reference AI agents do not have.

Before each day's use, a competent person named by the employer must inspect the sling and its fastenings and attachments. Workers must also stay clear of suspended loads. Both are hands-on duties done at the load, not through software.
Attaching and inspecting slings is physical rigging work done on the shop floor with hoisting equipment. Software only covers related paperwork, such as inspection checklists and records.
NIOSH sling checklists show that compliance depends on physically checking that the rigging is right and the load is within rated capacity.

The FAA's new AI tool from Air Space Intelligence supports traffic managers with routing decisions. The vendor's CEO says 'The machine never makes a decision. It's a human operator.' The reporting found no AI that gives pilots emergency vectors or weather reroutes on its own.

FAA-certified Garmin Autoland picks a suitable diversion airport by weighing position, fuel, terrain, weather and runway. This shows that choosing an emergency field can be automated, but it runs in the aircraft's avionics, not on the controller's side.
The FAA is spending $875M on AI air-traffic-flow software that is meant to support controllers' decisions, not replace them.

Under 49 CFR 240, anyone who moves a locomotive, including a remote control operator (RCO), must be a certified human engineer. Certification covers skills tests, rules tests and vision and hearing standards. Remote-control operation still needs a person on site using a belt-pack controller, and a 2026 bill would ban remote control locomotives on main lines.
The FRA final rule of April 2024 requires a minimum of two crew members on board most trains. Moving to one-person crews or to full automation would need special approval or an exemption.
Remote control locomotives move trains in yards only through a human RCO who is physically there. Driverless trains are purpose-built, railroad-specific control systems, not general software agents.

Under 49 CFR 232.205, a 'qualified person' must perform the Class I brake test on each train and car at points such as the initial terminal. Under the rule, both the test and the sign-off on it rest with a trained human.

Railinc's eABS tool records the date, time, location, number of cars and qualified person for each brake test. An agent could cross-check whether a test is on record, but the engineer's actual check of brake-pipe pressure and leakage happens in the cab.

Patent filings on automating brake inspection say an inspector usually has to walk the length of the train. They also say automated alternatives such as wireless sensors and camera systems have not been widely adopted.

Under 49 CFR Part 225, railroads must prepare accident/incident reports following the FRA Guide. When a railroad blames human factors, the employee can submit a personal supplement (Form FRA F 6180.78). That makes the engineer's own first-hand account and sign-off central to the report.

Software already structures and processes the formal reports. FRA's AIRGNET generates Part 225 accident/incident reports, and commercial tools such as PST's AIRS manage incident reporting. Neither supplies what the crew saw or heard.

Locomotive event recorders capture detailed operating data (speed, braking, signals) that could be used to reconstruct incidents. This data could feed a drafted report, but it sits inside railroad systems an outside agent would not normally reach.

Railroads such as Watco and Conrail put rulebooks, timetables, bulletins and special instructions on crew iPads through Comply365, with automatic updates, alerts and compliance tracking. Software can therefore check that the digital copies are current, but someone still has to check the paper binders and the device in the cab.

Under FRA rules, Form F6180-49A must be displayed under a transparent cover in a conspicuous place in each locomotive cab, and inspection records must be kept in the cab. These are paper items on the locomotive, so someone has to be there to confirm they are present.

ÖBB's infraDOAS tablet app downloads timetable data, orders and speed restrictions to the driver's cab, checks that they are valid and displays them. This automates the 'is the documentation current and available' part when the documents are digital.

Fully driverless (GoA4) metros open and close doors through dedicated signalling software and platform screen doors. This is purpose-built safety-critical rail automation, not a general software AI agent, and it requires replacing infrastructure.
On conventional lines, operators are responsible for safe door operation. They turn a key or physical control in the cab and look back to make sure nobody is caught in the doors.

Rules require each crewmember to be briefed on their door responsibilities, and doors must stay closed while the train is moving. Safety regulators report improper door openings as operator procedural failures.

Cat MineStar Fleet lets site controllers change tasks during a shift and send them straight to operators' in-cab displays. Written dispatch instructions are already digital, so an agent could read them, parse them or summarize them.

Modular DISPATCH sends task assignments to equipment operators through a touchscreen in the cab. The operator in the machine is still the one who has to take in and act on the instruction, so receiving it cannot be handed off to an agent that has no body.

MSHA Part 46 requires miners to be task-trained on specific equipment and tasks. Instructions go to the trained miner who does the work on site, often by radio or in person at the pit. The regulation does not require any signature for receiving them.

Tank truck seals are one-use tamper-evident devices put on valves, hatches and closures by hand after loading. Cable seals with metal locking bodies are recommended for valve outlets, so the work is hands-on at the vehicle.
Rail tankers and tank trucks normally have a place on the valve, or on the box covering it, where a seal such as a strap seal is attached by hand.
Bottom outlet valves are mechanical parts on the tank car. Their inspection and closure are physical work done on the car itself.

ASTM D1298 has a person measure density, relative density or API gravity of a liquid sample with a glass hydrometer. That means handling the sample, letting its temperature settle and reading the meniscus by eye.

The observed hydrometer readings are corrected to the reference temperature using the Petroleum Measurement Tables for custody-transfer volume conversion. An AI can compute that correction once a human has taken the readings.

The method is designed mainly for low-viscosity, transparent liquids. Viscous or opaque liquids need extra manual steps such as more time for temperature to settle and a meniscus correction, which adds physical lab work that a software-only agent cannot do.

Vendor material says a grain plant control system (PLC/SCADA) can run motors and route grain from the truck pit to a bin on its own. That logic is fixed automation built into the plant. It is not a general AI agent, and the physical work around the vehicle stays with people.
Truck receiving can be automated with RFID cards, photo eyes and driver touch-screens. This covers the paperwork and data side, but people still have to position the vehicle and open the hopper.
Loadout systems use a PLC to control the conveyor, but an operator still positions the equipment at the start with a handheld control pendant, so a person must be on site.

Governments publish their grain and agricultural tariff-quota allocation rules openly and run them through online systems such as Switzerland's e-quota and India's e-TRQ, so an agent can read the rules and apply the formulas digitally.

Grain quota allocation rules are documented formulas, such as first come, first served or shares based on past export tonnage. An agent can compute them from records, but it needs the firm's own trade history and access to the government portal.

US farm-program base and quota calculations follow published formulas, and university spreadsheet tools exist to compute them. Official figures still come from FSA allocation summaries, so a human needs to check the results against those.

Vendor pages say AI avatar video tools such as HeyGen can turn a script into branded financial-education presentations with an AI or digital-twin presenter. One vendor-reported case (Samsung Securities) cut video production from 2–3 days to 4–5 hours. These are recorded videos, not live, interactive seminars.

Under FINRA Rule 2210, a registered principal must approve a retail communication before it is used. Study-guide sources (not the rule text itself) say this covers a scripted seminar shown to more than 25 retail investors.

For seminars without a script, FINRA expects firms to supervise the human presenter through written procedures, training and surveillance. That fits a live, person-led session where the advisor answers audience questions and builds client trust.

Biomni is an agent built on large language models that writes and runs code. It completes biomedical research sub-steps such as causal gene prioritization, rare disease diagnosis and protocol generation without task-specific setup. These results are reported in the authors' preprint and have not been independently validated.

The ToolUniverse cancer-variant-interpretation skill takes a gene, variant and cancer type. It runs an 8-step workflow over CIViC, OncoKB, cBioPortal and ClinicalTrials.gov and outputs a report that tiers the variant's clinical actionability (T1 to T4). It was last updated in August 2026.

VariantBench tests agents on 118 variant discovery and interpretation tasks taken from published studies. The best reported pass rate was 42.1%, so expert review is still needed. Studying mutations also involves wet-lab work such as sequencing, cell and animal models, and mutagenesis, which agents cannot do.

As of 2026, AI and ODR tools mainly help human mediators with intake, scheduling, analytics and drafting. Commentators say AI should complement rather than replace human judgment, and that it struggles with parties' emotions and the dynamics of negotiation.

Research such as 'Robots in the Middle' found that LLMs can understand dispute scenarios, recommend interventions and draft neutral messages. That makes them capable assistants for some sub-steps of facilitation.
Court-annexed mediator rosters require qualified, trained people. Requirements include 40 hours of training, co-mediation experience, and in some cases bar membership or a behavioral-science degree.

OSHA 1910.269 applies to line-clearance tree trimming. It includes training (paragraph b) and job-briefing requirements, which an employer and a person in charge on site must meet. The search results did not give the exact wording of the training paragraph.

Arborist software such as ArboStar and Arbster handles crew scheduling, task assignment, risk-assessment forms and gear-inspection tracking. It supports supervision but does not oversee climbers or train them in the field.
GoCanvas form templates record safety meetings and training on PPE, pruning near power lines and climbing safety. They cover the paperwork side of training, not hands-on teaching.

OSHA tree-care guidance says only qualified, trained workers should run aerial lifts. It also says workers must stand to the side and feed material by hand when using chippers. Both are hands-on, on-site jobs.
OSHA lists the rules that apply to tree care, including 29 CFR 1910.67 for vehicle-mounted aerial lifts. ANSI Z133 sets requirements for trained and qualified operators.

The tree-cutting machines that exist are crane or grapple trucks run by a human with a remote control. Autonomous tree-trimming equipment shows up only in patents, not in products on the market. A software AI agent with no robotics cannot run this equipment.

OSHA 1910.269 sets fall-protection and line-clearance trimmer rules, including a required safety saddle and a second qualified trimmer nearby in some conditions. These rules assume a qualified human worker is climbing the tree.

A 2022 FWPA review found the range of robotic tree-climbing and pruning equipment very limited. Systems like the Patas still have problems with weight and agility, and UAV options need more development before they are usable. In any case these are robots, outside the software-only reference technology.
OSHA interpretation on safety saddles and body belts for line-clearance tree trimmers who climb, under 1910.269(g) and (r)(8).

Chainsaw maintenance is hands-on work: taking off the bar and chain, soaking and scrubbing them in degreaser, clearing the bar groove and oil holes, and filing the cutters with a round file or power sharpener.
Sharpening means filing each cutting tooth at its own alternating angle and filing the depth gauges every few sharpenings. A person has to handle the tool to do this.

Lubrication and pre-use checks (bar and chain oil, greasing the nose sprocket, chain tension, the chain brake, the air filter) are all physical inspection and adjustment on the jobsite. Software can only offer checklists or reminders.

OSHA 1910.269(r) sets rules for line-clearance tree trimmers: training, job briefings, minimum approach distances and a second-worker requirement. The work is done in person, physically, by trained workers.
AI tools that read satellite and LiDAR data, such as AiDash IVMS, only forecast vegetation growth and plan trim cycles. They do not do the cutting.
IBM Maximo vegetation management gives risk scores to rank where clearing is needed. This helps with planning but does not touch the physical cutting work.
The core duties are physical: workers climb trees or work from aerial lift trucks, run chainsaws while up in the tree, and use handsaws, pruners and rigging to trim and top branches.

AI-guided chainsaw drones for cutting branches are still a university research project (University of Canterbury, a 5-year grant), not a publicly available software agent. They are also robotics, which the reference technology does not include.
Arborist software only offers tree inventories and marking or tracking trees for pruning. This is a small planning aid, not the cutting and shaping work itself.
Tree trimmers do the work by climbing with arborist gear or from aerial trucks. They cut with saws, lower the cut sections with ropes and feed a chipper. All of it is physical work done on site.
Most US states require workers who apply pesticides and fertilizers to hold a licence, which usually means passing a test.

Drone pruning near power lines (UK Power Networks' Aero Prune, Dec 2025 to Sep 2026) is still a trial that needs hardware, not a software agent. It is not a commercial product that software alone could run.

Ground-worker duties are hands-on: tying saws, pruners, rigging lines and blocks for the climber, setting up port-a-wraps and lowering devices, and coordinating the lowering of wood by voice with climbers.

California Title 8 §3427 says a qualified tree worker trained in rigging must decide whether a tree can take the strain of lowering, and requires separate lowering ropes and block and tackle for heavy limbs. This governs how the physical work is done; it does not stop a machine from doing it.
In a NIOSH-investigated death, shock loading from a 330-lb section lifted ground workers off the ground. The lowering is a live physical control job that only a body on site can do.

OSHA's wood chipper bulletin describes operators feeding limbs into chippers by hand, which puts them right next to the infeed rollers and knives. It covers training and safe work practices, and it reports a fatal case where an operator was pulled into the machine.
ANSI Z133.1 requires quick-stop and reverse controls on the infeed that are within easy reach of the worker feeding the chipper. That assumes a person is physically at the machine running it.

WorkSafe NZ guidance says chipper operators must be trained and competent and should be protected from the infeed rollers by guarding and stop devices. The task is physical machine handling and has no digital part an AI agent could do.
O*NET lists this as a core task for Tree Trimmers and Pruners. It sits next to running chipping and shredding equipment and feeding limbs and brush into the machines.

A municipal job specification describes raking or shoveling debris into piles, loading it onto trucks or into a chipper, and hauling it away. Every one of these steps is manual or involves driving a vehicle.

Tree-service job postings for this duty require lifting up to 50 lb and working outdoors in all weather. A software-only agent can at most help look up a disposal site or plan a route, which is a tiny share of the work.

Photo-based AI tools such as Nyckel's tree-health classifier can screen uploaded tree photos for labels like Diseased or Dying. They are generic screeners, not reliable pest or pathogen diagnosis, so a human still collects the images and makes the call.

Standard tree inspection means physically examining the tree and its site, including sounding the trunk with a mallet, looking at the crown by eye or with binoculars, and climbing into the canopy if needed.
Even experienced TRAQ-qualified arborists disagree when judging decay, and instrument data such as tomograms changed their ratings. On-site expert judgment is still central to the task.

ANSI A300 Part 3 covers support system installation: cabling configurations, through-rod and dead-end bracing, guying with ground anchors, and propping. All of it means drilling and fitting hardware in the tree, and no software can do that.

Bracing, guying and propping are hands-on field jobs done at height or at ground anchors. Choosing hardware depends on inspecting the tree, its species and the site. An AI could at most look up the hardware sizing tables in the standard.
Employer groundperson job listings describe this work as raking and leaf-blowing the job site and cleaning up debris on site: hands-on work that has to be done in person.
Crew-member duties include raking, sweeping and blowing, and gathering brush, limbs and logs and carrying them to the chipping area. All of this is manual work on site.
O*NET lists collecting debris into piles and loading it onto trucks as tasks for Tree Trimmers and Pruners (37-3013.00). Nothing digital in the task could be done by a software agent.

O*NET lists 'Provide information to the public regarding trees, such as advice on tree care' as a task for Tree Trimmers and Pruners (37-3013.00). The occupation's core work is physical pruning, inspection and treatment, so advice is often given in person at the job site.

Consumer AI apps already identify trees from leaf photos, diagnose diseases, suggest treatments and give care advice on watering, sunlight, fertilizing and pruning. The developers' accuracy claims have not been checked independently.

General plant and tree care apps give pruning guidance and disease identification with treatments. They suggest checking with an arborist or extension service for valuable trees, which suggests a human still reviews advice that matters.

Job postings describe this work as picking up and carrying limbs, logs and debris by hand, feeding wood into chippers and running stump grinders. All of it is on-site physical work, so a software-only agent cannot do it.
Workers must regularly lift up to 50 lbs to load and unload equipment, and bend, walk, stand and stoop for long periods outdoors in extreme weather.

ANSI Z133 tree care safety rules, which state regulation adopts, cover on-site work such as tree removal, chipping, keeping clear of the work zone and using equipment. This is hazard management in the field rather than a sign-off that only a human can give.

Under OSHA, line-clearance tree trimming means pruning or clearing trees within 10 feet of energized power lines. It is regulated hands-on field work that only qualified line-clearance tree trimmers may do, and it requires the worker to be physically present.

29 CFR 1910.269 applies to line-clearance tree trimming done by qualified employees. Unqualified workers have to stay at least 10 feet away from overhead lines, so the work legally needs trained and qualified people.
Workers have died during tree trimming near power lines. That is why OSHA stresses qualification and on-site safe work practices for this kind of manual work.
Trimming stubs is done by hand on the tree, with the final cut placed just outside the branch collar so no stub is left. It requires using cutting tools on the tree in person.
On heavier limbs the cut is made in several steps: an undercut, removing the limb, then a clean final cut that keeps the branch bark collar intact. All of it is physical hand-and-tool work.

ANSI A300 section 5.3.6 says branches too large to support with one hand shall be precut to avoid splitting or tearing. This is about how the cut is done physically, not a licensing rule that requires a human.

To move a tree, workers drive hydraulic spade blades into the soil around the trunk, cut the roots, and box or wrap the root ball. Roots are often pruned 3 to 6 months beforehand. All of this is physical work with machinery on site.
Sources describe root pruning before the dig and preparing the planting hole (breaking up glazed soil, washing soil into gaps) as hands-on work done in the field.

Licensing differs by state. Louisiana requires a license for work on standing trees, while Connecticut does not count removals as licensed arboriculture. So licensing is not a general barrier, and the physical work is what limits AI here.

Chemical tree treatments need a state pesticide applicator license in general. For example, Washington's WSDA Commercial Pesticide Applicator license covers anyone applying pesticides on another person's land. In Connecticut, an arborist license also makes the holder a supervisory pesticide applicator.

Software calculators such as Toro's Sprayer Calibration Tool already handle tank-mix, nozzle-selection and application-rate math. This is the only digital part of the task. The actual mixing, calibration runs and spraying are done by hand with physical equipment in the field.

Connecticut requires a state arborist license for anyone advertising or contracting arboriculture work, and that license carries pesticide applicator responsibility. A licensed human has to perform or supervise the application.

The standard way to value a tree (CTLA Trunk Formula, Guide for Plant Appraisal) is a formula: Basic Tree Cost × Species % × Condition % × Location %. Software can calculate it, but the trunk diameter and the condition and location ratings must be measured and judged on site.
When 14 certified arborists valued the same ten trees, their results varied most on trunk area and condition rating. The weakest inputs are the field observations, not the arithmetic.
Tree-care platforms such as VilloAI and ArboStar already draft estimates from photos, suggesting line items and crew hours. When they aren't confident enough, they book an on-site visit.
Deep root fertilization is hands-on field work. Workers drill or air-spade a grid of holes in the root zone and inject liquid fertilizer into them. A software-only agent cannot do this.
Applying fertilizer alone usually needs no licence. A licence is required when the product contains a pesticide, so licensing is not the main barrier for this task.

Connecticut's arborist licence covers feeding and fertilizing trees and tests tree nutrition and how to diagnose deficiencies. AI could help with this knowledge, but a person still has to apply the treatment physically.

The task means putting a thin coat of sealant by hand (brush, tub or aerosol) on the exposed wood right after a cut is made on a live tree. That is physical manipulation an agent with no body or robotics cannot do.
Modern guidance mostly advises against routine wound dressing. The only digital part (looking up whether to seal, for example for oak wilt in season) is a small advisory share of the task's time.
Arborist sources describe sealant as a practice used at the site of the cut, with no licence or sign-off needed to apply it.

Older cavity treatment meant physically scraping out decayed wood back to sound wood and then filling the hole with cement, mortar or bricks. This is hands-on work done at the tree, often while climbing.

Arborists working by hand must remove the rotted wood carefully so they don't damage sound wood. Taking out too much weakens the tree, so the job depends on manual skill and judgment on site, which an agent without a body cannot provide.
Current guidance mostly advises against filling cavities. Software could at most help by looking up guidance, which is a very small part of the work.
Splitting is done by hand: you set an axe or wedge along the grain, hit it with a sledgehammer, then drive wedges into the crack. A software-only agent cannot do any of this.

The work means swinging a maul or sledge, judging knots and how thick the log is, and adding wedges as needed. It takes physical effort and carries a risk of injury, which is why a person has to be there.
Specialized tools like starter wedges and quartering wedges are physical devices that a person still has to drive into the wood.

Mindbody's ZeeZor app pulls per-staff numbers (retail sales, guest retention, service sales) from salon and spa point-of-sale systems. This automates the data side of performance reviews, but nobody has to watch the work being done.

General video tools can watch existing CCTV for staff productivity, uniform or SOP deviations and idle service points. They are sold for restaurants and retail, not built for personal services, and they only work where cameras and access already exist.

A study of AI video misconduct monitoring in restaurants found it can hurt operations. Feedback on individual misconduct such as uniform violations made things worse, so a human supervisor's judgment and delivery of feedback still matter.

AI agent skills and generators already draft performance improvement plans and disciplinary documents end to end from employee context and policy. Vendors say these tools do not verify facts or make the final decision, so HR keeps review and final edits.
A free AI PIP draft generator released in May 2026 produces structured drafts with goals and check-in schedules, and HR stays in control of final edits.

Employers remain liable for discriminatory outcomes from automated HR tools, even when a vendor promises compliance. This makes meaningful human review of adverse employment decisions necessary in practice.

Agentic booking tools are going live in 2026. Sabre, PayPal and Mindtrip are building end-to-end AI booking (flights from Q2 2026, hotels to follow), and Reservations Group launched an AI app for US hotels, flights and transport rentals. Coverage is still mostly individual and US-focused, with limited support for group bookings.

Expedition medical cover is arranged through specialist providers, who supply an on-site doctor or 24/7 remote support by satellite phone. An agent can request and coordinate this, but checking that the medic's credentials suit the expedition takes human judgment.

BS 8848 guidance says a registered medical professional must be involved and that their skills must match the expedition's needs. The model contract recommends settling medical and scheduling obligations in writing in advance, which needs a human to review and agree the terms.

Tour-operator platforms such as Bókun, FareHarbor, Rezdy and Checkfront include inventory or resource modules that track supplies and equipment records. An agent can reconcile these records against packing lists, but that covers only the paperwork part of the task.

Tour inventory software mostly manages seats, rooms and transport. It does not inspect gear. Checking gear quality (worn ropes, torn tents, safety equipment, fuel) and counting the physical stock requires hands-on inspection, and an agent with no body cannot do that.

Ramp's Agents for AP (launched October 2025) code, route for approval and process invoice payments in its Bill Pay product. Ramp says this is close to full automation, but that is the vendor's own claim, and humans usually still approve payments.
Tour leaders often collect local payments in cash at the start of a tour and pay for services with it during the trip. That on-site cash handling needs a person there.

Group leaders are expected to keep detailed logs of what they spend (date, who was paid, amount, purpose) and to reconcile them with receipts. An agent can keep this record digitally, but it works from receipts and inputs a human provides.

O*NET says Passenger Attendants (bus aides, bus monitors, transportation aides) work in person to keep passengers safe on ships, buses and trains and in stations and terminals. Their duties include answering questions, requests and complaints and giving route and timetable information.

Vendors say AI chatbots for airlines and rail already answer travel questions, take complaints and rebook trips, with claimed autonomous resolution rates of about 48% to 80%. These figures come from the vendors themselves, and the tools work through digital channels, not on board the vehicle.
Ada's own 2026 research found that only 24% of consumers said AI fully resolved their issue without a human, so harder requests and complaints still go to people.

Existing on-board systems use GPS geofences and text-to-speech engines to announce the next stop automatically, with no manual recording needed. This covers the route-and-stop announcement part of the task.
Audible stop announcements are often required by the ADA, but automated systems can meet that requirement. No law says a human must make the announcements.

A transit agency rolled out automated voice and LED stop announcements to replace drivers calling out stops. Greeting passengers at the door still needs someone physically on board, which an agent without a body cannot do.
Current AI agents can create unique coupon codes from shopper behavior and send them by email or other channels. This covers the digital part of the task.
Conversational agents can hand out redeemable coupons inside a chat session. In stores, however, demonstrators pass out samples and brochures in person, which an agent without a body cannot do.
Klaviyo's AI customer agent can find active coupon codes and share them during web chat and SMS conversations. The face-to-face persuasion at the point of sale still needs a person.
Demonstrators physically build and keep up display stations such as tables, carts and booths. They also prepare samples, arrange power and extension cords, and tear down and transport the displays.
AI merchandising tools such as PlanoHero, LEAFIO and Realgram can generate shelf and planogram layouts automatically. That covers only digital layout planning, not physically arranging a demo area.
Employer job descriptions list setting up booths and displays as a core in-person duty, alongside live demos and handing out samples.

In 2025, major retailers and AI companies launched agentic shopping assistants. Amazon's Rufus now buys products automatically, and ChatGPT added checkout. These tools find out what a shopper needs and suggest specific products without a human involved.
Reported uses of AI agents in consumer retail include personalized product recommendations. BCG reports a 5–15% conversion lift for retailers that run their own AI agents.

Agentic shopping tools moved from comparing products to recommending and buying them for the shopper. However, demonstrators and product promoters usually work in person, in stores or at events. There they read the customer and persuade face to face, which an agent cannot do without a body. No licence or legal sign-off is required for the task.

AI roleplay and coaching platforms such as FullyRamped and PitchMonster already run practice product demos with simulated buyers. They give automated feedback and push product knowledge to keep messaging consistent. That covers the scripting, practice and feedback parts of training.

Demonstrator work involves physical tasks like preparing and serving samples, using small appliances and keeping the station clean. Training for it therefore includes hands-on, in-person instruction that an agent cannot do.

Food-safety certification for demonstrators (provincial certificates, Costco's own test) is something the demonstrators themselves must hold. The person training them does not need a licence, so no rule says a human must deliver the training.

AI video tools such as HeyGen can produce retail tutorial and demo videos with avatars and voiceovers. That means an agent can write the instructional content, but the worker still delivers the live, in-person instruction.
Tools like TutorialAI generate step-by-step product guides and demo videos automatically. This covers preparing instructions for altering a product, not hands-on teaching on the shop floor.

Vendors describe AI demos that walk users through workflows and adapt to them. These work for software products; altering a physical product means a person has to handle and show the item, and the search found no evidence of in-store AI assistants doing this.

AI coaching apps released in 2026, such as NutriTracker, FitQoach and AllTrain, write meal plans and workout programs, track macros and adjust targets, but the user still has to eat, exercise and sleep in person. These are self-reported store listings.

Trainer platforms such as ABC Trainerize add AI workout builders and meal planners, link to wearables, and can produce a full 7-day meal plan with a grocery list in minutes. This covers only the planning and tracking part of the routine. The second source is a vendor blog.

A vendor guide on AI for personal trainers advises keeping a human's clinical judgment in the loop. Following a diet, sleep and exercise routine is bodily work only the model can do, and no law or license is involved.

A model voucher works like an invoice. It records the client, job details, dates, working hours and the pay rate, and both the client and the model sign it when the job ends. Filling in the fields is clerical work an agent can draft from booking data, but the hours actually worked and the client's signature come from the set.

Agency terms set the billing rules, such as a half day being 4 hours, overtime rounded up to the next full hour, and fittings paid at 50% of the hourly rate. An agent with software access could apply these rules to calculate the amounts.
Model booking apps let clients book and schedule models through the platform, so booking data such as rates and booked hours is digital and an agent could reach it.

Agency booking software such as Syngency handles scheduling, talent packages, contracts, invoice tracking and payments. That puts confirming a booking and checking upcoming jobs inside digital systems an agent could use if given the login.

Agencies often use client portals where models can see upcoming bookings and deadlines. Getting information about future appointments is mostly reading a portal, email or texts, which can be automated.

On platforms like Newbook, models run job search, contracts and payments through an app, and payment is processed after the job is completed. That suggests reporting a completed job is a routine digital step.
Consumer AI apps such as Flawless AI apply makeup virtually to a selfie and recommend products and looks for skin tone and face shape. The user still has to recreate the look by hand in real life.
Perfect Corp's AI makeup analysis detects skin tone, face shape and facial features and offers virtual try-on. That covers only the advice and planning part of the task.
Banuba's TINT face analysis and seasonal color analysis gives AI beauty advice. Actually putting on makeup and styling hair are physical jobs that an agent without a body cannot do.

H&M's 2025 campaign used photorealistic AI 'digital twins' of real models in some marketing images. The real models kept ownership of their likeness and a revenue share. This replaces the final image, but no agent poses in the model's place.

Zara uses AI to dress models virtually in variations of photos already taken of real models, instead of booking new shoots. It says AI will add to traditional shoots, not replace them, so a human still has to pose for the original shoot.

Zalando reportedly cut campaign lead times from up to 8 weeks to 4 days and costs by about 90% with AI imagery. That replaces the photo output, but the task itself, physically posing at appearances, filming or photo sessions, needs a human body.

Google's Try On tool, launched in June 2026, lets a user upload a photo and generates an image of clothing and accessories on that person. It only produces images. It cannot put real garments on a body.

Virtual try-on APIs such as FLUX Virtual Try-On Pro take a person image, a garment and a styling instruction (for example tucked in or layered). They can suggest styling for the accessory-selection part of the task, but a human model still has to physically put on the garments.
One 2026 vendor ranking covers virtual try-on tools for clothing, accessories and makeup. All of them work on images or video for previews and shopping. None of them dress a person.

Route-sales and DSD apps such as bMobile Route, Pepperi and inSitu can create invoices, process cash, card or check payments, capture signatures and sequence stops. The human driver still carries out the physical handoff and collects the payment in person.
Door-to-door selling means a person physically going to each door. Cities such as Woodinville require each individual seller to hold a peddler's permit, which assumes a human is there.
Peddler licensing usually includes a police background check on each person selling. That is a vetting and permit rule, not a requirement for a human to sign off on delivery or payment.

Voice agent lets a field rep dictate line items in front of a customer; the system creates the ERP order with the correct pricing tier, confirms totals and queues it for submission, with credit-limit and approval rules and escalation of exceptions to people (vendor claim).
Voice-to-CRM tools turn field reps' voice recordings into structured entries in Salesforce, HubSpot, Microsoft Dynamics and other CRMs (vendor claim).

A proof of concept for a Microsoft Dynamics 365 client used an AI agent to read order emails and attachments, validate them and post orders to the ERP, with a human customer-service rep approving each order; no results were reported.
AI video sales agents that run product demos and answer pricing questions are on the market in 2026, but they work only over online channels, not at a door or a street stall.

Door-to-door selling means a solicitor is physically present: cities require permits, a photo ID badge worn while soliciting, and set hours. This assumes a person at the door, but no law says a human must give the product explanation itself.
Cities require background checks and in-person license applications for each person selling door to door, which shows the job depends on face-to-face contact and trust.

Generic AI booking agents already capture and qualify leads, book appointments on a calendar, send reminders and re-engage past clients. That covers the scheduling and outreach steps of arranging parties.

AI receptionists for event businesses answer calls, book consultations and trigger follow-up sequences from CRM data. This is the closest match to booking parties, but no party-plan-specific agent for recruiting hosts turned up.

AI tools for direct sales cover lead generation, outreach drafting and follow-up. Recruiting hosts, though, relies on the seller's personal network and persuading people face to face, and the parties are usually held in person. I found no licensing rule that requires a human to do the work.

Salesforce's Prospecting Agent runs in the background, takes plain-language instructions about the target profile, and produces a ranked list of accounts and contacts. A customer reports that 60% of its North American pipeline was built autonomously.

Lead-list agents filter prospects by industry, size, location and job title, and remove duplicates already in the CRM. These tools are built for B2B contact databases, not household-level data for door-to-door territories.
AI SDR products such as Artisan's Ava and HubSpot's Prospecting Agent build prospect lists on their own. Reviewers still advise human supervision because list quality varies.

Vendors say telecom AI agents connect to billing systems, explain charges and apply simple credits or adjustments on their own. Disputes that need judgment or regulatory handling are still passed to humans.

A 2026 telecom billing-agent deck limits the agent to 'approved billing intents' as a guardrail and reports about a 20% drop in billing support calls. That points to partial rather than full automation.

For third-number billing, an operator must check that the billed party agrees to pay (for example, asking whether a called party accepts a collect call). Older patents say collect and third-number calls had not been fully automated. Speech-recognition systems already handled parts of these calls.

Multi-carrier shipping platforms such as Shippo connect to more than 40 carriers, including USPS, UPS, FedEx and DHL. They compare rates and generate labels through a web app or an API. An agent could run this through a browser or the API and pick the shipping method.

Shipping software compares carrier rates in one dashboard, bulk-prints labels, and remembers package weights and dimensions. This automates the software side of deciding how to ship and preparing postage.

Rate-shopping engines built on aggregators such as EasyPost, ShipStation or Shippo apply the shipper's carrier rules automatically and create labels by API. A person still has to weigh, pack, label, bundle and hand over the physical items. This last point is my inference; the page does not say it.

Good2Go Order Pilot (vendor claim) uses an OpenAI connection to read order emails and attachments. It pulls out page size, page count, quantity, colors, folding and paper, then creates the order in the system automatically.

Docparser offers a printing template that reads job orders and print specs arriving by email, fax or upload. It sends the extracted fields to job management systems, so reading production orders for item types and sizes is already automated.

Fiery JobFlow Pro analyzes job content to identify the job type and routes print jobs to the right presets on its own. Reading and classifying jobs is digital information work with no licensing or sign-off requirement.

FedEx's Pickup Request API lets software check pickup availability, schedule a courier pickup and cancel it. A successful booking returns a confirmation number, so the core booking step can be done end to end with no human.

Microsoft Dynamics 365 Intelligent Order Management lets users assign FedEx and UPS carrier pickup schedules to a fulfillment source. Its carrier API then sends the next available pickup time, so arranging pickups is already built into commercial software.

Logistics vendors sell AI agents that compare carrier rates, apply routing rules and confirm bookings on their own. This is the vendor's own marketing claim, not independent evidence that the agents work.
Cloud fleet tools such as UTAX Fleetmanager watch device status across a fleet, alert staff when a fault appears and update firmware remotely. This lets software take over part of the monitoring.

Epson Remote Services sends alerts and lets staff reboot devices and clean printheads remotely. Its stated purpose is to make field visits more efficient, which means hands-on visits are still needed.

PRISMA production-printer monitoring alerts operators when they need to act, for example to load media or add consumables. Many adjustments, like clearing jams, loading media and aligning feeds, have to be done by hand at the machine.

Loading a copier means doing things by hand: pull out the tray, adjust the length and width guides, fan and square the paper stack, place it within the fill line and reinsert the tray. A software-only agent cannot do any of these steps. Its only digital part is confirming the paper size and type on the control panel.
Manufacturers' manuals describe hands-on steps: setting the guides to the size marks in the tray and loading paper with the correct face up or down. A person has to be at the machine to do this.

Guidance for shared office copiers is about physically putting white paper in Tray 1 and colored paper in Tray 2, then picking the tray on the touch screen. AI could only help with the small digital step of selecting the tray or setting.

Optical sorters with cameras and AI already grade produce such as potatoes by size, shape, color and defects. These are dedicated machines with ejectors, not software agents, and the claims come from industry sources.
Vendor AI sorting systems, such as Robovision's, classify items from images and still need physical hardware with conveyors and ejectors to sort them. Feel and smell are not captured digitally.

USDA grading is voluntary for most produce. Licensed graders are needed only for official grades, for example under marketing orders, for import or export, or for government purchases. Ordinary sorting on a packing line needs no licence.

Optical sorting machines like TOMRA's Sentinel II and 5A already reject defects and foreign matter (stones, plastic, glass, rot, discoloration) on the line. They do it with cameras and NIR sensors plus mechanical air ejectors, which is dedicated machinery. A software-only AI agent can't do this.

The TOMRA 5A lets operators adjust accept/reject levels through software and sends sorter data to the TOMRA Insight cloud. That is the only digital part of the work an agent could touch. Picking items off the belt and putting good product into containers is still physical handling.
Combined NIR and color sorters on root crops can handle up to 100 tons per hour. This shows that automating the task depends on physical equipment, not on an AI agent working through software.

John Deere Expert Alerts and Remote Diagnostics analyze telematics data. With the owner's consent, they flag likely component failures to dealers and let dealers read or reset trouble codes and update software remotely. That covers the digital side of spotting faults and sending notifications, but not the physical repair.

The AI tools built for farm machinery, such as Deere Operations Center PRO Service and AGCO Fuse, mostly read fault codes and suggest likely causes through chatbots. Hands-on checks like listening for abnormal sounds, feeling vibrations, tracing hydraulic leaks and replacing parts still have to be done in person. This source is an opinion-style analysis, not vendor documentation.

Vendor 'AI diagnostic agents' announced in 2026, such as THINKCAR Tyler, help with diagnostic workflows and repair planning for road vehicles, not farm machinery. A technician still does the physical repair. These claims come from a press release and have not been independently checked.

Research on fault detection for combine harvesters uses vibration, acoustic and strain sensors with machine-learning classifiers. This shows AI can find faults from sensor data, but only when instrumented hardware is installed on the machine.

Predictive maintenance systems in agriculture use AI to compare sensor readings (vibration, temperature, pressure, torque) against a normal baseline and flag problems. This can support the operator's own monitoring by eye and ear, but it does not replace it.

John Deere collects sensor data from harvesters, tractors and planters and is adding computer vision and machine learning. The documented uses are mainly catching wrong settings, not judging machine sounds. The human operator in the cab is still the main detector.

FarmHQ's app lets users remotely start and stop irrigation pumps and solenoid valves, set schedules and get fault alerts. This only works where the retrofit hardware is already installed, and it does not cover laying pipe or digging ditches.

WiseConn's irrigation software schedules water by crop stage, soil moisture and weather forecast, and can control valves and pumps remotely. This covers the digital planning and control part of irrigation.

Valley's AgSense/ICON systems allow remote monitoring and control of pivots and pumps, but only through a smart control panel fitted on site. Moving portable pipe, setting siphons and ditch gates, clearing ditches and repairing pumps still has to be done by hand in the field.

Tank-mix apps already calculate product amounts per load and the correct mixing order. These are only the planning sub-steps; a person still has to measure, mix and pour the material into the machine.
Farm-management platforms such as Traction include a tank mix calculator linked to work orders that are assigned to operators, so the AI can help with planning but not with the physical handling.

Under federal rules, mixing and loading restricted-use pesticides counts as 'use'. It must be done by a certified applicator, or by trained workers under direct supervision, and some labels require the certified applicator to be physically present.
evidence.url: https://www1.maine.gov/dacf/php/pesticides/documents2/bd_mtgs/Feb23/6-40 CFR 171.201 Requirements for direct supervision of noncertified applicators by certified applicators.pdf

evidence.fact: John Deere sells retrofit autonomy kits for 8R/9R and 5ML tractors. Farmers control and monitor the machines through the Operations Center mobile app, but people still install the kits and the setup only works with certain equipment and implements.

Center-pivot irrigation can be started, stopped, scheduled and automated through apps such as Valley AgSense, FarmHQ and Agrico Web Control. This only works when a hardware controller has been physically installed on the pivot.

Autonomous tillage only works with John Deere implements fitted with the kits. Most of the work is still done in person: hitching, refuelling, adjusting, fixing breakdowns and tending machines in the field. A software agent can at most send commands through the app on connected equipment.

Deere's autonomous tractor app lets a farmer set implement width, speed, turn speed and tillage depth, and start or stop the machine remotely. This was shown at CES 2024 in a beta for specialized hardware, not general-purpose AI agents. The mechanisms on most machinery are still set by hand at the machine.

Cal/OSHA requires an operator stationed at the controls of a moving agricultural tractor. Driverless operation has only an experimental variance, and the staff recommended denying a petition to make it general.

Under federal OSHA (29 CFR 1928), operators must wear seat belts on tractors with ROPS and must receive safety instruction when first assigned and at least once a year. This assumes a human operator is physically present.

Crew-management apps already let managers assign jobs with a field location and instructions, record hours, and tag harvest entries to the crew that picked them. That digital scheduling and tracking is the part an agent could take over.
In AgCrew, foremen and field leaders still assign the tasks and send the daily summaries. The software supports a supervisor who is in the field and does not replace them.
FieldClock schedules and projects labor for seasonal harvest and H-2A crews. That covers the planning sub-steps, but directing and watching workers in the field still needs a person there.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(l), only trained operators whose competence has been evaluated may drive powered industrial trucks (forklifts). Employers must certify that each operator has had the training and re-evaluate them at least every three years.

Industry guidance for grain, feed and processing operations treats forklift use as hands-on work by a human operator. The training has to cover the hazards specific to the site, which here means the auger and hopper area.

OSHA's 1998 final rule requires both formal instruction and practical exercises for anyone who drives a forklift, including workers who only do it as part of another job. The work is physical, so an agent that acts only through software cannot do it.

Under federal rules, restricted-use pesticides may only be applied by a certified applicator or a trained noncertified person working under that applicator's direct supervision. The applicator must also follow the label and complete equipment training.

The AI spraying products that exist, such as Greeneye's see-and-spray system, are hardware mounted on tractor sprayers. Hand-sprayer work still means a person physically mixing, carrying and applying the chemicals.
Software such as Agremo builds prescription maps from drone or satellite images. That only helps a little with planning where to spray and does nothing for the hand application itself.

Hitching an implement is hands-on work on the machine itself: stopping the engine, leveling the lower links, setting the control valve to float, and making the PTO, hydraulic and lighting connections by hand. A software-only agent cannot do any of these steps. At most it can look up the procedure in a manual.

Even an automatic quick-hitch system that coupled the PTO and hydraulics as the tractor backed in was a mechanical device, not AI software, and it is no longer produced. Attaching implements still depends on physical tools and a person to handle them.

Deere's autonomous field work is aimed at tillage. Planting and spraying were only stated future goals, and there is no sign of a launched planting product. These systems also depend on robotic tractor hardware, with the farmer overseeing them through the Operations Center app. A software-only agent could at most help with planning and remote monitoring.

Autonomous operation requires camera and autonomy retrofit kits or factory-built autonomy-ready tractors and implements. This means the task depends on physical machinery, and someone has to be there to hitch, load and calibrate the towed implements.

Deere's autonomy was demonstrated pulling a field cultivator on fields that had already been mapped, with obstacle handling done remotely by a human. It is not a turnkey way to run seed drills or manure spreaders. Separately, US rules usually require a certified applicator to apply or supervise restricted-use pesticides.

Farm autonomy as of 2026, such as PTx Trimble OutRun, automates tractor-pulled grain carts in the field. An operator is still needed to unload into the truck, and the truck haul itself is still done by a human driver. In any case this is robotic hardware, not a software-only agent.

Driving a vehicle on public roads needs a physically present driver. Even under the MAP-21 farm CDL exemption, the farm truck driver must hold a valid licence (noncommercial at minimum), and a CDL is required beyond 150 air miles or for hazmat.
Covered farm vehicle rules are tied to the driver: there are age minimums, combination vehicles require a medical certificate, and a designation form must be carried in the cab.

Semi-automatic transplanters need people to separate seedlings and feed them into the planter by hand. Fully automatic transplanters are mechanical equipment, not software agents, and they still need humans to restock plants.
Automating seedling pickup and feeding depends on physical robotic mechanisms, and most fully automatic transplanters are still at the prototype stage.
Robotic transplanting machines were built to automate feeding and inserting seedlings, work that used to be done by hand. This shows the task is physical manipulation.

Field and bin scale systems already log each weighing digitally with picker RFID, date, time, weight and GPS. That leaves recording as the only digital sub-step, and a person still has to put the containers on the scale.
Libra Field Bin is an app that connects to bin load cells and logs each unload with weight, date, time and GPS, so the record-keeping is software-driven.

Weighmaster licensing in states like New York and California applies to issuing certified weight tickets for commercial or bulk sales. It generally does not cover routine on-farm weighing by equipment operators.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(l), forklift operators need hands-on practical training and an in-person evaluation on the employer's equipment. Operating material-handling equipment is physical work done in person.

PTx Trimble OutRun automates grain cart movement, but this is robotics built into the tractor, not a software-only AI agent. The cart is still sent to a truck unload zone where a person unloads it by hand.

A Purdue thesis says no existing system can fully automate a combine unloading on the go. Auger control relies on on-machine sensors and actuators, not on any digital system that a software agent could reach.

Dedicated optical sorting machines (cameras plus air-ejector valves) reject rotten produce on belt lines. This is automation built into the machine hardware, not something a software-only AI agent can do.
AI vision reject separators work as physical machines on potato and onion lines. Removing the product needs mechanical action on the conveyor.
AI-powered optical sorting requires installing dedicated sorting hardware to separate rejected material from accepted produce.
Agricultural bagging relies on hoppers, tunnels and grain-tank film tubes that are worked by hand at the machine itself. A software-only agent has no way to position boxes or attach bags.
Automatic bag feeders, sewers and heat sealers already open, fill and close bags. That is fixed mechanical automation, not something an AI agent can do through documents, messages or computer use.
Patented bagging gear uses grippers and clamps to physically handle bag mouths, so the task comes down to physical manipulation at the discharge point.

Remote water-level monitors (Farmbot) send tank and trough levels and rainfall data into AgriWebb's livestock software. An agent could read these dashboards and send alerts or reorder feed and water. That covers only the monitoring sub-step, and only on farms that have the sensors installed.

Automated feeding and drinking systems use level sensors, microcontrollers and apps to track supplies. The feeding and watering itself is still done by physical equipment or by workers, not by a software agent.

Systems that track drinking behaviour, such as RF-tagged water fountains, need hardware on site. Delivering feed, filling troughs, checking for frozen or broken waterers and seeing the animals in person all require someone physically there.

Dairy feed management software (FeedWatch, Cowconnect, Digi-Star TMR Tracker) adjusts rations and load sizes and tracks loading accuracy. The tractor or loader operator still physically loads the mixer wagon and drives it to deliver the feed.

A University of California study of 26 dairies using feed management software found ingredient loading deviations ranging from about -79% to +22%. The researchers linked this to feeder skill, which shows the core work is physical and done by a human operator.
Topcon TAP FEED software reports operator accuracy and refusals. It supports the human operator who drives the feed equipment but does not replace them.

Camera-based systems can score dairy cow body condition, mobility (lameness) and weight automatically, and in real-world tests did as well as or better than manual scoring. This only works where the cameras are installed on the farm.
In June 2026, SLU released an AI mobile app that measures and weighs dairy cows to help assess health and welfare. A person still has to be with the animal to capture the images.

Commercial vision products such as COW-AI claim real-time lameness scoring (1 to 5) and body condition scoring. These are vendor claims, so the AI analysis supports the on-farm hands-on exam (handling, palpation, temperature checks) rather than replacing it.

Feed-management software such as TMR Tracker builds rations in desktop software and sends the instructions to the mixer's scale indicator. The indicator shows a target weight for each ingredient, but a person still has to load the ingredients physically. Software can only help with calculating amounts and keeping records.

In Agrimatics' loading workflow, the operator starts a batch and adds each ingredient by hand while load cells track the weight. The system can recalculate the remaining ingredient amounts, but it cannot do the mixing.

FDA rules allow drugs to be mixed into feed only at approved levels. Medicated feed under the Veterinary Feed Directive needs a veterinarian's written order, but a farmworker can do the mixing on the farm without a licence when that order exists. The legal responsibility belongs to the veterinarian and the producer, so it does not require a human to do the mixing.

Barns are cleaned automatically today only by physical robots and scrapers, such as Lely's sensor-guided Discovery scraper that follows pre-programmed routes. These machines are robotics, not software agents, so they fall outside the reference technology.

Existing automatic barn-cleaning systems are autonomous vehicles or scrapers that move or collect manure on predefined tracks and timers. The task is physical manipulation of manure, bedding and equipment.

Vacuum robots like the Discovery 120 spray water and collect manure on solid floors. Even with automation, a machine has to be physically present, so an AI agent with no body can at most look up disinfectant dilutions or cleaning schedules.

Feed suppliers already run online ordering portals. MyForFarmers lets farmers place compound and blend feed orders at any time from a phone or computer and track delivery status, so an agent with computer use could do the ordering and delivery steps.
FeedX tracks tons of feed on the farm, projects the next delivery date from usage and lets users choose delivery dates. Scheduling and reordering are already automated in software.

MetaFarms Feed Mobile has staff place feed orders that a back office then reviews and approves. Human approval of orders is still common, and on-farm stock levels often still need someone to look at the bins.

OSHA logging rules (29 CFR 1910.266(h)) require planning and clearing an escape path before felling, then moving a safe distance away on it once the back cut is made. This is physical, on-site work by the faller.

OSHA's Logging eTool checklist lists chain saw work practices under 1910.266(e)(2) that include retreating with the saw and moving with a running chain saw. These are hands-on saw handling tasks at the stump.
Industry felling-safety guidance says the sawyer must plan two retreat routes to use when the cut tree starts to fall. The task depends on the person being physically present at the tree.

Under OSHA's logging rules, a back cut must be made in every tree being felled. It has to leave enough hinge wood to hold the tree to the stump for most of its fall so the tree falls in the intended direction. This is hands-on chainsaw work at the stump.

Errors in back-cut depth or height make the hinge fail, cause kickback or lead to inaccurate falls. NIOSH FACE investigations link these errors to logger deaths. Doing the cut correctly depends on real-time physical judgment and handling the saw.
The OSHA and state safety procedures for felling with a chainsaw regulate how the cut is done. They do not require any licence sign-off, so the main barrier is physical, not legal.

OSHA rule 29 CFR 1910.266(e)(2)(x) says the chain-saw operator must clear brush and other obstacles from the cut and retreat path before felling. The worker has to do this by hand on site with a chainsaw or axe, so a software-only agent cannot do it.
Kentucky's FACE hazard alert for loggers recommends clearing escape paths after the fall direction is set and before the tree is felled. This is a physical job done at the stump.
NCDOT's safety procedure for tree felling and chainsaw use under 1910.266 treats clearing and felling as hands-on chainsaw work. Software or AI agents have no part in carrying it out.

Systems that measure log length and diameter and choose where to cut stems (StanForD-based, e.g. Ponsse Opti, Waratah TimberRite) are built into mechanized harvester heads. They are machine control systems, not software agents. A manual faller checks logs on site with a tape and by eye, so an agent can only help, for example by checking photos or measurements a human supplies against the cutting specs.

A Skogforsk 2025 trial found that most shortfalls in bucking results came from errors in the machines' own length and diameter measurements. Even automated systems still need physical control measurements of the actual logs.

OSHA's logging guidance has the feller size and place the hinge, face cut and back cut on site, judging the tree's lean, diameter and condition. Wedges go into the back cut to fell against back lean, and timing them depends on how the tree is moving in real time.
Automated felling guidance (scanning a tree, estimating its center of gravity and rating fall directions) exists only as a patent concept, not a shipping product.
Research smartphone apps can estimate trunk diameter and lean direction from a photo, which could help a human decide, but they don't plan the cuts or wedges.
OSHA 1910.266(h) requires an undercut and a backcut on each tree, with enough hinge wood left to control the fall. Both cuts are made by hand with a saw on the standing tree at the stump.
NIOSH FACE reports recommend that fellers drive felling wedges on trees with back lean. This is physical manipulation done on site, so a software-only agent with no robotic body cannot do it.
State and agency chainsaw and tree-felling safety programs built on 29 CFR 1910.266 treat this as hands-on chainsaw and axe work done in the felling zone.
O*NET lists 'Trim off the tops and limbs of trees, using chainsaws, delimbers, or axes' as a core faller task. It is hands-on work with chainsaws, delimbers or axes at the felling site.

NIOSH reports describe deadly physical hazards in this work, such as a timber faller killed by a hung limb, and recommend following OSHA logging-standard chainsaw procedures. This confirms the task needs a person on site.

OSHA cited a logging company because an employee was limbing trees with a chainsaw without face protection. Limbing is done by hand with a chainsaw in the forest, outside any software system an AI agent can operate.

Maintenance happens by hand at the work site. The saw must be cooled, then the chain and bar cleaned and greased, for example every 3 days, and the chain brake kept working. An agent without a body cannot do any of this.
Sharpening means filing each cutter by hand at the correct angle with a file holder, after cleaning the chain and checking it for damaged teeth. All of it is hand work with tools.
Logging workers learn chainsaw sharpening and maintenance in hands-on courses, which shows these are physical skills with no software substitute.
