California Title 8 §6285 has the faller pump hydraulic tree jacks at the base of the tree and move wedges in progressively as the tree is jacked. This is hands-on manipulation done at the stump.

A NIOSH fatality report recommends that tree fellers use felling wedges along with proper felling technique on trees with back lean. It cites the OSHA 1910.266 requirement to leave enough hinge wood when making the back cut. The task is physical, done during the cut and in a dangerous spot.
Industry sources say jacking needs a competent faller on site who stays in control at the tree. Software agents with no body cannot insert jacks or drive wedges.

Oregon OSHA requires the hazard area around an unattended lodged or partly cut tree to be marked with hazard identification ribbon, and only qualified workers may fall danger trees. The ribbon must be bright orange and marked 'Danger' or with a skull and crossbones. Every cutter has to carry it.
California 8 CCR 6275(f) requires a qualified person to flag the hazardous area around an unattended lodged tree with warning tape or ribbon at the logging site.

Australian bushfire guidance says crews mark the zone around a dangerous tree on site with surveyor's tape or danger tape. The marked zone must be at least as large as the tree's height, so a person has to judge it on the ground and tie the tape by hand.
A choker setter is a logger who attaches cables to logs by hand so skidders or skylines can haul them out. The work is done in person on steep cutover ground.
A choker is a steel cable noose that the worker wraps around the end of a log and tightens before the turn is yarded. This requires handling the rigging physically.

Oregon OSHA cable-yarding rules require rigging crew members on site to carry transmitters while chokers are set, and a lone choker setter must stay in clear view of the yarder operator. These rules assume a human is physically present.

Automating log loading with machine control (reinforcement learning on a simulated forwarder crane) is still at the research-prototype stage. It requires robotic or hydraulic actuation, which a software-only AI agent does not have.

Remote operation of stationary knuckleboom loaders works through electric-over-hydraulic joysticks controlled by a human operator. It is physical machinery, not software an agent could normally reach.
Truck-mounted crane makers like Hiab offer only semi-automatic functions such as automatic folding. Full automation is still being developed through partnerships like the one with Forterra.
Logs have long been marked by striking an owner's mark into the log end or side with a stamp hammer. A lumberjack swung the hammer against the log to mark the trees they had cut.
Modern log identification uses paint, forestry hammers and tags applied by hand to the wood. The marks show origin, species, an inventory ID number and the licensee.
State harvest-marking procedure lists physical tools (marking guns, marking paint, a Biltmore stick) and requires marks that logging contractors and equipment operators in the field can understand.

OSHA's logging standard 29 CFR 1910.266 covers manual felling, chain saw use and machine use such as skidders as physical activities on the logging site. Its paragraph (i) requires training for workers who run chain saws and log skidders.
OSHA has an interpretation letter saying log skidder operators must be trained under 1910.266(i)(3)(ii). This is a training duty on the employer. It does not require a licensed human signature.

The University of Wisconsin Extension logging eTool describes chain saw felling and grapple skidder work as hands-on equipment work done in the woods. A software-only agent could not do any part of it.

O*NET lists 'Place supporting limbs or poles under felled trees to avoid splitting undersides, and to prevent logs from rolling' as a task for Fallers (45-4021.00). It is hands-on work with heavy material done on site in the woods.
A NIOSH fatality report describes a faller killed when an unstable log pivoted downslope while being bucked. Keeping logs from rolling is physical, on-site safety work that software cannot do.
Michigan's logging rules tell fellers to cut from the uphill side when a tree may slide or roll. This shows that handling logs depends on physical judgment at the site.
Automated rebar tying exists only as physical robotics. TyBot is a gantry robot on rails that finds rebar intersections and ties them with a robotic arm, and the reference technology excludes robots.
Even the robot needs a worker to supervise it, and it mainly pays off on large bridge decks and long rectangular slabs. Spacing and tying rods in forms is hands-on manual work done on site.

TyBot ties about 1,100 to 1,200 intersections per hour on bridge decks. A software agent cannot do any of the physical spacing or tying. At most it can help read blueprints or bar schedules, which is a small share of the time.
OSHA 1926.451(f)(7) requires that scaffolds be erected, moved, dismantled or altered only under the supervision of a competent person, by trained and experienced employees whom that person selects.
A competent person must inspect scaffolds before each shift and after any event that could affect their structural integrity. This needs someone physically on site.
OSHRC enforcement shows citations issued when a scaffold was erected with no competent person present. This confirms the human supervision and liability requirement.

Installing flat-roof insulation and vapor barriers is manual work on the roof: laying rigid boards in a staggered pattern, driving fasteners or placing adhesive beads, and taping or sealing the vapor-retarder seams. The fastener and adhesive layout is set by the product and the spec.

The roofing robots now on the market (for example Renovate Robotics' Rufus) lay shingles on sloped residential roofs and still need a human operator. No production system for installing insulation boards on flat roofs was found, and a software-only AI agent has no physical way to do this work.

Licensing applies to the roofing contractor business (state or local, often above a dollar threshold), not to an individual worker installing insulation. A human does not have to sign off on this specific task.

In aggregate surfacing, workers embed roofing gravel into one or two pour coats of hot asphalt at set rates (for example 3.0 kg/m2 of asphalt with 20 kg/m2 of gravel). The asphalt must cover the felts with no skips, and the gravel must cover the asphalt with no gaps. This is manual work done on the roof itself.
Manufacturer instructions describe single-pour and double-pour flood coat and gravel application as hands-on installation steps done with hot bitumen on site.
Built-up roofing is finished with a last flood coat that has gravel or granules embedded in it. The work is done on site and the surfacing step can take several hours.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1926.451(f)(7), scaffolds may only be erected, moved, dismantled or altered under the supervision and direction of a competent person. A competent person must also judge foundation adequacy and inspect the scaffold before each shift. This is hands-on work done on site by people.

Scaffold design software such as Avontus Scaffold Designer, scaffmax and CerTus can automate layouts, parts lists and assembly plans. It does not do the physical erection, which is the core of this helper task.
scaffmax generates scaffolding automatically wall by wall on 3D building models and produces parts lists, so only a small planning sub-step could be done in software.

How to modify grout mixing is set by each manufacturer's data sheet and by ANSI A108.10, for example water limits, pot life, discarding stiff batches and site-mix ratios. An AI agent can look these up and turn them into adjusted procedures for the helper.

Getting a consistent batch depends on hands-on mixing technique and on judging consistency on site. Sika even recommends having the same person mix every batch, so a human has to do and judge the physical work.

Premixed grouts follow separate standards (ANSI A118.19 and A108.22). Picking the right procedure for each material is an information task that software can support, but no licence or sign-off by a human is required.
Painter helper job postings list cleaning brushes and spray guns and keeping the work area clean among the essential manual duties.
Helpers operate, clean and maintain painting equipment such as sprayers, pumps and pressure washers. This is hands-on work that a software-only agent with no robotics cannot do.
Hawaii's state class specification calls painter helper duties routine, repetitive, manual and semi-skilled, and the role is entry level.

The machines that already automate sanding before painting are force-controlled industrial robots and cobots, which are physical hardware, not software agents. The reference AI agent has no body or robotics.
Sanding and buffing to prepare a surface for paint means applying the right pressure to the actual surface, swapping abrasive discs and controlling dust. A software-only agent cannot do any of this.

Even a dedicated aerospace sanding robot project still needed people for most of the work: the robot was grinding for only 8% of total processing time. Software can help at most with things like choosing abrasives or explaining the procedure.

State 811 centers take locate requests online. The request needs contact details, the work address, cross streets, the type of work (for example, a fence) and the equipment to be used, and a confirmation email is sent back. A software agent can do all of this on its own.

Before digging, the crew has to check on site that every utility has responded and marked its lines. Buried lines can sit up to 24 inches from the marks, so hand digging near them is advised. That checking and marking work is physical.

Free county GIS parcel viewers show property lines that an agent can look up, but they are not survey grade. A licensed surveyor or physical survey pins are needed to fix the exact fence line on the ground.

Hanging a chain-link gate is all hands-on work. The worker measures and cuts pipe, squares and bolts the frame, fits tension bands and bars, stretches and trims the mesh, mounts the hinges, lifts the gate onto the hinge pins, levels it, and adjusts the latch. This needs wrenches, pliers, cutters and a level, and an AI with no body cannot do it.

The gate is built from manufacturer kits and written instructions. Software can only help by finding instructions or working out cut lengths, such as the opening width minus about 6 inches. That is a very small part of the job.

Fence licensing applies to the business, not to the worker who assembles a gate. One example is California's C13 licence for jobs above a dollar threshold. Some Canadian sources say fence installation is not a regulated trade, so no law requires a human to sign off this task.

Under 49 CFR 213.233, track must be inspected on a set schedule by a person the owner has designated under §213.7. The inspection is visual, on foot or from a vehicle, and devices may only supplement it. The qualified inspector must start remedial action immediately when a defect is found.

Automated track inspection systems use sensors and AI mounted on rail cars and do detect geometry defects. In December 2025 the FRA approved a 5-year waiver that lets railroads reduce visual inspections where these systems are used, but it does not remove human visual inspection.
Automated track inspection depends on hardware mounted on rail vehicles, so a software-only agent cannot do it. Without a waiver it cannot replace required visual patrols.
The rail is cut with a hand-held hydraulic abrasive saw that an operator places on the rail and pivots to cut from either side. This is physical work done on the track.
Competency standards require cutting rail safely and accurately to procedure. That depends on hands-on knowledge: identifying rail by roll marks, defect length and depth limits, and pre-heating.
A rail-cutting incident investigation stressed on-site risk control and physical checks of the clearance gauge and the cut rails before the track goes back into service.
Pandrol sells petrol and hydraulic rail drills that a worker clamps onto the rail and runs by hand on the track to bore bolt holes for fishplates, so the task is done in person with a physical tool.

Patents describe a robot on a maintenance vehicle that positions a rail drill using sensors. This automation needs robotics, which the bodiless software agents in the reference technology do not have.
ROBEL and FANUC have rail-repair robots on track wagons as prototypes. I found no deployed autonomous rail-drilling system that a software-only agent could run.
Spike pullers are either hand-operated hydraulic tools or self-propelled machines run by an operator from a cab on the track, so the work has to be done in person.
Handheld hydraulic spike pullers such as the Stanley SPL31 deliver about 16,647 lbs of pulling force and kick back at the operator, so a person has to hold and handle the tool.

Patents show spike-puller jaws worked by hydraulic cylinders, with a mechanical tie finder that locates ties as the machine runs. The work is mechanical and done on the track, with no software step an AI agent could take over.

Plasser & Theurer's ALC automatic guiding computer controls lining and levelling on tamping machines. This automation is built into the machine itself and is not something a general-purpose AI agent can take over through software. An operator on board still runs the machine and handles its reference systems.

Correction values for the precision method are calculated in advance and fed to the guiding computer. That digital pre-calculation is the only part of the job that sits close to what a software agent could do. Turning wheels and working levers on the machine is physical work.
Inside the machine, lining and levelling are measured against steel chords, and outside it against a laser. Both have to be set up and adjusted physically at the track.

The Geismar LRH-5-SP hydraulic rail lifter is run by an operator at each end using local controls for the clamps and jacks. The work is done on site with heavy hydraulic equipment and has no software interface a remote agent could use.

The Unipart rail handler comes with manually operated rail grabs and threaders. Hydraulic control is optional, and radio control is offered as a remote option for an operator who is still on site. None of this is a networked digital system an AI agent could reach.
O*NET lists this task for occupation 47-4061 as pushing controls to close grasping devices on track so it can be raised or moved. It is direct physical operation of equipment on the track.

On track tampers and liners, the reference chord is a physical wire or cord. Its ends are held on bogies or buggies that are pressed against the rail, so someone has to string, tension and clamp it by hand on the track.

Modern machines use three-point chord measurement with sensors on buggies in front of the machine. Setting it up and attaching it to the rails is a hands-on job at the track, not something software can do.

Automated lining and raising systems, including light-beam chords, automate the measurement once installed. Mounting and attaching the reference system to the rails is still done physically by the operator.

Tie adzing means hands-on operation of a heavy machine on the track. The operator raises and lowers the cutterhead to offset the machine bouncing over uneven ties so the surface comes out smooth. An AI agent with no body or robotics cannot do this.
A 1937 archive photo shows railroad workers running Nordberg adzing machines to shave tie tops so tie plates can be fastened, which confirms the task is physical and done on the track itself.

Under FRA rules (49 CFR 214.341/214.355), roadway workers who run roadway maintenance machines must be trained and qualified by showing they can operate each machine safely in person, so the regulations require a qualified human operator.
Railroads paint stencils such as 'UPRR Main Trk' and 'No Trespassing' straight onto the rail web or onto signs at the track. This is hands-on work done in the field with paint and stencils.
Vendors sell ready-made rail stencils and regulation decals. An agent could at most order supplies or look up the required text, which is a small part of the task.
FRA rules (49 CFR Part 215 Subpart D) cover stenciling on equipment, but no licence requires a specific human to paint signs. The deciding barrier is that the work is physical.

On a rig, air from an onboard compressor blows cuttings out of the hole. This is part of operating the machine itself. Any automation of the step comes from control systems built into the rig, not from a general-purpose software agent.

Some rigs have built-in autonomous flushing procedures, but a remote operator can override them. Field data from the Telfer mine showed manual drilling cycles were 19% faster than automated ones, so automating this step depends on special rig hardware and controls.

Controlling drill dust takes physical work at the rig, such as keeping dust collectors working and drilling holes wet. Drill operators at the machine get the highest dust exposure, which shows the task has to be done in person.

Patents describe automatic jack-extension and mast-leveling systems that run on the rig's own sensors and hydraulics. A person still has to position the truck on site, and nothing here is driven by a software-only agent.
A federal drill rig operator job posting requires a Commercial Driver's License with air brake, tanker and trailer-towing endorsements, so a licensed human has to drive the truck-mounted rig.
A Driller industry column says most US states require a CDL to drive drilling equipment and a state well driller's license to drill.

Commercial core-image tools (ALS LithoLens, Seequent Imago) semi-automate lithology logging from photos and produce measurements such as RQD and fracture counts. Geologists still review and correct the results before they enter the geological record.

Image-based machine learning can classify lithology and alteration from core images, but results depend on photos taken on site and on lighting and image quality. Someone has to physically collect and photograph the cuttings or core at the rig.

In several US states, the licensed or registered well driller must keep a log of each stratum and file it with the state within 30 days of completion, so the driller stays accountable for the formation record.

O*NET lists 'Set up and adjust equipment used to excavate geological materials' as a task for Helpers--Extraction Workers. The same listing includes hands-on duties such as loading materials and repairing drilling equipment with hand tools, so the work is done in person on site.

Rig automation exists, but it is built into the machines rather than run by a general AI agent. Epiroc RCS 5 lets users make or edit drill plans remotely, and Cat MineStar automates drill cycles and tramming. Physically positioning, rigging and adjusting equipment still needs people at the site.
MSHA 30 CFR Part 48 sets training requirements for mine workers. These cover who may work on site but do not require a licence holder to sign off on equipment setup.

AI repair assistants such as iFixit's FixBot only give diagnostic advice. A hands-on review found it gave generic guidance on a TV repair that would not power on, while the human still does all the physical work.

Connecticut licenses television, radio and electronics technicians and service dealers. This is a licence for the business and worker in a few states, not a sign-off required on each repair, and most jurisdictions have no such rule.
California requires businesses that repair electronics such as TVs, radios and stereos to register with the state, but it does not require a licensed human to sign each job.

AI field-service tools can schedule appointments, plan routes and pull device error logs remotely before a visit. A human technician still has to go to the home and do the repair, with remote help available at most.
Salesforce's field-service AI handles scheduling and dispatch and offers remote help for onsite technicians. It does not do the physical repair.

California requires businesses that repair TVs and audio-video equipment for pay to register as electronic service dealers. This is a business registration and does not say a human has to sign off on each job.

The search found no AI tool that diagnoses tractor wiring faults on its own. The closest tools are AI troubleshooting and interactive wiring navigators for heavy machinery (Tweddle Troubleshooter/TRACER-X) and industrial panels (INTrouble). These guide a human technician; they do not do the meter testing, soldering or part replacement.

Commercial repair software adds interactive wiring diagrams that link components to location, testing and replacement procedures. This is information support only: a technician still has to be at the machine with meters and hand tools.

Farm equipment mechanics generally need no licence. Agricultural technician certification is voluntary in most Canadian provinces and only compulsory for heavy-duty work in some, such as Alberta. The search did not check US state rules or dealer certification programs.
Mounting an outboard is hands-on work. The technician sets the cavitation plate level with or just below the hull bottom and tightens the mounting bolts to spec with a torque wrench.

The sea trial checklist has the technician run the motor at trolling speed and full throttle, check the cooling water telltale, and inspect for fuel, water, exhaust and oil leaks. All of this needs someone on board operating the boat.
Under state law, a person operating a motorboat must hold a boater education card and carry it on board. California, for example, requires a California Boater Card for all ages since 2025.

Engine stand manuals say the engine is lifted with a crane or hoist, bolted through the stand's fingers at the mounting holes, then slowly lowered so the stand carries its weight. The mechanic has to do this with their hands.
Small engines are often taken out of the equipment frame so the mechanic can reach the parts. This is physical disassembly that software cannot do.
Lifting points, mounting bolts and torque values come from the engine service manual. Looking these up is the only part an AI could help with, and it is minor.

FieldStockPro is an AI-powered inventory tool for trade businesses. It sets loadout templates for each vehicle, monitors stock on each truck and sends automated restock recommendations when parts fall below minimum levels. Technicians still scan parts in and out by hand.
Fieldcode Plus shows part availability by van and technician, sends low-stock alerts and generates reorder suggestions automatically. This covers the digital tracking and reordering steps.

Field service stock systems deduct parts used on jobs and send replenishment alerts. They depend on data entered at the physical van and job site, and sources warn that tools get abandoned when data entry is cumbersome. Physical counting, picking and loading stay with the human.

AI diagnostic tools for appliance technicians, such as Marcone AI (built on OpenAI/ChatGPT) and aiventic, guide technicians step by step through troubleshooting and help identify parts. The human technician still does the diagnosis and repair.
An industry guide describes AI appliance-repair tools as decision-support aids for technicians, not definitive diagnostic solutions, especially for older equipment.

Most US states require no general appliance-repair licence. Exceptions include EPA Section 608 certification for refrigerant work and California's registration and licence rules for larger repairs, so licensing is generally not what requires a human for this task.
Boston: only a contractor with a valid, non-expired Massachusetts trade license may pull a Gas Permit and do any work installing or replacing gas lines or pipes.
Angi, a secondary consumer source, says gas grill line installations need permits that are usually pulled by certified plumbers, typically costing $100-$300.

The core of the task is hands-on work at the site: cutting, threading and fitting pipe, making the connections and leak-testing gas and water lines. An agent with no robotics cannot do this. It can only help with small side jobs like looking up code or ordering parts.

VendSoft lists automatic commission calculations for locations and route drivers, plus commission statements and sales-by-location reports. These cover the invoicing and account-settlement steps. The source is a vendor listing, so the claims are unverified.

Nayax telemetry and cashless systems send real-time sales and machine data, so an agent can reconcile expected takings and prepare settlements without visiting the machine. The source is vendor marketing.

Taking coins and bills out of machines is physical work done on site. No search in this check showed that an AI agent can do it. This part is my judgement, and it accounts for most of the task's time.

Vending telemetry platforms such as Nayax AMIT 3.0 monitor machines in real time, send alerts and allow remote device control. They read data through DEX/GSM, so an agent can check fault codes and machine status from a distance.

Remote monitoring software alerts operators when a machine is down or out of order and can reset errors remotely. It flags faults but does not physically test coin acceptance, product dispensing or game mechanisms.
DEX-port telemetry sends audit data to cloud reporting at set intervals. Checking that the machine really works still needs someone on site to insert coins, make test vends and watch the mechanisms.

Commercial diving work in the US, including underwater debris removal, falls under OSHA 29 CFR 1910 Subpart T. The rule requires human divers on site with dive teams, a designated person-in-charge and safety procedures. The work involves hands-on hazards such as cutting, material handling and cleaning.

Minnesota regulators apply the Subpart T commercial diving rules to underwater removal work done on scuba, such as aquatic weed removal. They issued a $730,369 penalty after a diver drowned. This shows the task is physical, in-water work that requires a human.

OSHA guidance describes diver hazards that come from working physically underwater and handling materials there. A software-only agent with no robotic body cannot do this. At most, it could help with paperwork or planning on the side.

Laser alignment systems such as the Easy-Laser XT app and SKF TKSA 51 compute alignment corrections and guide the operator step by step. A person still has to mount the measuring units and physically move, shim and bolt the machine.
SKF TKSA 51 uses a tablet app with a live 3D view of the measuring units to guide alignment of motors, fans and gearboxes. The app only processes readings and does not do the manual adjustment.
Rigger and millwright job postings describe very physical, hands-on work: setting machines with jacks, levels and lasers, building foundations with grout and steel, and lifting heavy loads.

Under AWS D17.1, aerospace welders must hold performance qualification for their specific process, material, thickness, position and weld type. This includes tube-weld tests for tubes of 1 inch OD or smaller and eye exams. Customers commonly require this qualification by contract, so a human welder has to do the work.

IPC/WHMA-A-620 covers hand soldering and crimping of cable and harness work. Operator and inspector credentials, and the NASA-aligned Space training, include hands-on practical exams. That shows the task is manual work done by a human.

The task means handling tack welders, induction brazing chambers and soldering tools on physical parts. A software-only agent has no body, so the most it can do is look up weld procedures or parameters, which is a small part of the working time.
O*NET lists this as a core hands-on task for Electromechanical Equipment Assemblers (51-2023.00), done alongside fastening units with hand and power tools.

Related tasks include measuring tolerances with micrometers and calipers and filing, lapping or buffing parts by hand to fit. This is physical work that a software-only agent with no robotics cannot do. At most it can help by reading blueprints or giving assembly-sequence guidance.
When this work is automated, it is done by robots or fixed automation that assemblers operate or tend, not by digital AI agents. No license or legal sign-off is required for the task.

O*NET lists 'file, lap, and buff parts to fit, using hand and power tools' as a task for Electromechanical Equipment Assemblers (51-2023.00). It is hands-on material removal and finishing on physical parts.

The same hand-finishing task is listed for Hand Grinding and Polishing Workers (51-9022.00). That makes it a manual shop-floor activity that only robotics could do, and a software-only agent has no robotics.
Descriptions of the role show assemblers filing, lapping and buffing parts by hand with hand and power tools as part of physical assembly work.
O*NET lists 'position or align components for assembly, manually or using hoists' as a core task of Engine and Other Machine Assemblers, along with setting and checking part clearances.

Assembler postings describe hands-on work: moving parts by hand or overhead crane, putting shims between parts to realign or level them, and checking alignment and clearance with micrometers and gauges. This needs a physical body, which a software-only agent does not have.

Mechanical assembler duties include positioning and securing engine block components with wrenches, hammers and power hoists, and running crane or hoist equipment. All of this is physical manipulation; an agent could at most help by looking up blueprints or alignment specs.
Trimming molded fiberglass parts is commonly done by hand. Automating it needs vision- and laser-guided robots, which is physical robotics and not something a software AI agent can do.
The UK occupational standard treats trimming composite mouldings with hand tools (cutting, sanding, drilling) as a hands-on, physical skill.
Automated trimming that does exist uses 5-axis CNC robot trimming centres, which is physical machinery and outside the reference technology.

Machinists sharpen end mills by hand. They clamp the cutter in a collet fixture and grind it against a bench grinder wheel, then index each flute in turn and finish with a diamond hone. All of this is physical work that software alone cannot do.
Reconditioning carbide and coated cutters carefully takes an experienced technician working at a benchtop grinding machine. Physical skill is the core of the job.

Hobbyist machinists describe grinding end mills by hand on a lathe, using a rotary tool and marked chuck positions. No step of the work is done in software, so an agent could only help by looking up details such as grind angles or tool specifications.

Automatic pressing plants, like rotating carousels that press trousers with steam or hot air, are physical machines that cut down on operators. That automation comes from the machinery, not from a software agent.
Commercial automatic shirt presses still need an operator on site to load the garment and press two start buttons at once for safety. This is hands-on work.

A low-authority job-risk site credits the gains in this job to automated buck presses, tunnel finishers and robotic loaders. All of these are physical robots or machines, and none is software reachable by an AI agent.

Curved pressing forms such as tailor's hams are used to shape sleeves, darts, collars and curved seams. The worker positions and moves the garment over the form by hand while applying heat and steam, so the task is entirely physical.
In pressing over a curved form, the garment is placed and held on the form and pressed with a hot iron and steam. A software-only agent with no body or robotics can't do any of these steps.

A standard ham can't handle every curve, so custom forms are made for different shapes. Each garment needs hands-on judgment about which form to use and how to manipulate it, which an AI agent can't do.

The right pressing heat depends on the garment's fiber content and finish. For blends, use the setting for the fiber that tolerates the least heat. Pressers often press a test scrap and compare it with unpressed fabric, so the check is hands-on and done by eye and feel. AI can give this kind of rule-based advice from care-label or fiber data.

Charts matching fabric types to industrial press machines and heat settings already exist. An AI agent could look up and apply them when fiber data is available, but the presser at the station still has to inspect the garment and choose the machine.
Some sources give conflicting temperature figures, so a quick physical test on the actual fabric is still standard practice. That keeps a human in the loop for the final choice.

Pressing involves misting fabric by hand with a spray bottle or using a dampened press cloth before applying heat. This is physical handling of the garment, and a software-only agent with no robotics cannot do it.

Extension guidance says to test the moisture and heat on a hidden area first and to use a dampened press cloth when the fabric can't take steam. These are hands-on judgments made while touching the fabric, not digital steps.
Water relaxes natural fibers so wrinkles press out, which means the task itself is putting water physically onto the textile.

Velvet is finished by holding steam a few inches from the fabric or steaming it from the back on a pile-down board, then brushing gently in the direction of the nap. Every step is hands-on work with the garment.
Velvet is finished by steaming and hand-brushing the pile with a soft brush, never by ironing. The work needs tactile judgment on a physical fabric.
The machines that steam and brush pile fabrics are physical equipment, so a software-only agent cannot run them.

Blocking means stretching the garment by hand on a board to the exact size it should keep, then applying steam with an iron and a damp cloth and leaving it in place until dry. All of this is physical handling of the fabric, so a software-only agent can't do it. At most it could look up target measurements, which is a tiny part of the time.

Steam blocking needs judgment by hand: the worker controls how close the steam gets so stitches don't flatten or go shiny, and pins and shapes the garment from the shoulders down. No digital tool handles this.

The task is done by hand. A worker presses ties using pressure, inserted metal forms or rods, and careful hand ironing so the rolled seams don't flatten. An AI agent that works only through software cannot do any substantial part of this.

In the O*NET listing for Pressers, Textile, Garment, and Related Materials (51-6021.00), the tasks are physical work with heated metal forms and hand irons on garments. I couldn't open this page directly because it redirected to O*NET's job-coding help page, so this comes from the search result summary.
Forum posts describe a heated metal 'Nek-Tie Iron' rod that a worker pushes into the tie to dry and press it at the same time. This is hands-on work, and the sources are informal.

O*NET lists using covering cloths so that equipment does not damage delicate fabrics as a core task for Pressers, Textile, Garment, and Related Materials (51-6021.00). The occupation operates steam and hydraulic pressing machines.
A press cloth is a thin cotton, muslin or organza layer placed by hand between the iron or press and the garment to prevent scorching, shine or melting, so the task is entirely physical manipulation.

Press cloths are physical products, such as the Dritz 594 silk organza cloth, which is dampened and laid over the fabric. Software has no role in performing the task, though an agent could at most look up fabric-care guidance.
O*NET lists pressing machine operator as a title for this occupation. The work means putting garments on heated presses and running them by hand, which is physical machine-tending.
Small garment presses, such as VEIT's collar and cuff press, are steam or electric machines that a person loads and runs by hand. No software agent can run them.
Making a necktie includes handling the fabric by hand, such as pinching the V-tip, which needs physical dexterity.

O*NET lists this task for Pressers (51-6021.00): workers select, install and adjust pressing forms, rollers and guides using hoists and hand tools. The work is hands-on mechanical setup, which an AI agent with no body cannot carry out. At most it could look up a manual or a part number.

Other duties in the same occupation are also physical: setting heat and pressure on the machine controls and finishing garments with hand irons. This shows the job is done at the machine, not through software.

The leading end of new fabric is joined to the trailing end of the fabric being processed by stitching transverse seams with a standby hand sewing machine. Someone has to physically line up the fabric and run the machine.
Comatex sells portable chainstitch machines for joining fabric at the entry to dyeing and finishing machines. These are hand-operated physical tools, not software.
Sewing tracks for joining pieces at the entry to finishing machines are mechanical gear that an operator loads and runs on the shop floor.
Vendor listings describe automatic shoe-upper cutters whose nesting software and defect-detecting camera plan the cutting path. The leather is still loaded and cut by dedicated CNC hardware.

Leather cutting systems such as Elitron Kudos use automatic nesting software (EliNest, NesCUT). This automates the layout planning, but the cutting itself is done by a machine, not by a software agent.

An EU project built a lay-planning system for shoe-upper parts that can feed manual or numerically controlled cutters. So software helps with planning, and a person or a machine still does the physical cutting.

Threading a machine is entirely hands-on: you raise the presser foot and needle with the hand wheel, then pass thread through the guides, the take-up lever, the needle eye and the presser foot. An AI agent that can only use software cannot do any of this.

Threading guides describe a manual sequence of steps that depend on the specific machine model. The only digital help is a threading diagram or manual, which a worker would already have, so AI adds little.
Common threading guides list only physical steps, such as snapping the thread into guides and pulling it through the presser foot. None of these steps can be done through software.
O*NET lists Sewers, Hand (51-6051.00) duties as physical handling of fabric: aligning parts, basting and joining material by hand with needle and thread. No software tool performs these steps.
The occupation is entered with little formal education and needs no licence, so no law requires a human to perform or sign the work. The barrier is purely physical manipulation of material.

ShadeBar Pro is an inline system that uses a spectrophotometer to measure L*a*b* values on moving fabric and calculate Delta E colour differences in real time. That covers the colour-measurement step, but it needs dedicated sensor hardware on the line.

AI vision camera systems detect fabric defects and shade variation, but they need controlled lighting and cameras installed on the line. A software-only agent can analyse the data these systems produce, but it cannot examine or feel the cloth itself.

Vision-based colour inspection reports Delta E and CIELAB colour-difference data, which an agent could read against standards. Judging tactile qualities such as hand and texture still requires a person handling the fabric.

One 2024 study used the Prophet time-series model on existing operating data to spot early impeller wear in pumps used for fabric dyeing. That is software helping with diagnosis. A person still has to do the repair.

Vendors sell AI predictive-maintenance and maintenance-management software for jet, jigger, winch and beam dyeing machines. It predicts pump and bearing failures and creates work orders. Technicians still do the cleaning, oiling and part replacement by hand. These are vendor marketing claims that no one has checked independently.

A Birlasoft case study reports that machine-learning predictive maintenance at a textile mill cut asset downtime by 48%. It used more than 2,000 sensor points and was not specific to dyeing machines. The software helps plan the work, but the maintenance itself is physical and done by people on the floor.

O*NET lists this as a task of Textile Cutting Machine Setters, Operators, and Tenders. In the occupation's work context, 72% use their hands continually and 73% stand continually, and the role needs finger dexterity and arm-hand steadiness.

Patents show that machine threading is done by hand or with built-in pneumatic and mechanical self-threading devices. Even with automatic threading, an operator still places the yarn end by hand, so the work is physical machinery, not software.
Older textile threading tools, such as hand-operated pumps for pulling yarn through ducts, are manual devices. None of the threading methods found involves a software or AI agent.

Stoll's knitelligence software covers design through production. Its Stoll-autocreate tool turns artwork into a knitting program, so part of reading a pattern and deriving a program is already automated. A job-risk analysis notes that the physical changeover on the machine is still done by people.

Weaving CAD tools such as WeavePoint, Pointcarre Dobby and DNC.GARM.DOBBY generate threading, treadling, tie-up and lift plans and produce spec sheets and loom-readable files. An agent could read these documents and work out setup parameters from them.

No source shows AI taking a mill's written specification and producing a complete loom setup. Most tools start from a drawn or image design. Checking physical fabric samples and talking with floor supervisors still needs a person on site.

Machines that change bobbins automatically (doffing and donning) are mechanical devices. Otherwise, putting empty bobbins on spindles and taking full ones off is done by hand. Neither is something a software-only AI agent can do.
Each spindle can have a mechanical gripper that lifts off the full bobbin and places an empty one. This is physical handling done by machinery, not by digital agents.
Automatic loading and unloading of bobbins on spinning and winding machines needs dedicated hardware, which shows the task is physical manipulation.

Industrial automatic winders handle unwinding from spools and rewinding onto take-up packages with mechanical tensioners, joiners and conveyors. This automation is mechanical hardware, not a software AI agent, and any manual work left over is hands-on handling of spools, bobbins and yarn ends.

Rewinding means pulling yarn off a bobbin, running it through a tension device and slub catcher, and winding it onto a tube driven by a traverse drum. Every step is physical manipulation of material, so a software-only agent with no body cannot do any substantial part of it.
A traversing winding device can rewind spindles on demand along a textile machine. This shows the task gets automated through machinery, not through digital tools an agent can reach.

Research systems use cameras and AI on extrusion lines to flag surface defects in real time, so shop-floor workers can respond quickly. Detecting the defect can be automated, but people still act on the alert.

A vendor proof of concept for extrusion quality control shows defect alerts to operators on screen and can feed real-time feedback to the line. It is not a verified production deployment, and directing workers to adjust the machines stays on the plant floor.

Vendor material says AI vision raises an alert on the first out-of-spec section, which supports automated notification. This is vendor marketing and unverified. It is not evidence that a software agent can direct physical machine adjustments.

StitchDesk is listed as an AI system for upholstery shops that automates fabric yardage calculations along with inventory and invoicing. This comes from a directory listing, and the features were not checked independently.

Fabric yardage calculators take piece sizes, roll width, piece count and allowances and return both the exact cut yardage and the amount to buy. An agent can repeat this from the measurements on a work order.

A supplier's furniture-shape yardage chart is only a general guide because real pieces vary. Getting an accurate estimate still means measuring or inspecting the workpiece, and only a human in the shop can do that.

Upholstery estimating tools exist that calculate yardage, labor and materials and produce PDF quotes. A vendor guide claims a vision model estimated yardage from photos to within about one yard roughly 80% of the time on standard pieces, but it struggles with curved, tufted or vintage pieces, so the upholsterer still checks yardage and sets prices.

AI reupholstery visualizers can show customers how candidate fabrics would look on their furniture, which covers part of the fabric, color and style discussion. The tool's article could not be read, so its fabric-swap handling is unverified.

About 9 states plus D.C. license upholstery businesses, with fees but no exams. These are business licenses and do not require a licensed person to carry out or sign the customer consultation or estimate.

Distressing is done by hand: hammers, chains or nails dent the surface, screwdrivers or chisels cut gouges, a wire brush scrubs out soft fibres, and sandpaper rounds edges, all before the stain goes on. An agent with no body can do none of this.

The antique look also comes from hand work during staining: stain is wiped off with a rag so it stays mostly in recesses, and wear marks are placed where use would naturally leave them. This needs hands and eyes on the actual piece.

The worker uses judgement on the actual object, for example not sanding through thin veneer on particle board. Software can only offer general advice, so it cannot meaningfully speed up the physical work. No licence or legal sign-off applies to this task.

O*NET lists 'Follow blueprints to produce specific designs' as a Furniture Finishers task. The occupation's core work is hands-on with the wood: sanding, stripping old finishes, repairing surfaces, and applying stain, lacquer or wax.

A Canadian furniture finisher job posting lists reading blueprints and drawings as one duty within physical finishing work in a shop. An AI could help interpret the drawings, but a person has to do the finishing.
The other Furniture Finishers tasks on O*NET include masking areas, removing accessories and repairing cracks and dents. Each needs physical handling, and an agent without a body cannot do any of it.

A search for automated reupholstery turned up only low-quality, copied pages from unreliable sites. They describe robotic upholstery in high-volume factory production, not stripping and re-covering existing pieces. No credible source showed software-only agents doing this work. A body-less AI agent could at most give marginal help, such as looking up fabric, adhesive or solvent specs or drafting cut templates.

The task is hands-on work on the object itself: removing old covering, cutting and fitting fabric, tacking or gluing it down, and applying softeners, solvents, stains or polish. It requires being there in person, and no law or licence requires a human to sign off on it.

Wood bleaching means mixing chemicals (two-part sodium hydroxide/hydrogen peroxide or oxalic acid) and brushing them by hand into the grain with a foam, nylon or scrub brush, then repeating and neutralizing as needed. All of this is physical work an agent without a body cannot do.

Getting an even result depends on judging the wood by eye and hand: testing on a hidden spot, deciding whether to reapply, wiping with vinegar to neutralize, and checking for embedded ferrous metal. Software can only offer step-by-step guidance on these steps.
The main constraints are safety ones (eye protection, gloves, ventilation, non-metal containers). No licence or sign-off by a person is required.
Graining metal means physically wiping thinned ink onto the surface with cheesecloth, combs or rollers, then lacquering it. Only hands or machinery can do this; software has no part in it.
Industrial graining transfers ink with etched plates and rollers. That is physical printing equipment, not something an AI agent can do through software.
Faux-grain technique depends on hand skill applied to wet glaze, such as dragging and rocking a graining tool, which takes practice to get right.

O*NET lists this as a core task for Model Makers, Wood (51-7031.00). It means fitting and joining wood parts by hand with glue, nails, dowels, bolts and screws. This is physical work that an agent with no robotics cannot do. At most, AI could help by planning joinery or assembly order, which is a small share of the time.
The duties around this task are also hands-on: trimming and sanding surfaces by hand, marking assembly details on parts, and finishing models with shellac, lacquer or wax.

Wood patternmakers build unit or sectional patterns for sand-casting molds. This is shop-floor work with no licence or sign-off required. The barrier is that it must be done physically, not any legal rule.

Building a box assembly jig means physically cutting a flat base and fixing rails or stops precisely square. That is bench work an agent without a body cannot do. It can only help with the layout and dimensions.
Assembly jigs use physical spacer strips and locating stops lined up with the slat ends. The worker has to place and check these by hand.
Box assembly jigs are physical tools that hold the sides upright so they can be glued and nailed. The work is hands-on, and no licence or legal sign-off is needed.

Yokogawa's eLogBook moves control-room logsheets into a digital system. It records operator observations and manually captured process data, supports shift handover, and can start maintenance requests, so the logs are machine-readable.

Pertamina's LEADS system at the Jambaran Tiung Biru gas plant uses an LSTM autoencoder on historical process data. It detects anomalies and sends early warnings, including flagging nomination (demand) changes and start-ups.

In a Baker Hughes/C3 AI compressor deployment, AI detected over 88% of anomalous events and cut alarms by 99%. Operators still confirm and act on the detections, and plant OT data is usually on restricted networks.

Air Liquide has run multivariable model predictive control (Yokogawa PACE) on its air separation units for over 20 years. The units adapt on their own to customer demand and power prices, and the vendor reports no operator intervention was needed in steady state or during load changes. The work an agent could take over is mostly this DCS/APC supervision, and dedicated control software already does much of it.

Field operators do rounds, inspecting equipment by sight, sound and smell and reading local gauges. They make local adjustments to valves, dampers and controllers, which is physical work an agent without a body cannot do.
ASU operators handle start-up and shut-down as well as preventive and corrective maintenance. These are the hands-on, non-routine parts of controlling the equipment.

Machine-learning anomaly detection on refinery process telemetry is already in use. Kaspersky MLAD was piloted on TANECO's CDU-VDU-7 unit, and a 2026 preprint describes adaptive online monitoring with LLM-assisted fault diagnosis, so the control-room part of monitoring can be largely automated.

Operator rounds mean physically walking the unit to read local gauges and tank levels, check valve positions and pumps, and notice leaks, noise, vibration and hot spots. These are physical sensing steps a software agent cannot do.

Under OSHA's PSM rules, operator rounds in covered processes check pressure, temperature, tank levels and samples against operating limits. Responsibility for these checks sits with trained operators and the employer's procedures, not with a personal licence or sign-off.

ASTM D4007 sets out a hands-on lab method for measuring water and sediment in crude oil with a centrifuge. Someone has to physically prepare the sample and run the centrifuge. The results are used to work out net volumes for sales and custody transfer.

Inline BS&W and watercut monitors already check crude quality automatically in LACT custody-transfer systems. This is fixed process hardware, though, not an AI agent. A software agent could at most help with calculations or record-keeping.

LACT parts and how they operate, including automatic sampling, are covered by API MPMS standards (Chapter 8.2 for samplers). These are industry standards, not licensing rules that require a particular person to sign off.

Slab-nesting and DXF-template software for countertop fabricators (e.g., SlabWise) automates turning templates into layouts and machine-ready files, but by the vendor's own account it does not deal with physical stone features like veining and remnants.
General AI nesting tools such as Nest&Cut automatically lay out shapes from DXF input to save material.
Machine-learning pipelines that read dimensions from engineering drawings reach about 81% accuracy, so critical dimensions still need a human to check them.

Inline analyzers paired with PLCs (BFI DynAcid, SensoTech LiquiSonic) can measure acid and iron-salt levels in pickling baths and dose acid automatically. That is dedicated plant automation, though, not something a software agent does through screens and documents. Where no such system is installed, an agent can only work out the dose amounts or log them.

In patented strip-cleaning line control, conductivity probes and an online titrator feed a PLC that adjusts acid and water additions. So the measure-and-dose loop is handled by plant hardware, not an AI agent.

OSHA rule 29 CFR 1910.94(d)(9) requires employees working around open-surface pickling tanks to be trained in hazards, protective equipment and first aid. The work involves handling corrosive chemicals in person, but no licence or human signature is required.

Tire building means physically placing the inner liner, plies and other rubber parts on a building drum, either by hand or with machine appliers on the factory floor. This is hands-on work that a software-only agent cannot do.
The O*NET profile for Tire Builders describes building rubber treads and layers onto tire casings in production and retread shops, which is manual or machine-operated physical work.
A process study of tire building notes that most steel-belted radial tires are assembled by hand: the inner liner and plies first, then the belts and tread.

In retreading, stitching means pressing a roller onto the newly placed tread to push air out of the bond line and make the bond layer an even thickness. It is a physical step done by hand or by machine.
Mechanical tire stitching machines exist. This shows the step is done by physical machinery, not by software agents with no body.
Older equipment for putting camelback onto tire casings is also mechanical, so the task is about physically handling rubber and the casing.

Speedcargo's Amplifi tool creates ULD-level load plans from booked cargo and aircraft type. Its Assemble tool gives ground handlers step-by-step digital build-up plans. Etihad Cargo has these in use in Singapore and is piloting them in Frankfurt, so the planning sub-step is automatable.

AI engines that use 3D spatial analysis and combinatorial optimisation can generate ULD build-up plans covering dimensions, weight, contours and dangerous-goods rules. This claim comes from a vendor explainer, so it is unverified. The physical build-up and placement of cargo is still done by people on the ramp or warehouse floor.

I found no federal certificate that an FAA load supervisor must hold. Load supervision and verification follow operator procedures under AC 120-85, and a 2018 FAA working group only studied certification for special cargo.

This task is done in person in the cargo hold during flight: inspecting restraints, watching for cargo shifting, smoke or leaks, then reporting to the pilots and taking corrective action. An agent with no body can't do these.
The loadmaster is a member of the flight crew. In-flight duties include visually checking interior and exterior clearances, running in-flight checks from the flight manual, and monitoring cargo.

Military loadmaster duties also include monitoring aircraft systems (fuel, hydraulic, electrical, environmental) and air traffic control radio while on board. These are crew-member responsibilities for a qualified person who is physically present. This source covers military roles, so it is only a rough guide to civil operations.

Launching a lifeboat is hands-on work done on deck and inside the boat: removing harbour pins, releasing gripes, working the winch brake, pulling the safety pin and working the hook-release lever, then steering the boat clear under engine. An agent with no body can't do any of this.

SOLAS Reg. III/3.2 requires survival craft to be handled by 'certified persons', meaning people who hold an STCW VI/2 Certificate of Proficiency in Survival Craft and Rescue Boats. The company and the master must make sure the crew assigned to these duties hold that certificate.

The STCW A-VI/2-1 competence trains a person to launch a survival craft or rescue boat and take charge of it in an emergency. This is a crew role in person, with a certificate that must be renewed every five years.

Removing rust on a ship means a person physically holds and runs pneumatic needle scalers (1.3–3.2 kg, 6–7 bar, 101–109 dB(A)) against steel decks and hulls. A software-only agent has no way to do this.
Needle scalers for shipyards are sold as hand tools with flexible needles that a person guides over uneven surfaces and projections. The task is manual work, not a digital process.

Marine autopilots already hold a course on their own: heading mode keeps a compass heading, and track mode holds a GPS course over ground by correcting for cross-track error. Operators still hand-steer in congested or tricky water, and these are dedicated onboard control systems, not something a software-only AI agent can normally operate.
Garmin documents autopilot heading-hold and route-following modes that run through the boat's own onboard hardware.
Carrying paying passengers on small vessels requires a USCG OUPV or Master credential held by a human operator. This requires sea time, an exam, a physical and a drug test.

Ships are usually controlled from the bridge, the engine control room or locally at the engine. Rules say only one location may control propulsion at a time, and local manual control must stay available if the remote system fails. Bridge control is built-in shipboard automation, not something a general-purpose AI agent can reach.
Vard's SeaQ Remote lets specialized class-approved systems run engines, propellers and thrusters remotely, but only on purpose-built autonomous newbuilds. Ordinary ships do not have it.

STCW and national rules such as 46 CFR 11.329 require a certified engineer to be in charge of an engineering watch, or to be the designated duty engineer when the engine room is periodically unmanned.

Factories do automate dosing. When manual addition is replaced, the work goes to dosing tanks and digital pumps, which are fixed hardware and not a software AI agent. The manual version needed extra manpower and physical handling of the chemicals.

In automated powder dosing, an operator types ingredient ratios and recipes into an HMI and a PLC controls the feeders. This setup screen is the only part a software agent could plausibly touch, and it depends on plant control systems that agents normally cannot reach.

Manual systems depend on an operator adding the chemicals by hand. Automated systems use sensors, controllers and pumps. Either way the task is physical or done by machinery, so a bodiless AI agent can only help with things like calculating amounts or looking up procedures.

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(l) says only trained, employer-certified operators may run powered industrial trucks such as forklifts. Training includes hands-on practice and an evaluation of the operator in the workplace, so the task is physical and a trained human must be accountable for it.

Automating this transfer work takes physical robots (AMRs and autonomous forklifts that move parts between machines). The software-only agents used as the reference technology here are not robots, so they cannot move the materials themselves.

ABB's Flexley Stack F712 autonomous forklift (2026) shows that robotics does this work in factories, not language-model agents. A software agent could at most help with dispatch or WMS/MES scheduling, which is a small part of the job.

Emerson's Winblend software runs batch blending by weight. Before a batch starts, it checks that raw materials, routes, flow paths and tank storage are available, and it logs alarms and completion data. This means the control and recordkeeping steps are already handled by software, not by an AI agent.

ABB's Regulatory Blend Control starts and stops blends, controls pump sequencing and adjusts flows to match a recipe. These functions run inside the plant's own control system, which an outside agent would not normally be able to reach.

In a 2008 case study, a PLC touchscreen panel let operators pick a recipe and dosed preset quantities. Lining up valves and hoses, connecting tanks and taking samples on site are still physical jobs for the operator, so an AI agent could mainly help with recipe calculations, checks and logs.

In practice, operators run chemical tests by hand on water at the plant using chlorine titrators, pH meters and turbidity meters, then adjust chemical feeds. This is physical sampling and instrument work.
O*NET lists 'Test materials and solutions, using testing equipment' as a task for Pump Operators, Except Wellhead Pumpers, next to collecting samples and adding chemicals to tanks.

Online analyzers can feed SCADA continuously. Under EPA Method 334, they can be used for compliance only alongside regular manual grab-sample checks, so an agent can only help with reading data, interpreting it and keeping records.

Atatus released Watchtower AI RCA in April 2026. The vendor says it finds anomalies and root causes from real traffic patterns without manual thresholds, so the detection and diagnosis steps of performance monitoring are already automated. This is a vendor claim with no independent benchmark.

A Tech Week Singapore 2026 session abstract describes multi-agent AI systems that detect performance regressions in production apps and locate their root causes. It also notes that diagnostics differ by platform, which makes the work hard. This is a conference abstract, not a peer-reviewed study.

A vendor comparison page credits Dynatrace's causal AI root-cause analysis with a 65% cut in MTTR. The figure is not independently verified. The task is done entirely in software, and I found no licence or legal sign-off requirement for monitoring program performance.
Agentic QA tools from 2026 plan, generate, run and repair software tests on their own, with humans setting goals and reviewing results. These claims come mostly from vendors.
Closed-loop LLM agents such as AgentDV generate hardware (RTL) testbenches, run simulations and refine them using coverage feedback. This work is simulation-based.

Agent-driven hardware-in-the-loop tests run on physical devices, and code that compiles can still fail on real hardware because of timing or peripheral behavior. Someone still has to set up the hardware, and a human has to validate the results.

A ScreenSkills career guide says AI tools can help hair and makeup departments track continuity across scenes. That is support work like reference photos and notes. Applying makeup to the performer is still done by hand.
The search found no dedicated on-set makeup continuity software that applies makeup. Current AI makeup tools only retouch photos or offer virtual try-on, not physical work on a real face.

Makeup continuity means keeping an actor's look consistent from day to day and shot to shot. A digital agent can check reference images, but someone has to physically apply products and prosthetics to the actor's face.
By 2026, AI agents can find, compare and buy products from a stated goal. Checkout support is still patchy: few merchants are live on in-chat checkout, and some large retailers block agents.
Professional suppliers of special-effects makeup, wigs and hair, such as The Costumer and Banbury Postiche, take orders online, so an agent could do the sourcing and ordering.
Custom wigs and hairpieces need precise head measurements and usually can't be returned. A person has to take the measurements, match colors on the performer, and check the goods when they arrive.
Continuity tools like SyncOnSet and DH Hair | Makeup handle continuity photos, notes and looks digitally. Someone still has to take the photos and enter the information on set.

Commercial tools such as Perfect Corp's AI Makeup Transfer can read color and texture from a reference look and suggest brand-specific product SKUs. These are guesses, not a record of the products the artist actually used.
Australia's CUAMUP412 continuity unit treats record-keeping and continuity photos as an on-set job, checking the performer's makeup at the end of each take. That requires being physically present.

ScreenSkills' AI guidance for hair and make-up designers says AI can generate hair and makeup concepts from character descriptions, a script or historical references and act as a visual sounding board. It also says interpreting character nuance remains a human skill.
Diffusion models can change facial attributes and cosmetic styles, including makeup for a period-drama setting, and are trained on large datasets of historical clothing and character designs.

Concept sketching, reference research and digital character mockups are listed as higher-risk tasks for automation. Prosthetic sculpting and hands-on application stay lower risk. Making physical models therefore still needs a person, and a designer has to check historical accuracy and the result for each actor.

Farm payroll platforms already handle blended piece-rate and hourly pay, minimum-wage top-ups, H-2A compliance, housing deductions and mobile time capture. That covers the main calculation and processing steps, which an agent can run through software.

Under 29 CFR 500.81, a farm labor contractor must pay wages when due and at least every two weeks (or semi-monthly). The law sets what must be paid and when, but it does not require a person to do the payroll work. The contractor is still legally liable, and a human usually approves the money going out.

MSPA requires an itemized written wage statement for each worker every pay period, including the employer's IRS EIN. Software can generate this automatically, but the hours and piece counts behind it come from crew leaders in the field. Many seasonal workers are also paid by paper check or cash handed out in person.

No AI tool turned up that inspects installed wallcovering seams. The closest machine-vision work checks the alignment of finished tile installations from images and is meant to replace subjective visual checks. That means a human would have to take photos on site before an AI could even assist.
Commercial AI vision tools check pattern alignment and defects only in textile manufacturing, not on wallpaper already hung in a building.
Pattern-alignment algorithms for repeating patterns exist, but they plan cuts for garment seams. They do not inspect finished installations.
Job postings say roofer helpers help experienced roofers tear off or remove existing shingles and other roofing materials, then clean the roof deck to prepare for installation.
The work requires climbing ladders, working at heights with fall protection, using hand tools, and lifting 50 to 80 lbs. This is manual work that an agent without a body cannot do.
Helpers remove old roofing materials under the supervision of skilled roofers on the job site. The task is done entirely by hand on the roof, with no part of it done in software.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1926.451, scaffolds may only be put up, moved, taken down or altered by trained workers supervised by a qualified competent person. That person has to judge on site whether the footing is adequate and fit ties or braces to stop tipping, so a person must physically be there.

A competent person must inspect each scaffold for visible defects before every shift and after any event that could affect its structural integrity. These are hands-on checks done in person, and the law puts the responsibility on a human.

OSHA's standard interpretations cover how scaffold and ladder access is physically erected and secured. The task is moving, placing and anchoring heavy equipment on a job site, which a software-only agent with no robotics cannot do. My search did not separately check the ladder or hoist rules.
Chopping tar into small pieces and heating it in kettles is a listed core duty of roofer helpers, along with hoisting tar and materials onto roofs. All of it is physical work done on site.

Running a kettle safely means physical work on site: setting the kettle on firm, level ground, keeping the temperature below the flash point, having a fire extinguisher at hand and putting up barriers to keep the public back.
Utah requires an attendant to stay within 100 feet of the kettle whenever the burner is lit. This is a safety-supervision rule, not a licensing requirement.

The only gutter-cleaning automation found was a hardware robot, the iRobot Looj. It is now discontinued and was driven by a person on site who had to place it in the gutter. Software agents with no body can't do this.
The Looj was remote-controlled or ran on its own only after a person put it into the gutter. Clearing debris means physically working on the roofline, so someone has to be there.
Sarine's machine-learning Clarity system maps diamond inclusions and blemishes. It needs dedicated imaging hardware with the physical stone placed in it.
GIA and IBM Research built an automated clarity grading system trained on tens of millions of graded diamonds. It was in limited use at GIA labs, covering only the most popular sizes at first.
Automated grading depends on hardware, lighting and stone orientation. A software-only agent cannot do that physical setup or the loupe and microscope examination.

AI tools for wheel-throwing feedback exist only as research prototypes (a CMU mixed-reality system using computer vision and LLMs). Researchers note that ceramics is embodied and its tacit knowledge is hard to pass on, so an AI can at most support a human teacher.

Studio job postings for pottery instructors ask for hands-on wheel-throwing and hand-building skill, prior teaching experience and a background check. The work is in-person demonstration and guidance in the studio.
Hiring sources ask for experience and a practice record, not a licence. Postings in the US and UK show no legal certification requirement for pottery instructors.

Royal IHC's dredging control system monitors and automates slurry pumps, gate valves and suction pipes. Its pump controller prevents pipeline clogging. This is onboard vessel automation run by the crew, not a general AI agent working through software.

Dragflow's Pumping Control System runs from a handheld tablet next to the equipment. It monitors density, flow and pressure and can switch components on and off. Line flushing still needs an operator on site to set valves and check that the pipeline is clear.

Automatic hopper-dredge controls start the pump with the overboard discharge valve open. These sequences are built into vessel control systems, which an outside software agent would not normally be able to reach.

O*NET lists this as a Dredge Operator task: directing or helping workers place shore anchors and cables, lay pipe from the dredge to shore, and pump water from pontoons. All of this is hands-on work on the water and at the shoreline.

A leverman job posting says the role includes directing or helping crew members place shore anchors and cables and assemble, position and lay pipe. This is physical rigging work done on site, not work done in software.

Related duties include running power winches, pulling in cables by hand and lowering anchor poles, all done at remote dredging sites. An agent that works only through software has no way to do or directly oversee this work.

MSHA rule 30 CFR 57.3200 says hazardous ground must be taken down or supported in the underground workplace before anyone else works or travels in the area. Taking down loose ground is physical work done on site.

30 CFR 57.3202 requires a scaling bar when scaling is done by hand. 30 CFR 57.3401 requires the mine operator to designate people experienced in examining and testing for loose ground, which means a qualified person must be physically present and accountable.

Commission case law says loose ground is judged by on-site tests such as sounding, visible fractures and popping noises. These checks require someone physically there to sense and handle the rock. A software-only agent with no body cannot pry rock or move it.

MSHA fatality reports describe workers who were killed while shovelling or cleaning conveyor spillage. Both blamed failures in safe spillage-removal procedures, such as not de-energizing and blocking the belt. This shows the task is hands-on physical work inside the conveyor area.

MSHA housekeeping standards (30 CFR 56/57.20003) require operators to keep work areas, including conveyor walkways, free of spillage. The requirement is met by removing material physically, not through documents or digital systems.

Underground coal spillage under belts and at transfer points builds up and becomes a fire or explosion hazard. Dealing with it takes physical cleaning on site underground, where a software-only agent cannot act.

Funeral-home software such as Memorion already covers scheduling, documentation, invoicing and workforce management, with an AI assistant whose output staff review. Search results showed no AI tools for funeral-home hiring decisions or for supervising staff.

In Kansas, each funeral establishment must always be under the charge and personal supervision of a licensed funeral director, who is responsible for staff conduct. No funeral arrangement may proceed without a licensed director or assistant director present.

Virginia requires a licensed manager of record for each funeral establishment, named on the establishment's license. Wisconsin requires a licensed funeral director in charge with full supervision of funeral directing and embalming.

Vendors sell AI colony-counting and plate-reading tools for water and environmental monitoring, such as Copan PharmaLab, Kikkoman CCS and Tailin ASC-2000Pro. They automate only the image-reading step, which happens after a human has physically sampled, plated and incubated the material. Accuracy figures come from the vendors and have not been independently validated.

Under state programs based on the EPA drinking-water lab certification manual, compliance microbiology analyses must be done by approved analysts. In Kentucky that means 30 days of supervised bench training, 60 more days of bench experience and passing proficiency tests. Ohio adds that each analyst must analyze at least 10% of routine samples. The requirements were read from state documents, not the federal manual itself.

UKAS has accredited automated colony counters such as Synbiosis ProtoCOL for counting microbes in water. That is still instrument-assisted counting inside an accredited lab workflow run by people, not autonomous testing.

Applied environmental research often includes hands-on field and lab work: soil and groundwater sampling, pilot tests, remediation monitoring, and lab tests of water quality. An agent cannot do these steps itself.

LLM multi-agent frameworks published in 2026, such as OpenAqua for early-stage water treatment train design and LLM agents for wastewater plants, already do the digital parts: literature retrieval, design options, modeling and optimization.
O*NET 19-2041.00 lists this task next to doing research or investigations to identify and abate pollutant sources. It is a research role with no required licensed signature for the research itself.

State boards require the PTA to complete continuing education hours personally to renew a licence. Examples: South Dakota requires 30 hours per 2-year period, and South Carolina requires 30 hours including ethics. Since the point is the worker's own learning, an agent cannot attend in their place.
Arizona requires 10 contact hours of continuing competence per compliance period for certified PTAs. Several states track compliance through CE Broker.

AI slide and video tools such as Prezi AI and 2Slides already turn policy PDFs into in-service training decks and narrated videos. Vendors still advise human checking for clinical accuracy, so AI can only help prepare sessions the PTA conducts.

Jail management systems already handle inmate movements, headcounts, cell checks, shift notes and incident reports digitally. Vendors list AI Copilot and generative AI features, which suggests that data entry and drafting can be automated.

Some analysts propose AI analytics that combine camera and sensor feeds into single incident logs. The source is an opinion piece, not a tested deployment, and officers still observe events on the unit in person.

Correctional policy requires each staff member who witnesses an incident to write their own observation report, sign it and send it to a supervisor for review and signature. This means a human must give the account and attest to it.

A patent for 'personalized chatbots for inmates' describes a server that answers inmate questions from stored data and offers counseling suggestions. This shows that answering routine written requests through tablets or kiosks can be automated in part.
Most prisons forbid inmates from going online. Official AI chatbot use on secure tablets is limited to pilots such as Northeastern's Prison Project, so agents rarely reach the inmate-facing channel.

A 2025 thesis finds that LLM chatbots on prison tablets can support inmates, but deploying them requires careful calibration against institutional constraints. Face-to-face counseling by officers in housing units is still done by humans.

O*NET lists 'Use nondisciplinary tools and equipment, such as a computer' as a task for Correctional Officers and Jailers (33-3012.00). Related job descriptions show the equipment includes radios, intercoms, phones, restraints and central control booth equipment, which are used on site inside the facility.

Jail management software already automates parts of the computer work, such as syncing arrest reports into the jail system, filling in charges automatically, sending warrant alerts and checking reports with AI. Officers still enter data, check it and act on it in person.
Officers in control centers watch inmates using CCTV and computer tracking systems. Much of the equipment use is tied to physical presence and live security operations inside the facility.
