Under Article II, Section 2, confirmation requires the Senate's advice and consent. Committees hold hearings, review disclosures and FBI background checks, and the full Senate votes. Only the legislators themselves can cast these votes.
In NCSL's 2026 survey, about 55-56% of legislative staff said they use generative AI for research and summarization. Staff also said AI output needs substantial human review.

Sen. Bernie Moreno's office uses an AI assistant for vetting work, according to a secondhand aggregator report of his remarks. He also said Senate rules currently bar integrating AI into Senate systems.

NCSL's preliminary 2026 survey: 55% of legislative staff use generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini and Claude. They use them for research, summarizing, transcribing meetings and some drafting. Staff are still told to verify all output, and nothing describes AI doing the negotiating.

Lawyers in the US House Office of Legislative Counsel are spending more time fixing AI-drafted bills with errors. In South Dakota, a lawmaker had Grok write first drafts of a bill that was later folded into a compromise package, but the senators still negotiated it themselves.

Lawmaking in 2026 is adopting AI for drafting and analysis support, while the actual bargaining between legislators and parties happens through human relationships, often face-to-face and behind closed doors.
AI tools such as Quorum's Quincy and ChatGPT prompt packs for congressional staff draft talking points, meeting briefs and media messaging. The legislator still delivers them and negotiates.
PolicyPage drafts one-page legislative meeting briefs, with citations, tailored to a specific legislator. This is preparation support only, not the representation itself.
Parliamentary mandates and votes are personal and cannot be delegated (for example, Article 79.6 of the Spanish Constitution). Representing a party is tied to an elected, accountable human.

Certified CT explosive detection systems already use an automated detection algorithm that makes a yes-or-no alarm decision. A screener reviews the flagged objects on screen and can override the alarm and clear the bag. Bags the screener does not clear go to secondary inspection: they are opened or swabbed for explosive traces.
The National Academies describe on-screen alarm resolution as a human step: the screener either clears the alarm or sends the bag on for more inspection. Each false alarm costs staff time.

Under 49 CFR 1544.207, TSA or its contractors must inspect property before it is loaded. Subpart E sets qualification rules for anyone who performs a screening function, so a qualified human screener must make and own the decision.
TSA's CT checkpoint scanners can detect explosives and other threat items automatically, but a TSA officer still looks at and resolves any bag the system flags.

A DHS S&T-funded AI algorithm piloted at Las Vegas flagged CT scans that might hold threats. It served as a second set of eyes for the officer doing the manual review and still needs TSA certification before deployment.

Regulators require people who operate X-ray or EDS equipment to hold certification and pass standardized image-interpretation tests. For example, CASRA reports that EU Regulation 185/2010 requires this.

Under TSA's checked-baggage process, CT explosive detection systems flag bags automatically. A TSO then reviews the images and decides whether to clear the bag or open it. Physical inspections are done by hand, on camera, and the officer leaves a Notice of Inspection in the bag.

Workers log every bag they physically handle, including who opened it and when. Fewer than 10% of bags are touched. Spotting tampering means handling and looking at the bag itself, which needs a human.

AI threat-detection tools for CT images (Pangiam/Project DARTMOUTH, SeeTrue) are in TSA trials. They are purpose-built vendor systems that help with image screening, not general software agents, and they do not physically check bags for tampering.

Purpose-built exit-lane systems at airports already raise real-time alerts to security staff when someone walks the wrong way through an exit lane (Kaba at McCarran; CheckVideo ExitSentry). That covers only one narrow type of breach and depends on fixed sensors and cameras, not a general AI agent.

Breach notification is tied to the screener's physical work at the checkpoint, such as following people who breach security until police arrive. The breach is usually spotted in person, and the alert is a quick radio or verbal call, so an agent adds little unless it has the camera and radio feeds.

Under 49 CFR 1544.405, no one may perform a screening function unless qualified. Checkpoint procedures are restricted as sensitive security information, which limits an agent's access to checkpoint systems.

In in-line systems, conveyors move checked bags through EDS machines. Bags that alarm are routed to resolution rooms or to a secondary area, where officers search them by hand. The automation that exists is conveyor and EDS hardware, not a software agent, and the searches are done by people on site.
TSA describes an image review step in a control room. Bags that need a physical search are then conveyed to an inspection area and searched by officers under CCTV.

Under 49 U.S.C. 44901, screening of passengers and property must be done by federal government employees, with listed exceptions (the current text cites section 44920), and supervised by uniformed TSA personnel.

In 2026 TSA put Ace, a Salesforce-built AI agent, on tsa.gov and the myTSA app. Salesforce reports it handles about 100,000 traveler conversations a month and resolves 96% of routine questions without a human. Harder cases go to live staff with an AI-written summary.
Since 2019, TSA's @AskTSA virtual assistant has answered common screening questions automatically around the clock, in English and Spanish. A human team handles complex questions.

Screeners mostly do this task in person at the checkpoint, pointing and guiding people in lines and lanes, often as part of the screening itself. A software-only agent can take over the informational questions through apps, kiosks or chat, but not the face-to-face directing, which needs someone physically there.

In a vendor case study, Ekimetrics' generative-AI ESG Copilot scored a client's existing reporting against about 1,200 CSRD disclosure requirements and recommended fixes for the gaps. The firm says this took 6 weeks instead of 6 months, a figure it reported itself.

Under the CSRD, the board, management and audit committee hold ultimate responsibility for sustainability reporting. The board must approve the management report that contains the sustainability disclosures, so a human still has to sign off on the compliance judgment.

CSRD reporting must get third-party limited assurance, which requires traceable audit trails. AI-generated metrics make that verification harder, so a human needs to review the AI's output before it is used.

AI and multi-agent systems in 2026 can extract, standardize and cross-check ESG KPI data. ESGAgent, for example, has tools for carbon calculation and checking alignment with regulations. This covers the data-gathering, tracking and analysis steps of program monitoring.

Research on agentic pipelines covers the whole ESG cycle: identification, measurement, reporting, engagement and improvement. It also notes that automation and continuous feedback are still immature, so a human still has to judge whether programs work and decide what changes to make.

Under CSRD the board approves the sustainability statement and auditors give limited assurance on it. Internal evaluation of program effectiveness does not legally require a human to perform or sign it, but external reporting does run through human approval.

AI tools already turn SOPs into training modules, videos and assessments. In regulated settings, subject-matter and quality reviewers still edit and approve the output before it is assigned, so the AI does not author unsupervised.
21 CFR 211.25 requires GMP training to be given by qualified individuals on a continuing basis. A qualified person must run and be accountable for the training.
Guidance for AI-generated GxP training calls for traceability back to the source SOP version, audit trails and human validation of all AI-generated content.

Commercial modeling tools such as OLI ScaleChem, OLI Corrosion Analyzer and Nalco Geomizer predict scaling and corrosion risk in geothermal plants and are used to design inhibitor programmes. An agent could run these tools or similar chemistry models and draft the selection analysis.

A DOE-funded project says no current tool accurately predicts both scaling and corrosion, and that turning model output into practical action still needs a separate advisory layer. Expert judgement and site validation therefore remain essential.

Corrosion control systems are generally designed and installed by, or under the direction of, a qualified person such as a PE or an AMPP/NACE specialist. Implementation means physical installation, monitoring coupons and site work, which needs human sign-off and presence.

Power-plant maintenance software (CMMS) vendors say their products set reorder points from supplier lead times and past usage, and create purchase orders automatically when stock falls below those points. These are vendor claims and have not been checked independently.
Maintenance software already handles safety stock, reorder points and automated purchase requests. AI adds changing reorder levels based on usage trends and how reliable each supplier is.

Vendor pages describe AI that predicts delivery delays, builds parts kits for planned shutdowns and flags obsolete stock. People still have to count stock on site, receive and inspect deliveries, and approve spending on critical spares. No law or licence requires a human to manage inventory.

Commercial electronic logbook software for power plants (Yokogawa eLogBook, MCG Versify OpLog) replaces paper control-room logs. It records events and compliance items, keeps audit trails and links to plant information, maintenance and lab systems. Some process data, such as tank dips, is still entered by hand.
MCG Versify OpLog logs events, activities and compliance requirements into a single tool and captures, stores and analyzes critical operational data.

Under Title V (40 CFR 70.5(d)), a designated Responsible Official, such as the plant general manager, must certify that compliance reports built from these records are true, accurate and complete. A human therefore keeps responsibility for signing off on the recorded data.

Plant startup and shutdown are still done mostly by hand. AI-agent control of startup and shutdown is at the research stage, mainly reinforcement-learning work on nuclear plants, with no commercial control-system deployment found. The researchers also say it is hard to retrofit onto existing plants.

Shutting a boiler down for maintenance means physically isolating every energy source (electrical, fuel, steam and water pressure) and applying lockout/tagout devices under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147. When several crews work on the same equipment, a group lockout is used.
Boiler operator licensing comes from state and local rules, not OSHA. Employers remain liable for unsafe conditions. OSHA cited a biomass plant in New Hampshire for lockout/tagout training failures.

A study used machine learning on SCADA data from a biomass power plant. An Isolation Forest flagged anomalies and a Random Forest sorted operating states at about 96% accuracy. The data covered only one 24-hour period at one plant.

A peer-reviewed study pulled startup, shutdown and failure events from short operator log entries with F1 scores of 80-92%. Specialised NLP beat generative AI used alone, so log review can be automated but still needs a human to check it.
Vendors are selling agentic AI and copilots that search historians, CMMS data and shift logbooks and produce ranked alerts and work orders. Their performance claims are not independently checked.

Hydro O&M platforms such as GE Vernova APM and Andritz DiOMera already offer ML-based anomaly detection, predictive maintenance alerts and a CMMS module for digitising maintenance work. An agent could use these to plan maintenance, schedule work, track work orders and write reports.

Maintenance on generation equipment falls under OSHA 1910.269(d) hazardous-energy control (lockout/tagout). That rule requires on-site isolation, verification and authorization by qualified people, so a human has to oversee the work and sign off on safety.

Remote or unmanned hydro sites still need on-site servicing and coordination with the system operator for energy isolation. Supervising installations means being physically present to direct crews and contractors.

Gym maintenance software such as UpKeep and BlueFolder already handles the arranging side of the job: logging problems through QR codes, scheduling preventive maintenance by usage or date, assigning work orders to outside vendors, and keeping asset and warranty records. An agent could run these steps end to end.

The maintenance itself is hands-on. Job postings describe inspecting, cleaning, lubricating and tightening machines, checking electrical connections, and lifting equipment over 50 lb, so a person has to be there.

Postings ask for CPR/AED and sometimes OSHA training, but no licence requires a human to do or sign off fitness equipment maintenance. A person still has to inspect the machines and do or check the repairs.
Vendor gym software says its AI reads member preferences, usage and attendance data to suggest new class offerings and forecast how renewals and class participation affect revenue.
TeamUp says it launched an AI Business Advisor: a monthly report built from a studio's own performance data and industry benchmarks that recommends business actions.

A vendor example shows AI spotting that evening yoga classes keep filling up and prompting the gym to add sessions or hire instructors. Analysis and recommendations can be automated, but approving the offering and committing budget remains a human management decision.

Current AI fitness tools use a phone camera to check a user's form and give feedback on lifts like squats and bench presses. That is coaching help after the fact, not a physical demonstration of the equipment.
AI workout coach apps record sets and show joint and angle overlays with tips, so they can support instruction, but a person or the equipment itself still has to do the demonstration.
Developers can build real-time vision agents that count reps and give voice cues, but these need the trainee to be physically present and moving, and they cannot adjust or operate machines.

O*NET lists this task for Fitness and Wellness Coordinators, together with a related duty to manage and train staff of wellness specialists, health educators or fitness instructors. The work combines people management with in-person oversight.

Gym instructor-management software such as NetGym automates instructor scheduling, substitute requests, communication and analytics on instructor behaviour. These are administrative sub-steps an agent could run.

AI tools for gyms forecast class demand, balance instructor workloads and link instructor-level factors to member retention. They support supervisory decisions, but the evidence that they give useful coaching feedback in practice is thin.

AI dosing systems already exist: CURATE.AI generated individualised capecitabine dose recommendations, and clinicians accepted close to 97% of them in a 10-patient pilot. Clinicians still made the final call.

Under 21 CFR 312.60 the investigator is accountable for running the study according to the protocol and for protecting subjects. FDA guidance says the investigator stays responsible for any task delegated to staff, so a physician must review and decide on any dose change an agent advises.

Duties on clinical research teams are split by role: coordinators support and document under the investigator's oversight, while clinical decisions such as dose changes stay with qualified investigators.
RTSM/IRT platforms like ClinPhone Pro track site stock and automate restocking, which covers the digital inventory side of supply management but not physical storage.

Viedoc's trial supply management sends alerts when stock at a trial site falls below set threshold levels. An agent could use this for inventory planning, but a person still has to shelve, label and set up the equipment.
Signant's GxP Inventory is a 21 CFR Part 11-compliant software tool for tracking inventory. Arranging the physical space still depends on hands-on work at the site.

Clinical trial management software (CTMS) already works out each subject's protocol visit dates and windows, warns when a window is about to close or a visit is overdue, and texts subjects confirmations and reminders automatically. This covers the routine calculation and reminder parts of the task.

Once a protocol visit schedule is assigned to a subject in a CTMS, the system predicts when each visit should happen. A visit outside its window is a protocol deviation, so a human still has to judge edge cases and documentation.

AI scheduling agents that find open slots and book through Epic FHIR APIs exist but are mostly at proof-of-concept stage. Booking procedures and inpatient stays in hospital electronic health record systems depends on integration and permissions, and an agent often won't have that access.

Nomic's AI drainage-study review checks drainage reports against local criteria and flags mismatched drainage areas, storm events, pipe sizes, elevations and assumptions. It checks that documents are consistent but does not independently solve the hydraulics.
Arcadis is piloting AI with NYC DEP to flag inconsistencies and non-compliance in SWPPP reviews. NYC DEP staff keep professional judgment.

Local codes (e.g., Michigan, Kentucky, Georgia, Washington) require that a licensed professional engineer prepare and seal stormwater detention designs, and that a city engineer review the plans and calculations.

Vendor tools say they can turn compliance policy documents into structured, interactive courses with auto-generated quizzes and role-based learning paths. This covers the content design and e-learning delivery sub-steps.
AI voice and chat agents are being pitched for interactive compliance training tailored to each employee's role and risk exposure. Most of this evidence is vendor marketing, not independent testing.

The DOJ guidance on corporate compliance programs judges training by risk-based design and measured effectiveness. It does not require live or human-delivered training. Even so, human review of AI-written content and live facilitation still help with credibility and with leadership setting the tone.

Compliance platforms like Vanta say they automate evidence collection, parsing and continuous control monitoring for audits through 400+ integrations, and cite an IDC figure of 82% less time per audit. Both claims come from the vendor.
A practitioner case describes building an AI agent to answer customer audit requests by gathering compliance evidence automatically.

Vanta's own guidance says organizations should not fully rely on automated evidence without independent review. Its comparison page also says a competitor's automation is brittle and non-deterministic, so a human still has to check the work, explain processes to auditors in walkthroughs and stand behind management's representations.

Accenture (Dec 2025, vendor forecast) describes PE teams moving from AI-assisted analysis to agent workflows that scan markets, test scenarios and flag diligence issues, with diligence becoming a continuously updated model.

DiligenceSquared, a Y Combinator startup, uses AI and voice agents to produce M&A commercial diligence research and claims, without independent verification, quality comparable to consultancies at much lower cost.

Epiq sells an AI assistant for HSR premerger compliance that tags and queries deal documents. Epiq says it can cut data-related filing costs by up to 80%, but the HSR filing itself still goes through counsel and the parties.

Vendor sources (unverified marketing) say 2026 TMS platforms embed AI agents. Trimble's dispatch optimization has agents across seven modules, and project44 offers an Intelligent TMS. These agents optimize routing and load consolidation and act on the results, not just recommend.

Agent-based load planning re-plans routes and consolidation against capacity, hours-of-service, traffic and weather limits. Agents handle routine cases and pass unusual ones to human operators, so a human still reviews strategic and exception decisions.

A TMS overview credits route optimization, load consolidation and carrier rate optimization with 5-15% lower transport costs (figure not independently sourced). This is software work with no physical step and no licensing or sign-off requirement found.

In a Nov 2025 arXiv prototype, an agentic inventory system handled forecasting, supplier selection and negotiation in a mid-sized store. Against baseline heuristics it cut stockouts and holding costs and improved product-mix turnover. This was a prototype, not a live deployment.

A June 2026 industry description says agentic AI uses ERP data, supplier portals and logistics APIs to optimize inventory on its own. These are vendor claims, and no independent field data on inventory turns was found.

Supply-chain agents check stock against lead times and safety stock. They order on their own only within set authority limits and send larger decisions to humans for approval, so a human still signs off on major changes.

Optilogic, a vendor, says its AI-native supply chain design platform has autonomous agents that build network models, generate scenarios and weigh tradeoffs. This covers the analytical design steps of the task.
A 2026 trends piece expects companies to let agents recommend critical supply chain decisions but not commit to them. Humans still approve and carry out redesigns.

A Databricks-hosted vendor paper cites a Gartner prediction that 50% of supply chain management software will include agentic AI by 2030. This suggests agentic supply chain tools are still being adopted rather than fully autonomous.

In 2026, AI recruiting agents can source, screen, reach out to candidates, schedule and run structured AI interviews (for example Paradox and HireVue) with little human involvement. Vendors still recommend that a human review final hiring decisions.
Vendor buyer guides describe autonomous hiring agents covering top-of-funnel steps. Supervising staff day to day, coaching them and managing their performance on the store floor stays a human job.

NYC Local Law 144 requires bias audits and candidate notice for automated employment decision tools but does not ban them and does not require a licensed human to sign. This is a regulatory burden, not a rule that a human must do the work.

Warranty claims software now includes AI agents that handle claims end to end, with claim scoring and anomaly detection. These products are generic and built for the OEM side, not wind-specific, which suggests the paperwork and tracking parts of the task can be automated.

In wind, warranty management relies on continuously collecting turbine data (such as SCADA and condition monitoring) and filing claims throughout the warranty period. These are digital steps an agent could carry out.

Turbine-by-turbine physical inspections at end of warranty, plus filing on time with OEMs, decide whether claims get honoured. Field crews do the physical work, and commercial negotiation with OEMs stays with a human.

Budgeting tools for wind O&M already exist: K2 Management and Emerson's P50 Booster, built on multi-brand SCADA data, forecasts maintenance needs to show owners when to budget for maintenance and to address rising opex.
In the vendor guide, agents run the annual planning process while finance keeps decision authority and the budget still goes to the board for approval. A human remains the final reviewer.

As of August 2026, FP&A agents from Cube, Datarails, Vena, Anaplan, Pigment and Workday work on top of existing Excel or planning models, but some deeper planning agents were still in beta. This is a vendor-written ranking, not an independent benchmark.

Vendors describe AI design-compliance agents that read specifications, drawings and regulatory documents, check designs against standards, flag likely violations and produce structured compliance reports. Vendors present them as first-pass reviewers, with engineers keeping the final judgment.
Florida DEP requires remedial action plans and engineering documents to be prepared by, or under the direct supervision of, a Florida-registered professional engineer, who must seal and sign them.
New Mexico requires a professional engineer to design and seal final remediation plans that include engineered systems such as mechanical or electrical equipment.

In 2026, AI permitting tools mostly check applications before filing. For example, Yuma AZ's January 2026 pilot reviews plans and documents for missing information and inconsistencies before submission. Vendor tools such as PermitOS and Datagrid claim to pre-screen applications against regulations and to connect to permit portals. Fully automated approval has only been announced, by Dubai in August 2026 for villa permits.

Dubai Municipality is building an AI agent to issue villa building permits without human review, which shows agencies are moving toward digital end-to-end processing. That example covers villa building permits only, not demolition or remediation permits.

Demolition permit applications usually need an owner or applicant signature, sometimes notarized. They also need an asbestos survey done beforehand by a certified inspector or licensed contractor, and some jurisdictions require a licensed PE or architect certification. So a human has to sign the application and provide licensed inputs, even though an agent can compile and file it.

Cleanup cost estimating already relies on parametric software such as RACER. It produces repeatable, documented remediation estimates from available site data, with yearly cost-data updates. An agent could run this kind of structured estimating work.

In New Jersey, remedial cost estimates for NJDEP Site Remediation Program work must be signed by a Licensed Site Remediation Professional (LSRP). Other remedial work must be certified by a licensed Professional Engineer (PE), with the preparer's license number listed.
Ohio's brownfield grant program requires remedial cost estimates from a certified professional or engineer.

Commercial hazardous waste platforms (e.g., Triumvirate ADVISE, ERA EHS, ChemicalSafety) already automate manifests, waste profiles, pickup requests, return-manifest tracking and compliance calendars, so the paperwork and scheduling sub-steps can be handed off to software.

The generator, or the person acting for it, must sign the manifest certifying that the waste is properly classified, packaged, marked and labeled. EPA e-Manifest accepts electronic signatures, but they are tied to an accountable person's identity.

Under EPA's interpretation, the person who signs a manifest must have hazmat training under DOT rules. Signing is also usually done when the transporter picks up the waste at the site, which needs someone there in person.

RACER is a parametric remediation cost tool used by agencies and consultants. It calculates technology quantities, localizes unit costs and applies markups, so the cost-estimating sub-step is already automated and can be run through software.

New York remediation feasibility study reports carry a licensed Professional Engineer's certification under 6 NYCRR Part 375, and NYSDEC has sent back a report that was missing it. A human must still sign.
Texas rules list a feasibility study as a required part of a remedial investigation. These studies are formal regulatory documents that the agency reviews.

Industry sources describe AI agents in 2026 that read inbound carrier emails, pull out lane, rate and capacity details, send quote requests and place voice calls to carriers. Vendors claim 60-94% no-touch automation. Edge cases that depend on relationships, such as capacity crunches or negotiating favors, still go to humans.
C.H. Robinson's Navisphere real-time rating calls carrier APIs with a standard payload, and carriers return rates automatically. No human contact is needed for routine rate and schedule requests.
Loadsmart's API inside the Kuebix TMS returns instant, bookable truckload spot quotes. Asking carriers for rates is already a software-to-software step.

AI demand forecasting in supply chains has moved from pilot to production at leading companies. The step from decision support to autonomous action is still in progress, and in the common model humans review and approve the agents' actions.
Gartner projects that by 2030, half of cross-functional supply chain management solutions will use agents to carry out decisions on their own. This means fully autonomous control is not yet standard.
Logistics analysts need no legal certification or license. Voluntary certifications such as ASCM's CPIM, CSCP and CLTD and SOLE designations exist, but nothing requires a human signature.
ReadiNow won a BCI Global Award in 2025 for a platform that uses autonomous AI agents trained in risk, compliance, continuity and incident response.
PagerDuty's Spring 2026 release includes an SRE Agent that investigates and resolves complex incidents at enterprise scale. Vendor sources say audit trails and human override are becoming standard.
BCP credentials such as CBCP and ISO 22301 are voluntary professional certifications. The search found no legal requirement for a licensed human to sign off on monitoring or resolution methods.

AI-generated or AI-assisted sustainability claims on websites, packaging and ads can draw regulator scrutiny if they are inaccurate, vague or unsubstantiated, and agentic AI with little human review is flagged as a concern. This points to a human review step before publication.

The EU EmpCo Directive (2024/825) applies from 27 September 2026. Under it, general claims such as 'green' or 'sustainable' must be proven by the business. The Green Claims Directive's mandatory prior verification of claims is still a stalled proposal. Liability falls on the company, and no rule requires a licensed human to author or sign the material.
Implicit environmental claims made through imagery, branding and design must also comply, so a human still has to check generated visuals and wording against evidence and brand approval.

Banks report that agentic AI coding and legacy-code work runs 2 to 20 times faster for some tasks (Citi). Morgan Stanley's DevGen.AI reviewed 9 million lines of legacy code and turned them into plain-English specifications. Agents can do the code changes but did not take over model ownership.

US model risk guidance (SR 11-7, reportedly replaced in 2026 by SR 26-2) requires model development to be documented, validation to be independent, and human governance structures to approve model changes. Sources disagree on whether GenAI and agents are inside its scope, and I could not check the Fed's own text.
One bank's AI coding trial reported up to 20% less boilerplate coding effort, including code review and refactoring. That points to large help on sub-steps, with humans still reviewing the work.

The COSO/ACFE Fraud Risk Management Guide sets out a structured fraud risk assessment: find fraud schemes, then judge their likelihood and impact against existing controls. Much of that structured work can be done with software and documents, though it still needs judgment about incentives, opportunities and rationalizations.

Fraud risk assessments now need to cover AI-enabled methods such as fabricated documents and fake approval requests. The UK's 'failure to prevent fraud' rule has applied to large organisations since September 2025. It makes the organisation accountable for its controls, but it does not require a licensed person to carry out the assessment.

The CFE Code of Professional Standards is an ethics code that individual fraud examiners apply to their own cases. It does not legally require a licensed human to perform or sign a fraud risk assessment.

Nokia's Gemini-powered agents (triage, anomaly reasoner, action reasoner) are said to cut telecom troubleshooting time by 50-80% for some issues. Operators still approve critical actions, and only low-risk cases run in closed loop.
TeamViewer's Tia agent, launched in November 2025, combines remote connectivity with finding and fixing IT and device problems on its own, which covers remote diagnosis and software fixes.
Agentic service desks handle routine L1 tickets through system APIs and pass non-routine issues to humans. Hardware faults that need on-site work are still done by people.

Commercial AI assistants such as dbForge AI Assistant already find inefficient or missing indexes, generate indexing scripts, explain the causes of SQL errors and suggest fixes. That covers the main technical sub-steps of answering a support question.
Practitioners say AI SQL optimization works well as an assistant but still needs human checking and testing before anyone trusts it on production systems. So a human review step remains.
A developer at a company with no DBA used AI to fix SQL Server performance problems. This shows AI can stand in for some of the support a senior database person would give.
Microsoft's Teams Facilitator agent writes live notes, posts the agenda, runs agenda timers and records decisions and open questions. It is generally available with a Microsoft 365 Copilot license.
Cisco's Webex AI agents turn meeting summaries into action items, such as creating Jira tickets or scheduling follow-up meetings, and carry them out for the user.

Meeting-notes agents do not make decisions or invent commitments, and they flag unclear points for a human. Steering the discussion and settling stakeholder conflicts still depend on a human facilitator.

Atlassian's Jira Delivery Agent (Rovo) analyzes Jira spaces and connected data to report on progress. It runs inside automation rules and can be set up for different audiences, from team summaries to executive updates.

Atlassian ships automation templates for Daily Standup, Delivery Health Check and Stakeholder Status Summary. They compile progress, risks and completed work and post the result to Confluence or Slack, which automates the recurring parts of carrying out a communication plan.

Atlassian's 'Harper' workshop shows how to build a custom agent that writes project-health, milestone and risk summaries for PMOs, executives and team leads. A human still decides stakeholder priorities, handles sensitive messages and leads the live meetings.

AI policy-generator agents (Lyzr, GeneratePolicy.com, ISMS Copilot) draft security and compliance policies mapped to frameworks such as ISO 27001, SOC 2 and GDPR. Their workflow still has a human review and customize the draft.

PCI DSS Requirement 12.1 requires a formal security policy that is established, published, maintained and distributed. Management endorsement is recommended and an assessor reviews the documents, so organizational sign-off stays with humans. The strategist in this task only assists, and no licence is needed for that role.
Policy ownership and governance sit with named officials such as the CISO or Treasurer, who approve the final policies and do annual reviews.

Itembase, launched in April 2026, is a game economy design workspace. It centralizes currencies, stats and items, models how players acquire and progress through them, and supports AI plugins. This means drafting and simulating currency and item catalogs can largely be done in software.

Seele AI generates virtual economy and in-app purchase designs, including currency sources and sinks and limits on inflation. It describes the output as a prototype for early design review rather than a finished system, so a human still has to review it.
PlayFab Economy provides standard catalog and multi-currency tooling. The agent can configure it digitally, and no physical presence or licensing is required.

Saama's SDTM-RAG uses several AI agents to map source fields to SDTM domains and variables, check the mappings, and write SAS or R code. In vendor-reported pilots, about 75% of mappings were generated automatically, with roughly 70% accuracy. Users still approve or reject each suggested mapping.
A PharmaSUG 2026 paper argues that AI alone cannot resolve sponsor conventions or ambiguous metadata. It recommends combining deterministic rules with review by a programmer.

Under 21 CFR Part 11 (FDA rules on electronic records), clinical electronic records must run on validated systems with audit trails. Each change has to be traceable to an identified user, so a qualified human typically reviews and accepts formatted datasets before use.

By 2026, vendors were selling agentic AI for clinical data management. Examples: Veeva's Study Builder Agent configures EDC forms, visits and edit checks from a protocol; Hexaware's agents propose CRFs and validation rules; Clinion's assistant answers natural-language questions about live study and operational data. These tools could support data-driven review of processes and technology, but the efficiency gains are still mostly vendor claims.

Hexaware's agentic CDM offering automates sub-steps such as CRF design, CDISC mapping and edit-check suggestions. That shows agents can analyze workflows and suggest changes, but humans still decide what to adopt.

Under ICH E6(R3), the sponsor keeps ultimate responsibility and must run risk-based oversight of computerized systems and data governance. Process changes therefore need human review and approval before rollout, although the task of suggesting revisions does not itself require a human signature.

Vendors in 2026 sell AI and agentic tools that scan EDC and other trial data for discrepancies and draft queries. In each case a data manager approves or rejects the results, so the human keeps final review. These claims come from vendor marketing.
Clinion describes a multi-agent setup: one agent reads the protocol and case report forms, and another flags discrepancies and drafts queries. Clinion won the ACDM 2025 innovation award.

This is a secondary summary, not the primary text. Under ICH E6(R3), a responsible party must set the scope of audit-trail and data review on a risk basis and document it. Data corrections must be attributed and justified. This calls for human accountability, but no licence or law requires a human to perform each QC check. QC work runs inside validated, access-controlled GxP systems.

Veeva announced its Study Builder Agent on September 24, 2026. Veeva says it configures EDC forms, visits and edit check rules directly from a study protocol, and automates testing, including generating test data. Early-adopter access is planned for December 2026, so it is not yet generally available in October 2026. The time savings come from the vendor and have not been independently checked.

A Medidata-sourced opinion piece from April 2026 says AI can cut study build timelines from 10 to 12 weeks down to a few days, and that it can flag common data inconsistencies and suggest edit checks. This is promotional commentary.

Clinical trial databases covered by 21 CFR Part 11 must be validated, with defined roles that include an approver. Failing to validate can lead to regulatory citations. This means a qualified, accountable person still has to review and sign off on the database and edit-check validation before go-live. The source is a secondary university guide, not the regulation itself.

Agentic HEC-RAS is an MCP server for Claude Code and Codex built on the open-source ras-commander library. It lets an agent inspect, edit, run, read, compare and plot 1D/2D HEC-RAS models from a plain-language goal without opening the GUI. The author says it was checked end to end on HEC's Muncie 2D example. This is a self-description and I found no independent test.

RAS Commander is an MIT-licensed Python library that automates HEC-RAS plan runs, HDF result extraction and geometry operations. Its documentation says it was developed with LLMs including Claude and GPT-4. The search did not show whether agents can reliably build and calibrate a model from scratch, rather than edit an existing one.

Under 44 CFR 65.7, all analyses submitted to FEMA must be certified by a registered professional engineer. Floodway no-rise certifications must also be signed and sealed by a PE. So for regulatory flood models, a human engineer has to review and take responsibility for the work.

Commercial AI tools (TuMeke, ConductVision, Human Focus) already score RULA, REBA and the NIOSH lifting equation automatically from workplace video. Agreement with expert human reviewers has been reported as good, but it has not been fully established.

Studies of the reliability of AI video-based REBA against human raters show the agent can do the analysis step, but a human still has to check the results. Recording the video and taking force or anthropometric measurements on site needs a person to be there.
No ergonomics certificate (such as the BCPE's CPE) is legally required to do ergonomic analysis, and the search found no rule that a licensed person must sign the assessment.
AI 'synthetic user' agents, such as Adobe's UXCascade, now produce and gather usability feedback at scale. These tools can supply the evidence and arguments used to advocate for users.

In an April 2026 experiment, synthetic users diverged from real users, and the authors concluded the results can't be trusted without checking against real users. A human still has to judge and stand behind the user advocacy.
HF/E certification through BCPE (CPE/CHFP) is voluntary and private. It is not a legal licence, so no signing barrier applies to user advocacy.

Standard and harmonized fuel cell test protocols and design-of-experiments methods are published and can be used to plan tests. An agent can draft test matrices, factorial designs and procedures from them.
Commercial ML tools such as Monolith already predict test outcomes and recommend which fuel cell tests to run next. This speeds up the planning sub-steps.

Running a test program means designing and building physical test rigs, often automated in LabVIEW. It also involves handling hydrogen safely on site and using station hardware, which needs people in the lab.

Vendors such as dSPACE showed generative and agentic AI for SIL and HIL validation, test generation and automated CI/CD test pipelines at CES 2026. These are vendor claims. They show that test-case creation and SIL execution can be partly delegated.

In a Volvo/Chalmers study of generative AI for HIL test automation, only 23–36% of AI-generated test cases passed. Hardware-specific benches limit autonomy, so humans still have to review and run tests on physical rigs and vehicles.

US FMVSS uses manufacturer self-certification based on due care. No licensed individual is required to perform or sign system tests, but vehicle-level testing still relies on physical vehicles, test tracks and instrumentation.

AI agent tools such as Powerdrill Bloom and multi-agent slide generators turn raw files (Excel, CSV, PDF) into reports and presentation decks. That covers the drafting part of reports and slides. One analysis notes that much of the time saved goes into checking and refining what the AI produces.

Vendor tools say they can process raw data, run statistical analysis and produce slides ready to present. These claims come from the vendors and have not been independently tested on engineering-grade results.

State rules on engineer seals, such as Florida's, require a licensed PE to sign and seal reports that contain professional engineering work. Most nanosystems R&D and program-review reporting falls outside these rules, so this is not a typical legal barrier for this task.

Enphase's Solargraf says its AI-assisted tool builds complete permit plan sets, including single-line and three-line diagrams, in under 10 minutes. It also says the tool pulls NEC code automatically and exports DWG files. These are vendor claims, so the drafting steps can be automated by software that an agent can operate.

Solargraf generates single-line, three-line and detailed calculation pages that it describes as permit-ready. No independent check of how accurate they are or how often permit offices accept them was found, so an engineer still needs to review them against the NEC and local rules.

Some permit offices require a single-line diagram stamped by an electrical engineer, for example when a line-side PV connection modifies electrical distribution equipment. Engineering documents for larger systems often need a PE stamp, so a human has to sign off.

In 2026, PNNL's AutoLabs multi-agent LLM system wrote chemical procedures for a liquid-handling robot and corrected its own errors, reaching an F1-score above 0.89 on multi-step syntheses. This shows agents can handle protocol and experiment-design sub-steps, though the authors also describe limits.

Self-driving labs, such as NC State's catalyst lab, design, run and analyze iterative chemistry experiments with little human input. Researchers note that true experimental autonomy is still limited and that the field has not settled on what 'autonomous' means.

Interactive robot training relies on kinesthetic teaching, where a person physically guides the robot, or on human teleoperation with VR controllers or spacemice. These demonstrations require a human operator with the physical robot.

A Japan Science and Technology Agency (CRDS) study from August 2026 describes specialized AI agents that split research work while another AI coordinates the overall research process. These are mostly prototype systems. They support coordination but have not replaced how human scientists coordinate with each other.

Coordinating interdisciplinary research is still advertised as a human role. A 2026 Know-Center job posting asks a postdoc to coordinate scientific collaboration across an interdisciplinary team, which relies on interpersonal trust and scientific judgment.

Writing about AI research agents in 2026 presents them as partners that speed up searching, drafting and analysis. They are not described as independently negotiating collaborations, dividing work between scientists or aligning their priorities.

FutureHouse's Robin multi-agent system generates hypotheses, proposes experiments and interprets experimental data, which are the design and interpretation sub-steps. FutureHouse says its designs are not yet detailed enough to execute without human lab work, and the RPE-cell experiments were run by humans.

Secondary reports say OpenAI and Ginkgo Bioworks had GPT-5 design about 36,000 cell-free protein synthesis experiments that robots in a cloud lab carried out, with the results fed back to the model. This shows execution can be closed-loop only where robotic cloud-lab access exists.

An Active Site study found that AI help did not significantly change novices' ability to complete a complex wet-lab virus-production workflow. Hands-on bench execution and oversight still depend on people.

ClimatePolicyGen (2026) is a multi-agent framework that analyzes environmental, socio-economic and infrastructure data to produce climate policy recommendations. It is validated only by automated metrics and has not been deployed by a government.

Research benchmarks test AI agents on climate policy reasoning, including treaty interpretation and adaptation policy, which shows they can do the main analytical sub-steps but have not yet been shown to replace an analyst from start to finish.

Ready-made agents already market themselves as environmental policy advisors that produce policy recommendations, so the drafting step can be delegated. Working out what is politically feasible and persuading stakeholders still depends on human judgment and trust.

Research from 2025–2026 shows LLM agents being used to build and run agent-based travel and traffic simulations that match standard benchmarks. The authors call the work preliminary, and multimodal networks and other complex settings remain untested. So agents can do the coding and simulation steps, but production planning models still need human checking.

Under federal conformity rules (40 CFR 93.122), network-based travel models must be validated against observed counts for a base year no more than 10 years before the determination. The task therefore depends on agency count and survey data and on calibration judgment. No search result showed that a licensed engineer must seal or sign model development.

An FHWA peer review found that many travel demand models give too little attention and effort to validation. This supports keeping a human expert to review calibration and validation before a model is used.

Instrument vendors build diagnostics into their own software. Shimadzu's Nexera spots flow and pressure faults, purges the pumps and re-injects the sample on its own, but it still stops and passes the problem to a person when the fault persists.

Research systems with several AI agents watch instruments and keep troubleshooting histories for lab QC. These are proteomics and mass-spectrometry setups, not HPLC, and one agent's precision was low (0.41), so it raised many false alarms. I found no independent test of an AI agent fully diagnosing real HPLC faults from start to finish.

US drug-manufacturing rules (21 CFR 211.68) require automated and electronic equipment to be routinely calibrated, inspected or checked under a written program, with records kept. In practice, fixes such as replacing seals, fixing leaks and swapping columns are done by hand at the instrument.

Industry guides and vendors describe AI drafting GxP SOPs, flagging unclear wording and tracking guideline changes to find affected SOPs. They stress that a human must review the drafts, because AI cannot know what actually happens on the floor, so process owners have to supply the facts.
Vendor tools such as CaseMark sell GMP SOP generation workflows and claim the first draft takes minutes instead of 20-40 hours. This is unverified marketing.

Under 21 CFR 211.22, the quality control unit must approve or reject procedures that affect identity, strength, quality and purity, and its procedures must be in writing. This means a human from that unit has to approve the work.

ICH Q14 and USP <1220> frame the work as lifecycle management: set an analytical target profile, find critical method parameters, monitor performance continuously and improve. Much of this means analysing data and documents, which an agent can do from a goal: reviewing SOPs and validation reports, trending system-suitability and OOS data, searching the literature and drafting improvement proposals. Vendor tools such as ACD/Labs AutoChrom already digitise method development.

Under GMP, the quality unit is responsible for approving procedures and results, and lab records must reference method validation data. A qualified human must therefore approve and sign off on proposed method changes. Checking a proposed improvement also needs bench experiments in the physical lab.

Uptake of Q14's enhanced, data-driven tools is still low, at about 19% in an ISPE poll. Method data usually sits in LIMS and chromatography data systems that an agent may not be able to reach. Search results showed no autonomous AI agent doing regulated method evaluation from start to finish.

OpenEduCat sells an AI lesson-plan generator for PE. Its marketing says it produces inclusive stations, changes difficulty through distance, ball size or target size, and adds modification notes and progressions. That covers drafting the planning step, which is only part of the task.

A practitioner guide for special education teachers presents AI as a drafting assistant for adapting lessons. Teachers have to review, verify and personalize every output and remain responsible for what reaches students.

Some states require a licensed physical educator to deliver adapted PE services. Wisconsin requires an adaptive PE license, and Connecticut requires a certified physical educator to serve students with IEPs. Adapting instruction means watching motor performance and adjusting it live in the gym.

Autonomous research agents from 2025–2026 (OpenLens AI, Medical AI Scientist) run the steps from literature review through data analysis, coding and manuscript writing end to end. These are mostly preprints and have not been validated in peer review.
BioWorld reported two Nature papers from May 2026 showing autonomous AI agents working across the biomedical research cycle: forming hypotheses, designing experiments and analysing data.

Under 21 CFR 312, a qualified human investigator must sign Form FDA 1572, personally conduct or supervise the study, and ensure informed consent, IRB review and adverse-event reporting. Patient exams, biopsies and bench work also require a person to be physically present.
Applying a chemical that alters living tissue counts as the practice of medicine. Doing a chemical peel needs a physician, or a licensed practitioner the physician has delegated to.
State rules limit chemical peels to physicians, PAs and CNPs, and some procedures need a prescription from a licensed clinician.
AI tools for chemical peels only analyse skin and help with planning, for example measuring pigmentation and texture before a peel. A clinician still makes the call and does the procedure.

Skin Analytics' DERM holds an EU Class III CE mark to make skin-lesion decisions on its own. A UK hospital trust says it uses DERM to discharge patients with benign lesions without a dermatologist's input, so lesion-image diagnosis can be delegated. Both sources are promotional and independent validation is limited.

In the US, the FDA-authorized AI skin cancer device DermaSensor only assists clinicians. Its output reads 'investigate further' or 'monitor' and is not a standalone diagnosis, so a licensed clinician still makes the diagnosis and treatment decision.

A JAMA Dermatology review found that none of 41 consumer dermatology apps had FDA approval and that their performance was inconsistent. Without a licensed human in charge, AI diagnosis and treatment carry liability and reliability risks.

FDA has authorized autonomous AI systems that screen fundus images for diabetic retinopathy (LumineticsCore, EyeArt) and return results in under 30 seconds. Medicare pays for this under CPT 92229, so AI can already do part of the interpretation work.
Billing for OCT interpretation (CPT 92134) needs a signed interpretation and report written by a physician. The device printout alone is not enough, so a licensed human must review and sign.

Comparisons of retinal AI tools show that autonomous authorization covers only narrow screening uses tied to specific cameras. Most ophthalmic tests, such as slit lamp exams, tonometry, gonioscopy and dilated exams, are done in person with physical equipment.

Digital pathology platforms such as Proscia Concentriq AP-Dx (new 510(k) in August 2026) and PathAI AISight Dx (July 2025) are FDA-cleared for primary diagnosis from whole-slide images. They are image management systems, so a pathologist still reads the slides and makes the call. The search turned up no autonomous AI diagnosis product.

PathAI's AISight Dx digital pathology system received FDA clearance for primary diagnosis in clinical settings, so slide images and lab data can be reached through software where labs have gone digital.

Under CLIA (42 CFR 493.1273(d), as quoted in CMS survey reports, not checked against the regulation text), a tissue pathology report must be signed by a qualified person. An electronic signature has to be authorized by the person who did the examination and made the diagnosis.

A randomized trial found an AI agent that reviewed primary-care registries for hereditary cancer risk and handled genetic-counseling follow-up for more than 3,000 patients performed about as well as the manual approach. A 2025 review says AI's potential for population health management is still largely untapped and calls for rigorous evaluation.

A 2026 JMIR feasibility study used an agentic AI platform on a claims database to estimate the prevalence of six conditions. This shows agents can run the data-analysis step of an evaluation, but the work still needs validation and access to protected data.

ACPM's privileging standards and ABPM's competencies list health services planning and evaluation, and evaluating a health system's delivery of preventive services, as specialty competencies. Employers expect board-certified physicians in these roles, but no law requires a licensed person to sign this kind of analytic work.

The ASA 2008 Pre-Anesthesia Checkout Recommendations list 15 items to check each day or after the machine is moved or serviced, and 8 items before each procedure. Machine-builtin automated checkout covers only some of these steps; it is device firmware, not a general AI agent.

APSF reports a machine that passed its automated self-test and still failed during ventilation. It recommends a manual functional test of the breathing circuit and ventilator, using the breathing bag as a test lung, so physical hands-on work is still required.

Automated self-tests check internal transducers and circuit compliance. They cannot replace manual checks of vaporizers, suction, cylinder reserves and backup bag-valve devices (secondary study-guide source).

Nebraska's anesthesiologist assistant standards list inserting pulmonary artery catheters and interpreting data from invasive monitors as tasks the supervising physician anesthesiologist delegates. That is hands-on bedside work done under supervision.

South Carolina requires a direct, continuous and close supervisory relationship between the anesthesiologist assistant and a sponsoring anesthesiologist, who is responsible for the assistant's activities at all times.

FDA-cleared AI tools exist for parts of the analysis, such as EEG trending and artifact reduction (Ceribell) and automated echo measurements (Us2.ai). They support clinicians' decisions but do not place devices or replace the clinician in the operating room, which limits AI to helping interpret the data.

Commercial drug-diversion and supply-surveillance products (Bluesight ControlCheck, Wolters Kluwer Sentri7, Iatric DetectRx, Imprivata) pull data from dispensing cabinets, EHRs and timekeeping systems. They reconcile dispense, administration, waste and return records, and use machine learning to flag problems. Most still send the flags to a human to review, so an agent could handle the data-monitoring part but not the whole task.
Cloud software from Kit Check and Omnicell tracks controlled substances and combines charting and dispensing records so deviations show up as they happen.

DEA rules (21 CFR 1304.11) require a physical inventory of controlled substances at each registered location, with exact counts for Schedule II drugs. That is hands-on counting and record-keeping by the registrant, so someone has to be physically present and a licensed person is accountable for it.

Harvesting cultures for cytogenetic analysis is a manual, multi-step bench process that averages two to three hours. The automation that exists is lab hardware (harvesters, metaphase spreaders, stainers), not software agents.

Automated harvesters such as the HANABI-PIII handle blood and bone marrow suspension cultures by physical robotics. A human still loads and handles the specimens, and a software-only AI agent cannot do these steps.

Cytogenetic technologists who process patient specimens and perform tissue culture must meet the CLIA high-complexity testing personnel requirements (42 CFR 493 Subpart M), and employers often also require ASCP CG certification.

FDA-cleared AI for digital cytology (Hologic Genius Digital Diagnostics / Genius Cervical AI) only triages cervical Pap slide images for a cytotechnologist or pathologist to review. It is a specialised device, not a general agent, and it does not do hormonal or maturation-index evaluation.

Under CLIA, 42 CFR 493.1274, individual cytology screeners must examine the slides, with a cap of 100 slides per person in 24 hours and records of each person's workload. This means a licensed human must do the screening and be accountable for it.

The digital workflow still needs glass slides to be physically prepared, stained and scanned, or examined under a microscope. A general software agent would usually not have access to lab scanners or the LIS.

Lab scheduling software already assigns staff automatically by credentials, competencies and bench requirements, and fills open shifts. AI workforce tools forecast lab demand, but a human still reviews their recommendations before schedules change.
Rostering software for pathology labs coordinates benches, on-call shifts, couriers and collection centres, so the main sub-steps of coordinating assignments are already done in software.

CLIA cytology rules cap screening at 100 slides per 24 hours and require each person's workload limit to be reassessed at least every 6 months, with documentation. Surveyors cite labs for gaps, so a qualified human supervisor stays accountable for workload assignments.
Consumer labor apps such as Freya and ONA already coach breathing through each contraction and play relaxation audio, so software can deliver the breathing and music parts.
Continuous labor support is mostly hands-on, in-person work: massage, warm baths and encouraging the mother to move. Its benefits are tied to a supportive human being present.
Hydrotherapy, touch and massage, and movement and positioning are effective comfort measures, and all of them need someone physically there to carry them out.

Pipelines already pull EHR data automatically into REDCap-based registries for rare diseases. A multi-institution rare-tumor registry imported 482,450 lab results for 1,109 patients with high accuracy.
Vendors sell LLM and agentic workflows that find registry cases and extract data from clinical notes. They still put a human abstractor or reviewer in charge of the final decision.

Under HIPAA, patient data can be shared for research only through a signed patient authorization, an IRB or Privacy Board waiver, de-identification, or a limited data set with a data use agreement. These steps need human consent, oversight and accountability.

A leak test has to be done on the physical endoscope before cleaning or disinfection. The scope is pressurized and the tester watches for a pressure drop, so it has to be connected and handled by hand, either dry in air or wet under water.

Automated leak testers exist (Olympus ALT-Pro, Medivators Veriscan LT) and cut down on operator subjectivity, but they are physical devices. A person still has to connect the scope and run the test. A software agent has no way to do this.

Automated leak-test systems reduce variation between users, but staff still have to set up the equipment and inspect it. An AI agent could only help with checklists, logging results and looking up manufacturer instructions.
Pre-procedure room setup is hands-on work: setting up the endoscope and video tower, laying out supplies and getting specimen-management supplies ready.
Techs pick the correct endoscope and run a physical quality-control check on it before each procedure.

Techs choose the equipment, supplies and instruments for each procedure based on the procedure type and the patient's needs. An agent could only help with the planning side, such as drafting checklists from the schedule or preference cards.

Endoscopy technicians do hands-on maintenance work. They leak-test and take apart scopes to the manufacturer's specs, pull scopes that fail from service, check machine water pressure and change filters. An agent with no body can't do any of this.

Software only supports the work. Tracking systems record a device's damage, test results and repair history, and a deep-learning model reviewing borescope video of working channels caught 91.4% of the problems endoscopists found. That model only flags scopes for a person to check and send for repair; it doesn't do the inspection or the repair itself.

An agent could take on the paperwork side: filling in repair logs, keeping records, sending scopes out for repair and coordinating with the manufacturer. That is a small part of the time, while the physical inspection, troubleshooting and repair make up most of it.

Endoscopy technicians physically handle biopsy forceps, polyp snares, clips and retrieval nets, and collect and label specimens, all under a physician's direct supervision. This is bedside manual work that a software agent with no body cannot do.
The role is performed under the supervision of a registered nurse and physician, and snare positioning and polyp removal are framed as actions taken under physician direction within clinical scope.

The existing AI in endoscopy is FDA-cleared polyp-detection software (GI Genius). It overlays alerts for the clinician and does not do the technician's hands-on assisting, and the clinician makes the final decision.

AI articulation apps (Sara for SLP, SpeechLP, TikTalk) can run practice drills that the SLP sets up and give automatic error feedback. They cover only home or drill practice, not full treatment sessions.
SLPAs carry out specific parts of care plans written by an SLP, under supervision. The supervising SLP keeps full legal and ethical responsibility.
State law (Illinois) defines the assistant's role as carrying out the SLP's documented treatment plan under supervision. Assistants may not work with clients outside that plan.

AI articulation apps such as Sara for SLP, SpeechLP and TikTalk generate practice sets, listen to speech, find phoneme errors, give real-time feedback and report progress to SLPs. They support drill practice between sessions, but the SLP programs and directs them. These claims come from the vendors and press coverage, and I did not check them independently.

Under ASHA's scope of practice, SLPAs do tasks that a certified or state-credentialed SLP prescribes, directs and supervises. Training, credentialing and supervision requirements govern the role, and state rules decide the binding details.

A state guideline defines direct, immediate and indirect supervision for SLPAs. For some direct work with clients and families, such as with medically fragile infants, immediate supervision is required. That points to in-person interpersonal care, though teletherapy also exists.

SLP documentation tools such as Ambiki's Tenalog record and transcribe session audio and produce SOAP notes. They also pull out structured data for progress tracking, analyse errors and draft progress summaries. That covers much of the compiling and documentation work.

SLPAs collect performance data during therapy sessions and prepare records under the direction of a supervising SLP. Much of the raw data comes from watching client responses live, often in person, and judging each trial and the level of prompting.

ASHA recommends that the supervising SLP regularly review the data for every client the SLPA serves, and the SLP keeps overall responsibility. A human therefore reviews the data, but no rule requires a human to collect or compile it.

Esri's ArcGIS now has agentic AI. External agents can connect to ArcGIS tools over MCP/A2A, run geoprocessing tools and complete multi-step GIS workflows with little user input. AI assistants also write ArcPy/Arcade code.
AI-generated ArcPy scripts for GIS automation often fail on the first try and need a human to debug them. That means a human still has to review the work before it is used.

As of 2026, US intelligence agencies are still working to get agentic AI onto classified networks, where accreditation is a very high bar, and officials say humans will keep making key decisions. This limits an agent's access to the databases analysts normally use.

Loss prevention store audits are on-site walkthroughs. The auditor checks the entrance, stockroom, CCTV, EAS tags, display locks, fitting rooms and receiving dock security, and watches staff follow procedures in person. An agent without a body cannot do this.

Audit templates cover about 60 checks across physical security, cash/POS controls, inventory shrink and corrective actions. They also include reviewing earlier findings and incidents, which is digital prep work an agent can do.
AI tools already group POS exceptions, assign risk scores, link transactions to video and flag shelf and inventory mismatches. This covers the data-analysis part of finding problem areas.

Guard-management platforms such as TrackTik, Guardix and SecurityTime already handle scheduling, dispatch, digital post orders, patrol-tour checks, incident reporting, and automated AI calls to guards who are late.
In retail security, AI video analytics run alongside human agents. Humans check the alerts and coordinate dispatch, so people still direct the response on the ground.

Interface Systems reports that interactive remote video monitoring resolved 62.4% of high-priority retail events without police dispatch. This shows that much of the coordination of the response can be done remotely through digital systems.

Appriss Retail runs a generative AI tool on Azure OpenAI that automatically links theft, fraud and abuse incidents into cases by matching suspects, narratives and vehicles. Its case-management module captures incidents and evidence, and manages suspects and resolution.
My LP Portal offers an AI loss prevention assistant along with incident reporting and investigation management, aimed at small retailers that have no LP department.

LP incident reports bring together a timeline, the people involved, and evidence from CCTV, POS records, alarms and witness notes, written in neutral factual language. Because such reports may be used in later legal proceedings, the investigator who saw the events needs to confirm and attest to the account.

Vendor AI video analytics running on existing CCTV say they can flag unauthorized removal of goods, shipment mismatches, loitering and entry into restricted zones at loading docks and in warehouses. This covers much of the work of watching and reviewing footage. These are vendor claims and were not independently checked.

Covert surveillance in loss prevention depends on hidden cameras built into walls or ceilings or disguised as objects such as exit signs, so someone must physically install them. This physical setup, along with in-person stakeouts and undercover observation, is outside what a bodiless agent can do.
A practitioner post on an industry forum says covert cameras are widely used in retail loss prevention to watch areas the everyday camera system cannot see. This is an anecdotal account, not a study.

Camera health monitoring software already checks each camera, NVR and network link on a set schedule. It reports tampering, blurring, blocked views and equipment failures in near real time, so an agent could handle the CCTV status-check part of this task through software.

Remote monitoring for sensor-tag (EAS) systems shows up mostly in patents, not in shipping products. The patents describe extra hardware such as acoustic or optical sensors to detect alarms, and they note that store staff have little control over these systems. Checking that EAS gates and locks actually work still usually means someone walking tags through the gates and trying the locks on site.

NFPA 72 requires alarm inspection and testing to be done by qualified, trained or certified people, and many states also license the companies that do it. This applies to fire alarms that contractors service. It does not require a loss prevention specialist to sign off on routine checks of security systems.

Critical event management platforms such as OnSolve use AI risk intelligence to scan many data sources, flag events like severe weather, estimate their impact on people and operations, and send multi-channel alerts. These are the monitoring and notification steps of the task.

Rave Mobile Safety lets retail staff send mass notifications by email, text, digital signage and broadcast, and links incident administrators with first responders. Its materials describe retail stores as highly susceptible to violence, active shooter events, outages and weather-related closures.

Retail incident case management tools such as Appriss Retail Incident handle evidence capture, alerts and documentation. The response itself still happens on site: securing the store, evacuating people and working with police.

Under Food Code rules, cleaning is hands-on work. Utensils and equipment must be scraped, washed in detergent, rinsed, sanitized with chemicals or 171°F water, and air dried. Surfaces must be clean to sight and touch, and equipment used with TCS food must be cleaned every 4 hours.

Cleaning automation is built into the machines themselves, with timer-triggered cleaning cycles for the coffee and milk systems. These cycles do not require a software agent, and staff still have to do the manual steps.
Cafe software can only schedule and track maintenance. It cannot do the physical cleaning, so an AI agent's role is limited to checklists and logs.

Vendors sell wireless sensors that log fridge and freezer temperatures around the clock to cloud dashboards. They send text or email alerts when a reading is out of range or the power fails, and produce reports for inspectors. Where these are installed, an agent with dashboard access could do the monitoring, alerting and record-keeping. These are vendor claims I have not verified.

Alerts can be set to fire only when a freezer stays above a set temperature for a set time. That supports automatic detection of faults, but someone still has to be on site to check the equipment and fix it.

State guidance (Minnesota's sample plan, not the FDA Food Code itself) has the person in charge or a trained employee check product temperatures with a probe thermometer about every four hours. That is hands-on work, and many cafes have no sensors for an agent to read. Neither source requires a licensed human to sign the check.

Square launched an AI voice-ordering kiosk in October 2026. It has payment processing and Square Loyalty built in, so a customer can order and pay for card or wallet transactions with no barista involved.
At a café POS, customers insert, tap or swipe their own cards. For cash, the barista enters the amount handed over and physically gives back the change, which software alone cannot do.
Shared tap-to-pay terminals can put a payment on the wrong tab, so a person still has to watch over payment handling in a busy shop.

Sandwich and salad assembly is being automated only with dedicated physical robots (Nala Sandwich Bot and Bowl Bot, Bizerba's two-arm station at EuroShop 2026), which are outside the software-only reference technology. Even Sweetgreen's robotic line still has staff handle the start and end of the process and add final toppings.

Salad robots like Sweetgreen's Infinite Kitchen and Chowbotics' Sally work by physically dispensing ingredients, which shows the task is physical manipulation that a software agent with no body cannot do.

The FDA Food Code requires a Certified Food Protection Manager on site. Food-handler cards for line staff are a state-by-state choice. These are food-safety rules, not a requirement that a licensed human perform or sign off on each item.

Slicing fruit, vegetables, desserts or meats means a worker handles knives or slicers and the food itself. Food Code 3-301.11 governs how workers physically touch ready-to-eat food, which an agent with no body cannot do. It only requires utensils or gloves and does not require a licensed human to carry out the task.
Cut fruits and vegetables and sliced deli meats count as ready-to-eat foods. They must be handled with deli tissue, tongs or single-use gloves, which are all physical hygiene steps at the station.

The FDA's rationale is that touching ready-to-eat food with bare hands can spread foodborne illness, so the task depends on hands-on food handling. A software agent could only help at the edges, for example with prep lists or portion guides.

Connected spa systems like SmartTub can remotely detect power failures, GFCI trips, heater malfunctions, open covers and nearby moisture, and send alerts through an app. This is the part of the work an agent could monitor through software.

Patents for remote spa control describe sensors that track temperature, turbidity and chemical levels and raise alerts when they detect a fault. This sensor data is the only equipment check that happens digitally; the rest needs someone on site.
Remote diagnostics only flag problems. A person still has to inspect and test the equipment on site, including saunas, steam rooms, massage tables and treatment devices.

Third-party guides say HubSpot's Breeze agents take one campaign goal, plan a multi-channel campaign, and draft and schedule content. They also warn that drafts often need editing to match brand voice, so a human still reviews the work.
A med-spa vendor (unverified claim) says AI agents can run live Meta and Google ad campaigns through official ad-platform connectors, but says the campaigns still need daily management.
In 2026, spa and salon AI tools are mostly sold for booking, reminders, loyalty and follow-ups; much spa marketing is still done by hand.

In February 2026 athenahealth launched agentic patient-communication tools that give patients 24/7 access to front-office AI agents. Vendors also describe agents that sync patient information across EHRs, calendars and messaging platforms, which covers the routing, scheduling, reminder and status-update parts of coordination.

A 2026 industry guide places AI agents in administrative communication such as scheduling, referral and result tracking, and triage, and treats clinical judgment separately. A survey it cites shows lower comfort with autonomous AI beyond administrative tasks.

Under 42 CFR 482.13, hospitals must run a grievance process with set timeframes and written responses. The hospital's governing body must approve the process and is responsible for it, so a human stays accountable for grievance outcomes. Routine coordination messages do not need a licensed signer.

Healthcare learning platforms already use AI to build role-based compliance courses from policy documents. They also offer AI roleplay for sensitive patient conversations and simulated patients for training patient-support staff, which covers drafting materials and running practice sessions.
AI authoring tools turn uploaded policy and regulatory documents into structured training outlines and draft content, including HIPAA training for front-line patient interactions.

The CMS patient-rights rule (42 CFR 482.13) sets the hospital's grievance process and the staff training required for restraint and seclusion. Searches found no rule that a licensed person must deliver guest-relations or patient-rights training. The hospital still has to approve and stand behind its policies, so a human reviews the content.

Customs iX's Classify module suggests HS codes with duty rates and preference eligibility, and its 2026 release adds declaration generation. Vendors also say OCR models pull entry data from invoices, packing lists and bills of lading.
