Vendor sources describe a hybrid workflow: AI proposes classifications and declarations, and a human reviews them before filing. The accuracy figures they give come from vendor blogs and have not been independently verified.

In the US, 19 CFR Part 111 governs broker licences and permits, including the rules for doing customs business without a licence. Since the 2022 rule, a brokerage firm must employ enough licensed brokers to keep its customs work under responsible supervision and control. This points to a human with legal responsibility for clearance filings.

Weather sealing is hands-on rooftop work. The installer sets flashing, fastens the mounts and injects sealant through the mount ports until it comes out, removing the mount to seal by hand if needed. An agent without a body cannot do any of this.

Installers fill the pilot holes with MS polymer, silicone or butyl sealant and then seat the flashing. Software can only help with the edges of the job, such as looking up which sealant a manufacturer specifies.
Roof penetrations are checked in rough-in and final building inspections, and permits name licensed contractors. However, no law specifically requires that a licensed human apply the sealant.

Under the IRC, every penetration through the roof plane must be flashed. Installers generally fit flashing according to the roofing manufacturer's printed instructions. This is hands-on work done on the roof.

Michigan's rooftop PV rule requires penetrations to be flashed and sealed following the manufacturer's instructions. The cited version was listed as effective until 8/29/2025, so it may no longer be current. It describes code requirements for the work, not a rule that only a licensed person may do it.
Penetrations sealed only with mastic or silicone are not considered durable, so flashing devices have to be physically installed around the hole.

DOE Weatherization Job Aid 20-1, which follows Standard Work Specifications 5.0107.1, has the installer seal the ducts and then fasten the insulation mechanically with wire or twine. The installer also tapes the vapor-retarder seams and must avoid compressing the insulation. All of these are hands-on steps done at the duct.

Job Aid 20-2 has the installer wrap metal fittings such as boots and elbows separately with vapor-retarder duct wrap. It also requires at least R-8 on new flex duct and support for ducts exposed in unconditioned spaces, which means physical work in attics and crawlspaces.
The ROCKWOOL ductwrap installation guide describes cutting, wrapping and fastening the wrap by hand. Software or AI can't do these steps; an agent could only look up specs or R-value requirements.

BUCHI's NIR-Online sensor measures quality parameters such as water, acid value and glycerol continuously in biodiesel production. Once a plant has these sensors installed, the monitoring is done by instruments and software, so an agent could watch and interpret the data.

Producers hesitate to install in-line analysis because the systems are complex and costly to maintain. Many plants still rely on sampling and lab or at-line testing, which needs a person on site to collect and handle the samples.

The BQA 1000 is an at-line analyzer for feedstock and B100 quality. Someone has to draw a sample and feed it to the instrument, so the measuring step is physical. An agent could only help by logging the readings and flagging values outside spec.

Commercial wetstock monitoring systems such as TankStream read tank contents and sensor packs every 20 seconds and upload the data automatically. An agent could watch that data, flag problems and keep the logs.
Biofuels take up water, which makes sensor-based water detection unreliable. Degradation can also speed up later in storage, so physical sampling and lab tests are still needed.
Good practice calls for physically sampling the tank bottom at several access points, draining free water and checking visually for haze, darkening or particulates. All of these need someone on site.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.22, employers must keep workrooms and walking-working surfaces clean, orderly and as dry as feasible, free of spills and leaks, and inspected regularly. Meeting this takes physical cleaning on site, which an agent without a body cannot do.

Housekeeping guidance focuses on hands-on work such as cleaning up spills, clearing clutter and preventing slips, trips and falls. An AI agent could only help with peripheral parts like checklists or logging.
Housekeeping duties also come from the flammable liquids standard (1910.106) and combustible dust guidance, and these too are met by physically cleaning the site.

Housekeeping for combustible dust is physical work. Plants clean by vacuuming, sweeping or water wash-down, and they clean and inspect priority areas daily. Compressed air is allowed only after ignition sources are shut down. An agent without a body cannot do this cleaning; at most it can help draft the written housekeeping schedule.

Federal OSHA has no standalone combustible dust standard. It enforces housekeeping through the General Duty Clause, 1910.22 and a National Emphasis Program that covers wood dust. These rules require a clean workplace, not a licensed human to do or sign the cleaning.
Guidance for 2026 on combustible dust points to NFPA standards and dust hazard analysis. The cleaning itself is still done by hand with approved vacuums and similar equipment.

Cameras and AI mounted on collection trucks, from vendors like Prairie Robotics, automatically detect contamination, overfilled carts and bins that weren't set out. They send photos and feedback to residents. More than 20 North American cities use them, so the monitoring and notification steps can be automated.
Coordinator job descriptions include field inspections of drop-off sites and facilities, and investigating and documenting ordinance violations. These steps need someone physically on site.

Some postings say coordinators issue violation notices and work with compliance departments on code violations and illegal dumping. These are enforcement steps where a human with authority has to act.

Upper's AI Dispatch software builds the schedule from the user's rules and gives a confidence score for each assignment. This suggests matching drivers to routes can be automated from a goal and a set of rules.
RouteNow describes an AI dispatch system that suggests truck and route assignments using real-time data. A human still accepts or adjusts the suggestions, and the claim comes from vendor marketing.

Wastehero's route software plans routes around vehicle capacity, time windows and road limits, then sends the plan to the driver. Assigning routes is digital work and needs no one on site. No search was run on law or licensing; no rule requiring a human to sign off on route assignments is known.

Commercial AI and geospatial platforms (e.g., Solonic on ArcGIS) and open planning tools (e.g., WaPla) already model waste flows, costs and emissions, simulate operations and redesign collection systems, which covers the main analytical sub-steps of program design.

Planning tools such as WaPla map municipal waste flows and estimate greenhouse gas emissions and costs per process, which supports scenario design for reduction, recycling, composting and disposal programs.

US state statutes require solid waste management plans to go through public comment periods and hearings, be adopted by local governing bodies and be approved by a state agency, so stakeholder engagement and human adoption stay essential. A licensed professional's signature is not typically required.

Grants-management platforms such as Appian, REI GovGrants and EY Grants Accelerator (FedRAMP-authorized) offer AI for compliance guidance, document classification and summarizing progress reports. This supports partial automation of the monitoring and reporting sub-steps.

EPA grant administrative conditions require recipient performance reports under 2 CFR 200.328 and route them through designated authorized representatives. A human official stays accountable for submissions.
State solid-waste grant forms require the applicant to certify deliverables and designate an authorized project representative. This means a human signs off on progress and compliance.
Pactum's AI negotiates supplier contracts on its own, mostly long-tail and low-value deals for companies like Walmart and Maersk. Strategic negotiations are still largely handled by humans.

In Nashville, the Metro Council must approve by resolution any solid waste collection or disposal contract worth $500,000 or more a year, and an authorized official executes it. A human sign-off is therefore required.
In Monroe, the city council selects the solid waste collection contractor and approves its contract and any addenda.

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(l) says only trained operators whom the employer has certified and authorized may run forklifts and other powered industrial trucks. Training includes hands-on practice and an evaluation in the workplace.

Autonomous forklifts (for example DHL's 15 units) are robots with LIDAR and camera hardware, not software-only agents. The search found no recycling facility using them, so the reference technology, which has no body, cannot move materials itself.
Recycling facilities are messy, unpredictable places where items arrive overlapping and in random positions, which makes physical handling hard to automate.

Commercial and public AI grant tools such as Polco's Grant Writing AI Agent and Massachusetts' GrantWell already match municipalities to funding, summarize funding notices, draft narratives and letters of support, and help with budgets. That covers most of the writing and research steps.

For local-government recycling grants such as EPA SWIFR, the governing body typically passes a resolution naming an official to sign the application and later grant documents. So a human authorized representative has to approve, certify and sign.

State recycling grant signature pages require an authorized representative to certify that the governing body approved the project. Applications also depend on internal program data, budgets, matching-fund commitments and partner letters, which a person has to gather and review.

LoopWorks MRF OS scale-house app records gross, tare and net weight, material type, contamination, supplier and driver in one form, and traces each ton from the scale through the baler to the outbound load. Log capture and reconciliation can be done digitally, but someone on site still has to confirm what physically arrived or left before the log is accepted.
AMCS Scale House connects directly to scales to weigh incoming and outgoing material and feeds transaction records, so an agent working through software could keep the logs from system data.
ReMatter's scale-ticket product automatically takes pictures of scales for compliance documentation, which cuts down manual ticket transcription.

Indonesia's grid code requires automatic generation control on plants above 5 MW. Since 2017 many geothermal plants follow load according to the dispatcher's daily plan. Because reservoirs differ, the AGC mode has to be chosen carefully to protect production wells. Software already handles the routine load following, but people still have to judge the reservoir and steam constraints.

At PLN/Pertamina geothermal plants, the Yokogawa control system automates startup and shutdown sequences, which cuts down on operator intervention. Setpoint and control changes are made through the control screens, so an agent with that access could in principle make them.

NERC's PER-003 certification rule covers reliability coordinators, transmission operators and balancing authorities. A 2008 NERC drafting document says certification of generator operators was left out of it. No licence rule was found that requires a human to make geothermal plant adjustments.

Manual J load calculations are routinely done in software such as Wrightsoft Right-J. The software handles the math and recalculates loads as inputs change, and vendors say many contractors now use AI heat load tools. Software still cannot give accurate loads if the user does not apply Manual J procedures correctly, so a human has to review the inputs and assumptions.

Many US jurisdictions require a Manual J report with the permit, and it must come from ACCA-approved software. The search found no general rule that a licensed engineer must sign it, and enforcement varies widely by locality.

Remote services sell permit-ready Manual J calculations made from plans and owner-supplied data. This shows the calculation can be done without being on site, but it depends on accurate measurements of the home's envelope, windows and insulation.

Geothermal loop fields use HDPE pipe made to ASTM standards. Installers join it by hand on site, using socket fusion for smaller pipe and butt fusion for larger pipe. That means cutting, facing, heating and joining with fusion equipment.

PE industry guidance says operators who do butt fusion or electrofusion should be trained, pass an exam and hold an approved-operator badge, renewed every one to two years, following ISO/TR 19480. National schemes include Germany's DVGW GW 330.

ISO/TR 19480 sets out how PE fusion operators are trained, assessed and approved, which makes fusion jointing a qualified human trade. Software can only help with side work such as looking up fusion parameters or reviewing joint logs.

Agentic AI in regulatory affairs can run a linked chain of detecting regulatory changes, analysing them, drafting, sending notifications and keeping audit trails. It can also check internal policies against new or updated regulations. Qualified regulatory affairs, quality assurance and qualified person (QP) staff remain responsible for decisions.

Generative AI speeds up drafting of GxP standard operating procedures (SOPs), but it may not know the company's own processes and can produce outdated or wrong text. The sponsor stays fully accountable for any content the AI drafts.

Under 21 CFR 820, executive management is responsible for the quality policy and must set up quality system procedures. A designated person has to review, approve, sign and date the documents. Implementing a procedure also involves management approval and training.

Dillon Consulting and Toronto Metropolitan University are building an AI system that moves site-visit data into pre-formatted Word templates and writes report text from past reports. They aim to automate 75–80% of the energy audit report. This is a project description, not a finished product.

Existing audit tools already run ASHRAE Level 1–3 analyses and produce standardized reports automatically: OptiMiser Commercial does measure analysis and reporting, and simuwatt/NREL generates standardized reports. Neither is described as AI-driven. The report-writing part of the task is digital, but the input data comes from physical site visits.

NYC Department of Buildings rules for Local Law 87 limit who can submit Energy Efficiency Reports to Registered Design Professionals. A human therefore has to certify and sign the report, though secondary sources disagree on the exact qualifications.

Research agent systems such as MetaChat (Stanford) and VortexChat turn photonic design goals written in plain language into device designs by running simulate-and-iterate loops. They are research prototypes, not turnkey products for deciding on applications.

OptiAgent's authors report that LLMs often fail to turn what they understand from text into workable optical designs without physics-based checks. That points to a continued need for human expert review.
A PE licence is generally needed only to sign and seal plans submitted to public authorities. Photonics R&D and product design work inside a company usually does not require a licensed signature.

Climate FieldView already builds zone-level variable-rate seeding prescriptions from historical yield data and satellite imagery, using known optimal seeding rates for commercial hybrids. An agent can drive this kind of software or reproduce the analysis in code, which covers the core GIS-to-prescription steps.

A patent family describes software that identifies management zones in a field and generates planting plans for each zone. It can use a yield-based model (seed hybrid, target yield, historical yield) or an economics-based model, and the two can give different recommendations. Choosing between them and checking them against local agronomic knowledge still takes human judgement before use.

No law was found that requires a licensed or Certified Crop Adviser to make seeding-rate or variety recommendations. The licensing rules found in Arizona, Louisiana and California apply to pesticide advice and nitrogen management plans instead.

AI dosing guidance tools such as UpToDate Expert AI exist in 2026. They are built to keep a clinician in the loop, and hallucination in unusual dosing cases is seen as a high risk. I found no autonomous prescribing systems in use.
Clinical decision support tools built into the EHR read current medications and lab results and return dosing and interaction suggestions. A clinician still approves any change.
State law and board rules set who may prescribe, and only licensed people such as nurse practitioners and physicians qualify. Some states require a physician to cosign or work under protocols.

Joint Commission guidance says the bedside two-person check before a blood transfusion is done by a qualified transfusionist whom the hospital designates under professional guidelines and state law. A barcode or other automated system can stand in only for the second person.

Children's hospital policy requires the whole blood verification to happen at the patient's bedside with two people, a transfusionist and a witness, before the product is hung and the patient is monitored.

AI tools for spotting and predicting adverse transfusion reactions are still mostly research models. They support a clinician's decisions but do not replace physical administration or bedside assessment.

Before a transfusion, two people (a transfusionist and a witness) must check the blood product against the patient at the bedside. Administering blood requires an authorized licensed provider such as an RN, LPN or physician.

Bedside barcode systems such as BloodTrack Tx (FDA 510(k)-cleared) electronically match the patient to the blood unit and record vitals and reactions. These are documentation and checking aids, not autonomous administration.

Current reaction detection uses rule-based alerts on vital signs that nurses enter, which can start a reaction work-up. The search found no autonomous AI tool that detects or manages transfusion reactions.
The AANA Scope and Standards say the CRNA must inspect the anesthesia machine and monitors before use and record the check in the patient's chart. The task is a hands-on, licensed one.
Automated machine self-checks have missed leaks and failures, so a clinician still has to do manual checks before each case.
Closed-loop anesthesia systems can adjust drug delivery, but they are device-integrated and still need a human in the loop. Software agents cannot prepare drugs or set up equipment physically.

Library technician job profiles describe first-level, often in-person troubleshooting of copiers, printers, microform readers and AV equipment, with harder problems sent on to IT. Clearing jams, swapping cables and replacing parts takes hands-on work that an agent without a body cannot do.

Products shipping by 2026, such as TeamViewer Tia and the Ivanti and ServiceNow service-desk agents, find and fix software and endpoint problems on their own. That covers the computer part of the task: remote diagnosis, fixes, logging tickets and contacting vendors. Independent data on how often they fix things without help is still thin.
O*NET lists this as a core library technician task. No licence or sign-off is needed, but the agent would need remote-management access to library machines, and it may not have that.
OCLC WorldShare Acquisitions can claim serial issues automatically through saved searches and scheduled jobs. Claims only go out when a vendor contact email is set.
SirsiDynix Symphony serial control produces claim notices for missing issues as reports and can send EDI claims to vendors that are set up for EDI.

In Voyager-style workflows, check-in patterns flag missed issues into a problem file that staff review before claiming. This includes physically confirming whether an issue arrived but was not checked in.
Alma Analytics reports can be exported to CSV, Excel or PDF, and can be scheduled and emailed to staff. An agent can collect and compile this data through software alone.
Alma can harvest COUNTER usage data through SUSHI automatically. Its built-in fulfillment dashboards cover loans, returns, requests and course reserves.

Usage data has known problems: items migrated from an old system may show only their most recent loan, and some canned reports were inaccurate. A person who knows the data still has to check the numbers before reporting to ACRL or IPEDS. Access requires staff analytics roles.

Hotel AI tools such as Accor's ALL Concierge and Yanolja's AI concierge already answer property questions, help with bookings and in-stay requests, and give recommendations. Yanolja lets human staff take over a conversation in real time when needed. Accor reports more than 1 million guest conversations in its pilot.
Canary Technologies runs AI voice and text agents for the front desk, concierge and reservations. They both answer guest questions and act on requests through hotel systems.
Vendors say LLM agents handle 80% or more of guest messages and up to 80% of call volume. These figures are unverified marketing claims, and unusual or in-person cases still go to staff.
O*NET lists this as a desk clerk task. A DOL job filing describes it as physically moving pre-packaged breakfast items and coffee supplies to a self-serve area. Clerks don't cook.
Breakfast attendant postings describe the work as setting up and breaking down breakfast items and brewing fresh coffee. All of it is hands-on work that software can't do without a robot.
AI inventory tools such as WISK.ai can forecast food and beverage demand and suggest purchase orders. That covers only the small planning and restocking part of the job, not the setup.

The only AI paint-defect inspection systems found run on factory paint lines, not in collision shops. Nissan AUTIS uses fixed high-resolution cameras that take about 15,000 images per car, and technicians still confirm and classify each flagged defect. A software-only agent cannot use this kind of camera hardware or check a car in person.

Factory systems that pair AI paint inspection with robotic repair, such as EINES ESFI with AutoRepair, need dedicated inline hardware and robots, which are outside the reference agent's abilities. The task's other main parts, test-driving the car and checking fit, function and dimensions on site, are physical work by nature.

The search found no collision-repair product that does post-repair inspection end to end. An agent could only help in small ways: comparing photos or measurement and scan printouts against OEM specs, and drafting the QC checklist and records.

When payment systems are connected to the hotel's property management system (PMS), payment events are sent to the PMS automatically and the guest's bill updates without staff input. Refunds update it the same way.

Charges from linked systems such as point of sale, minibar and spa are posted to the guest's bill automatically through PMS interfaces. When systems use different identifiers, posts fail and staff have to clean them up by hand.

A vendor says its AI agents match card batches, cash and booking-channel payouts against PMS postings and keep an audit trail. This is the vendor's own claim and has not been independently checked. A PMS records a charge but does not prove the money was collected, so a human still has to review discrepancies and count the cash.

PNNL's PermitAI and SearchNEPA tools use AI to search and analyze NEPA documents. About 30 DOE evaluators are testing them, and an EIS drafting assistant and a comment-sorting tool are due in 2026. Agents can already do substantial review sub-steps, but under human oversight.

A 2025 practitioner paper describes AI in US environmental impact assessment as still at a very nascent stage. Expert biologists still have to check the ecological adequacy of reports before they are used.

Some local agencies, such as Ventura County under CEQA, accept biological work only from approved qualified biologists. That is an accountability barrier: a human must stand behind the adequacy findings.

AI and software tools exist for planning which gear a shoot needs. Studiovity turns script breakdowns into shot lists with lenses and camera setups for each shot. CineBag builds equipment lists that can be exported to rental houses. These cover only the selection and planning sub-step.

Camera operators rig and operate camera equipment and work with grip and electric crews to rig supports, dollies, track and lighting flags. They also lay out sets and furniture and handle heavy equipment. This is hands-on work that a software-only agent cannot do.

Career descriptions say the job is physically demanding and involves assembling studio sets and arranging cameras and lighting on location or in the studio. No law or licence requires a human to perform or sign off this task.

AI rehabilitation apps such as MED-EL ReDi and Neurotone LACE AI Pro already run personalized listening, speechreading and speech-in-noise training on their own. These are sub-steps of the instruction part of the task, though the claims come mostly from the vendors.

ASHA places aural rehabilitation for adults, including counseling, within the scope of licensed audiologists and SLPs, who are expected to be specifically trained for it. State practice acts define it as licensed audiology practice.

Trade guidance says AI training apps work best when the clinician frames them as rehabilitation and persuades patients to take part. That keeps the person-to-person counseling and motivation with a human.

Medicare-certified home health agencies must use aides trained in a state-approved program of at least 75 hours, including 16 hours of supervised hands-on practice, and evaluated by an RN. The task is hands-on care that a person must physically do, but no rule requires a human to sign off on these chores.

The laundry-folding robots shown at CES 2026 (such as LG CLOiD and SwitchBot Onero) are general household prototypes, and reviewers found their speed unconvincing. They are robots, not software agents, so they are outside the reference technology anyway.

Robots that help with bathing have only reached early research, such as adapting an industrial arm to help with showering. Personal care still needs a person who is physically present and someone the patient trusts.

Psychiatric institutions began controlled trials of ambient AI scribes that draft notes for clinicians, including nurses, in August 2026. This shows AI can draft documentation, but clinicians still review it. No product specific to inpatient aide or nursing notes was found.

Psychiatric hospital records must show the degree and intensity of treatment, and surveyors cite missing 15-minute observation-check records. These records come from staff who observe patients in person on the unit.
Under CMS rules for psychiatric hospital records (42 CFR 482.61), entries must be authenticated by an accountable author. A human has to observe the patient and sign the note.

The machines that do automate sandwich, bowl, salad and drink prep are dedicated robots (Nala Robotics Sandwich Bot and Bowl Bot, Rolo Robotics micro kitchens). That is physical hardware, not a software AI agent without a body.

Even 2026 automated micro kitchens do the frying, baking, salad and beverage work with physical modules. The task is hands-on handling of food, so an agent that acts only through software cannot do it.
The FDA Food Code requires a designated Person in Charge on site during operation, but no licence requires a specific person to do the food prep itself. The decisive barrier is physical, not legal.
Cleaning food-contact surfaces is hands-on work: pre-scrape, wash, rinse, sanitize, then air dry. A software agent with no robotic body cannot do any of these steps.
Under the Food Code, all surfaces must be washed and rinsed, and food-contact surfaces must also be sanitized. All of this is physical work done in the kitchen.
Food-safety software such as Xenia only covers digital side work like cleaning schedules and checklists. The cleaning itself still has to be done by a person.

Washing, peeling and cutting produce in commercial kitchens is automated, where it is automated at all, by physical machines such as the IMC MF5 peeler/washer and vegetable processors with cutting discs. These need a person to load and run them; software agents do not do this work.
Industrial automatic peelers, such as onion/garlic peelers rated at about 240 kg/h, are mechanical equipment that only does the physical handling of the food.

Even dedicated automatic peelers struggle with produce that is non-spherical or has tough skin. This shows the task is a matter of physical handling and dexterity, which a robot-free AI agent cannot provide.

Vendors sell AI voice agents for restaurants that answer the phone, take reservations (checking availability, party size, time and special requests) and send takeout orders straight to the POS. Unusual or large-party requests are passed to staff. These are vendor marketing claims, not independent evaluations.

Restaurant voice agents can update reservation systems and route calls to a person when needed. That covers the phone part of the task end to end, while greeting, seating and thanking guests still happen in person on the restaurant floor, which the agent cannot do.
Vendor posts describe 24/7 AI handling of restaurant phone orders and bookings. None of the sources mention a licence or legal rule requiring a human to take reservations or orders.
AI feedback agents for dine-in guests open from a QR code on a table tent, check presenter or receipt. They collect satisfaction feedback in the guest's phone browser.

A restaurant feedback chatbot vendor says its bot passes serious complaints to staff with the conversation history and does not try to resolve them itself. Humans still handle the in-person resolution.
POS-linked and QR survey platforms such as Ovation detect negative sentiment in real time and route it to managers so staff can act during or after the visit.

A patented vision system watches dining tables through existing surveillance cameras and flags plates, utensils and spills left behind. It labels each area as normal, possibly needing cleaning, or needing cleaning. This is a patent, and I found no current product for dining-room tables.

Commercial AI camera systems for restaurants, such as Dragontail, check sanitation mainly in kitchens and food-prep areas, like glove and mask use and how often surfaces are cleaned. They work only with cameras installed on site. They do not walk the floor, touch surfaces or fix table settings.

Wobot connects to a restaurant's existing CCTV and checks conditions and activities in real time. The examples it shows are mostly kitchen and counter tasks, so an agent could only help with visual checks where these cameras exist. The host still has to walk the room, look closely, touch surfaces and fix the setup.

Childcare software such as KidKare and Brightwheel already handles the digital parts of the task: CACFP-compliant menu planning, flagging missing meal components, and logging meals. Preparing and serving the food is still done by hand.
Illinois licensing rules require staff to be present to supervise children at mealtimes and require food service to be managed by a state-certified food service manager.
Ontario requires at least one trained food handler or supervisor on the premises of childcare settings that serve meals, and food handlers must meet personal hygiene requirements.
Caring for children with disabilities involves hands-on physical help: tube feeding, suctioning, toileting, diapering, and moving or positioning the child.
Supported child care workers help with feeding, lifts and transfers, grooming and toileting, and carry out exercise and mobility care plans.
AI is used for side tasks such as drafting support or IEP plans and giving children learning or schedule aids. A human still reviews the plans, and the people involved decide the services.

Funeral home community outreach is in-person: staffing booths at local events, handing out giveaways and collecting contact details face to face. The task's core needs physical presence and personal relationship-building.

Funeral marketing software can already schedule posts and newsletters, invite people to in-person events and send automated follow-up emails. This covers support sub-steps like promotion and follow-up, but not attending or presenting.
Brand and preneed material tools work with general AI assistants such as Claude and ChatGPT. That supports drafting presentation and promotional materials while a human delivers them.

Funeral home software such as Kindred, FuneraliQ+ and Osiris already includes built-in accounting, financial performance reports and QuickBooks integration, and some products add AI assistants. Most of this is vendor marketing, and I found no independent test of how well the AI insight features work.

General AI agents (ClickUp, Taskade) are sold for profit-and-loss analysis and cost-reduction planning. They flag costs that look too high, compare spending with industry norms and watch budgets for overruns. The same sources say humans still need to review nuanced, sector-specific cases. No independent case studies were found.

Reviewing internal performance data is a management analysis task. It needs no physical presence, and no licence or signature rule requires a human to do it. The agent's output still has to be checked by the manager, who knows local context such as families, staff and how services run on the ground, before anyone acts on it.

Funeral home management platforms such as The Smart Director already automate death certificate filing through state Electronic Death Registration Systems (EDRS) and track merchandise inventory, so an agent working through this kind of software could do most of the record work.

In Colorado, the funeral director or person acting as such who first takes custody of the body is responsible for filing the death certificate. Electronic submission counts as the signature, so accountability stays with a human filer.
Washington's EDRS requires each funeral director to get an identity-verifying digital certificate before filing, which limits direct agent access and keeps a human in the loop.
Commercial AI exit-interview agents run the offboarding conversation by chat, email or voice. They adapt questions, analyse sentiment and send summaries to HR dashboards.

Offboarding automation starts checklists from HRIS termination events, generates documents such as COBRA notices, final paycheck acknowledgments and state wage notices, routes them for e-signature and files them back to the HRIS.

HR platforms and access tools each cover only about half of offboarding tasks, and coordination between functions often falls through the gaps, so a human still needs to oversee and close out the work.

Vendors describe recruiting agents that source candidates by analyzing profiles and career signals. They also watch pipelines and, when a role falls behind, add sourcing channels or re-engage passive candidates on their own. Most deployments are still shallow (job descriptions, basic screening), and the autonomy claims come mainly from vendors.

Korn Ferry's 2026 Talent Acquisition Trends report says 52% of talent leaders plan to add AI agents to their teams. Recruiters' time is expected to shift toward turning hiring data into business strategy, so humans keep the strategic alignment and approval steps.

The EU AI Act classes recruitment AI as high-risk and requires human oversight; sources disagree on whether this applies from August 2026 or, under the AI Omnibus, December 2027. NYC Local Law 144 requires only bias audits and notice to candidates. Neither law requires a licensed human to write or sign off a recruiting strategy.

The search found no product where an AI agent negotiates for a union or employer. The 2026 sources describe unions bargaining over how employers use AI, and AI used to prepare or support union work. They do not describe AI conducting the talks.
The NLRA duty to bargain in good faith includes meeting at reasonable times and places, which can be in person or by video conference. Physical presence is therefore not strictly required.
Commentary lists negotiators without real authority as a sign of bad-faith bargaining. In practice the other side expects an accountable human representative who can commit the party.
Canva's Magic Design builds editable event posters from a text prompt and uploaded images. Its Magic Switch feature turns one design into matching social posts and an email newsletter.
Figma Make can build nonprofit websites from a plain description of the fundraising goal and page sections, including event pages, RSVPs and volunteer signups.
Eventnook's AI builder makes event sites for charity galas and fundraising events, with registration and ticketing, from a text prompt or an uploaded design.

Blackbaud says its Development Agent, built into Raiser's Edge NXT, finds, cultivates and contacts donors, and that the platform surfaces recommended actions and donor briefings. This is a vendor claim.

DonorSearch Ai trains custom acquisition and retention models on an organization's own giving history and returns ranked prospect scores, which automates a core analytic step in planning for new or larger gifts.

Salesforce Nonprofit Cloud offers Agentforce-based fundraising agents, including a Prospect Research Agent. Strategy approval and how well it fits with relationships, the board and the mission still depend on humans.

Customizable bid sheet templates in PDF and image formats are widely available. They list the item description, starting bid, bid increment and bidders. An agent can fill them in and lay them out from an item list without help.
Mobile bidding and online form tools pick the winning bidder automatically and send bids straight into spreadsheets. This means much of the digital prep around bid sheets can be done in software.
The printed bid sheets still have to be placed next to each auction item. Stuffing envelopes and assembling gift bags are also hands-on work at the venue that an agent without a body cannot do.

SpeakUp, a speaker-matching platform, says it offers an MCP server that lets ChatGPT or Claude agents find, shortlist, contact and book speakers within a chat. This is the vendor's own claim and has not been independently checked.
Event-platform guides describe using AI to research speakers, draft personalized invitation emails and handle logistics, which covers most of the digital sub-steps of securing a speaker.

AI email agents can already send personalized outreach at volume and schedule follow-ups automatically. Choosing which speaker fits the cause, persuading high-profile or unpaid speakers through personal relationships, and committing to fees or contracts still need a human.

Bandwidth-planning tools and AI document-analysis tools for network architecture exist, but they give only rough, early-stage estimates. Sizing still has to be checked against vendor specs and measured traffic, which supports partial rather than full delegation.
Traffic from AI agents breaks the usual assumptions about peak hours and oversubscription. Requirements therefore depend on site-specific traffic data that sits inside the organization's systems.

A licensed professional engineer must certify the network design for some government-funded broadband projects, such as USDA ReConnect. For typical enterprise network requirements, no license or sign-off is required.

Community health workers hand out flyers in person, door to door: they leave them on homes and car windshields and give them out at community events. An agent with no body cannot do this core activity.

Automated SMS and AI-driven outreach already reach targeted families digitally. In one trial, a GPT-4o phone agent booked visits. This means agents can handle the digital side of distribution, such as texts, emails and social posts, plus list targeting and logistics.

AI can draft health-education texts, but researchers found that expert review is essential for accuracy and appropriate language. This supports the view that agents help with preparation but do not carry out the whole task.

Vendors such as Opalite Health (YC W26) and No Barrier AI sell real-time speech-to-speech medical interpretation between clinicians and patients in 150+ languages. These claims come from the companies themselves.

A Boostlingo/Fierce Healthcare survey found most healthcare leaders accept AI interpreting for scheduling and billing, but far fewer accept it for emergency, inpatient or emotionally sensitive care. Their main concern is whether it performs well in real situations.

Under the US Section 1557 rule, a qualified human translator must review machine translation when the content is critical, technical, or affects a person's rights, benefits or access (for example consent forms and patient instructions).

AATA guidance says the therapist must get explicit written consent before using a client's artwork, including how the client wants to be identified, and must watch for subtle coercion caused by the therapist's greater authority. Choosing clients and getting their consent is relational clinical work that a human has to lead.
CATA/ACAT standards forbid publicly displaying client art without a dated, signed written release from the client or guardian, and forbid identifying clients in public.

Agentic event tools released in 2025-26 (Cvent agent Skills, Bizzabo, RainFocus Nexus) handle scheduling, vendor emails, RFPs, registrations and reminders end to end. These match the logistics sub-steps of a showcase, but hanging the work and running the event in person still need a human.

A 2026 preprint used automated PubMed retrieval and NLP to organize the music therapy literature. The authors say AI should support retrieval and professional judgment, not replace clinical expertise, so an agent can do the search and synthesis but the clinician still applies the findings.

Some US states require music therapists to hold MT-BC board certification and a state license. A credentialed human is therefore responsible for clinical decisions about using research-based interventions with clients.
Turning research into practice includes delivering and adjusting music interventions in live sessions with clients, which needs physical presence and a therapeutic relationship.
Researchers scored ChatGPT against an ACSM-based rubric for 26 clinical populations. Its exercise recommendations covered only about 41% of the content expected in a gold-standard prescription.

A systematic review of generative AI for exercise prescription found that it complements expert guidance but does not replace it. In expert-rated studies, LLM programs were generally safe but not individualized enough to each person's health conditions and goals.

In Louisiana, clinical exercise physiologists hold a licence from the State Board of Medical Examiners and work under a licensed physician's direction, approval and supervision. Their licensed scope includes formulating and developing exercise protocols for cardiopulmonary rehabilitation.

AI fitness tools I found, such as Virtuagym's Max AI Coach and TrueCoach-listed assistants, generate workout plans and content or check exercise form. They are built for one-to-one client coaching. I found no product that mentors or trains staff to lead group classes.
AI4Fit, a university research project, only supplies workout data to support a human coach's feedback. The trainer stays the one who gives it.

The ACSM group exercise instructor credential is a knowledge exam taken online or at a test centre, and the results showed no practical component. This suggests no licence requires a human to do the mentoring. The hands-on parts of mentoring, such as demonstrating, cueing, observing classes and correcting staff, remain physical and in person.

Software MRI simulators (Corsmed, ScanLabMR) already provide virtual scanner training with built-in course creation, grading and progress tracking, so the didactic and protocol-practice parts of instruction can be handed to software.
Hands-on training for positioning, coils and patient comfort uses physical mock scanners or real equipment, so a person has to be physically present to demonstrate and correct.

ARRT requires clinical competencies such as MRI safety, positioning and quality control to be verified by an ARRT-registered MR technologist or another qualified person, so a human has to sign off on trainee competence.

Ocular motility tests such as the prism cover test are done in person. The examiner holds occluders and prisms, sets fixation targets and coaches the patient, and getting a young child to cooperate is a known difficulty. A software-only agent cannot do this hands-on work.

Dedicated eye-tracking hardware, such as the University of Auckland digital cover test, can automate the measurement. These systems are separate physical devices, not general AI agents, and a 2025 review notes several barriers that keep them out of routine clinical use.

One eye-tracker system reports a nine-point comitancy screen in under two minutes. An agent could help with recording and reading the results, but a person still has to set up and run the test with the patient.

In low vision acuity testing, the examiner moves the patient closer to the chart (to 2 m, then 1 m) and uses single cards. With very poor vision, the examiner also counts fingers, checks hand motion and tests light perception. All of these need a person in the room handling materials and the patient.

Smartphone and at-home acuity tests (Peek Acuity, Vision at Home, and the three home tests compared in JAMA Ophthalmology 2022) came within about one line of in-office ETDRS results. But validation mostly involved people with normal or mildly impaired vision, and accuracy varied with the level of impairment. Software can therefore help with chart display, scoring and records, but it cannot replace in-person low vision and blindness testing.
A full low vision assessment covers history, acuity, refraction, contrast sensitivity, color vision, glare and visual fields, using physical charts and devices with the patient present.

Bedside voice AI products like OrbitaASSIST already take spoken patient requests (for example 'tell the nurse I need a pillow' or 'I've fallen'), then triage, prioritize and route them to care-team devices. This covers the call-answering and needs-intake sub-steps.

AI virtual triage is used alongside nurse triage call centers to collect symptoms and prioritize requests. In a 54,587-encounter study it cut unnecessary consultations, which shows automated needs-assessment works for remote, verbal interactions.

Many calls still need an aide at the bedside to see the patient (falls, incontinence, pain, confusion, patients who can't speak). A human therefore performs essential steps, but no license or signature is required to answer call lights.
CNA support work is hands-on: setting up suction equipment, giving oxygen with tents and masks, turning and positioning patients, and moving them with wheelchairs, walkers and lifts.
Current AI tools cover only the digital side, such as ambient sensing for fall risk and virtual nursing for documentation, monitoring and education. Clinicians still do the bedside care.
In 2026, nurse ambient AI produces flowsheet entries that a nurse must review, and only 22% of nurses surveyed said they trust AI tools for safe patient care.

Hospital room disinfection is done by people with their hands, sometimes helped by dedicated UV-C robots. UV robots are hardware, not software AI agents, and the vendor itself calls them a supplementary device that assists cleaning staff.
A 2025 hospital study found that UV-C robots and hydrogen peroxide vapor methods fall short on shaded areas and surface contamination, so physical wiping is still needed.
Even an autonomous UV disinfection robot needs a physical platform to clean a room, which a software-only agent does not have.

State nursing boards list specimen collection as a hands-on CNA skill: clean-catch and 24-hour urine, stool and sputum. This means being physically present with the patient and handling the containers.
Training modules describe bedside steps such as having the patient rinse their mouth before giving sputum and collecting it in the morning. These are physical, interpersonal care steps.
Robotic sputum and urine collection systems exist only as research prototypes. Automation is mainly found in lab processing after collection, not at the bedside.

Oracle Health's Clinical AI Agent for nurses is commercially available in the US. It writes short nursing summaries for shift handoffs from physician notes, medications, labs and orders. This covers the record-review part of gathering patient information.

Handoff-summary tools such as Pokee AI build summaries from notes, vitals, labs and care plans, but they keep the output as a draft until a nurse reviews it. The search found no tool built for nursing-assistant handoffs.

Nursing assistants work under a licensed nurse's delegation and follow the plan of care. Instructions from physicians or family go through the nurse. Much of the information comes from verbal report and huddles on the unit, and the aide has to understand it personally before giving care.

CNAs pick up skin changes such as redness, swelling and bruising, and blood in urine, while giving hands-on personal care at the bedside. They report these to the supervising nurse and do not diagnose them.

A smartphone AI app that staged pressure injuries from photos reached only about 63% accuracy in validation. It also needs a human to take the picture, so the AI can only help with images someone else captures.
CNA skills are carried out under the direction and supervision of a licensed nurse.
Surgical positioning means physically moving the patient, keeping the body aligned, and padding pressure points. RNs direct technicians and assistants, who do the physical moving.
Positioning is a shared responsibility of the perioperative team. The RN applies the positioning devices and the surgeon chooses the position, so licensed professionals stay accountable for the work.

Pressure injury is the most common positioning complication. Preventing it depends on hands-on placement of padding and devices, and OR documentation records skin condition and devices used. A software-only agent could help only with that documentation.

The bedpan procedure is hands-on work: gloving, placing a barrier, positioning the pan under the patient, then emptying it into a toilet or graduated cylinder and recording output. Only the recording step is digital.

Debilitated, obese or post-surgical patients often need two or more staff to move on or off the pan. Forcing the pan under a patient risks friction injury to the skin, which takes careful physical handling.
State nurse aide checklists test this as a physical skill. Toileting is offered every two hours and calls for sensitive, therapeutic communication because incontinence is embarrassing for patients.
O*NET lists changing soiled linens, drapes and cubicle curtains as a hands-on orderly task, alongside collecting soiled linen and trash.
Florida's hospital rules require soiled linen to be collected in a way that limits the spread of microbes. This is physical handling done under infection-control procedures.
A York hospital (UK) guideline sorts linen into used, soiled and infected, and each type needs physical bagging and handling at the bedside.

At Cleveland Clinic, the infectious-waste transport that does get automated is done by physical robots (AGVs) that move regulated medical waste to a sterilization room. Software-only AI agents without a body can't do this.
Research robots such as Siriraj Hospital's 'Wastie' use robot arms to lift and carry infectious waste bins. This shows the core work is physically handling closed containers.

A 2025 review of medical-waste technology says automation of traceability is still not widely adopted. Logging and tracking paperwork is the only part a software agent could help with, and it is a small share of the task time.
O*NET lists 'Position or hold patients in position for surgical preparation' as a hands-on orderly/aide task done in person with the patient.
Orderlies help position patients under staff direction. This is physical handling of the patient, not work done through software or documents.
Today, surgical positioning relies on people holding limbs by hand or on mechanical positioner devices. Neither is a software or AI agent capability.

Hospital food services use TUG robotic carts to move meal trays through hallways and elevators. Staff watch the carts on iPads and meet each one at drop-off, then take the trays to patients themselves. Robots are physical systems and fall outside the software-only reference technology.

Tray-delivery software uses barcodes on trays and patient wristbands, so staff can make sure the right diet goes to the right patient. Software can help with checking, but a person still physically hands over the tray.
At UCSF, the food-service TUG robots do not enter patient care areas. People still do the bedside serving and the collection of trays.

Hospital PAR software such as Cognosos ProPAR tracks room-level stock against PAR thresholds, sends alerts and builds pick lists for the staff who restock. People still carry and place the items. Software only helps with the counting and planning step.
Automated PAR-room systems record usage and trigger restocking with no manual counts, but they do not physically restock shelves or carts.
Linen and supply carts are refilled every day to set quotas. This is hands-on work that takes physical presence in storage rooms and on carts.

Hospital delivery robots such as Aethon TUG/ZenaRx and Relay carry specimens and medications with locked compartments and logged chain of custody. These are robots, and the reference technology has no robotics. A software agent could only handle the logging and tracking part.

Automated chain-of-custody software records who loaded and delivered each item, along with times and locations. This digitizes the documentation step, but someone still has to move the items physically.

Relay Robotics advertises secure autonomous transport with chain-of-custody tracking for medications and lab specimens. Even with these robots, the core of the task is physical handoff to authorized staff.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030(d)(4)(iii), contaminated sharps have to go into closable, puncture-resistant, leakproof, labeled containers. These containers must be replaced routinely and not overfilled. Each of these steps is physical handling at the point of use.

Reusable sharps containers may not be opened, emptied or cleaned by hand or in any other way that puts workers at risk. Final disposal must follow federal, state and local regulated-waste rules, so the work is done by physically segregating and moving the material.

OSHA governs how waste is contained and handled where it is used, and state medical-waste and EPA rules govern what happens after that. Only small digital sub-steps, such as looking up the rules or filling in waste logs and manifests, could go to an AI agent with no body.
California BPC §1246 requires state certification to collect blood. Under the CDPH tiers, skin-puncture collection needs at least a Limited Phlebotomy Technician or CPT I credential.

The first FDA-authorized autonomous blood-draw robot (Vitestro Aletta, August 2026) is a physical robotic device. It does venous draws only, not capillary heel or finger sticks, and it still needs a trained phlebotomist to start and supervise each session.
Capillary dermal puncture is a hands-on skin procedure on the patient. Training programs teach it as a practical clinical skill, and a software-only agent cannot carry it out.

CLSI GP41-based practice puts the explanation at the bedside, just before the draw. It sits alongside spoken patient identification, implied consent (for example, the patient rolls up a sleeve after the explanation) and stopping if the patient withdraws consent. So the core explanation is an in-person exchange with the phlebotomist and is part of the draw.

CLSI says blood collection must not go ahead against the patient's consent and treats patient-centred communication as part of the collection procedure. This makes the explanation a trust and care step built into the physical procedure.

In lab medicine, AI chatbots are documented for explaining results and for scheduling blood tests. I found no products that give the bedside explanation of a collection procedure, so AI is limited to support work such as pre-visit instructions (fasting, urine or stool collection kits) and written handouts.
Blood-donor canteen roles involve physically serving snacks and drinks, restocking and sanitizing tables, and talking with donors face to face. Listings say mobility is needed to serve refreshments.
Canteen staff watch donors in person after donation for adverse reactions and tell staff right away. This needs someone physically present in the room.
This is often an unlicensed role done by volunteers or attendants, so there is no licensing barrier. The work is greeting donors and handing out refreshments in the refreshment area.

Under OSHA directive CPL 2-1.36, workers climbing communication towers must use a fall arrest system (1926.502) or a ladder safety device (1926.1053(a)), and they must be trained. This is a physical task that a person has to do in harness.

Drones can cut down on climbs for inspections, but the tower erectors' association (NATE) and AT&T say drones cannot do rigging, antenna work or line work. Climbers are still needed, and drones are not software agents anyway.
Drone-based digital twins can reduce the need to climb for site audits, but they do not climb towers to reach components. They are also robotic hardware, which the reference agent does not have.

Heidelberg's Predictive and Remote Monitoring use sensors and algorithms to detect developing faults and flag them. The cause is then fixed by technicians or operators, so software handles detection but not the physical correction.

Prinect Inspection Control finds defects, sounds an alarm, inserts a tab in the pile and shows the defect on the console for the operator to correct. The response to the alert is left to the operator.

Press fault messages show where the fault is and guide the user through physically clearing jams or fixing components, and the manual warns against forcing paper out of the fuser or rollers. Resolving these faults requires hands-on work at the machine (evidence is from a Xerox digital production press, not an offset press).

Fiery Scribe, announced in March 2026, is an agent that watches an email inbox for print job requests, works out the job specifications and loads the jobs into Fiery Command WorkStation. That is automated intake of job requirements.

AI quoting tools can read customer files uploaded to web-to-print portals and pull out dimensions, page count, orientation and color space. This automates part of the requirements discussion. The claims come from vendors and have not been independently verified.

Chat-based intake agents for print shops list missing specs, write follow-up questions and handle exceptions. Talks about binding plans still usually involve physical samples or dummies and judgment about the shop's own equipment, which is why a human stays in the loop.

O*NET 51-5113.00 lists this task as a core task (importance 87). It is done by hand or with a machine: stitching or gluing endpapers, bindings, backings or signatures using sewing machines, glue machines, or glue and brushes.

The work includes forming book bodies by folding and sewing printed sheets into signatures and assembling them in order. These are hands-on, physical steps that a software-only agent with no robotic body cannot do.
The usual entry requirement is a high-school diploma. The occupation profile shows no licence or sign-off rule that would require a human to do the task.

VueScan's software automates dust and scratch removal using the scanner's infrared channel. Its auto-crop and auto white balance are meant to keep manual adjustment low when batch scanning slides and negatives, so an agent using a computer could run the scanning settings and post-processing.

Batch film scanners such as PowerFilm Plus still need a person to physically load the filmstrips (up to 10 strips of 6 frames per batch). After that, the scanner removes dust and scratches with infrared Magic Touch cleaning on its own, so handling the media remains a human step.

The Plustek OpticFilm 135i batch scans groups of up to 4 slides or 6 negatives and corrects dust with an infrared channel. Software handles the scanning, but someone must physically feed the film or slides into the machine.

Remote management systems for minilab photo equipment have existed since the 1990s. They let a central site control how lab-shop processors run and manage production and quality, so some setting changes can be made through software.

Processors can adjust developer replenishment automatically from control-strip density readings. That covers part of the parameter adjustment, but these controls are built into the equipment rather than reachable by a general AI agent.

On a Kodak DKS digital minilab, replenishment rates are set on the machine's own chemical parameter screens, and some changes also require physically modifying the replenishment lines. That means a person usually has to be at the machine.

To make timed prints, a person loads the conformed negative on a Hazeltine analyzer, picks printer-light settings for each scene, and sends them to a contact printer. Today the timer types the corrections into a computer that the printer reads, but the film handling, printing and review are still physical.

Printer lights for each scene are set on a 1 to 50 point scale for each of red, green and blue. Automatic timing from densitometer readings has existed since 1956. Even so, a skilled timer usually needs two or three trial prints to get a balanced result.

Software tools such as Resolve's Shot Match and scene-cut detection can suggest color matches between shots. Guides say to treat the result as a starting point, not a finished grade. These tools are digital and do not run photochemical printers.
Beam AI says its compliance agents gather ESG data, flag policy gaps and produce disclosures for SFDR and similar frameworks. This is a vendor claim and has not been independently checked.

ESGAgent.ai says it automates sustainability compliance, including tracking EU Taxonomy and SEC climate-rule changes and reporting aligned to GRI, SASB and TCFD. This is company-reported in trade news.
Compliance & Risks markets AI-native sustainability compliance intelligence that monitors regulations. The task is digital oversight work that needs no physical presence or professional licence.

University of Washington researchers built multi-agent AI that generates life-cycle inventories and carbon footprints for electronics from just a product name. Error ran 5-19%, close to expert LCAs, but it covers only cradle-to-gate emissions, not a full LCA.

Commercial LCA tools (Makersite, Sphera, One Click LCA) use AI to fill data gaps, match bills of materials to background databases, import files through an AI agent and run scenarios at scale. Primary data from suppliers is still needed.

Consultancy summaries of ISO 14044 (I could not check the clause text) say that when an LCA supports a public comparative claim, an independent expert panel must review it. For other studies a single independent expert may review it. No licence is needed to conduct an LCA, so a human reviewer is needed only in some cases.

Procurement sustainability agents, such as Dcycle's, rate suppliers using public ESG data (CDP, SBTi, controversy databases) and compare them against purchase history. This is a core sub-step of weighing environmental aspects of competing suppliers and merchandise.

myclimate Smart PCF uses AI to estimate the carbon footprint of individual retail products from attributes like category, price, weight and materials. This makes it possible to compare competing items automatically.

AI LCA tools for fashion and retail, such as Carbon Trail, fill data gaps with AI estimates, and no independent accuracy benchmarks turned up. A human still needs to check the outputs, get proprietary supplier data and make the final buying call. There is no licensing or physical requirement.

Stantec/Page describe an AI framework that speeds up early-stage energy modeling, which normally takes up to 80 hours. It is built on Honeybee/Ladybug parametric tools, so performance analysis can run inside design exploration.

A review of generative AI and optimization methods for sustainable architecture reports energy reductions of about 23-28% in studies. This suggests software can automate design-option generation and performance optimization.
A licensed architect must prepare or directly supervise building permit documents and sign, seal and date them. Plans without proper seals are returned without review.

Cistern sizing for rainwater harvesting can already be done with existing calculators and spreadsheet methods: roof catchment area, rainfall data and a water-demand balance. An agent can find the rainfall data online, run these calculations, and write the specifications and narrative documents.

Landscape architects are expected to calculate how much rainwater a project can reuse and what size cisterns it needs, using the project's annual rainfall (LEED context). This is analytical, desk-based work that an agent could largely do.

Technical submissions for permits or construction must carry a licensed landscape architect's seal and signature. Greywater systems may also fall under separate plumbing or health codes, so a licensed human still has to review and sign the work.

Modular green roof trays are placed by hand on rooftops. Installers lay them over a root barrier on a sound, watertight membrane, clip them together and level them. The trays weigh about 75 kg/m² when saturated, and the plants must be installed within about 24 hours of unpacking. All of this is physical work an agent without a body cannot do. Software can only help with side work such as layout planning or load checks.
Patents for modular living roofs describe trays that sit on the roof membrane, with drainage holes and adjustable leveling devices that the installer sets on site.

Many US states and localities require a license or registration to do roofing work, so a licensed human contractor is accountable for it. California's C-39 license covers installing waterproofing surfaces. Search found no green-roof-specific licensing rule, so it is only inferred that these rules cover green roof installs.

Heavy-duty diesel smoke testing uses the SAE J1667 snap-acceleration procedure. A light-extinction smokemeter is attached to a stationary vehicle that has reached normal operating temperature, at the roadside, a depot or a repair shop. Someone has to be there to fit the probe and work the throttle.

Under California's HD I/M program, newer vehicles can meet the requirement with OBD data sent through CARB-certified telematics, with pass criteria of no MIL-on events, no active codes and no permanent codes. That part could be automated in software. Non-OBD vehicles still need opacity tests at set intervals.

Tests submitted for compliance must be run by HD I/M Approved Testers using registered tools, or by certified remote OBD devices. This means a credentialed person or device is responsible for the result.
Kentucky law says no one may install, erect or repair boilers without a state license, and getting one requires passing an exam.
Michigan licenses boiler installers in classes based on boiler size and type, and an applicant needs at least 5 years of installation experience.

Installing a boiler is physical on-site work: rigging and moving a heavy vessel, leveling it so the water-level controls and steam separation work properly, and fitting seismic restraints. An agent can only help with document steps such as reading the manual or planning, which take up little of the task's time.
NSW's energy-efficiency retrofit scheme says any electrical work on an air conditioner must be done by a licensed electrician, and every upgrade must meet licensing requirements.
In British Columbia, replacing or upgrading complete light fixtures in an LED retrofit generally needs an electrical permit tied to a contractor installation permit or operating permit.
AI tools help with the planning steps (finding retrofit opportunities, ranking upgrades by return, recommending lighting retrofits). The physical installation itself still needs a person on site.
AI-CMMS tools only predict boiler faults and generate work orders with suggested parts and timing. A human still does the physical repair.
In Michigan, boiler repair needs a permit from the state boiler division, and permits go only to licensed boiler repairers. Unlicensed workers must be directly supervised by a licensed person.
In NYC, some boiler and burner work must be done by a Licensed Oil Burner Installer or a Licensed Master Plumber, under permits issued to licensed tradespeople.

Coupa says it has built more than 20 AI agents, and its 'prescriptions' combine agentic AI with mathematical optimization to assess transportation networks and warehouse capacity. A Bain executive says this cuts the work from 4-6 weeks to 4-6 hours. These figures come from the vendor and a conference talk and were not verified independently.

KPMG describes AI network optimization agents that decide how many distribution centers to have and where, set inventory for each site, and simulate what happens when a distribution center changes. These are the main sub-steps of facility and capacity planning.

Supply chain planning agent designs are moving from human-in-the-loop to human-on-the-loop, but humans still check the assumptions and approve the results. No licence or sign-off is legally required for logistics capacity analyses. This is a general assessment, with the article available only as a paywalled excerpt.

Fleet telematics such as Kärcher Fleet and Diversey Taski IntelliTrail give managers each cleaning machine's run time, location and condition, and flag machines that need attention. An agent could read this data and schedule maintenance.

Janitorial Manager's equipment-tracking software records equipment location, usage and repair costs, and takes repair requests through QR codes. This covers the digital record-keeping part of the task, but the inspection and repair are still done by hand.

Preventive maintenance checklists for floor scrubbers and sweepers involve physical inspection: checking batteries, squeegees, brushes, hoses and filters. That needs a person on site, which an agent without a body can't do.
Cleaning a kennel is hands-on work: scooping waste, washing bedding, scrubbing, applying disinfectant and letting it sit, then rinsing. Only physical presence gets it done.
Where cage cleaning is automated, it is done by physical cage-washing machines, not by software agents.
Software only helps at the edges, with things like cleaning schedules and digital checklists. That is a very small share of the task's working time.

Vendors describe AI connected-worker platforms (Augmentir, IFS/Poka) that turn videos, PDFs and notes into step-by-step digital work instructions, track training and skills matrices, and show KPI dashboards to managers. That speeds up the documentation and tracking parts of training and supervision. These are vendor claims, not independent evidence.

Augmentir says its AI skills matrix lets managers see their team's skill gaps and act on them. That is decision support, but a human supervisor still oversees the line on the shop floor and demonstrates the procedures.

Federal OSHA has no single general-industry rule requiring supervisor training, so a human signature is not generally required. Training best practice still calls for hands-on practice and workers showing in person that they can do the task, which needs someone physically present.

Google DeepMind's Aletheia (arXiv 2602.10177, March 2026) is described as a mathematics research agent that works end to end in natural language. Its authors say it produced several papers of publishable quality, one of them with no human intervention. These are the authors' own claims and have not been checked independently.

ICMJE, COPE and the major publishers say AI tools cannot be authors because authorship requires being accountable for the work. Human authors stay responsible for all content and must disclose any AI use. This summary comes from secondary sources, not the ICMJE or COPE documents themselves.

COPE's position, as quoted on a journal's authorship page, is that AI cannot take responsibility for a submitted work, declare conflicts of interest, or handle copyright and licence agreements. This is a secondhand quote.

Under NFPA 10, the monthly check is a hands-on, on-site visual inspection. It covers whether the unit is in its assigned spot, nothing blocks access, the gauge reads in range, seals are intact, weight (by weighing or hefting) and visible damage. The inspector's date and initials must be recorded on a tag, a checklist or electronically.

NFPA codes allow electronic monitoring of extinguishers (location, access, pressure) instead of the physical 30-day inspection. This only works where sensors have already been installed, so an agent could review monitoring data and logs but could not check equipment without sensors.

A vendor (Keltron) says the 2026 edition of NFPA 10 allows technology in place of monthly physical inspections. This is the vendor's own claim, and the change still depends on sensor hardware being installed.

Canada's correctional service (CSC) is piloting an Accenture AI tool that reviews and organizes information from intake files to draft offender profiles. Staff still review the output, and critics point to the risk of automation bias.

South Korea's correctional service plans AI that combines counseling, disciplinary and medical records to flag signs of violence, self-harm and escape. The service says the AI's analysis will not decide treatment by itself, so humans keep the decision.
In job descriptions, supervisors read inmate records for health, safety and security concerns and recommend classification changes. This is document-based work in internal corrections systems.

Trade press such as Premium Beauty News and CosmeticsDesign publishes ingredient, research and trend coverage online. An agent with browsing can watch these sources and write summarized digests on its own.

Much industry learning still happens in person: trade shows (in-cosmetics Global, Paris, April 2026), hands-on treatment training and trying products on skin. An agent with no body cannot do these, and the specialist still has to absorb what is learned.

Some states require license holders to complete continuing education themselves to renew. For example, Oregon requires 5 hours a year for advanced estheticians, and self-study is allowed. Other states require none. This is a personal learning requirement, not a sign-off that an agent could do instead.

In 2026 OpenTable says its voice-AI partners have seated 3 million diners. It also reports about 450,000 monthly users for its Concierge AI assistant, which shows routine dinner booking by AI is already common.
AI concierge and voice agents such as Inhotel Golf Assistant and Courserev book golf tee times from live availability and guest preferences, and can put players on waitlists for open slots.

Google Duplex showed AI phoning businesses to make reservations, so venues without online booking can also be reached by an agent. Businesses could opt out of these calls, though, which limits coverage.

Hotel guests can already book vetted, background-checked babysitters for their room through an online app (Sitters UK), with bookings from 2 hours and arrival in as little as 90 minutes. The booking part of the task is fully digital.

Agencies like Aunty.sg match a vetted sitter for in-room hotel care and email the sitter's details, reviews and references. An agent could handle the request, matching and confirmation by web or email, but a parent's trust in the choice of caregiver usually rests on the concierge's own vetted agency relationships and personal judgement.

Voice and AI agents can already answer questions, take bookings and send confirmations for babysitting services. I found no turnkey AI concierge that books and vouches for childcare from start to finish, so a human still reviews the choice of sitter and gives the guest the final assurance.

Vendors describe AI data-entry agents that run the whole pipeline: they take in email and uploads, extract data into a schema, validate it and write it to a CRM, ERP or spreadsheet. Cases where the agent is unsure still go to a human, which supports L2 rather than L3.

Airtable's Omni builds base structure and field agents, and its field agents fill in cell data automatically. Tools connected over MCP, such as Claude, can create and edit fields. This covers both creating a database and entering data into it.
Airtable runs a developer page aimed at agents, so agents can reach databases through software access alone. No physical presence is needed.

Commercial AI CAM tools exist that work from CAD models. Siemens NX AI feature recognition finds holes, pockets, slots and contours, then suggests machining strategies. CloudNC CAM Assist generates 3 and 3+2-axis strategies. Cimatron's CAM agent, shown at IMTS 2026, reads part geometry and the tool library to produce complete 3-axis toolpaths. These are vendor claims, and fully autonomous end-to-end process planning is still mostly in research (TUM AI4CADCAM and TU Darmstadt autonomIQ, both running through late 2026).

Siemens NX AI feature recognition uses machine learning to classify features in 3D models, and the CAM system then proposes toolpaths. A machinist still has to check the plan against the shop's own machines, fixtures and stock, and against physical sample parts that may have no CAD model.

A third-party licensing site, not an official government source, reports that states such as Delaware do not require a state license for machinists. Employers set requirements such as NIMS credentials and apprenticeships, so no law requires a human to sign off on a process plan.

Construction-intelligence platforms such as Buildots combine site data, BIM, schedules and daily reports to forecast delays and show their root causes at the activity level.
