AI can also link schedule updates, RFIs, change orders and weather records to support delay analysis. These are vendor claims and have not been independently checked.
AI agents can collect the reports, inspections, photos and training records tied to a safety incident and draft a root-cause analysis. Construction safety professionals still make the final call.

OSHA rule 29 CFR 1926.20(b)(2) requires the employer to name competent persons to inspect job sites, materials and equipment frequently and regularly. A competent person must be able to identify hazards and have the authority to take prompt corrective action. Employers must also investigate recordable injuries and document them. This is based on secondary sources; the regulation text was not checked on OSHA.gov.
Automated cell culture incubation relies on dedicated robotic incubator hardware, not software agents. Vendors note its value comes from reducing human physical handling and contamination.

Automated slide preparation (inoculating, spreading, heating and drying slides) is done by specialised mechanical cartridge or robotic platforms. It needs physical manipulation, which a bodiless AI agent cannot do.

Lab automation for incubation means physical hardware (e.g., Thermo Fisher Cytomat incubators). An AI agent could at most schedule runs or look up protocols, which is a small part of the working time.

CodeSignal sells AI interviewer training. It runs simulated interviews with AI candidates, an AI tutor gives feedback on how each interview was structured and what to improve, and it is pitched as a replacement for live shadowing and as a way to certify interviewers. This suggests the training part can be handed off in large pieces.
CodeSignal's launch announcement says the training can be tailored to an organization's own scorecards, question frameworks and standards, so an agent could build and deliver custom training modules.

A vendor blog (marketing, unverified) describes post-interview reports on question effectiveness and recorded clips for peer coaching. AI can help with quality monitoring, but decisions about performance and staff and day-to-day supervision still need a human manager.

The Cabrillo National Monument visitor center SOP lists physical opening steps: unlocking doors, updating the passport stamp dates and filling in a whiteboard with the date, tide times, scheduled programs, groups due in and the weather forecast.

The Lookout visitor centre closing checklist covers turning off equipment and lights, lowering the blind, locking up, bringing in the flag and collection box, logging the shift, cleaning, and a radio announcement that the site is closing.

General facility opening and closing guidance includes a perimeter security check, disarming and setting alarms, starting lighting and HVAC, checking the cash float, reconciling cash and locking doors. These are mostly physical steps. An agent could only help with digital parts like workstation startup, shift logs and status updates.

Cities such as Kelowna, B.C. and Abu Dhabi use generative-AI permit assistants that answer code questions and point applicants to specific code provisions. Kelowna says this cut early staff questions. These tools cover the 'explain regulations' part of the task.

A 2026 Florida League of Cities buyer's guide says AI permitting tools flag issues and cite the rule, but a person still makes the decision. In a Seattle study, the tools' compliance checks were about 87-92% accurate, so a human still has to review the output.

Local codes give the building official the power to serve notices of violation and stop-work orders. These must be written and signed by the inspector, so the authority behind the remedial requirements stays with a human official.

EarthCam Control Center 9 uses AI on jobsite cameras to report usage of 50+ equipment and vehicle types, detect 85+ types of equipment and materials and their status, and flag labor utilization issues. An agent could watch these feeds remotely, but only where such systems are installed.

Telematics shows machine and operator productivity, but a Dodge study found only 17% of contractors use technology that monitors operator behavior. Most field monitoring is still done in person by the supervisor.

OSHA's excavation rule requires a competent person to inspect the site daily and to have authority to take prompt corrective action. Courts have held that this must be a human with real power to stop work, and it is often the foreman.

Ramp-design software such as K-MINE generates ramp geometry, grades and switchbacks automatically. That is the planning side, done by engineers. The operator's task is physically cutting, pushing and compacting material with machines.

Under MSHA 30 CFR 56.9300, mine operators must build and maintain berms at least mid-axle height of the largest equipment on elevated roadways. That is earthwork done on site. The rule binds the mine operator; it does not require a licensed individual to sign off.

Autonomous haulage changes ramp specifications, such as tighter crossfall and rutting tolerances. But ramps are still built by heavy equipment working physically on the ground, which a software-only agent without robotics cannot do.

Agents can operate Revit through MCP connectors with over 226 Revit functions. Add-ins such as Glyph CoPilot and BIM Engine automate parts of construction documentation, like sheets, views, tags and dimensions. No independent benchmark shows agents reliably producing a complete permit-ready set without a human checking it.
Glyph CoPilot is sold as an AI assistant that automates construction documentation inside Revit.

In Washington State, a registered architect or engineer must sign and stamp each page of construction drawings submitted for a permit. They may seal only work they prepared or reviewed, and they carry full responsibility for it.

Procore's AI agents, sold as Digital Coworker packages, can turn site photos and voice notes into a draft daily log, flag schedule, sequencing and float risks, and handle RFI and site-safety tasks. Procore says human teams still review and approve everything.

Procore's May 2026 launch says its Digital Coworkers automate construction workflows inside the platform. This covers the paperwork and coordination around site management, not directing crews in person.

State licensing rules for engineers define 'responsible charge' as direct control, personal supervision and legal responsibility for engineering work. The licensee must review the work and approve, change or reject it.
I couldn't verify anything online. The search tool returned an API error, so this rating is based only on what I already know about the task.

Setting up equipment for site testing means physically moving, placing, connecting and calibrating instruments such as soil probes, sensors, sampling gear and lab apparatus. An AI agent with no body can't do this. It can only help with planning, checklists, setup instructions and configuring the software or data loggers.
I don't know of any licence or law that requires a human to sign off on this routine setup work in typical jurisdictions.

Axon's Draft One uses AI to write police report narratives from body-camera audio. A human officer must review and approve each report. A San Francisco pilot used it for citations and misdemeanor cases.

eCitation software fills in citation fields automatically from a scanned licence and syncs the data with records, dispatch and court systems. A sworn officer still has to issue and serve the citation in person in the field.
No source showed AI report tools being used specifically by game wardens. For this occupation, AI exposure was described as limited to the documents around the field work, not the work itself.

In state electronic death registration systems, the funeral home starts the death record and picks the physician. The physician then logs in from anywhere to enter the cause of death and sign, and gets email alerts for records waiting on them. Clerks can update the record but cannot sign it, so an agent can start and chase the record but the licensed certifier has to sign.

When a certifier is not online, funeral or clinic staff print an attestation form, get the certifier to sign it, and fax it into the system. Some cases still involve paper handling and getting signatures by hand.

Insurance assignment services connected to Passare pull case data automatically, generate the assignment paperwork, submit claims electronically and talk to insurers. The family still has to sign the assignment, and the vendor acts under a limited power of attorney.
Vendors say AI tools can check product bills of materials for errors in part numbers, revisions and sourcing. That is the main sub-step of checking whether a materials list is accurate.
AI takeoff and material-list tools such as Beam AI and 2by4.ai produce line-item lists, but the vendors still keep a human expert to check accuracy before the list is used.
Home Depot's AI Blueprint Takeoffs tool generates complete material lists and quotes, and a human Pro team member reviews the scope with the customer before the estimate goes out.

Commercial AI tools such as BuildCentrix 3D Blueprint Takeoff analyze 2D drawings and pull out sheet metal dimensions and materials for fab shops. This covers the materials and scope sub-step. The source is vendor promotion published by SMACNA.

Civils.ai's AI duct takeoff produces only a draft from plans and schedules. The vendor says human QA is essential and the tool does no 3D coordination or clash detection, so a human still has to review the output before it is used.

In official trade descriptions, this duty means reading blueprints, sketches or specifications to decide fabrication and installation sequence and methods. That is mostly document interpretation. Field measurement is treated as a separate competency, and none of the sources says the plan needs a licensed sign-off.

Taking off lug nuts and wheels is hands-on mechanical work. The automated systems that do it are physical robots with sockets and arms, not software agents. The reference AI agents have no body or robotics, so they cannot do this task.

A TechCrunch article from September 2026 reports that PitPro's tire-changing robot went live in Canada, aimed at commercial fleets. This is dedicated robotic hardware, which falls outside the software-only reference technology.

A 2026 deployment of SkySelect's AI procurement agent at Magnetic MRO reportedly fully automated 79% of parts purchases through two-way ERP integration. Other platforms, such as AAR's Airvoyant, still keep a human reviewing recommendations.
CMMS systems track stock levels and automatically create purchase orders when parts fall below a set threshold, and some can send POs directly to suppliers.
Grainger accepts electronic orders through punch-out catalogs, cXML, EDI and an API, so a software agent can place orders with a major maintenance supplier.

2026 agent systems such as ArtiCAD and ToolCAD turn text or image descriptions into editable CAD parts and assemblies, including multi-part assemblies with moving parts. That covers the drafting and modelling steps of designing a repair aid.

The ArtisanCAD authors (July 2026) note that text-to-CAD agents still struggle when design intent is vague or underspecified. Shop-floor repair aids are usually specified that loosely, so a human has to measure on site, try out prototypes and correct the design.

Industrial exemptions, such as Texas Occupations Code §1001.057, generally let employees design tools and equipment for their own company's facilities without a PE licence. A sealed design is required mainly for structural or load-bearing items in some places, such as Ontario after it repealed its exemption.

Vendor product pages say AI document tools pull fields from bills of lading, check that required fields and signatures are present, and match driver-uploaded BOLs and PODs to load records in a TMS. This covers the check of the documents themselves. These are vendor claims; no independent tests were found.

Freight-audit software from VektorTMS checks required BOL fields, verifies signatures and matches each BOL to its load, flagging missing data. This shows the completeness check can run end to end once the paper is digitized.

Under 49 CFR 177.817, a carrier may not accept or haul hazardous materials without a correct shipping paper, and the driver must keep it within reach in the cab. At pickup the driver still has to compare the paperwork with the actual freight (piece counts, seal numbers, placards) and sign the BOL, which needs a person on site and a responsible human.

Commercial workforce platforms advertise AI agents that assign shifts automatically by availability and skills, reschedule after absences, fill open shifts and flag labor-rule problems. These are vendor claims, not independent tests.
Fraunhofer IKS and ATOSS built a reinforcement-learning shift-planning agent that automates hospital staff scheduling, so the core scheduling step can be handed to an agent.

Predictive-scheduling laws such as Oregon's set rules for how far ahead schedules must be posted and for premium pay when they change. They do not require a human to write or sign the schedule, and posting can be electronic.
Bain says AI agents can track supplier performance, market shifts and supply risks in real time. This covers the KPI, delivery and spend-vs-budget monitoring sub-steps.
Industry outlooks say semi-autonomous procurement agents still need human approval for sensitive judgments such as supplier evaluations and contract recommendations.
On-site supplier visits are usually limited to critical, high-risk or sole-source vendors, and remote audits are common for lower-risk suppliers. No general legal rule requires on-site audits.
AI tools draft OKRs and goals from a company's priorities, check them for weak key results and test how well they align. That covers the drafting and analysis steps of setting departmental goals.

Company law commentary, including Delaware case law and the views of White & Case, says AI can raise issues and make recommendations. Directors or officers still have to make and approve policy decisions themselves and cannot outsource that judgement.

Directors and their delegates should not rely on AI output without checking it, and they lose their legal protections if they hand their judgement over to AI. A human therefore has to review and approve policies before they take effect.

In 2026, AI recruiting agents handle top-of-funnel hiring on their own: sourcing, screening, outreach, scheduling and first-round structured interviews, which end in a ranked shortlist for human review. Most deployments are only partly autonomous, and humans keep the later decision stages. These figures come from vendor sources.

The EU AI Act classes AI used for recruitment, selection, performance evaluation, promotion and termination as high-risk. That brings oversight, documentation and risk-management duties, so humans must stay responsible for personnel decisions.
NYC Local Law 144 bans automated employment decision tools unless they pass a bias audit each year and the results are published. This adds compliance limits on fully automated selection.

Sources from 2026 describe agentic marketing systems that take a high-level goal and plan, run and adjust campaigns across channels. Humans still set the goals, budget, brand voice and compliance limits, and they oversee the strategy.
Industry reporting expects marketing operations to be run more and more by multi-agent systems, with human marketers keeping strategy and oversight while agents handle execution at scale.

Vendor guides describe AI marketing agents that create content, sequence campaigns and optimise them in real time. These are vendor claims, not independently verified, and none show agents formulating marketing policy or directing people without a human.
AI tools like Realgram AI and PlanoHero can generate store-specific planograms and layout plans automatically. That covers only the planning step, not the physical build.
Leafio uses image recognition to check shelf photos against approved layouts. Store staff still take the photos and set up the products by hand.

O*NET lists the core task as setting up displays in store space using lighting, colors and props, along with building displays and maintaining props and mannequins. All of this is hands-on physical work.

Job postings say ticket takers spend about 85% of their time greeting guests and scanning tickets in person at the gate. They also spot fraudulent tickets, check bags, and redirect guests whose tickets are invalid.
The role involves repetitive hand and arm motions to scan tickets and tear stubs, standing at entrances, and working in outdoor weather. It is a physical, on-site job.

Self-service scanning turnstiles and kiosks already check tickets and passes against the ticketing database without staff. That is fixed automation hardware, not a software AI agent, and staff still handle the exceptions.

Nail robots such as Nimble only scan and paint nails. Reports say they do not remove polish, buff, file or treat cuticles, so no machine does the soaking and orange-stick prep step, and software-only agents can't do it at all.
Nimble's device paints base, colour and top coats and dries them, taking about 10 minutes per hand. It does not prepare the nail beforehand.
Nail technicians need a state license almost everywhere, earned through 300 to 600 hours of training plus theory and practical exams, for example in South Carolina and Nevada.

Mississippi board rules say anyone using an electric file in a manicure must first hold board-approved proficiency certification and display it to the public. A human must be licensed and certified to do this work.

South Dakota requires at least 8 hours of training, including hands-on practice and infection control, before anyone may operate an electric nail file or drill on clients. The task is physical, hands-on work.
Robotic nail machines such as Clockwork only paint nails. Reports say none of them shape or buff nails, and the task needs a body anyway, which software agents do not have.

Consumer apps such as Nail Health Scanner and Nails AI can score nail and cuticle condition from a photo. Only the assessment part is covered, it only gives information, and the vendors' accuracy claims have not been checked independently. None of these apps can remove dead skin or massage hands.
In states such as Tennessee, manicurists must finish about 600 hours of training and pass both a written and a practical exam before they can be licensed.
Licensed nail technicians do hands-on work on clients, including massaging the hands, feet, forearms and lower legs. This requires being physically present with the client.

Even dedicated manicure robots (Clockwork) only paint polish: they cannot cut or shape nails, and they do not offer acrylic extensions. A software-only AI agent has no body to apply powder, solvent or nail forms at all.
No full salon-type manicure with shaping and buffing was offered by the robotic players Clockwork, Coral or Nimble.

Nebraska requires a state nail technology licence to attach, shape or adjust artificial nails using acrylic, resin, fabric or gel systems. Other states similarly require licensed nail technicians for paid acrylic services.

Dealer management software (Autologica Sky DMS) already produces parts-order suggestions using 14 methods, including sales level, part value, aging and purchase frequency. This covers the digital side of maintaining stock without a person doing it by hand. Source is the vendor's own description.

A 2025 IEEE conference paper simulated AI demand forecasting with IoT/RFID tracking at a car dealership. Stock-outs fell from about 9.7% to 4.2% and inventory accuracy rose from 85% to 93.3%. These are simulated results, not a live deployment, and the setup still needs tagging and storage work on the warehouse floor.

A trades-business guide describes AI agents that log parts used, check stock levels and trigger reorders on their own. Physically finding parts on shelves, attaching labels and doing counts still needs a person, and an agent with no body cannot do those steps.
Parts counter job postings list keeping the department and work area orderly, neat and clean, and stocking shelves, as hands-on duties done in the store or warehouse.

Employees may be given a section of the showroom or storage area to keep clean, stocked and orderly. This is physical work that software-only agents without robotics cannot do. They could at most make cleaning checklists or schedules, which is a small share of the time.
Housekeeping in a parts counter area is a general workplace duty. Typical jurisdictions do not require a licence or a human signature for it.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1926.451(f)(7), a competent person must supervise and direct anyone who erects, moves, dismantles or alters a scaffold. A competent person must also check the scaffold for visible defects before each shift, which requires someone on site.

Scaffold planning software such as Avontus Scaffold Designer and Layher LayPLAN can generate layouts, tie and bracing plans, and parts lists automatically. This only touches the planning sub-step. Someone still has to put up the scaffold by hand.
softtech's scaffmax models a building and fills it with scaffolding wall by wall, accounting for ground conditions. It produces plans and material lists, not the physical assembly.
In RV dealer and rental orientations, a person typically walks the customer through the vehicle and shows how its systems work. These sessions often last 40–60 minutes.

Video orientation courses already deliver standardized explanations of RV systems to customers. This shows that much of the explaining can be done with pre-made content rather than a technician on site.
AI agents built for the RV industry answer customer questions from brochures and spec sheets and route service requests. No dedicated AI tool for walking customers through RV systems was found.

Rigging control cables means physically setting the controls to neutral, adjusting turnbuckles, and measuring tension with a calibrated tensiometer and the correct riser. The reading is then corrected for temperature using rigging charts and checked again after the controls are cycled. An agent could only help with the chart lookup and the temperature correction.
Tension values must be checked against the approved maintenance manual or manufacturer data for the specific model, using hand-held tensiometers such as the Tensitron units.

Under 14 CFR Part 43, only certificated persons, or people they personally supervise, may do maintenance on aircraft, and a person authorized under §43.7 must approve the aircraft for return to service. In production, a human quality inspector likewise has to sign off on flight-control rigging.

With SCADA or DCS, operators can start and stop equipment such as pumps and motors from a central HMI. This makes remote software starts technically possible in automated plants. Controllers then send the start signals to actuators in the field.

SCADA HMI mimic screens show whether a pump is running and its flow, so the operator can confirm a start or switch the pump off. An agent could read these screens, but plant control systems are usually walled off from general IT and AI tools.

Centrifuge operator jobs are hands-on, on-site roles: pre-start walkdowns, local start buttons, checking guards, lubrication and valve settings, and watching vibration and noise after the start. These need physical presence that a bodiless agent cannot provide.

In 2026, an MCP-based agent workflow connected to EnergyPlus cut energy-model inspection and modification tasks from 1-2 hours to under 15 minutes, and an agentic mode automated parametric analysis. The authors say professionals should stay in charge of decisions.

UMD's Rapid Energy Auditor produces a preliminary audit from utility data alone and flags which facilities need a follow-up onsite assessment. This shows the analysis part of advising can be automated, while site-specific data still depends on people visiting the building.

Programs such as Energize Denver require audits and recommendations from credentialed third parties (a licensed PE, AEE CEM/CEA or ASHRAE BEAP) following ASHRAE Standard 211 Level 2, so a human remains accountable for formal advice.

USDA ARS Yield Editor 2.0 automates yield-data cleaning, including flow-delay correction and removing overlapped end-row data. On 50 test maps, its automated cleaning was not significantly different from cleaning done by an expert.

GeoPard imports harvester yield data directly from John Deere Operations Center. It then cleans the data, including outlier removal and striping correction, and builds yield maps, so the whole process runs in software.

Automated methods such as Climate Corp's patent on expert filters plus spatial outlier detection generate accurate yield maps from raw monitor data. No licence or sign-off is needed, but a human usually checks for calibration and multi-combine problems.

Private household cook duties include keeping records of menus, finances and other business matters. A typical posting asks the cook to log purchases, menu costs and kitchen expenses, stay within the household budget and report variances to the household manager.

Consumer AI apps such as Famally, EasyGrocery and Zenkitchen say they plan meals, build grocery lists, pull items and prices from receipt photos, and track pantry and budget. These are the main sub-steps of menu and expense record-keeping. The claims come from app listings and have not been independently verified.

Bookkeeping guides for personal chefs describe digital logging of grocery costs, fees and expenses. They also say household and business spending must be kept separate, which is a judgment call that may need a human check. No licence or sign-off is required for this kind of record-keeping.

Zenoti salon software tracks stock from sales and how much product services use. It flags products that reach a reorder level, can create purchase orders automatically and stores supplier details so orders go out from the system. This covers the ordering sub-step from start to finish. Source is vendor marketing, not independently checked.

Meevo builds purchase orders automatically from stock levels and usage rates before items run out. An agent with computer use could run this and send orders with no one stepping in. Source is vendor marketing, not independently checked.

Salon inventory guidance still assumes in-person stock counts (audits), and these software estimates are reset against those counts. Setting up retail displays, restocking shelves and storing backbar products are physical jobs that an agent without a body cannot do. No licence or sign-off is needed to order supplies.
Travel CRMs already use AI to enter data from booking confirmations, and supplier integrations bring confirmation numbers, schedule changes and service updates straight into client records.

Agency software offers AI-driven CRM updates, including automatic logging of emails and calls, removing duplicates and cleaning data; vendor CRMs also track supplier rates, allotments and package quotes. These are vendor claims, not independent case studies.
California's Seller of Travel law requires the business to register (owners, trust account or bond), but no rule says a person has to do the data entry or sign each client or vendor record.

Fitting brakes means removing the wheel and loosening and tightening pad bolts with an Allen key. The mechanic also has to line each pad up with the rim, set cable tension with barrel adjusters, then spin the wheel and test the brakes by hand. All of this needs hands on the bike, and an agent without a body cannot do it. At most it can look up specs or the right pad type, which is a very small share of the time.

Each brake has to be set to its own measured fit: the pad sits flush and square to the rim about 1-2 mm below its top edge, and the barrel adjuster is turned until the pads stop rubbing. These are hands-on adjustments, and no software or AI tool performs them.

Bicycle mechanics need no licence in the US or Canada. Certification, for example from UBI or Barnett, is voluntary, so there is no legal or liability rule requiring a human to do or sign off the work.

Software can work out spoke length from hub and rim measurements (flange diameter, flange-to-center distance, effective rim diameter, or ERD), but a person must take those measurements on the actual parts.
Online spoke calculators cover J-bend and straight-pull hubs but tell users to measure carefully and check the numbers before cutting spokes. Cutting and threading are done by hand with a machine.
Wheel builders say different calculators give slightly different results, so the final call on length and the hands-on build (lacing, tensioning, truing) stay with the human.

Operation Lifesaver's RISC-LE rail safety course for law enforcement is mostly taught in person in 1, 2 and 4-hour versions. Some sessions are restricted to sworn officers, and the 4-hour version holds IADLEST/POST certification. That points to a human instructor delivering the course in person under a certification framework.
AI avatar video tools are marketed for turning police SOPs and scripts into training modules. This shows that agents can do much of the work of creating course materials.
A custom GPT for police academy instructors helps build scenarios, quizzes and presentations, but instructors still lead the training.

At Halton Healthcare, software creates the meal ticket from the patient's barcoded record and wristband (diet, allergies) and gives tray-assembly instructions. Staff still assemble the tray by hand and scan it before delivery.
Computrition's Tray InMotion software tracks trays from ticket creation, alerts staff to diet-order changes and checks wristbands. The physical work of putting food on trays stays with people.

On tray lines, printed menu tickets from the CBORD system list exactly which items go on each tray based on that day's menu and the patient's requirements. Workers then plate and assemble the trays by hand.

AI documentation tools such as AutoNotes and Mentalyc already draft SOAP, DAP and treatment-plan progress notes from session input or dictation, and AI note generation is described as reaching recreational therapy session documentation. The agent can write the note, but a human has to supply the in-person observations of how the participant is doing.

CMS therapy documentation rules for PT, OT and SLP require progress reports and treatment notes to carry the signature, professional identification and date of the qualified professional who provided the service. No CMS rule specific to recreation therapy turned up; the closest rules found were state ones (Texas, Arkansas).

State program rules (Texas YES Waiver) require recreational therapy progress notes with participant, date, times, service and location, written by licensed or certified providers such as a CTRS, so an accountable human has to review and sign.

In 2026, AI scheduling agents such as Carly, Blockit and Skej are sold as tools that read email threads, negotiate times with outside participants, then book and reschedule within set rules without approval at each step. These sources are vendor blogs, so they are marketing claims, not independent tests.

Microsoft 365 Copilot in Outlook can check attendees' free/busy times, suggest time slots, book a room, draft an agenda and send invites from an email thread. It is a guided chat that the user starts. According to a competitor's comparison blog, it does not negotiate times by email on its own.

Gemini's 'Help Me Schedule' in Gmail suggests meeting times from the email thread and the user's calendar. The user starts it, and an article that may be out of date says it only works for meetings with two people.

USDA AMS released a free Log Truck Route Planner in March 2026. Its log allocator assigns logs from forests to mills at the lowest cost, and its truck scheduler builds trip plans from the user's delivery requests.

Trimble LogForce links forest owners, haul contractors and mill receivers. Planners use it to split orders into loads, send loads to trucks, manage daily and weekly schedules and message the other parties.

An ORTEC case study describes a timber producer that switched from manual planning to optimized routing, load building and a driver app with electronic proof of delivery. This suggests the digital coordination steps can be automated. Confirming informal deals with small haulers and mills by phone, and checking log grades in the yard, still falls to a human.

Under 30 CFR 75.211, the roof, face and ribs must be visually examined, and sound or vibration tested where supports go in. Loose material is taken down by hand with a scaling bar from a safe position underground. All of this is physical work an agent with no body cannot do.
MSHA enforcement cases treat scaling as manual barring by a miner at the working face, using a scale bar or drill steel.

Under 21 CFR 211.84, workers must physically open, sample and reseal component containers so nothing gets contaminated, using sterile equipment and aseptic technique where needed. Samples taken from the top, middle and bottom of a container must be kept separate. All of this is hands-on work.

Each lot is held until the quality control unit has sampled, tested and released it, and sampling plans need a scientific justification that they are representative. That leaves accountability with a human or QC unit. An AI could still help work out statistical sample sizes and draft sampling plans or chain-of-custody paperwork.
Automated sampling systems in pharma are robotic hardware, such as isolators and aseptic bioreactor samplers, not software agents. A software-only agent with no body cannot physically draw samples.

Cloud-connected electronic shelf labels update prices straight from POS/ERP systems. This is fixed automation, not a software agent, and it covers only the price-marking part. Stores without ESLs still need someone to put tags on by hand.

Autonomous robot restocking is still a pilot as of Oct 2026. In Salling Group's Føtex trial, humanoid robots need human operators to guide every movement, and independent restocking is targeted for early 2027. Either way, robots fall outside the no-body reference technology.
Shelf-scanning systems such as Simbe's find gaps and pricing errors, but store staff still do the physical restocking. The work requires someone in the store moving goods by hand.

Farm inventory software already tracks feed use, sends reorder-point alerts and drafts purchase orders for the user to approve. Bin-level sensor systems such as BinMaster FeedView automate feed inventory tracking and online ordering. This covers the monitoring, comparison and ordering steps but not receiving or putting stock away.

BinMaster FeedView combines wireless laser bin-level sensors with cloud software that forecasts feed use and supports online ordering. Without such sensors, someone has to check stock levels in person.

In the US, medically important antibiotics for livestock (in feed, water, injectables and boluses) can only be bought with a veterinary feed directive (VFD) or prescription from a licensed vet under a vet-client-patient relationship. The vet authorizes the drug, but the buyer does not need a license to place the order.

The machines that automate dog bathing (PuppyWash and patented washing and brushing enclosures) are physical robotic devices. They are not software agents, and a human still has to load and handle the animal, so a software-only AI agent can't do this task.
Patents for automatic dog washing and brushing describe tubs, brushes, sprayers and motors. Bathing and grooming are hands-on physical work with live animals.
AI-driven wash-cycle adaptation (Woofwoof Lux) is built into dedicated hardware. A software-only agent operating a computer can't reach it or do the work.
Exercising animals is physical work: a person leads, rides, lunges or hands the animal onto equipment. Even automated horse walkers need a human to load, tether or supervise the animal on site.
Programmable exercisers can run preset speed and direction programs for groups of horses. Software can help with scheduling and settings, but it cannot do the exercise itself, which needs a body.
Free-moving walker systems still need a physical work area and someone to watch the animals, which an AI agent without a body cannot provide.

NWCG S-130 Firefighter Training includes a required field exercise that can be arduous. The lead instructor must be a qualified Single Resource Boss and unit instructors must be qualified FFT1, so training is delivered in person by credentialed humans.
AI in wildland fire training appears as immersive simulation and visualisation tools such as UNSW iFire 1.0. These support human-led exercises; they are not autonomous instructors.
Commercial vendors offer virtual and simulator-based wildland fire training (FS3D/Intellic, DAS USFS simulator), but in-field hands-on instruction is still done by human instructors.

Consumer AI pet-health assistants, including Daisy, PawHealth AI's Evie and Pack Pet Health (built on Gemini), already give owners care tips tailored to breed, age and history. They also triage cases and tell owners when to see a vet. Most accuracy claims come from the vendors themselves.

In a vendor-run blinded test with UK vets, a specialised AI triage tool scored 81% accuracy, against 69% for Gemini and 50% for ChatGPT. Quality is useful but still imperfect, so a human should review the advice.

State veterinary practice acts stop non-vets from diagnosing, recommending specific treatments or prescribing. General care advice from a caretaker (feeding, grooming, exercise, hygiene) does not need a licence, but advice must stay below the level of diagnosis.

Under BLM policy, the authorized officer (a human official) sets priorities for NEPA and other legal requirements before grazing permits are issued. Renewal needs a finding that the permittee has a satisfactory performance record, and the officer must consult with permittees and the public, so a human has to sign and stay accountable.
BLM renewals check each allotment against rangeland health standards, which depends on monitoring data collected in the field.

Satellite and AI tools such as Enriched Ag Insights, the Rangeland Analysis Platform and GrassSignal already produce stocking recommendations, recovery periods, overgrazing estimates and rotation plans. An agent could handle the analysis, planning and paperwork, but field compliance checks and work with ranchers in person still need a human.

LLMs such as ChatGPT-4 produced understandable cataract-surgery education material at about a 5.75 grade reading level, and none of it contained dangerous information. This shows that drafting and answering FAQs can be delegated, but the material still needs clinician review.
A question-answer chatbot for cataract education tested with 18 patients was rated acceptable (mean SUS 78.6/100), although the sample was small.

COMT job descriptions say the technologist answers patient questions with information as directed by the provider and supports patients and families in person in the clinic. That keeps a human doing the in-person teaching and following the provider's direction.
Glaze chemistry software such as Insight-Live and Glazy can calculate recipes and batches. This is the only digital part of the task that an AI could help with.
Spray glazing is done by hand with HVLP spray guns in a ventilated booth, using a turntable and a respirator. The person has to judge glaze thickness and keep the strokes even.
Glaze is applied by physically handling the pieces through dipping, pouring, brushing or spraying. It takes a lot of practice to get an even coat.

AI vision at pack stations can confirm SKU, slot and orientation from overhead cameras and flag errors before sealing. This is dedicated camera-and-gantry hardware built into the line. It is not a software-only agent, and a human still handles the items.

Machine-vision systems inspect packaging for item counts, presence/absence and defects. They depend on installed cameras, lighting and line integration, so physical inspection needs either on-site hardware or a person handling the product.

Vendor material describes AI vision as best suited to checking count, presence and placement. Physical checks such as handling, opening containers and testing seals or weight stay with the human packer. No licence or legal sign-off requirement applies to this task.

Market Logic added a Persona Builder and Synthetic Panel to DeepSights Personas in April 2026. It includes an AI interviewer agent, and the vendor says new concepts can be tested across audience segments in hours.

Attest launched AI-moderated interviewing (Attest Explore) in June 2026. An AI research assistant drafts the interview guide, and an AI moderator then runs video or audio consumer interviews and probes for deeper answers. Similar tools include User Intuition, Conveo and Echovane.

Quantilope's August 2026 blog presents synthetic consumers as a complement to traditional research, not a replacement. Accuracy has not been independently benchmarked, so a human still has to check the findings and target-audience choices before use. The work is fully digital and needs no licence or sign-off.

Interact's 2026 release added agentic tools: one lets communicators ask questions about engagement data in plain language, and an Executive Assistant Agent sorts employee tasks by priority. This covers the analytics sub-steps of internal relations.
Lyzr sells an AI Internal Communication Agent that summarizes announcements and tracks employee engagement and sentiment. Its claimed results are the vendor's own marketing figures.

A vendor blog cites survey data saying 52% of internal-comms practitioners use AI at least weekly. It frames the buyer's question as who reviews what the agent sends to employees, which means a human still reviews the output. This is a vendor source, so I treat it as opinion.

Prophix markets autonomous FP&A agents, launched in September 2025, including a budgeting agent that updates plans from plain-language input and a reporting agent that writes variance commentary. A reviewer says their accuracy in production is still unproven.

Agentic marketing-budget tools, such as Domo's Budget Allocation agent, analyze channel and campaign performance and reallocate spend using data from BigQuery, Snowflake and Salesforce. The search found no tool aimed specifically at PR or communications budgets.

Agents for budget variance tracking can flag overspends and draft explanations automatically. Final approval of spending priorities and negotiations over agency retainers stay with managers, and this needs no physical presence.

AI video tools available now, such as Synthesia (avatar videos built from a script, at scale) and Runway (generating and editing scenes), can produce substantial parts of corporate video products from a written brief. They are weaker on creative range and pre-production.

AI digital asset management systems transcribe, auto-tag and index video libraries, and offer rights and licensing workflows (for example Veritone, Bynder and Canto). That automates much of running a film library and controlling distribution, but tags often lack campaign or channel context, so a human still reviews them.

AI video platforms automate transcription, scene and face detection, and tagging for searching and distributing video assets. Live filming of real events, executives and facilities still needs crews on site, and distribution decisions that affect the brand need human approval.

Microsoft's Copilot onboarding uses a 'Learning Agent' that walks users through role-tailored practice tasks in about 10 to 15 minutes. AI can tutor the person, but the human still has to do the learning.
Vendors such as VisualSP sell in-app, in-context AI guidance so employees can learn new tools while they work. This speeds up human learning step by step rather than replacing it.

Microsoft Learn's onboarding guidance for organisations relies on training strategies, champion programmes and rapid-enablement training of people. The human's own skill-building is the essential output.

Cisco, Microsoft and Zoom announced meeting agents in late 2025 that can take part in calls, for example updating tickets and finding files. A 2026 vendor review says most meeting AI is still a notetaker and does its work after the call, so agents do not yet represent a person in meetings.

Service-desk agents create, categorize, route and fully resolve some employee requests (one vendor self-reports 15-25% resolved end to end) and escalate the rest. Vendors say this extends to HR, finance and procurement requests.
Agentic ticketing systems pass exceptions to humans when judgment is needed. Handling complaints and representing the unit in person still depends on human negotiation, trust and attendance.

AlertMedia's AI Plan Builder (August 2026) lets security teams generate response plans from a natural-language prompt and check current regulations, with users reviewing or reverting the AI's changes. This shows plan drafting can be largely delegated but still goes through human review.
Swimlane's investigation agent uses the NIST incident response framework and the customer's own runbooks to produce a prioritized plan covering containment, eradication, recovery and hardening.

NIST SP 800-61r3 (aligned with CSF 2.0) is guidance, not law. It calls for defined roles and escalation authority but does not require a licensed human to write or sign the plan. Approval is an organizational governance step, not a legal one.
Agent systems can already turn an incident report into a draft response plan with actions, owners and deadlines, but they are mainly research prototypes, and human review is the usual design.
Vendors offer no-code agent templates that update evacuation plans and coordinate with emergency services. These cover the documentation part of contingency planning.

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.38 makes the employer responsible for the emergency plan, choosing and training evacuation staff, and reviewing the plan with employees. This is work done by people in the workplace and on site, so it can't be fully delegated to an agent.

Vendor pages say AI compliance agents continuously test controls such as access reviews and configuration baselines. They also say these agents collect evidence from identity providers, cloud and ticketing systems, flag drift and keep audit trails, and that high-risk fixes need human approval. This covers the digital part of compliance monitoring.
Agents run on a schedule to monitor controls, gather evidence and fix configuration drift within guardrails set by people, with human approval for high-risk changes.

Under the NISPOM (32 CFR 117), organizations in the National Industrial Security Program must run their own self-inspections, including an insider threat self-assessment. DCSA checks that findings are documented and fixed. Physical items such as GSA security containers, Closed Area accreditation and alarm/intrusion detection upkeep need checking on site, and a named human official is responsible for the program.

In 2026 KnowBe4 launched AI Defense Agents (AIDA), including an Orchestration Agent that it says fully automates administration of security awareness training programs and a content agent that builds custom training. These are vendor claims.
Adaptive Security's platform uses generative AI to create personalized security training content and simulations. This is also a vendor claim.

State security-officer rules often require classroom hours taught by licensed or certified instructors. Florida allows live online delivery only when Class DI instructors teach from a physical location in Florida.

Vendor sources (to be read with caution) say AI agents in 2026 automate month-end narratives and risk-memo drafting and can produce a full first-draft management pack. A human still signs off on the numbers, and the CFO typically reviews the pack.

Microsoft's release plan says Copilot for Finance can run variance analysis in Excel against ERP data (Dynamics 365, SAP) and produce reports with comments for stakeholders. Users review and adjust the results, and Microsoft's own estimate is 30% faster reporting. The feature entered public preview in June 2025, and its current availability was not confirmed.
Agents can model the impact when assumptions change, find ways to reduce risk, and alert stakeholders. A human still checks the figures before they are used.

Generative AI tools already draft, update and rebuild manufacturing SOPs and work instructions from source material. Vendors say subject-matter experts must review the output and check it against how the work is actually done on the floor before it becomes official.

A patent describes a generative model trained on libraries of industrial process specifications (SOPs, work cell layouts) that turns natural-language descriptions into draft process specifications. This makes the 'develop' part of the task largely automatable.

OSHA 1910.147 requires the employer to inspect each energy-control procedure at least once a year and certify it. The inspection must be done by an authorized employee who watches workers carry out the procedure and talks with them. This means the 'enforce' part needs a human on site and a human who is accountable.

Vendor material describes AI agents for manufacturing that find recurring OEE drops and create improvement tasks on their own, and that do predictive maintenance and OEE optimization. This means the analysis and recommendation steps can be delegated when the plant's data systems are connected. The performance figures are vendor claims and have not been independently checked.

OSHA puts safety duties on the employer, such as checking workplace conditions and keeping equipment safe. Plant manager job postings make the manager responsible for OSHA compliance across plant operations. So putting cost changes into practice requires human accountability and on-site checking.

Environmental permit documents such as Title V and NPDES must be signed and certified by a human responsible official or an authorized representative. An agent cannot be the one who certifies regulatory compliance.

SAP Transportation Management reportedly has AI agents that plan, run and optimise shipments on their own, from route planning to resolving problems as they happen. That covers the main sub-steps of comparing routing and carrier options.

Agents described in industry sources handle multimodal routing and freight-rate negotiation using live market data. Survey data citing Trimble says 31% of carriers and logistics providers use AI for route planning, and poor data quality (57%) is the top barrier.

BCG reports that AI in logistics often fails to deliver ROI because of data and integration problems. This supports keeping a human to check assumptions and approve the financial impact analysis before it is used.

Vendor products such as Fountain's AI Recruiter (Anna) and Interviewer.AI already run structured first-round screening interviews for high-volume frontline and warehouse hiring and score the answers. A human team still reviews the results before deciding (the efficiency figures are vendor claims).

Interviewer.AI markets AI video interviews built specifically for hiring warehouse workers and claims a large cut in recruiter time on first-round screening. This is a self-reported, unverified figure.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(l), forklift operator training must include hands-on practical training and an in-person evaluation on the site's own equipment. Online material can cover only the classroom part, so much of the training needs a human trainer on site.

IFS Softeon's Fulfillment Flow, launched in 2026, uses AI digital workers coordinated by a central operational agent across warehouse functions and nearby areas such as manufacturing line feeds. Human managers still set priorities and make the final decisions.

SAP's 2026 outlook describes role-specific planning agents (material planner, commercial, demand forecasting) that work together to recommend actions across sales and operations planning. The cross-department decisions stay with humans.
Agents now handle routine purchasing, generating purchase orders and suggesting transfers from forecasts, while humans keep strategic relationships and negotiation.

AI warehouse-design simulators exist and handle layout and planning work. GreyOrange's GreyMatter Foundry, launched in April 2026, combines flow design, technology sizing and layout planning, and includes a conversational AI design assistant. Addverb's tool generates 2D layouts from dimensions and storage needs. An agent with tool use could run sub-steps like these, along with capacity analysis, equipment comparisons and ROI work.

No AI tool was found that handles a whole facility expansion end to end. Current tools cover the concept and simulation stages. Site assessment, capital approval, vendor negotiation and overseeing implementation still need humans, and some of that work is physical, such as site walks and supervising construction and installation.

Structural changes to buildings usually need plans signed or sealed by a licensed engineer or architect before a permit is issued. That signature falls to outside licensed professionals, not to the logistics manager, so it limits only the structural part of the task.

Making the case for warehouse automation capex is a standard desk analysis: define the scope (volumes, WMS/WCS interfaces, building and power work), then calculate payback, NPV and IRR against WACC. An agent with code execution and web access can do this from operational data and vendor quotes.

Companies usually approve capex through a delegation-of-authority matrix. Named roles have monetary limits, and large purchases go to the board. Approver roles are kept separate from initiators, so a person with that authority must sign off.

Delegation-of-authority approvals are increasingly built into ERP workflows such as SAP S/4HANA. Software sends the request through, but the approval itself still comes from a human who holds the authority.

Regulatory horizon-scanning products (for example FinregE's 'Regulatory Operating System') already watch for new regulatory developments. They link that intelligence to policy, control and implementation workflows, so most of the monitoring and summarising can be automated.
Vendors such as CUBE say the hard part is deciding which changes actually matter to a firm's products and policies. That relevance judgement still needs human context and review.
AI tools can process large volumes of outside material and find patterns faster. Human judgement is still needed to supply context and to answer 'so what, now what, who owns it'.

Current security-architecture guidance and products cover designing integrated control layers (identity, access control, data governance, enforcement points). This is the kind of design and integration recommendation an agent can research and draft. Vendors still advise keeping AI advisory, with humans reviewing decisions in mission-critical physical security settings.

Physical security integration recommendations depend on site- and system-specific factors such as video availability, door access, incident response and operational continuity. Getting that information usually takes site knowledge and access to client systems, which a human typically provides and verifies.

Licensing for low-voltage security design varies by state. California, for example, requires a C-7 licence for CCTV design and a C-28 licence for access control installation by the contracting entity, while several states have no statewide licence. Advisory recommendations by themselves are generally not required to be signed by a licence holder.

Vendors sell investment-analyst AI agents that run screens, pull filings and transcripts, summarize earnings, refresh models and draft coverage notes end to end. Analysts still review the output, and live agentic deployments remain early-stage.

Multi-agent equity research setups (document analyzer, model-building analyst agent, a portfolio-manager agent that challenges the thesis) are described for producing investment theses. The post is promotional and gives no outcome data.

In the US, research analysts who publish recommendations must hold FINRA Research Analyst registration (SIE plus Series 86/87), so a registered human has to be accountable for and approve published recommendations.

Third-party leaderboard trackers report that frontier models score about 95-96% on SWE-bench Verified (as of July-Sept 2026). The benchmark asks a model to write patches that fix real GitHub issues without breaking existing tests. These rankings were not checked against the official leaderboard.

Spotify built 'Honk', an autonomous AI coding agent that runs codebase and framework-upgrade migrations across thousands of repositories. It handles the edge cases that deterministic scripts could not.

An MSR 2026 study of 33,580 PRs written by agents found that 2.66% contain reverting commits, ranging from 0.7% to 7.6% depending on the agent. A separate 2026 study says many agent-involved fix PRs depend on maintainers to merge them. Both point to human review still being needed before use.

Esri describes agentic mapping apps where a user asks a plain-language question and the agent picks and runs the spatial analysis tools, then returns results. Its ArcGIS Pro assistant, which can generate ArcPy and Arcade code, is still in beta, so map-and-layer production can be partly delegated.

A USGS presentation shows Esri's AI assistants for Pro, Survey123 and Arcade code generation still at Preview or Beta stage in 2026, so a human still has to review cartographic quality and data correctness.

A surveyor's seal is required only for survey products such as plats and boundary maps. General-purpose GIS maps, tables and reports usually need no licensed sign-off, though some states define surveying broadly.

Physical penetration tests of offices, plants and server rooms are done on site. Testers work in person under signed authorization and try tailgating, lock bypass and sensor bypass, and they test fire and cooling systems. None of this can be done through software alone.

Software and sensors can already monitor temperature, smoke, humidity and floods and send alerts automatically. An agent could review that data, the floor plans and natural-hazard data, and draft findings against frameworks such as ISO 27001 control 7.5.

The DISN facility STIG requires physical penetration testing at least once a year, recommends an outside tester and has results reported to the site commander. A person is expected to carry out the test and own its results.

ReqGenie is a GPT-based research prototype that runs text-based stakeholder interviews and turns them into requirements. In a preliminary test, its outputs compared well with two existing SRS documents. This suggests an agent can carry out the elicitation and summary steps on its own.
A 2026 study of multi-agent requirements generation still has stakeholders review and refine what the agents produce. Human sign-off on requirements is still essential.
Commercial requirements tools present AI as an assistant. It pulls out candidate requirements, flags ambiguities and suggests clarifying questions, while humans make the decisions about requirements.

Google's AI co-scientist is a multi-agent system that generates and ranks biomedical hypotheses, and some of its proposals were confirmed in wet-lab tests. It is still built to keep a scientist in the loop, and human checking is still needed.
Multi-agent tools such as SciAgents can build new hypotheses from more than 1,000 studies, but these systems are mostly at the research stage and are not yet routine lab tools.
Most biomedical engineering work does not require a PE license. A license is mainly needed to stamp designs or to testify as an expert witness, neither of which applies to research consultation.

Maritime predictive-maintenance tools connect to planned maintenance systems and can create work orders and schedule maintenance around voyages and port calls. They do not handle the hands-on repair, and they say little about dispatching repairs, spares or shipyards.
Planned, predictive and breakdown maintenance of ship machinery is done to classification society rules (e.g. Lloyd's) and flag state law, under the responsibility of the engineers on board.
Under survey requirements and the ISM Code, maintenance and repair records must be completed and engine room logs signed by the chief engineer, so a human has to sign off.

Vendors describe CAPA agents that classify nonconformances, link related events, assign action priority from AIAG/VDA severity, occurrence and detection scores, and draft root-cause suggestions and corrective-action recommendations. Their capability claims are unverified marketing.
An industry guide for FDA-regulated biopharma says AI does not write CAPAs or decide on corrective actions. Qualified people review and decide, so a human review step is still needed.

In regulated QMS settings, a named person in the company must approve and sign quality documents and CAPA. This is an approval duty inside the company, not a licence needed to make the recommendation.

BLS says these technicians help mechanical engineers design, develop, test and manufacture devices. Their listed duties include setting up and running tests on units and their parts, logging the results, reviewing drawings and building mechanical parts. Testing and building are hands-on work.

MecAgent V2 is a commercial agent that runs inside SolidWorks. The vendor says it can turn text into CAD, convert models to drawings, build assemblies, check standards and generate bills of materials, including an assembly of about 56 parts built without supervision. These claims are not independently checked, so a human still has to review the output.

Research from 2026 (TOOLCAD, ACL Findings) says a fully autonomous CAD agent that works with real design platforms does not exist yet. CoLab argues that making the geometry is only the first step and the harder engineering work comes after it.

Robotic total stations, which have existed since 1990, use servomotors and a tracking sensor to follow a prism. The operator controls the survey from the prism pole, so the instrument operator is no longer needed. Even so, a person still has to carry the pole and hold it plumb over each point. That work is physical and a software-only AI agent cannot do it.

The Leica iCON robot 50 is sold for one-person surveys run from a field controller mounted on the prism pole at the point being positioned. Setting up and holding the rod still takes a human in the field.

AI change-detection tools combine aerial and satellite imagery with existing map data to flag areas that may have changed, so specialists review fewer places. Comparing new imagery against an existing map is being automated, but people still review the results.

Methods that turn features extracted from aerial images into vectors and compare them against existing map vectors to find mismatches are documented. Manual visual comparison by analysts remains the slow baseline.

Under state law, technical staff prepare survey and mapping work under a licensed surveyor in responsible charge, who seals the final product. The technician's comparison step itself does not need a licence, but a human reviews the final product.

Chesapeake Conservancy reports that its deep-learning model maps wetlands at 1-metre resolution with 94% accuracy. It still needs local training data from state wetland inventories and the National Wetlands Inventory (NWI), so automated mapping covers a large part of determining wetland extent from existing data.

A 2025 practitioner presentation says AI wetland-probability layers are being added to the NWI update process, but their boundaries do not consistently match NWI standards. A human expert therefore still has to review and correct the output.

Regulators such as the Corps and state agencies make the final call on wetland boundaries and verify delineations by consultants. That formal step applies to regulatory delineation, not to compiling or interpreting biodata for planning.

The FDA has cleared AI-based computerized cognitive screening tools such as CognICA, a 5-minute iPad test for early dementia, and Cognivue. These screen for impairment. They do not diagnose CNS disease or treat it.
Georgia rules treat neuropsychological testing and diagnostic opinions on organic brain disorders as the practice of psychology, and unlicensed people may not provide them.
According to AACN, most U.S. states restrict who may use psychological and neuropsychological tests, and some limit them to licensed clinical psychologists, for example Illinois.

O*NET lists this as a task for Geological Technicians. Related tasks for the same job include taking part in exploratory drilling and well-logging surveys and collecting or preparing solid and fluid samples, which means physical fieldwork.
AI and ML workflows already automate main desk sub-steps of CO2 storage site work, such as seismic horizon and fault interpretation, filling gaps in well data and building reservoir property models.

A CCS site assessment workflow that combines well and seismic reservoir properties was designed to be as automated as possible and was applied across more than 6,000 sq km. Compiling existing data is largely digital work.

Minnesota DNR: when work in public waters is done without a permit, enforcement can include a civil restoration order, and the area hydrologist prepares these orders. An agent can draft such legal documents from templates, statutes and case facts, but the agency issues them and they can be contested in hearings.

Under Minn. R. 6115.0255, the commissioner or agent reviews the evidence, including evidence from the landowner, inspects the site if needed and makes the determination. That requires a human on site and a human decision.

In a real case (Maple Lake, 2015), a conservation officer and an area hydrologist investigated a complaint in person: cattails had been removed and sand and fabric placed below the ordinary high water level. The investigation depended on field visits and talking with the landowner.

A vendor (OpenEduCat) says its AI planner builds 5-day lesson plans with IEP goal alignment, accommodation notes and pacing for co-teaching and resource-room settings. It also says it flags curriculum months where a goal has no planned activity. These are the vendor's own claims and were not independently checked.

A small peer-reviewed study (Education Sciences, Aug 2025) found ChatGPT made IEP goals clearer and lesson plans more structured. Teachers said human oversight was needed to fit the plans to real classroom conditions.

State co-teaching guidance treats co-planning as a live meeting between the general and special education teachers. The meeting covers curriculum, student data, supports and who leads each part of the lesson. Planning time comes from state, district or union rules, not a federal IDEA requirement, and no rule requires a human signature for the plans.

Library policy work is mostly research and drafting: comparing peer libraries' policies, surveying common practice and writing staff- and patron-facing text. ALA's 2026 guide and WebJunction materials describe this as document work that an agent can largely do end to end.

Public library boards of trustees hold the legal authority to adopt policies, for example under Washington RCW 27.12.210. Adoption means first and second readings at a public meeting, public comment and a majority vote, so humans must approve the result.
Staff and legal counsel review a policy before it is adopted. Trustees set the policy and the librarian and staff carry it out, so building agreement with stakeholders stays a human job.

Kirkpatrick Partners says AI can create and refine Level 2 learning assessments and automate Level 1 surveys and feedback. It also says a human should check those AI outputs against the performance objectives, so a person still has to review before use.

Kirkpatrick Partners offers an 'AI-Powered Evaluation Specialist' certification built with UnDesto AI, with 2026 sessions. This shows AI-assisted design of evaluation tools is established practice. The course also covers bias, privacy and validity risks that call for human oversight.

Training-evaluation survey guides note that Level 3 (behavior) and Level 4 (results) measures depend on organization-specific performance data and stakeholder agreement. An agent can draft these instruments, but a human has to validate them in context.

Districts already run field-trip, yearbook and club fees through online portals such as SchoolCash Online. Parents pay by card or e-check, get automatic notices, and the money goes straight to the school's bank account, though many schools still accept cash and checks.

Under state auditor guidance, a teacher or coach who collects money has to use a pre-numbered receipt book and keep a list of cash and check payments. That makes the in-person handling of cash a physical, hands-on step, while the record-keeping is digital work an agent could do.

District procedures let elementary teachers collect small amounts of cash or checks from students. School policies require the cash to be stored securely and handed to the office, and ask for receipting, banking and reconciliation to be split between staff. These are internal controls, not licensing rules.

Free AI design tools such as Canva AI, Venngage and Pixa generate classroom labels, bin labels and bulletin-board letters for printing. Only the design and printable-file step can be done in software.
O*NET lists this as a core teaching assistant task: organizing and labeling materials and displaying students' work at eye level, which is physical work done in the classroom.

UK teaching assistant job descriptions describe preparing, mounting and presenting displays of pupils' work and laminating materials. These are hands-on duties with no licensing or sign-off requirement.

Reviews describe AI tools for teachers, such as MagicSchool and Eduaide.AI, that generate worksheets, lesson materials and other teaching resources from a short specification. The sources found did not confirm that these tools make charts or graphic organizers.
Brisk works inside Google and Microsoft documents and webpages. It creates learning materials, changes reading levels and translates content without leaving the browser.

Teacher guides say AI-generated materials should be fact-checked and approved before classroom use, and that private student data should not be uploaded to unapproved tools. This means a human still reviews the output, and some classroom aids are physical items such as posters.

AI tools such as Alongside's Kiwi chatbot, SchoolAI 'spaces' role-play bots and Gemini Gems are used for SEL and social-skill practice. These tools are run by teachers alongside regular teaching. Educators worry that AI could weaken relationship-building, and most of the efficacy evidence comes from the vendors themselves.
CASEL presents AI-powered tools as a support for human-centered SEL work, not a replacement for it.

Under ESSA Title I, paraprofessionals work under the direction of a certified teacher and may not be given full responsibility for instruction. No licence requires a human to sign off on teaching social skills.

A two-year randomized trial in 18 Tennessee middle schools found that Khanmigo can tutor students on its own during remedial math sessions. Gains were modest, about 0.06 to 0.08 SD per year. Students used it little, and the authors say low engagement was the main limit.

When Khanmigo asked guiding questions instead of giving answers, students often stopped using it. This suggests that a human's in-person presence and motivation still matter, especially for young children.
Under ESSA/Title I, paraprofessionals must work under a certified teacher's supervision. No licence is needed to tutor, so this rule would not stop an agent from doing the tutoring.

Tools such as AbleSpace, SyncIEP and IEP Insight automate data logging, mastery calculations, graphs and AI-written progress notes once someone enters the observations. The direct observation itself still has to be done by a person.

The special educator decides what data to collect and builds the tools. The paraprofessional watches students in the classroom (prompting level, engagement, behaviour) and records the data on the spot with those tools, so physical presence is required.
Paraprofessionals give informal assessments and collect classroom behaviour data as the teacher directs. Accountability for the data stays with the teacher, not with a licence held by the aide.

Special education paraprofessional job descriptions list hands-on help with toileting, diapering, feeding, lifting and repositioning students, and wheelchair assistance, as required by the student's IEP.
Aides do health procedures such as tube feeding, catheterization and suctioning when the school nurse delegates them, and they work under the direction of a teacher or administrator.

AI tools in special education mainly adapt materials, support communication and tutor students. Reviews say they support special educators and do not replace them, and that teachers need to oversee them.

Camera-based attendance systems that use facial recognition exist, including a reported rollout to 48,000 government schools in Assam. Without an installed camera, though, someone in the room still has to see which students are present. Research prototypes report roughly 85-96% accuracy and raise privacy concerns.

Under English school policy, schools must keep an attendance register by law. Class teachers mark it at the start of morning and afternoon sessions, and entries are kept for 6 years. This is a record-keeping duty, not a rule that a specific licensed person must sign.

In one New South Wales (NSW) school's procedures, the roll is printed weekly and the principal signs it to certify that it is accurate. The person who signs is the principal, not the teaching assistant.

AI script-breakdown tools such as Filmustage and RivetAI can find and tag props, costumes, wardrobe, locations, vehicles and other production elements, and link them to schedules and budgets. That covers the 'identify' part of the task from start to finish, but the breakdowns still need human review for accuracy and creative fit.

Approval is a creative authority held by the director: production guidelines say the director gives final approval on props, and scenic elements must satisfy the director and production designer before tech rehearsal. In practice, sets, fittings and lighting are often reviewed in person.

Production policies set the director's prop list and approval deadlines inside an internal workflow run by people. These are institutional rules, not legal ones, so no licence or law requires a human to sign.

Commercial RFP agents (Folio3, Lyzr) already handle intake, extracting requirements and deadlines, pulling from past winning proposals, drafting, compliance screening and approval routing as separate automated steps.

Vendors say their tools cut RFP response time a lot: Beam AI claims about 40 hours down to 8 per RFP. These are the vendors' own figures, not independent results, but they suggest a human still spends real time reviewing and finishing the work.

Under FAR-based rules, an offer must be signed by a person with authority to bind the offeror, and the contracting officer must confirm that authority. So a human has to commit to the price and terms and sign the bid.
Existing AI tools such as Orb Composer can harmonize and orchestrate an imported MIDI melody into a full arrangement. The user then edits the result, so a human is still involved.
AI orchestration tools turn a piano or melody MIDI file into a multi-track orchestral score. Voice-leading quality is claimed by the vendor, not verified, so an expert still needs to review it.

Copyrighted works need the rights holder's permission before they can be arranged, because an arrangement is a derivative work. That is a copyright licence, not a rule that a licensed human must do or sign the arranging.

SignNow sells templated DJ contracts covering performance, payment and scheduling. It presents electronic signatures as legally recognized under ESIGN/UETA (vendor claim), so no wet-ink or in-person step is needed.
Cal.com's DJ booking workflow guide says a booking tool can trigger a DJ contract template sent through DocuSign or a similar e-signature service when a booking is made.
AI drafting agents and generators produce service agreements from a plain-language description or a structured set of questions, with Word/PDF export (vendor claims, not independently tested).

SoundSwitch software analyses tracks in batches to build light shows automatically (AutoScripting) and keeps lighting in sync with the beat (Autoloops) through USB-DMX alongside Serato, Engine DJ and VirtualDJ. This means software can already handle much of the live light cueing.

US laser shows need an FDA variance under 21 CFR 1040.11(c). They must be under the direct and personal control of trained operators who are positioned where they can see all beam paths, so a human has to run the lasers.
The FDA has checked at events that laser operators hold an approved variance and follow its conditions.

Current DJ software handles stem separation, BPM matching and transitions. Commentators from 2025 and 2026 say that reading a live crowd is still done by human DJs. The webcam 'crowd-reading' features are an April Fool's joke, not real products.
djOS (April 2026) is presented as an AI co-pilot that plugs into DJ platforms and responds to the crowd. It is a press release only, and I found no proof that it works on its own in real venues.
Public performance licenses (ASCAP/BMI/SESAC) are usually held by the venue. No law requires a person to be the one who selects or plays the music.
Bloomberg Law built an LLM tool that copy-edits articles to match house style, to cut editors' copy-editing time.
NZ Herald's in-house AI checks grammar and spelling, enforces house style and condenses press releases into articles under an editor's direction, with review before publication.

Newsroom AI policies such as WEHCO's, based on AP standards, require a human editor to review AI output before publication. This is a newsroom norm, not a legal or licensing rule, but it means a human still has to approve or correct the work.
Jotform's Copywriter Intake AI Agent template runs conversational intake with clients. It gathers project details and brand information and accepts uploaded brand guidelines.
Monday.com's creative brief agent builds briefs from Slack threads and voice-note transcripts. It states its assumptions where information is missing and flags conflicting stakeholder feedback.
Jasper's Creative Brief Agent organizes goals, audiences and deliverables into a brief for stakeholders and applies the user's brand voice settings.
