O*NET lists 'Install electrical cables or wire fixtures' as a core task for Lighting Technicians. The work is hands-on: running cable, wiring fixtures and patching them to dimmers at the venue. An agent with no body cannot do it; at most it can look up wiring diagrams or load calculations.
Lighting technicians rig, wire and focus fixtures on site following the designer's plot. In theatre they work under a master electrician, and in film and TV under a gaffer.
Licensing rules differ by US state. Temporary production wiring is often allowed under a limited stage-electrician license or exemption, while permanent wiring requires a licensed electrician.

Focusing moving lights is done on the lighting console using stored position and focus palettes. Software such as FocusTrack helps check and touch up focus cue by cue, but a human programmer runs it. The search found no fully automatic focus feature in current consoles.

Rigging and electrical work in many venues must be done or supervised by ETCP-certified people, under venue rules and IATSE agreements. This is an industry and union requirement, not a general legal licence, and it assumes human hands-on work.
ETCP certifies Riggers and Entertainment Electricians as experienced practitioners of the physical work: hanging, cabling and powering fixtures.

Vendors describe AI that reads referral documents, ranks urgency, fills in EHR referral forms and tracks referral status. That covers the paperwork and coordination steps, but no peer-reviewed evidence shows an agent completing ED-to-specialist referrals end to end.
In a 2025 ED pilot, an AI tool (Mediktor) recommended referral to urgent care for 43.6% of 427 non-severe patients. Clinicians and patients still made the final decision.
Medicare allows only PECOS-enrolled physicians or non-physician practitioners, each with an individual NPI, to order or refer services. A licensed human therefore has to be the referring party.

Software from AI vendors (e.g., Opmed.ai) plans operating-room staffing and changes schedules in real time. This covers the administrative scheduling part of the task, not hands-on clinical direction of the surgical team. Most evidence comes from vendors.

Under CMS teaching-physician rules, the attending surgeon must be physically present for the key or critical parts of surgical procedures done by residents. Supervising the team is an in-person duty that a licensed physician must carry out.

Vendor reports describe AI agents that coordinate hospital staff workflows, such as refilling cancelled slots and updating schedules, without a human involved. These are logistics tasks, not directing clinical staff at the bedside or in the operating room.

Automated stainers such as the Leica BOND RX run IHC, immunofluorescence and multiplex protocols that users program. A person still has to load the tissue sections, slides and reagents, so the automation is in the hardware, not in a software agent.

Users can edit the temperature of individual steps in BOND RXm IF and multiplex protocols. An AI agent could help draft or tune these protocols, but the bench steps (fixation, sectioning, antigen retrieval, mounting) are physical.

Under CLIA, 42 CFR 493.1489, people who perform high-complexity testing, including histopathology tissue work under 493.1449, must meet set qualifications and hold a state license where the state requires one.

Staining means physically moving slides through reagents such as xylene, alcohols, hematoxylin and eosin. Automated stainers can do this, but a person still has to load slide racks and reagent containers. A software agent can only help program protocols (for example, the Histo-Tek SL takes 15 programmable protocols of up to 35 steps), look up procedures or keep records.
Special stains are chemically sensitive and need reagents applied in a set order. That calls for hands-on bench work and quality control, which an agent with no physical body cannot do.

Anatomic pathology counts as high-complexity testing under CLIA, so the people performing it must meet personnel requirements. Several states, including Florida, Nevada and New York, also require a state licence.

Histotechnology training is mostly hands-on bench practice (microtomy, embedding, frozen sectioning, staining), plus about 10 hours of lectures a week in the first months. That puts most of the teaching at the physical bench.

A 2025 review sees large language models and multimodal AI personalizing pathology education and cutting content-development work, but with ongoing human oversight so AI supports educators instead of replacing them.
Curricula combine lectures, tutorial demonstrations and rotations through hospital labs, so demonstrating techniques and coaching in person stay central.

Konica Minolta's commercial 'Positioning i' AI measures how far key positioning points deviate and grades radiographs as Acceptable, Tolerable, or 'Re-radiography must be considered'. This supports the reject/repeat decision but does not take the exposure.
GE's AI gives real-time mammography positioning feedback before exposure, with about 96% validation accuracy. A technologist still positions the patient and fires the exposure.
New York Public Health Law §3502 allows only licensed practitioners and licensed persons to apply ionizing radiation to human beings.
AI voice agents sold in 2026 answer clinic calls and book visits straight into clinic calendars or scheduling systems, and pass complex cases to staff.
Vendors say AI scheduling agents write bookings into EHRs through HL7/FHIR standards and native connectors, for example NextGen. This is a vendor claim.
A vendor guide on AI scheduling agents deployed by health systems reports an 89% drop in call abandonment at one system. This result has not been independently checked.

AI registry products already automate case finding, abstraction and NAACCR-format reporting from clinical data. Vendors report cutting per-case abstraction from about 2 hours to 10–20 minutes, with human validation still in the loop. These are vendor claims.

Statistical analysis of registry data runs on standard software (NCI SEER*Stat, SEER*DMS, CDC EDITS). An agent with code execution can drive tools like these to produce tables, charts and narrative summaries.

The credentialing rules found (CTR requirements from CoC and state registries) cover abstraction and registry staff, not who prepares statistical reports. Registrars prepare and submit reports to SEER/NCDB under those standards, so in practice a human still reviews and is accountable for the work.

Under NWCG, the Cost Unit Leader gathers incident cost data, runs obligation reports from the ICARS database, builds cost reports and charts, analyzes cost-effectiveness and recommends savings. These are data and reporting steps that an agent with system access could carry out.

Line officers, agency administrators and incident commanders must review costs daily and document those reviews. Unresolved cost concerns go to the Agency Administrator or Line Officer, so a human holds the accountability for deciding whether spending is necessary.

Incident business follows the NWCG SIIBM (PMS 902), and federal expenditures of $10M or more trigger formal cost reviews. These rules give an agent clear criteria to check spending against, but delegated authority and sign-off stay with people.
This federal fire job posting says crew carrier drivers must hold the state licence the state DOT requires before they are assigned, and they are subject to DOT drug and alcohol testing.
This posting says firefighters who drive fire engines as alternate drivers must have a commercial driver's license before the assignment.

At CES 2026 Oshkosh showed an AI collision-warning system for firefighters, not a driverless truck. The searches found no driverless crew carriers or fire trucks in service, and in any case the reference AI agents have no physical body.

Fire alarm testing is usually done in person: designated inspectors walk the whole building, set off each device and log pass or fail. Self-test detectors and cloud platforms such as Honeywell CLSS cover only some devices and work through the vendor's own systems.
NFPA 25 allows automatic or remote inspection and testing only through electronic devices installed for that purpose. Everything else (valves, sprinklers, pumps, extinguishers) needs someone on site.
NFPA 25 requires inspection, testing and maintenance (ITM) work to be done by qualified personnel. The local fire authority (AHJ) decides what training, certification or licence each ITM task needs.

Commercial AI deterrence products (Verkada, Alarm.com AID) detect trespassers on camera and give automated spoken warnings that escalate. This covers detection and warnings only. It does not cover physically removing or detaining anyone.
AI video analytics combine human classification with line-crossing detection to give real-time perimeter alerts and automated deterrence. A human still has to respond in person.

When licensed security officers detain or arrest someone, they do it as private citizens under state law. Unlawful detention creates personal liability for false imprisonment, which assumes a human performs the act and answers for it.

Vendor pages for security scheduling software describe filling posts automatically. The tools check each guard's licence class, site clearance, training and overtime limits, then message the best-matched candidates. These are marketing claims, not independent evaluations.

Teambridge sells 'Security Operations AI' that matches available guards to armed or clearance requirements and contacts them to cover open posts. Its rule engine warns rather than blocks, so a supervisor can still make a judgment call, and each override is logged.

Guard scheduling is built around posts: each post has a location, hours and required certification. Putting a guard with an expired licence on a post is a regulatory violation, but no law found requires a human to make the assignment.

A vendor (DocsBot) markets an AI agent trained on a security company's post orders, SOPs and client instructions. It answers guards' questions and sends issues that need judgment to a human supervisor, so the written explanation step can be automated.
General HR policy agents already explain company policies to employees from the uploaded documents and cite the source, with no human answering each question.

Security guard licensing is set state by state and covers guard training and registration. The search found no state rule requiring a licensed human to personally explain company policies. Supervisor duties such as giving direction and motivating staff are set by employers.

AI video and audio alarm verification is sold commercially to cut false alarms. Vendors say 2026 AI agents can assess an intrusion, sound an alarm and write incident reports, but a human operator still decides whether to call police.
Alpha Vision launched an AI security agent at ISC West in March 2026. It offers real-time video analysis, structured incident reporting and natural-language queries to speed up investigations.
Security supervisor postings require responding to alarms in person, doing on-site checks, calming altercations and holding a state security licence.

Electronic key control systems such as KeyTrak and Traka replace manual key logs. They record every key removal and return automatically, tied to the user's PIN, card or biometric, and produce an audit trail and overdue-key alerts.

Access control software like Genetec and Gallagher Command Centre manages cardholders and credential assignments digitally, including importing data and exporting card assignment records for audits. An agent using a computer can operate these tools.

Someone has to physically hand over the key or card and check the recipient's identity in person. Without an automated cabinet or reader event, the agent needs a human to tell it what was handed out before it can record it.

Guard tour software already checks guard compliance automatically. It records timestamped checkpoint scans (NFC, QR, GPS, RFID) tied to each guard's badge, and sends alerts when a tour starts late, ends early or misses a checkpoint. An agent can review this data and report on it without a human.
Patrols are linked to the guard's badge login and the data syncs automatically, so the digital record of each guard's adherence is available to software.

Guard licensing is set state by state, with no federal license, and no separate licence tier for supervisors was found. That suggests no legal rule requires a human to do the monitoring, but on-site observation, coaching and corrective action still depend on being there in person.

AI recruiting agents can work toward a hiring goal on their own: they source and screen candidates, schedule interviews and run adaptive voice or video interviews with scored evaluations. They hand control back to a recruiter at set checkpoints, and most companies keep a human overseeing AI-run interviews (71% say a human always oversees, 6% let the AI run the process alone).

Hiring security guards requires state-regulated steps that the agent can only coordinate. In Michigan, for example, the licensed employer must fingerprint prospective guards and submit the prints to state police and the FBI; in California, guards need DOJ Live Scan fingerprinting, training and a state ID card. The licensee is responsible for meeting these requirements.

Laws on automated hiring tools add obligations: NYC Local Law 144 requires bias audits and candidate notice, and Colorado's AI law provides human review of adverse AI-driven employment decisions. This pushes the final hire decision back to a human.

Gamma's AI agent can take an uploaded budget spreadsheet and build a full formatted budget presentation with charts and category breakdowns. This is the vendor's own claim and was not independently checked.
Microsoft's adoption guidance says its Office Agent (Copilot) can draft budget performance presentations from financial analysis and earlier meeting notes. This is also vendor material.

Security budgets depend on post-coverage minimums written into contracts and on overtime driven by staff turnover. Those inputs come from internal scheduling and payroll data, and a supervisor has to judge them and defend them to management.

Fire departments use NFPA 1582 to require medical and physical fitness exams for firefighters. The standard covers aerobic capacity, strength and endurance, and a physician must confirm that the person can do essential tasks such as rescue. This shows the task is physical work done in person by certified people.

Departments give the NFPA 1582 medical exam at hire and then every year. A physician reports whether each firefighter is fit to do the job's essential physical tasks, so a certified human is held responsible for doing the work.

The fitness requirements set by the standard (grip and limb strength, muscular endurance) reflect the main parts of a rescue: carrying victims, forcing entry and getting people out of water. An agent that works only through software cannot do these things.

Firefighters reach the seat of the fire by physically stretching and advancing hose lines inside burning buildings. Crews read the flow path, stairwells and building layout on the spot, so the core of the task is bodily movement under IDLH conditions.

AI navigation aids for firefighters (deep-learning thermal imaging with AR overlays) are still mostly academic prototypes. They only advise the firefighter, who still does all the moving, and are not standard tools.

Fire department operating guidelines put interior attack and entry decisions in the hands of trained, certified crews and officers on the fireground. A software agent has no body and could at most do pre-incident building lookups.

AI in fire service is mostly at the dispatch level: computer-aided dispatch adds AI on top of rule-based routing and zoned alerting. That is the dispatcher's job, not the firefighter's on-scene response.
Plans for AI-based dispatch of the nearest fire truck are still proposals. Trucks, drones and people still carry out the physical response.
Responders must hold certification to NFPA 1001 Firefighter I/II, which requires passing practical skills exams plus hazmat and first aid/CPR credentials. This is a human licensing requirement.

NFPA 1583 sets up mandatory fire-department fitness programs with an assessment at least once a year of aerobic capacity, strength, endurance, body composition and flexibility. The firefighter has to do the exercise in person, so it can't be delegated.

AI fitness apps can write workout plans and adjust them over time. That only touches planning, a small part of the work. The person still does all of the training. No firefighter-specific AI training tools turned up.
Exercise only improves the fitness of the person doing it. An agent with no body can't do any substantial part of the task.

Salvage means hands-on work at the fire scene: pumping out basements, draining water pooled in ceilings, covering contents with salvage covers, and sealing broken windows and doors with plastic sheeting.
Salvage activities include expelling smoke, controlling runoff, removing water, and covering broken windows and doors, all carried out by crews on site.
Crews remove smoke by physically ventilating the building and keep ventilating during overhaul; the building's HVAC system is usually shut off rather than used.

Automatic pump pressure governors are built into pumper apparatus, not run by general-purpose AI agents. They hold the discharge pressure the operator sets by adjusting engine speed. The operator still engages the pump, sets the pressure and watches for cavitation at the panel on the truck.
Newer integrated pump panels such as REV Smart Flo cut pump engagement down to a button press. The controls are on the apparatus and a person has to operate them there.

Under NFPA 1002, pump operators must hold Driver/Operator–Pumper certification. That requires Firefighter I, written and hands-on practical exams on the apparatus, a medical evaluation and a driver's license.

Crime scene protocols say the first officer gives the investigator taking control a detailed briefing at the scene and records the handover. The investigator asks what was done and what changed. This is a face-to-face exchange inside a secured scene.

Department policy has the securing officer go over the scene and events with the detective once the detective arrives, while making sure no one touches the physical evidence. This requires being physically present and moving carefully around evidence.

Axon Draft One turns body-camera audio into draft reports, but officers must review and sign each one. Some deployments leave out felonies and arrests, so AI only helps with documentation and does not replace the briefing itself.

Baton Rouge police policy: once a responding officer discovers or identifies a crime scene, that officer immediately becomes responsible for protecting it from contamination. Yellow perimeter tape is the preferred first barrier, so the work is physical and done in person.

Fairfax County police set up two perimeters on site: red 'Crime Scene-Do Not Cross' tape for the inner one and yellow 'Police Line' tape for the outer one. Officers have to place and check both by hand.
Burleson, Texas policy: the officer keeps an entry log recording each person's time in, time out and purpose. This log is the only part of the task software could help with.

Under Crawford v. Washington, testimonial statements are barred unless the witness is cross-examined at trial or was unavailable after an earlier chance to cross-examine. So the officer who saw the events must testify under oath in person.

AI tools like Axon Draft One only write first drafts of reports from body-camera audio. The officer reviews and signs the report, and prosecutors want officers to stay responsible because they may have to testify about what they witnessed.
The COPS Office says AI report tools cannot parse or summarize the visual content of video. That limits AI to a supporting role in preparing evidence for testimony.

AI camera systems such as Rekor's Argos Guardian combine radar, video and AI plate reading to flag violations and build citation evidence packets. These systems sit outside the agent and only cover detecting and documenting violations. They do not drive a patrol or make arrests.
A July 2026 NCSL/CDT report says AI-upgraded license plate readers are now used to pick which vehicles to pull over. Officers still have to make the physical stop.
Arizona AG opinion: only a POST-certified peace officer can exercise the authority to detain and arrest. A non-certified person has no more authority than any citizen.

Since February 2026, the San Diego County Sheriff has run an AI agent around the clock on its non-emergency line. It decides whether a call goes to a dispatcher or the communication center and points wrong-agency callers to the correct agency. The 71% deflection rate is the vendor's own figure.

AI agents on non-emergency lines in Ontario (Halton's SARA, Owen Sound's CARA) pass emergencies or calls they don't understand to a human. In El Cajon, California, a human still reviews every call the AI handles.

Officers in the field relay information to dispatch by radio and through the mobile data terminal (MDT) linked to the dispatch system (CAD). Some departments forbid using the MDT in place of radio, and high-priority calls go by voice. That means relaying depends on what the officer gathers on scene and on secured police systems.

AI agents for skip tracing are sold to law enforcement (ICE has contracted vendors whose AI agents locate people and map their associates), so the search-and-locate part can be sped up. The arrest itself still has to be carried out by people.
In California, arrest warrants are addressed to peace officers, and only the officers or authorized public employees who receive the warrant can carry it out.
In Louisiana, only a peace officer with authority in the place where the person is found can execute an arrest warrant.

Jail management systems already speed up booking. Kologik says arrestee data syncs automatically from CAD and RMS. SmartJAIL can import arrest and charging reports to fill in cases, charges and bond details. This makes the records side digital, but a person still runs the system.

CentralSquare says automated intake cuts booking from about 45 to 15 minutes per inmate. This is a vendor claim. The physical steps still need a person on site: searching the arrestee, taking prints, photos and property, and keeping custody.
Booking still involves capturing fingerprints in person with livescan devices linked to criminal-justice databases such as FBI/AFIS. Some agencies still fill out hard-copy forms by hand.
D.A.R.E. sends specially trained, certified police officers into schools to teach the curriculum in person. Instructors must complete an 80-hour training course, and lessons run weekly in classrooms.
Local police departments run these as officer-led classroom programs that finish with a culmination ceremony. The officer's own presence and relationship with the students is the core of the program.

AI lesson-plan generators such as MagicSchool and Eduaide can draft lessons, activities and assessments, but sources say a human must review the drafts. Locally specific curricula need more rework. This supports the prep work only, not the in-person delivery.

Wheelchair securement is a hands-on job. Staff position the chair, center it between the floor tracks, lock the brakes and attach the straps. The bus must not move until the chair is fully and properly tied down.
District procedure says two adults should take part in loading and unloading. The bus driver or bus aide is responsible for making sure the student and equipment are secured before the bus moves.

Guidance requires a 4-point tie-down with a separate occupant restraint, following the manufacturers' instructions. Staff must not improvise a securement. This is physical work with nothing an AI agent can do through software.

O*NET describes school bus monitors as helping students board and exit safely, opening and closing doors, operating wheelchair lifts, securing seatbelts and tie-downs, and directing evacuations. All of these need a person physically on the bus.

Existing software, such as RFID card scanning with cloud logging and alerts, only records who gets on and off. It does not direct students, so it covers a small digital part of the job and leaves the in-person direction to a human.
Job postings require monitors to help children get on and off at the right stops in a safe, orderly way, using in-person supervision and behavior management of minors.
District procedure: the driver and trained safety monitors physically shut off the engine, set the brake, use extinguishers and supervise unloading of passengers on site.
Bus monitor policy: a monitor near the front takes authority if the driver is injured, shuts off the ignition and keeps passengers calm, which requires being in the bus.
Ohio Admin. Code 3301-83-15 sets out required emergency and evacuation procedures and drills, and only trained personnel may transport pupils.

The Ontario MTO bus handbook says the backing spotter must stand behind the bus where the driver can see them in the mirror. Without a spotter, the driver must leave the bus and check the path. The task requires someone physically there, outside the vehicle.
Industry guidance recommends an adult outside the bus to help with backing. Backup alarms and cameras are presented as extra measures that do not replace that person.

Help for drivers when backing up comes from cameras, mirror monitors and radar sensors built into the bus. These are hardware systems, not general-purpose AI agents that a monitor could reach through software, so an agent cannot see the rear of the bus or signal the driver.
Wendy's FreshAI voice ordering is expanding to up to 600 restaurants and reportedly handled about 86% of drive-thru orders without staff stepping in. The remaining orders were passed to human staff.

A May 2026 vendor blog (a possibly biased source) reports AI drive-thru order accuracy of about 83%, against 87% for human-taken orders, rising to 95% when staff help. Yum!/Taco Bell has used voice AI on millions of orders, and McDonald's ended its pilot over order errors. Human review and correction are still needed.

Square released a quick-service kiosk in October 2026 with a voice layer that understands the menu. Vendors say systems like this send orders to the POS and kitchen display systems and print order numbers or stubs, so no hands-on ticket writing is needed.

Casino AI surveillance systems (EagleSight, Dallmeier, Xsen) already flag past-posting, bet capping, pinching and dealer payout errors. This takes over part of the cheat-spotting work but does not keep the supervisor's own knowledge current; that still needs a human.
At G2E in October 2026, operators such as MGM and Resorts World were using AI and RFID table-game monitoring alongside human staff, not instead of them.

Game-protection training (card counting, past-posting, collusion, chip fraud) is something the human learns, and it sits alongside surveillance training. An AI can gather research and write briefings, but the familiarity has to stay with the licensed floor supervisor.
Cash recyclers in casino cages are hardware that accepts, validates, stores and dispenses cash, and they handle bill breaking. This automation is physical machinery, not a software AI agent.

Glory sells cage recyclers and self-service kiosks that count, authenticate and dispense notes and coins for buy-ins and payouts. Doing this without a person to handle the cash takes dedicated physical hardware.
In this patented cage method, a cashier chooses the denomination and quantity and the recycler dispenses it. Software only sends the order, and handing the cash to the customer stays a physical job.

Regulator-approved totalisator software works out the pool totals, takeout and winning payouts. A Wisconsin rule requires the mutuel manager to produce a daily summary of pari-mutuel operations as the original record of wagering, so most of the compiling is already done by software.

Nevada's race book rules require anyone acting as race book manager or supervisor to register with the Gaming Control Board, so oversight of wagering records is tied to an accountable, registered person.

Nevada Regulation 22 covers how wagers are accepted, how winners are paid and how computerised bookmaking systems are used. Records are produced in approved systems that an agent could only reach if the operator granted access.

Casino accounting systems such as Konami SYNKROS and G+D CashView already automate revenue audit and drop/count reconciliation. One case study says revenue audit went from 4-5 days behind to 24 hours, so the reconciliation sub-steps can be done by software.

Under NIGC MICS (25 CFR 543.17), drop and count must be supervised by an agent with equal or greater authority, and results must be documented. This keeps a human supervisor accountable for the final review and sign-off.
Nevada MICS require supervisors to authorize and document transfers and other accounting steps. Initials do not count as a valid signature, so a named human must attest to the records.

Casino workforce software such as UKG Virtual Roster automatically matches staff to shifts by skill and handles labor-demand forecasting, union rules, labor laws and internal policies. This means the scheduling part of the task can be delegated end to end.

New Jersey requires anyone with supervisory responsibility over casino areas, such as a pit boss or shift manager, to hold a casino key employee license before starting work. Supervisory authority therefore has to sit with a licensed human.
Washington's rules require a licensed floor supervisor for each gambling area. Supervising and evaluating dealers on the floor means being there in person.

InMoment's entertainment and recreation product collects feedback from surveys, social reviews and calls. It uses AI sentiment analysis to pull out themes so teams can act on them, which covers the analysis sub-steps of this task end to end.

Arch Amenities Group uses InMoment's XI Platform and its AI hub to collect and analyze survey and review feedback from gym and spa visits. The goal is location-level insight for improving the customer experience, which shows feedback-to-insight work already being delegated in recreation facilities.

TrustYou uses AI on surveys and reviews from across the web to improve service quality and to help respond to all feedback. Putting the changes into practice with staff and on-site operations is still the supervisor's job.

Camp management platforms such as CampDoc store participants' allergies, medical needs and accommodation details in digital profiles. An agent could pull these together and turn them into staff briefings.

Regpack keeps one profile per camper with health data, forms and group assignments. Group-specific needs are already in systems an agent can reach, which supports end-to-end drafting and sending of briefings.

AI communication and accessibility tools for special-needs populations exist, but no recreation-specific AI product for staff briefings was found. Delivering the briefing in person and judging group sensitivities still rest with the supervisor.

AI onboarding and training tools already draft training modules, keep onboarding consistent across hires, and answer new-hire policy questions around the clock. That covers the explaining-policies part and the preparation of training materials.
AI agents can act as digital coaches that guide frontline workers in real time and personalise their training content. They support the training but do not replace hands-on supervision.

Recreation and aquatics training includes site-specific policy training, skills demonstrations and in-service drills. These need a supervisor present to demonstrate and check the skills, and the training has to be documented.

evidence.fact: Apaleo and THE FLAG use an agentic AI 'Trace Agent' in live hotel operations. It reads reservation comments and creates about 30 housekeeping tasks a day without a person, so routine task creation and dispatch can already be handed to an agent.

Housekeeping tools such as HelloShift learn from past room assignments to assign cleaners automatically, by zone or floor and with checkouts first. Supervisors still handle on-floor problems and changes in real time.

Salon scheduling software matches stylists to services, checks real-time availability and notifies stylists. This covers the scheduling side of coordinating stylists but not in-person direction, coaching or quality checks.

Arterial embalming is done by hand. The worker places the cannula and drainage, injects and massages the fluid, aspirates the cavities, sutures the incisions and disinfects the body. An agent with no body or robotics cannot do any of this.
The full process uses arterial, cavity, hypodermic and surface embalming. All of these are hands-on work on the body, followed by dressing and cosmetic preparation.
US states license embalmers, with requirements such as accredited mortuary-science training and an apprenticeship (Oregon example). This makes embalming a licensed professional activity.

Funeral-home AI chatbots handle logistics and questions about services, pricing and documents, often around the clock, and pass families to staff when needed. They serve as a supportive first contact, not a replacement for human comfort.
A funeral-industry source recommends using AI chatbots for supportive administration rather than counseling. It notes safety limits and that conversations with a chatbot are not confidential.
One funeral home added EverGrace.Ai, a voice chatbot described as empathetic, to help families with early planning. This is a single anecdote from a podcast description.

Retort controls already run temperature and timing through a fully automatic cremation cycle, and some systems allow off-site monitoring and alarms over the internet. Loading the body, opening the door and removing the remains are still done by hand, so software could at most help monitor the cycle and keep records.
Virginia requires anyone operating a crematory retort to hold CANA, ICCFA or another board-recognised certification, and trainees must work under a certified operator.
In South Carolina, a person may not perform cremations before receiving a Crematory Operator Registration, and the crematory must remove all remains from the retort at the end of each cremation.

Processing means attaching a stainless steel drum to the drive unit, taking off the lid, loading the bone fragments by hand and running the blades, which take about 30 seconds or less. Every step is physical.

Before grinding, metal has to be sifted out by hand because the high-speed rotor would be damaged by it. A magnet misses gold, copper and aluminum parts, so the sorting needs hands and eyes on the remains.

Operators move the remains to a tray, run them under a magnet, pick out implants and joints by hand, then put the bone through the processor. A software-only agent with no robotics cannot do any of this.

Florida's standard procedure says that once the cremation finishes, all remains must be taken out and the retort swept clean. The ID tag goes into the recovery tray, and the brushes and tools must be checked for bone fragments. All of this is hands-on work done by the operator.
Remains have traditionally been taken out of the chamber with handled tools such as rakes and brooms. The only automation found is mechanical equipment, not software or AI.
The bone fragments are left to cool and then collected by hand from inside the chamber. The job requires being physically at the cremator.

Vendor comparisons for 2026 list AI agents that generate invoices and run billing, collections and cash application from start to finish. They say these agents check outgoing invoices against customer records and past invoices. These figures come from vendors and have not been independently checked.

Agentic AP/AR platforms in 2026 claim 70-90% of invoices go through with no human touch at scale. This suggests the main sub-steps are already automated, though McKinsey reports that only about 6% of finance functions have scaled AI.

E-invoicing rules usually ask for a digital or qualified electronic signature tied to the issuer, not a human's handwritten one. India, for example, drops the signature requirement for e-invoices, so the law does not require a person to issue each invoice.

Vendor blogs describe AI agents that watch for rule changes, collect evidence, propose edits to policy and procedure documents, send them for review and keep an audit trail. A named person still accepts, changes or rejects each edit. These are vendor claims and have not been checked independently.

Agentic AI tools for managing standard operating procedures are said to draft, update and send out revised procedures when requirements change. A human review step is still recommended. This is also a vendor claim.
One guide says generative AI can do up to 80% of the work of updating policy documents, with a human expert doing the final review. The guide gives no independent evidence for this figure.

GovGuard (a Y Combinator company) says its AI agents search years of city records, flag sensitive information for redaction and draft response letters for staff to review. This suggests humans still review responses before they go out.
Datagrid describes AI agents that handle public records requests end to end: intake, search across systems, redaction, deadline tracking and updates to requesters.

A village ordinance names the clerk-treasurer as records access officer, who must grant or deny requests within five business days and certify true copies or that no record was found after a diligent search.

Onboarding platforms already generate whole training courses, with sections and lessons, from a single topic prompt. That covers the material-drafting part of training without step-by-step human work.

Vendors sell AI agents for government onboarding that claim to produce onboarding materials and track required training and certifications. These are unverified marketing claims, so I read them only as signs of partial automation of coordination.

Guidance on court staff training says role-specific, hands-on instruction and supervision are still delivered by people. In practice, clerks teach judges and colleagues directly, which points to human-led live training and coordination.
Municipalities are moving bid solicitation, receipt and contract management onto e-procurement platforms such as OpenGov, which gives an agent digital access to most of the paperwork.
Public-sector procurement vendors advertise AI-powered features, including automated bid tabulation and compliance support. These are the vendor's own claims, not independent evidence.

Municipal codes require the city clerk or a designee to open bids and publicly read them aloud at a set time and place, which can be done virtually. The award is made by the council, so a human still has to perform and sign off on key steps.

Vendor AP agents already take in invoices, run OCR and line-item extraction, check the data and post it to an ERP, either as a draft for review or with no human touch. This is the same mechanism needed to post a sales slip to a customer's account.

Agent platforms advertised on AWS Marketplace cover the whole chain from intake and OCR through checking to ERP posting. Vendors claim 80–90% of items pass straight through without manual handling, but these figures are not independently verified.

AR agents check extracted billing data and act on it, for example by filling in ERP billing records. If the slips are paper, someone still has to scan them and file the physical copies, which is a hands-on step.

Commercial APIs from vendors such as Middesk, CRS (sourced from LexisNexis) and D&B already return liens, judgments and bankruptcies for underwriting, so the core lookups can be automated. These are vendor marketing pages, not independent checks.

Court-record API coverage is patchy. Cobalt's Court Records API covers only New York State and Miami-Dade County, so some places still need manual searches of county portals or courthouses, and a person has to confirm the records match the right applicant.

The FCRA requires a permissible purpose and reasonable procedures for maximum possible accuracy, especially for criminal records. These sources did not show any law requiring a human to do the search or sign it, but mistakes create liability, which supports a human review step.

Central issuance software takes card requests from the bank's card management system and sends print jobs to card printers in branches. The data and job steps are digital and an agent could do them, but the printing itself happens on local hardware.

Instant issuance covers data preparation, magnetic stripe encoding, embossing, and chip or contactless personalization. Data preparation can be automated, but embossing and encoding produce a physical card.

Vericast's SaaS platform personalizes EMV chip and dual-interface cards in the branch in about a minute. A person still has to load card stock, take out the finished card, inspect it and hand it over or mail it.

Voice and chat AI agents in 2026 take first notice of loss, check coverage, send out assessors or contractors and update claimants. Vendors report that 45–65% of interactions are resolved without a human, and that agents hand coverage disputes back to people.
In April 2026 Hippo rolled out Clara, an AI voice agent for first notice of loss. Hippo expects more than 70% of homeowners claims to be filed digitally as a result.

Staff without an insurance licence may give routine, clerical and claims-processing help. They may not sell, negotiate or advise, so giving limited claim instructions does not usually require a licensed human.

Policy administration workflows already sort each termination by type (client-requested, insurer-initiated, non-payment, cooling-off), produce the matching communications and update the policy record at each step. This is the core of notifying the parties involved.

InsuredMine, an agency CRM, has cancellation workflow automation that tags cancelled policies with a cancellation date and sends notifications by email, text or task. Its knowledge-base page is vendor release notes, not an independent source.

A vendor guide from 2026 (marketing material, with no cancellation-specific metrics) says AI agents handle policy servicing: they process policy changes and deliver documents through software alone, with no physical step. The notices to the agent and accounting are internal messages; statutory cancellation notices go to the insured, so no licensed human signature is needed.
Duck Creek launched Agentic FNOL in Sept 2026. It uses coordinated AI agents to process claims information from digital, mobile and voice channels, targeting manual entry and incomplete data.

Vendor guides describe AI agents that capture loss details, look up policies, and open and update real claim records in core systems such as Guidewire, Duck Creek and Snapsheet. Coverage decisions are left to licensed adjusters. These are vendor claims, not independent measurements.

A 2008 New York DFS legal opinion treats data entry and processing as ministerial work that needs no adjuster license. Only discretionary acts such as loss evaluation and payment authorization require one. Rules vary by state.

FarmKeep lets a manager assign chores such as feeding animals and cleaning water troughs to farm members, set up recurring routines and track them in calendar, list or kanban views. This is the digital core of the task, which an agent could run end to end.

Farmbrite supports team schedules, task-assignment notifications and tracking tasks for individual livestock. An agent could build and send rosters from goal specifications, but someone still has to check animal condition and crew availability on site.

AgriWebb pushes planned livestock tasks and feed records to workers' mobile task lists, so assignments can be fully digital where the crew uses the app. Many farm crews are still directed verbally at the barn.

Commercial aquaculture farm-management platforms keep a daily fish or shrimp inventory with egg-to-harvest traceability tied to regulatory reporting. That means an agent could do the record-keeping, reconciliation and reporting digitally.

ERP and Odoo aquaculture modules link fish batches from hatchery to dispatch, along with harvest grading, stock entries and sales invoices. Records of fish sold and shipped can therefore be generated automatically from transaction data.

State rules require stocking receipts listing date, species, length and number stocked, signed and dated by the hatchery. The counts come from physical observation on site, and a human signature is needed, but the rules do not require a licensed professional.

Camera-based AI that detects missing PPE and people in risk zones exists, but the agribusiness deployment found used existing CCTV in fixed grain-handling areas. The vineyard field study was only a preliminary image-based study, and no forestry tools turned up. That means open-field, remote crews mostly have no camera coverage an agent could watch.

Under OSHA, the employer that directs and controls the workers is responsible for their safety. That employer must get workers to comply and can discipline them, and fines fall on the employer, not the employee.

A model logging safety program requires a competent supervisor on each jobsite with authority to enforce the safety program. Violations can lead to discipline or termination, so a human with on-site authority is expected to give warnings and discipline.

Herd-I's commercial dairy system films each cow as she leaves the milking shed and uses cloud models trained by veterinary experts to score lameness and send dashboard alerts. This covers only one narrow part of the task and needs camera hardware installed on the farm.

A Queensland government prototype camera system for beef cattle is being trained to alert producers to injuries, lameness or emergency disease symptoms. It was still in development, not widely deployed.

University research on gait images from depth cameras reports detecting dairy-cow lameness with 99% or higher accuracy. Lameness is the most developed use case, and wider detection of illness and unusual behavior still mostly depends on in-person observation in barns, pens and pastures.

Ace Aquatec's A-BIOMASS uses AI with underwater cameras to measure salmon size and track growth in real time. Its A-HARVESTCAM estimates weight, weight distribution and quality on harvest lines. These need dedicated hardware installed at the site.

Roboflow's vision AI counts fish, estimates their length and weight, and detects sea lice, lesions and fin damage from stereo and mono cameras on an edge device, then sends results to farm systems through an API. An agent could analyze this output, but only where cameras are already installed.

Fraunhofer's image-based monitoring picks out individual fish in dense schools and measures their length and volume in tanks and net pens. It needs underwater cameras in place. Without them, a person has to observe the fish, beds and ponds in person.

OSHA's logging standard 29 CFR 1910.266 has its own training section. As I understand it, that section requires a qualified person to train workers, including on-the-job, and to certify the training. My searches showed the standard has a training section but did not return its text, so this detail is my reading and is not quoted here.

OSHA's eTool checklists for chain saws and felling are keyed to 1910.266(e) and (h). They cover physical field practices such as planning a retreat path while the tree falls, which are taught at the work site.

Digital forestry training exists as VR hazard-recognition simulators (for example Mills Skills VR, Scion and harvester simulators). I found no evidence of generative AI or an autonomous agent delivering hands-on felling or machine-operation training.
AI livestock tools such as Gau Swastha, Betty and Jaguza only suggest likely diagnoses and treatment protocols from photos, questionnaires or sensors. Farmers or vets still carry out the treatment.
On-farm treatment plans have caretakers follow the veterinarian's or the label's directions. Staff trained on SOPs physically give the drugs to the animals.
Prescription animal drugs can be used or dispensed only within a valid veterinarian-client-patient relationship, so a licensed vet has to authorize the treatment.

Digital training in aquaculture is mostly VR simulation. One fish-farm VR and photogrammetry project stopped at proof-of-concept and said the technology 'requires further development'. That means hands-on training is still mostly done in person, though an agent could write the materials.

Under OSHA, employers must train tractor and farm-equipment operators when they start the job and at least once a year after that, on safe operating practices. The source I found does not say a licensed trainer is needed. However, the training covers equipment on the farm, which points to in-person demonstration.

University farm safety programs require supervisors to keep records of training dates, the trainer, the topics covered and the equipment each worker is certified to run. An agent could do this kind of paperwork, but the practical training and certification happen on site.

Under EPA's Worker Protection Standard, pesticide safety training must use EPA-approved materials. It must be given by a qualified trainer, such as a certified applicator or someone who completed an EPA-approved train-the-trainer course, before workers enter treated areas and again every 12 months. Records must be kept for 2 years.
The EPA's training checklists cover worker and handler topics, including the Application Exclusion Zone. The delivery format is a person presenting to workers, not standalone software.

AI video tools such as HeyGen and Miraflow can generate multilingual farm safety and crop-management training videos. This covers the materials-preparation part of the task, but not the hands-on field demonstration of planting, harvesting or insect identification.

2026 AI agents (Intelinair AGMRI, GROWMARK myFS Agronomy) combine field-level soil, weather, imagery, input-application and yield data to support decisions on nitrogen timing, fungicide use and replanting. GROWMARK says its agent is meant to support crop specialists, not replace them.
The Taranis Ag Assistant is a generative AI tool that draws on in-season crop intelligence, weather maps, machinery data and university research to give agronomic answers to producers.

In California, anyone recommending agricultural pesticide use needs a PCA licence. Property operators and their employees making recommendations for land they control are exempt, so an internal discussion between a supervisor and managers does not require a licensed human signature.

Trimble CFHarvest is web and mobile software that sends work instructions, schedules and resource updates to harvesting crews' devices. An agent could draft and send this kind of written, scheduled communication.

Remsoft Operations, used at Forico, offers drag-and-drop crew scheduling. Forico reports it cut scheduling time by about 50%, a figure that comes from the vendor. This shows plan and schedule communication is already largely digital.

NZQA standards for crew foremen say the operational plan should be passed to the crew at a pre-start meeting on site. WorkSafe NZ also reviews daily tailgate meetings. This in-person part needs a human on site.

Landus SkyScout flies fixed-wing aircraft and drones over fields every 12 days and uses AI to flag low emergence, weed pressure, stress, nutrient deficiency and disease. Landus agronomists review each scan before it becomes a recommendation, so a human still makes the decision.

In Taranis-style scouting, drone operators collect leaf-level images in the field. The AI detects weeds, disease and insects and suggests actions, but the farmer or agronomist makes the in-season management decision.
A 2024 GRDC paper calls autonomous agronomy (drone-in-a-box scouting, language-model recommendations) emerging but not yet established, and agronomists remain central to the work.

Crew-and-equipment dispatch software such as B2W Schedule has an 'Equipment Move Planner' that sends text and email notices to drivers and transport crews. This shows the planning, scheduling and messaging parts of the task can be done entirely in software, which an agent could run end to end.
Farm labor scheduling tools handle crew transport to remote fields and shift timing. They only coordinate logistics. The supervisor still directs the dismantling and setup on site.

No-code farm tools build scheduling, equipment tracking and field logs from general parts. No product we found automates the on-site physical work of taking equipment apart and setting it up again, which still needs a person there.

Sawmill software such as Tally-I/O tracks log and lumber inventory, production and yard management with barcode scanning. An agent could use these records to match logs in storage to production needs and transport schedules, then send out the selection and movement plan.
Yard and dock scheduling systems let dispatchers plan loading and unloading against shipments and yard space, and let carriers book appointments. This covers the scheduling part of the task.

No product turned up for log merchandising, meaning checking log grade, condition and species on site. Log-yard records are often patchy, and the loader operators have to be directed in the yard. So a human is still needed on the ground to confirm the selection and supervise the moves, and no law or licence requires a human sign-off.

Farm scheduling products such as FieldClock already do job-based crew scheduling and piece-rate tracking. One 2026 review says FieldClock's schedule shows the work but not which worker is doing it, and it sends no notices when plans change, so a person still assigns crews and passes on changes.
Vendors are marketing AI agents that catch crew and equipment conflicts across several fields. The figures they publish look like demo output, not measured results.

Good farm scheduling has to account for weather, crop growth stages and whether equipment is available. That information often comes from what the supervisor sees in the field and from talking with crew leads, not from systems an agent can reach.

Driverless tractors such as John Deere's autonomous 8R/9RX tillage system rely on machine-mounted cameras, GPS and the vehicle's own robotic hardware, started and monitored from the Operations Center app. That is physical robotics, not the software-only agent this rating assumes. A software agent could at most help with route or field planning.

Driving a truck or tractor on public roads requires a licensed human driver. Farm vehicle operators still need a valid driver's license, though states may waive the CDL requirement under 49 CFR 383.3(d).

John Deere's autonomous tractor is a dedicated robotic machine controlled through a smartphone app, with live video and metrics. It cannot be done by a general-purpose software agent working only through digital systems.

Farm platforms such as QuickBooks, Xero and farm-specific suites are becoming more autonomous. Tend sells one AI-driven platform for crop planning, sales, accounting and inventory, so agents can carry out accounting and sales sub-steps end to end.

Farm Focus put an AI agent ('Daisy', built on Salesforce Agentforce) into service for about 10,000 farm customers, covering CRM and marketing workflows. This shows marketing and customer management can be delegated in part.

H-2A job orders show that personnel work for farm supervisors is done in person: directing crews, giving warnings and discipline, safety training, and transport that needs a Farm Labor Contractor license. Employers must take responsibility for licensing and compliance, so this part depends on human trust and a person who signs.

Livestock transport management systems such as Tracx and AMCS Livestock Planner already schedule, dispatch and re-plan loads, track species welfare transit limits, and take transport requests through portals. That means the 'arrange for transport' part can be handled digitally.

Hauling livestock requires a human driver working under FMCSA hours-of-service rules, with agricultural exemptions. Loading animals, equipment and feed and driving them to work sites are physical jobs an agent without a body cannot do. The rules govern the drivers, so they do not require a human to make the arrangements.

Dispatch tools for livestock and feed haulers include driver apps, GPS tracking and ETA notifications. An agent with access could book carriers and coordinate logistics, but farm supervisors often move supplies themselves on informal or offline systems.

No-code AI platforms such as FlyPix analyze satellite, aerial and drone images. They flag stress and anomaly hotspots, weeds, pests and gaps in crop stands, and produce geolocated scouting points and walking routes. This speeds up field inspection, but a person still has to collect the imagery and check the findings on the ground.

Drone Ag's Skippy Scout app runs AI analysis on drone photos to report green area index, crop cover and weed percentage. The farmer has to fly the drone, so field inspection is only partly digitized and still depends on someone being there.

Tools that interpret drone imagery are reported to be about 10 times faster than walking crops. They cover crop fields, not checks of buildings, fences, supplies or equipment, which still need someone on site to look and handle things.
Nursery management software (Tend) says it lets growers build production plans and automatically sync inventory updates with the crop plan and customer orders.
Mprise Agriware's ERP for growers advertises AI (Copilot) that generates orders and automates sales-order entry.

Folio3's nursery software claims to assign, track and optimize field and greenhouse tasks by crop stage, crew and work zone. An agent can turn orders and inventory into a task list, but a supervisor still has to check it against crop readiness, weather and crew that day.

Vendors say drone and computer-vision software can find anomalies and assess damage in imagery, but a person or robot has to capture the imagery on site first. The agent only analyzes what it is given.

One pre-seed startup builds drone and software systems that analyze aerial images of farms and infrastructure. This is narrow vendor tooling, not a general agent that can walk through barns, grain bins, irrigation systems or equipment.

AI drone inspections can flag problems in infrastructure, but the evidence comes from vendor and industry-blog material without independent accuracy checks. For farm buildings, a human still has to look, touch and test things in person.

AI planning agents in farm platforms such as Granular and Trimble Ag can weigh field readiness, equipment availability and storage capacity to suggest harvest windows and logistics. That covers the prep work for the meeting, but the meeting itself is still between people.

In 2026, agentic AI in agriculture is mostly used for field operations, fertility prescriptions and directing autonomous equipment. No product was found that handles the supervisor-manager talks on labor schedules or production requirements.
Even with growing interest in AI for farm workforce management, there is still a clear gap between the tools on offer and what farms actually use.

Farm timekeeping software already handles the crew-level time data. Croptracker's Punch Clock groups workers into crews with crew leaders and produces pay and cost reports by crew, person or activity. Its records are also used for performance reviews, but the reviews themselves are rule-based and no AI agent writes them.

Farm payroll services such as OnPay and Netchex already process payroll for W-2, 1099 and H-2A agricultural workers, so an agent can compile and run the payroll reports. Evaluations, discipline and hiring decisions still depend on what the supervisor saw in the field, and a human has to review and approve them.

H-2A employers must keep records of each worker's earnings, hours offered and worked, and work locations for 3 years. The rule is about keeping the records, not about who prepares them. Secondary sources describe this rule, and it does not explicitly require a human to prepare or sign the reports.

Agents for food and supply-chain buying (Instacart's agentic checkout, Infios supply-chain agents) already handle cart building and purchase orders within set rules. Agents built specifically for buying farm supplies are mostly still forecasts.

Under federal rules, only certified applicators or people they directly supervise may buy restricted-use pesticides, and dealers may not sell them to anyone uncertified. So insecticide purchases often need a licensed human buyer.
Some states go further. Kansas requires private applicator certification to buy restricted-use pesticides, and Wisconsin allows no supervisory exemptions.

AI progress-monitoring tools (DroneDeploy Progress AI, OpenSpace, Buildots) read drone and 360° site imagery and compare it with the schedule. They depend on someone in the field capturing that imagery, so an agent can help with tracking but cannot do the on-site oversight.

Irrigation installs need on-site inspections, operational demonstrations and as-built checks. A licensed irrigator signs, dates and seals the completion certificate. That licence duty falls on the installer, not the farm supervisor.
From 2026, San Antonio's water utility (SAWS) requires a licensed person to supervise new irrigation installs and inspects each one on site. Physical presence is central to this kind of oversight.

Equipment checkout software for agricultural clients records inspections and signatures at each check-in and check-out. Software handles the logging, but a person still has to hand over and take back the equipment.
Tool crib systems record which worker took which tool and when it is due back, using barcodes on both tools and employees. Scanning and handover are still done in person.

Tool crib software can check out tools against a specific technician's work assignments, so an AI could plan the issue lists and track returns. It cannot move or inspect physical implements, ladders or containers.

Farm safety SaaS (Safe Ag Systems) digitizes the paperwork side of this task: training records with expiry alerts, risk assessments, incident reporting and compliance audits. Spotting hazards in the field and fixing them is still left to human supervisors.

AI camera safety monitoring (e.g., OpenBlue Worker Safety Advisor) runs on existing CCTV and is aimed at industrial, oil and gas, and construction sites, not open fields, forests or boats. Agricultural options such as AirAgri cover mainly lone-worker IoT alerts.

Under the Worker Protection Standard, agricultural employers must instruct supervisors on which protection duties they are responsible for. OSHA's field sanitation rule and General Duty Clause put responsibility for on-site compliance on the employer and the supervisor.

FieldClock and similar farm labor tools already handle crew scheduling, attendance and piecework tracking. One review notes that FieldClock's schedule shows what work needs doing but not which workers are assigned, so the supervisor still has to make the assignments.
Toolhouse markets an AI agent that reviews harvest schedules and flags crew or equipment conflicts. This shows agents can take on key sub-steps, although the vendor shows no independent results.

Agriculture workforce software generates schedules from worker availability and skills and says it adjusts them for weather and crop cycles. Real crew and equipment availability is still often known only informally on the farm, which limits what an agent can reach.

Transplanting and potting are automated only with dedicated physical machinery, such as vacuum or gripper transplanters and mobile robots that move container-grown plants. A software-only AI agent cannot do this work.
Patents for automatic transplanting describe physically moving plugs and seedlings from one container to another. The task is mainly hand work with plants and soil.
Patents describe autonomous mobile robots that carry container-grown plants to stations for re-potting, grading and sorting. Robotics is required, which the reference agent does not have.
Fruit-picking robots such as Fieldwork Robotics' raspberry harvester are still on commercial-farm trials. Fleets are only expected from 2027, and they are physical robots, not software agents.
Commercial robotic harvesting is only now moving from pilots into early scaling, mostly in berries and apples. Hand harvesting is still a physical field job.
Washington's tree-fruit industry expected it to take 5 to 10 years before growers could hire a robotic apple harvester. This is an older source, so the timeline may be out of date.

A Department of Labor seasonal job posting for this occupation (SOC 45-2092) lists 'clean work areas and maintain grounds and landscaping' among duties that are manual, done with hand tools, and include moving pots and flats of up to 50 lb.

O*NET describes the occupation as manual planting, cultivating and harvesting with hand tools. It points to a separate occupation, Landscaping and Groundskeeping Workers, for grounds upkeep. Both are physical, on-site work.

Autonomous commercial mowers such as the Husqvarna Automower 560 EPOS (2026) are robots, which fall outside the reference technology. A software agent could at most schedule or monitor them, which is a negligible share of the task.

AI agent templates already take plant orders from start to finish: they help customers pick plants, take payment and collect delivery details. That covers the digital selling step. Loading plants and handing them over still needs a person.

An online garden center put an AI agent on its repetitive customer questions about delivery costs and times. The vendor claims this saved about one full-time employee, a figure that has not been independently checked.
States require a nursery or plant dealer license to sell rooted plants. The license belongs to the business, not to the worker, so no human has to sign off on each sale or delivery.

In Wageningen's Autonomous Greenhouse Challenge, teams' AI algorithms set climate setpoints remotely, and a climate and irrigation process computer ran the actuators. In the cherry tomato trial, all AI-supported teams outperformed a greenhouse run by human growers. This shows setpoint control can be delegated where the greenhouse already has automated actuators.

Commercial controllers such as GrowDirector advertise AI software that runs climate control, irrigation/fertigation and EC/pH dosing through dry-contact relays, with app-based monitoring and control. This is vendor marketing, not independent performance data.

Cloud systems such as Click2Cloud's Greenhouse Pilot say they automate climate, humidity, lighting and irrigation for small growers. But for a crop laborer, the task also includes manually opening vents, adjusting valves and moving hoses, which needs a person on site.

Commercial greenhouse control software, such as AgriLogiq's ZoneLogiq, already handles climate and irrigation control, real-time alerts and remote monitoring. That covers the digital side: diagnosing faults and adjusting setpoints. The physical repair still has to be done by a person.
In farmworker job postings, irrigation repair means hands-on work in the field, such as replacing sprinkler heads and drive chains. An agent with no body cannot do this.
Texas requires a license to repair irrigation systems, but it exempts work on commercial agricultural irrigation systems. No licence barrier was found for farmworkers doing this repair.

Farm management software such as Croptracker already records spray applications by block, tracks chemical inventory and costs, and logs harvest yields by block and commodity. An agent could fill in these records and analyse them from data a worker provides.

Federal rules for restricted-use pesticides (7 CFR 110) require the certified private applicator to keep a record within 14 days. The record covers product, EPA registration number, quantity, date and location. The applicator is responsible for the record, but the law does not require a human to physically write it.

The source data, such as what was sprayed, how much, where and what was harvested, comes from physical field work and observation. A human or a sensor still has to capture it before an agent can record it.

O*NET lists mending fences and farm buildings as part of this occupation's work. A DOL H-2A posting for this job says workers repair buildings, fences and other structures by hand with tools such as shovels, trowels, hoes and tampers.
The H-2A job posting lists repairing farm buildings, fences and other structures as a hands-on field duty.

There are autonomous robots that inspect fences, but none were found that repair them. Since a software-only agent has no body, it could only help with small parts like looking up materials or repair methods.

Getting a cold frame ready means digging out topsoil by hand, sifting it through wire screen to remove grass and rocks, loosening the subsoil with a pitchfork and working in compost. All of this is manual work done on site.
Hotbeds heated with manure are dug 16 to 24 inches deep and cold frames 6 to 15 inches deep. The pit is filled with manure and then about a foot of soil, which also requires physical labor.

Before sowing, the soil surface is raked and leveled and weeds are removed. The only parts that can be done digitally, such as looking up soil mixes or temperature guidance, are a tiny share of the working time.

Machine-vision plant grading exists only as dedicated machines that have cameras and sorting mechanics, such as Carnegie Mellon's strawberry plant grader and the patented bin-to-bin sorter. A software-only agent has no body to handle plants or check bud ties in the field.

Commercial AI vision systems like Aris grade potted plants on health, size, shape, colour and defects. They need fixed camera hardware installed in the facility, so an agent could at most review images a human or a machine has already captured.

Human grading of nursery seedlings is subjective, with no consensus on about 1 in 4 trees. This suggests AI could help as a second opinion on photos, but a person still has to do the physical inspection.
Bunching flowers is automated only by dedicated hardware, not by software AI agents. Bercomex sells machines that cut, count, bunch and bind stems.
Bercomex says its Furora Nova line sorts and bunches cut flowers fully automatically using a physical processing line. This automation depends on robotics and machinery, not on a software agent.
Packing bouquets into boxes, including taping or wrapping the stems, needs physical equipment such as conveyors, drop mechanisms and taping machines, as described in a US patent.

Autonomous nursery work is done by dedicated robots, not software agents. The first commercial machine went to a Swedish nursery in late 2025 and is doing border spraying in 2026; that spraying was previously done by hand. A software-only AI agent cannot do this physical work.
Robotic weeding for nursery seedling beds, such as the University of Idaho prototype, is still years from commercial production. Planting, weeding and pruning remain hands-on work done with tools.

Restricted-use pesticides may only be applied by a certified applicator or someone under their direct supervision. Routine planting, watering, weeding and pruning need no licence, so this applies only to part of the spraying.

Cellular trap sensors such as the Skyhawk Trapmate send an alert to a phone when a trap is triggered. They only send the alert. Someone still has to go to the trap, remove the catch and reset or move it.

In a field trial on dingo foot-hold traps, a satellite or cellular trap-alert system reported 91% of captures. It helps decide which traps to visit but does not do the physical inspection, catch removal or resetting.
Trap-check laws, such as Arizona's daily inspection rule, require the trapper to inspect traps in use. Licensed people handle the inspection, removal of animals and resetting.
onX Hunt's private-land data usually lists the landowner's name, mailing address and property boundaries. An agent could do the research step of finding who to contact.

Online permission forms, such as Typeform's template, collect the hunter's details, dates and a liability acknowledgment, and can be sent by email or link. An agent could draft them and handle the paperwork.

In Tennessee, the landowner issues the written permission slip and the hunter carries it. The landowner is the one who signs, so no law requires the hunter to sign anything personally. Getting a yes still depends mostly on building trust with the landowner, often face to face.

Software such as onX Hunt only supports the trip. It offers offline GPS maps, land-ownership layers, trails, waypoints and track recording, but a human still has to walk, drive, boat or ski to the hunting area.
onX navigation (GPS, compass mode, tracker) assists a hunter who is physically travelling through unfamiliar terrain, so the help is limited to planning and wayfinding.

Phone apps can download offline maps up to about 150 miles wide for areas with no coverage, but they don't move the person. The task itself is physical travel by foot, vehicle, boat, snowmobile or skis.

Dedicated marine autopilot and autonomy systems, such as Robosys VOYAGER AI SMARTPILOT (waypoint tracking, route following, collision avoidance) and Simrad AutoCaptain, already handle some steering. But they are built-in onboard systems. Simrad AutoCaptain is described as an assisted system that helps the operator, so a human still runs the boat. A general software AI agent would only help with planning routes and reading charts, weather and AIS data.
Simrad AutoCaptain, shown at CES 2026, is an assisted system for docking, low-speed maneuvering and route planning. The operator stays in charge.

Navigation watches on larger fishing vessels are expected to include a licensed deck officer and a lookout. In Washington State this is a voluntary standard for vessels of 300 gross tons and up, not a confirmed federal rule. The person in charge of the vessel answers for its safe navigation.
Pelts are stretched and dried by hand on wire frames or wooden boards. They have to be centered and held under light tension, with pins, tacks or the stretcher's arms, all done physically.
Preparing a pelt involves skinning, turning it fur-side in or out depending on the species, tacking the legs and lips, and stuffing the paws. All of these are manual knife and hand steps.
The only automated stretching is done by industrial pelt-board machines for farmed mink, which are robots, not software agents. Trappers stretch pelts by hand.
Maintaining traps is hands-on work. Traps are boiled, dyed and waxed, then the dog and pan notch are filed down. Baseplates, springs, chains and swivels are inspected and repaired by hand.
Lobstermen do off-season 'gear work' on their traps: they build new ones, replace worn parts and fix doors, bait bags and broken laths. All of this is physical work on the traps.

Regulations set some trap features, such as breakaway or bio-vent panels that corrode open. They do not require a licensed person to do or sign off on repairs. The software-only part is limited to looking up specs or rules and ordering parts.
In fleshing, the worker drapes the raw pelt over a fleshing beam and pushes fat and meat off with a fleshing knife. It is hands-on manual work with sharp tools, which a software-only agent cannot do.

Trapper-education guides describe fleshing as a physical skill: the knife is used with the right pressure so it doesn't expose hair roots, and all fat has to come off to prevent grease burn. A person has to handle the pelt directly.

State wildlife guidance on processing fur covers skinning and fleshing by hand with knives or draw knives. It names no software or automated digital tool for this step, and no licence is needed for the scraping itself.
Fishing hands cast and lower nets, pots, lines and traps into the water, attach running gear and bait, and set lines into position by hand on deck.
Longline deployment is done on deck with machinery, under a supervisor's instructions, using floats, dan poles and weights so the gear does not foul. This is physical seamanship work.

Automatic baiting and setting machines such as Mustad Autoline are vessel-mounted mechanical systems that crew run on board. They are not software agents, so a non-embodied AI agent cannot do the deployment.

O*NET lists 'Maintain engines, fishing gear, and other on-board equipment and perform minor repairs' as a core task of Fishing and Hunting Workers. Career guides say it covers hands-on work such as mending nets, replacing lines and doing basic engine checks on board.

AI marine engine diagnostic and predictive-maintenance tools exist, such as ioCurrents MarineInsight and Yanmar SHIPSWEB. They flag faults and suggest maintenance from sensor data, but they need onboard data connections and crew to do the physical repairs.
Yanmar SHIPSWEB offers chatbot help and engine diagnosis for vessels, which supports troubleshooting, not the repair itself.

Camera and machine-learning systems that measure fish length on board (iObserver, CatchMeter, NOAA's camera chute, UMass discard chute, CatchCam) are mostly research or pilot monitoring tools. They measure fish only after a human or a conveyor has handled them. None of them removes catch from fishing gear, which a software-only agent cannot do anyway.
Measuring fish and estimating their size from images on board needs dedicated chutes or conveyors with cameras: physical equipment that a general AI agent would not normally have access to.

Size rules require undersize fish or crustaceans to be released immediately and, as far as possible, alive. That is physical work done at the gear while it is being hauled. The law sets what must happen to the fish but does not require a licensed human to do the measuring.

Kongsberg and Viam's Sonar AI works with Simrad fishing sonars such as the SY60. It watches sonar data streams on its own, detects fish automatically, alerts captains and crews when targets appear, and logs fishing activity.

Furuno commercial sonars (FSV-85 Mk2, CSH10) can lock onto a school and track it automatically, and can estimate a school's size and density. A human usually has to pick the target first, and the crew still steers the vessel and runs the equipment on board.
AI species classification from echosounder data is still at the research stage. AZTI's tool reaches about 63.5-80% accuracy on pelagic schools, so a human still has to check what it finds.

M-44 sodium cyanide is a restricted-use pesticide. Users must be trained and certified, warning signs must be posted at the application site, and residents within half a mile must be told in person or by a door tag. That means a licensed human has to carry it out, and some steps are physical.
