Some state wildlife agencies, such as Georgia DNR and New Jersey, now let people apply for trapping licences and permits online. An agent could fill in and submit those forms digitally.
Massachusetts trap registration uses a mail-in paper application, and the registration number has to be marked on each trap. Some approval steps are on paper or physical.

Garmin chartplotters already plan routes automatically. Auto Guidance builds a path from vessel settings and chart data, and a connected autopilot can follow it. Garmin warns that this does not ensure clearance from obstacles or the bottom, so a human still has to check the route.

Under the STCW-F Convention, every officer in charge of a navigational watch on a fishing vessel of 24 m or more in unlimited waters must hold a certificate. The skipper must ensure the watch arrangements are safe. Legal responsibility for navigation therefore stays with a certified human on board.
STCW-F is the IMO treaty that sets certification and training standards for crews of seagoing fishing vessels. The Code was revised by Resolution MSC.562(108) in 2024.

Software only monitors traps after they have been set: cellular or LoRaWAN devices report when a trap closes, and some use AI to identify the species caught. Choosing, baiting and setting the traps and laying the poison on trails is still physical work done by people in the field.
Wildlife toxicants such as 1080 and strychnine need a state permit plus pesticide applicator certification. In the US, restricted-use pesticides require a certified applicator under 40 CFR 171.
About 23 US states require a wildlife control operator license, and the Canadian job bank says a provincial pesticide applicator licence is required in all provinces.
Alaska's seafood harvesting career guide lists attaching nets, slings, hooks and other lifting devices to cables, booms and hoists as a hands-on deckhand duty on fishing vessels.

A U.S. Department of Labor seasonal job posting describes deckhands attaching nets, slings, hooks, blades or lifting devices to cables, booms, hoists or dredges. This is physical rigging work done on deck.

A Department of Labor shrimp and oyster vessel posting describes attaching and detaching apparatus devices to cable, boom, hoists, lines and nets. The work is manual and done on board, and software-only agents cannot do it.

USDA APHIS Wildlife Services' damage control and disease work is done in the field: trapping, sampling wild birds for avian influenza and other surveillance, and sending people to sites within 48 hours. The 2005 directive bases this work on the Act of March 2, 1931.
Field deployments for disease response add up to thousands of person-days, such as 1400 deployed days for HPAI and over 2000 for ASF. That work needs a person physically present and handling animals.

Software tools like ClassifyMe and TrapTagger already classify camera-trap images, filter out empty frames and write detection reports. This covers only the digital data-processing part of the research work.

Fish reach processors and buyers by physical means: pick-up trucks, boats, lorries, refrigerated trucks, reefer containers and air. Keeping the cold chain intact in transit is a physical job, not a software one.
Fishers who deliver direct need their own refrigerated van to transport the catch, so the core of the task is driving and handling the fish.

The digital side of a delivery (landing reports and fish tickets in eLandings) is mostly done by the receiving processor. The tickets are printed for signature, so this leaves only a small paperwork share an agent could help with.

Weathernews' SeaNavigator for Master is an onboard AI tool for ship captains. It reads wave and wind forecasts, grounding risk and route simulations, and suggests route changes. A human meteorologist still checks its suggestions in fast-changing storms, and the sources show no use in fishing fleets.

SOLAS Regulation 34-1 and ISM Code section 5.2 give the master overriding authority and responsibility for safety decisions, including how to handle heavy weather. Commercial weather routeing advice does not replace the master's decision.

Heavy-weather practice expects the master to change course and speed as good seamanship requires, based on what is observed on board. Judging the vessel's condition means being physically present to watch sea state, stability, icing and gear.

To transfer an animal, the trapper lines up a sliding-door transfer cage with the trap's release door, pulls the door up, then closes and latches it once the animal has moved across. This is all physical handling.
Releasing or handling trapped animals means wearing heavy gloves, covering the cage, and holding or carrying the animal, so someone has to be there in person.
Guidance for birds caught in multi-catch cages has the handler go into the cage with gloves and a towel, then hold the bird by its body and legs to release it.

The Idaho trapper course tells trappers to kill trapped animals in person, with a .22 firearm or a small club struck at the base of the skull. Both methods mean being physically at the trap and handling the animal or a weapon, which a software-only agent cannot do.

Washington requires trapped wild animals to be killed or released immediately. Anyone buying a trapping license for the first time must pass an exam on humane trapping technique, so the person doing the trapping must be a licensed human.

Wisconsin requires live furbearers taken in season to be released unharmed or killed immediately. California bill analysis says animals should be shot where permitted and bars drowning, chest crushing and non-euthanasia chemicals, which shows the methods themselves are regulated.
Deckhands wash vessel decks by hand with high-pressure hoses and brushes, using marine soap to remove mud and biofouling. This is physical work done on board.
Processing surfaces and equipment on fishing vessels have to be cleaned and sanitized every day, and ice holds after each fishing period. This means physically handling the equipment on the boat.
OSHA treats deck housekeeping and the safe handling of cleaning chemicals as hands-on crew practices for preventing injuries. It describes no software role in doing the cleaning.

Maine requires trap/pot gear to carry physical colored marks on buoy lines (for example 4 purple and 1 green in federal waters, with both trawl ends marked) and weak links of 600 lb or less on buoys. The worker has to attach these by hand on the boat or dock.

Massachusetts requires a solid red mark at least 3 ft long in the surface system and red marks no more than 60 ft apart along the line, with breaking-strength limits. The job is rigging rope, floats and weights by hand. Software can only look up the rules.

The rules are about how gear is built and marked, not about having a licensed person sign off. Any crew member can attach the accessories. The real obstacle for AI is the physical work, which a software-only agent cannot do.

Guiding is mostly done in the field: the guide leads clients through terrain, shows them stalking, calling and shooting techniques, and keeps them safe. In many jurisdictions anyone guiding for pay must be a licensed human who meets age and first aid/CPR requirements, passes a background check and a written law exam, and is sponsored by an outfitter.
Montana's Board of Outfitters requires guides to be licensed, hold current first aid certification and be sponsored by a licensed outfitter.

Existing AI tools only help with background learning, such as IHEA's experimental Scout assistant for hunting regulations and apps that recommend strategy. They do not teach in the field, so the parts an agent could take over are mainly prep materials and answering questions.

An Alaska state description of fishing deckhand work says deckhands attach nets, slings, hooks and other lifting devices to cables, booms and hoists. They load equipment and supplies by hand or with hoisting equipment and signal coworkers to position the loads. All of this is physical work on the vessel.

Seasonal fishing job postings from the U.S. Department of Labor list loading and unloading equipment, catch and supplies at the start and end of each day. The work includes attaching gear to the cable, boom and hoist and lifting up to 100 lb.

A crab deckhand posting includes loading and unloading supplies and offloading product among the duties. It says some boats may require crane operator certification, and gear such as crab pots can weigh 850-1150 lb. No software can stand in for this hands-on handling. The most an agent could add is small planning help, such as supply checklists.

AI on fishing vessels in 2026 does only digital support work, such as reviewing electronic-monitoring video to count catch, and human reviewers still check its results. The harvesting itself is done by hand: diving, dredging, setting traps and working rods and tackle.
Commercial harvest needs fishery-specific federal and state permits held by eligible persons or entities, plus vessel monitoring and logbooks. That ties the work to licensed humans and vessels.

EU projects pairing AI cameras with robotic arms for catch monitoring are still in research (OptiFish, 2024-2028). They involve robotics, which the reference agents do not have, and they monitor the catch rather than harvest it.

AI fishing tools such as Catchwise combine catch history, AIS and ocean conditions to suggest where to fish, and are presented as supporting the skipper's judgment rather than replacing it. Its reported 6% efficiency gain across 3,800 trips comes from the company's own analysis.

ILO Convention C125 says fishing vessels it covers must carry a certificated skipper on board. National rules, such as Denmark's, set certificate-of-competency requirements for the master and the mate.

AI sonar products such as Kongsberg's SYAI on Simrad sonars detect fish, predict their movement and log detections. They are decision aids that run the equipment the crew uses. They do not direct the crew themselves.

Vendor material for 2026 describes procurement AI agents that find a supply shortfall, pick pre-approved vendors, draft purchase orders and send them for approval without step-by-step human input. These are vendor examples, not studies of real deployments.

Maritime software such as Kongsberg K-Fleet Provision and its C-Purchase and C-Spares modules already handles vessel provision ordering, inventory and stock control, and syncs order data between ship and shore.

Marine procurement software such as DNV ShipManager is built to stop over-ordering and stock-outs of spares and stores. Deciding which gear is worn and needs replacing still means someone has to inspect it on board.

Home Depot's AI Blueprint Takeoffs tool (Nov 2025) produces a full material list and quote for single-family projects from plans, but a Pro team reviews the scope before the list is final. That shows the work can be partly delegated with human review.
Commercial AI takeoff tools such as Attentive.ai (vendor claims 98%+ accuracy), Autotakeoff and Beam AI automatically pull material quantities and dimensions from multi-page blueprints.
Most US states do not license carpenters directly, and no licence requires a human to sign off on reading plans or doing material takeoffs.

OSHA 29 CFR 1926.703 says forms must be built, supported, braced and maintained to carry all expected vertical and lateral loads. Erected shoring must be inspected before, during and after the pour, and sills and base plates must be in firm contact with the ground and the form. All of this is physical work and inspection done on site.

Formwork automation is still physical robotics and only semi-automated, for example the DokaXbot Lift and the DoKart 3 table-form mover. That is outside what a software-only AI agent can do. At most, an agent could help look up specs or bracing layouts, which takes up very little of the task's time.
In precast plants, formwork robots run from CAD data place parts automatically. These are physical machines, not software agents.

Cutting, notching and boring framing members for pipes is hands-on work that the code limits: hole diameter at most one-third of joist depth, hole edge at least 5/8 inch from the stud edge, notches no deeper than 25% in bearing studs. A worker has to measure and cut on site with tools. Software can only look up these limits.

Retrofit cutting during re-piping must stay within code limits. Cutting into shear walls may need a building permit, and changes to engineered lumber need manufacturer approval or a registered design professional.
Almost all US states license journeyman and master plumbers, and apprentices work under supervision, so licensed humans must perform plumbing work.

Scan tools now include AI assistants, such as TEXA IDC6 AI Smart Diagnosis. They walk the technician through each diagnostic step and suggest repair paths from validated case data and technical service bulletins (TSBs), but the technician still connects the tool and carries out the tests. This is augmentation, not autonomous troubleshooting.

Bosch is adding a conversational AI assistant to ESI[tronic], previewed for 2026 with rollout in release 2026/4. It cross-checks live vehicle diagnostic data against OEM repair information and Bosch's experience-based repair database. It helps with interpretation, while the physical measurements stay with the technician.

The federal EPA technician certification found (Section 609) covers motor-vehicle A/C service, not fuel, ignition or emissions troubleshooting. State smog-repair licensing was not checked, so a human sign-off requirement is not established for typical diagnostic work.

Bosch's ESI[tronic] diagnostic platform is getting a conversational AI assistant, set for global rollout with the 2026/4 release. It checks vehicle diagnostic data against OEM repair guidance, schematics and Bosch's repair database. So an AI can interpret scan data and choose tests, but a technician still connects the tool to the car and takes physical measurements.

The TEXA IDC6 AI Diagnostic Assistant uses a control-unit scan and VIN confirmation to pick the vehicle, then guides the technician through each stage of diagnosis and suggests repairs. The software does the analysis, while hands-on testing stays with the human.

Most US states have no general mechanic license, and ASE certification is voluntary. Licenses are required only for specific jobs such as state safety or emissions inspections and handling refrigerant under EPA Section 609. So no law requires a human to perform or sign routine electronic component testing.

ALLDATA Diagnostic Intelligence is an AI-assisted tool. Starting from a trouble code or a symptom, it returns ranked probable causes, OEM diagnostic procedures, shortcut tests, technical service bulletins (TSBs) and wiring diagrams. This means software already does the main lookup and sequencing sub-steps of planning a repair procedure.

Mitchell 1 ProDemand takes the technician from a trouble code or component search straight to test procedures, specifications and diagrams. A browsing or computer-use agent can operate this kind of shop software the technician already has access to.

Judgment call, not a sourced fact: the plan depends on what the technician finds on the physical vehicle and on hands-on experience (seized parts, condition of the vehicle, shop equipment). So a human still has to supply observations and review or adjust the agent's draft before using it. In most US jurisdictions no licence or signature is required to plan the work.

Installation manuals show the job is mostly hands-on work: mounting and leveling the unit, attaching duct collars and insulated ductwork, running sloped condensate drains with traps, and connecting electrical power. An agent can only help by looking up specifications and sizing.

Under EPA Section 608 (40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F), anyone who services equipment that could release refrigerant, or adds or removes refrigerant, must hold technician certification. Uncertified apprentices must work under close supervision.

Commercial dehumidifier manuals require specific electrical connections, drain piping and service clearances to be done on site by qualified installers. No current software product does any of this physical work.

Maintenance software such as UpKeep schedules preventive maintenance and recommends service intervals from failure history and sensor data. It also creates work orders with checklists attached. Vendor claims say users build these checklists from templates. No source showed AI writing procedures from scratch. Only the 'recommend or develop procedures' part of the task can be done in software.

HVAC preventive maintenance software provides checklists and seasonal schedules for chillers, air handlers and boilers. People still have to clean, oil parts and change filters by hand at the equipment.

EPA Section 608 certification covers only work that could release refrigerant, such as attaching gauges or adding refrigerant. Routine cleaning, oiling and filter changes generally do not need a licence or a human sign-off.

The task is hands-on. A worker has to physically mount the compressor and condenser on frames using hand tools and acetylene welding or brazing equipment. A software-only agent with no robotics cannot do this. At most it could look up specs or mounting diagrams, which is a very small share of the time.

In the US, anyone who installs, maintains, services or repairs equipment containing regulated refrigerant must hold EPA Section 608 technician certification. This works as the main occupational licence for HVAC technicians.

To get Section 608 certification, a technician must pass an EPA-approved test given by an approved certifying organization. Installation work on refrigerant-containing systems falls under this requirement.

Leak testing means hands-on work. The technician isolates and seals the system, connects a nitrogen tank and regulator to a service port, pressurizes it to a set test pressure, watches the gauge for 30-60 minutes or longer, and brushes soap solution on joints to find the leak. All of this needs physical presence.

Under EPA Section 608 (40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F), anyone who attaches hoses and gauges to measure pressure, or adds or removes refrigerant, must be a certified technician. Uncertified apprentices need close supervision by a certified technician.
Under F-Gas rules, engineers must be able to show that leak checks were done before and after charging. That puts the record-keeping and responsibility on a qualified human.

OSHA 29 CFR 1926.451(f)(7) says scaffolds may be erected, moved, dismantled or altered only under the supervision of a competent person, and only by trained workers that person selects. Setting up a scaffold is physical, on-site work that a human is legally responsible for, and it also involves hands-on hazard inspection.
An OSHRC enforcement case issued a serious citation because a scaffold was put up with no competent person present or supervising. This confirms that a human has to be on site.

Scaffold safety programs require physical inspections and erection by trained people. Software agents with no robotics can only help on the side, for example by pulling up checklists or manufacturer instructions.

AI vision and machine-learning inspection is used in jewelry production, but it runs on dedicated cameras and machine controllers built into the production line. A software-only agent cannot pick up and examine a piece.

In jewelry quality control, computer vision and laser measurement can flag defects in metals and stones and check that a design is consistent. This is a promotional source with no accuracy figures. An agent could analyze images and measurements a human captures, but the human still handles the piece with a loupe and gauges.

AI visual inspection systems output a defect class, location and confidence, and compare these to tolerance data to accept or reject a part. An agent could do this comparison against the specification once a human supplies the images or measurements.

Straightening a bent ring is hands-on work: the jeweler bends it gradually with pliers, a mandrel or a ring stretcher, protects the stones and polishes off tool marks. A software-only agent cannot do any of this. Caveat: this source is a low-quality, auto-generated how-to page and is used only to show the steps involved.

Harder metals such as platinum and titanium need more force or special heating equipment. Badly damaged pieces may need cutting and soldering, which is skilled bench work done by touch. Same caveat: low-quality source.

An October 2026 demo at the Bharat Diamond Bourse (BOTS.Ai) showed AI agents that price stones from the 4Cs using live market and recent-sales data. Rapaport is testing agentic AI for diamond market analysis and trading search. Both suggest an agent could handle research, pricing and online matching of buyers and sellers, though neither is shown to be in full production use.

Buying secondhand precious metals and jewelry falls under state rules: sellers must show government ID, dealers keep records and must hold items for set periods. These are compliance steps, not a requirement that a licensed human sign. Florida even allows ID checks through a national verification provider.
Maine requires dealers to check a government-issued ID and hold acquired precious metals for a set time. Handling the goods, inspecting them and keeping custody still need a person on site.

Pencil, a parametric CAD platform for jewelry, has released an AI jewelry CAD design agent. It produces rendered, parametric CAD designs meant for printing and casting, so the digital model-design sub-step can be delegated.

One vendor's AI text- or image-to-3D workflow exports STL files for 3D printing and investment casting. Its own guidance says a human still has to review stone settings and wall thickness before production, so the output needs checking.

RhinoArtisan 7.0 includes a Generative AI Studio that makes images and organic 3D models from text prompts. Physical fabrication (molds, printed or carved models, machine accessories, modified hand tools) still needs hands-on bench work.

Patching a plaster mold is all hands-on work: roughen the damaged spot, wet it, mix the plaster to a paste, press it onto chipped edges, let it dry and sand it smooth. An agent with no robotics can't do any of these steps.
Repairing chips and cracks in plaster means applying and shaping setting compounds by hand in layers, letting each dry and sanding between them. No software can do this.
Guidance on chipped edges and corners covers stiff setting materials, the right consistency and drying between layers. These are manual skills, and an AI could only help by looking up instructions.

Vendors describe AI crew-planning agents that can roster crews, check schedules against qualification, duty-time and union rules, and propose or make reassignments behind approval gates. This covers the scheduling and coordination sub-steps, but these are promotional product pages, not independent evaluations.
AI matching of available, qualified crew to assignments is described as the most mature AI use in 2026 aviation crew scheduling. This source is a vendor blog.

FAA Part 121 requires minimum flight-attendant staffing and on-board positioning for safety and evacuation. Directing attendants in the cabin during operations needs physical human presence, and the certificate holder is accountable for the crew's duties.

The AI cabin-inspection tools that exist need a person or a robot on board to capture images. Diehl's ACIRTo classifies defects from photos that crew take. DrumView, a research project running until the end of 2026, uses a mobile robot to find surface defects. A software-only agent would still need someone physically present to inspect or photograph the cabin.

DrumView is still a research project. It uses a robot that moves through the cabin and cameras with anomaly detection to find scratches, seam deviations and discolorations. Fully automated inspection is not yet a mature, available product.

A flight attendant union document describes 14 CFR 121.309 as requiring a preflight inspection. Crew must confirm that the required emergency equipment is on board and readily available, and must report anything missing or inoperative to the Captain. Under this reading, crewmembers do the check in person and are accountable for it.

Vendor material for 2026 says AI recruiting agents can source candidates, screen them against set criteria, send outreach and book interviews on their own. This covers most of the administrative recruiting work. These are vendor claims and I did not check them independently.

The EU AI Act classes AI used for recruitment, screening and candidate evaluation as high-risk and requires human oversight. A human therefore keeps responsibility for the hiring decision. Sources disagree on when this applies: one says enforcement starts 2 August 2026, while later ones say the Digital Omnibus moved it to 2 December 2027.

NYC Local Law 144 requires an independent bias audit and candidate notice for automated tools that substantially assist or replace hiring decisions. This limits how far hiring can be handed to AI without people in charge. The sources found did not say whether a human must make the final hiring decision.

Transfinder's Wayfinder driver app is tied to its Routefinder PLUS routing software and gives school bus drivers turn-by-turn directions with voice guidance on a tablet. Edulog's tablets do the same with Edulog Routing and Planning. This software can take over most of the map-reading and route interpretation, but it only helps the driver.

Under federal rules, every school bus driver must hold a CDL with passenger and school bus (S) endorsements. That means the person following the route behind the wheel has to be a licensed human, since the agent has no body and cannot drive the bus.
Vendors sell school-specific turn-by-turn navigation for drivers. The driver still has to physically follow the directions while driving and deal with verbal changes from dispatch.

Dispatch platforms for chauffeur, limo and private-hire fleets already sell AI auto-dispatch, smart driver assignment and 24/7 AI voice booking agents. That covers much of the request routing and information exchange between dispatch and drivers.
Industry writing on AI dispatching says routine trip assignment and status updates can be automated, but exceptions and situations happening on the road still need human judgment.

FMCSA rules ban drivers of commercial vehicles from using handheld phones while driving and allow only hands-free use. This is a safety rule on how the driver uses the device. It does not require a human to do the communicating, which supports automated, hands-free status messaging.

Fleet incident apps already guide drivers through accident reporting at the scene. Crashwise uses an AI guide and turns the driver's photos and videos into a standardized digital report that goes to fleet managers. The driver still has to gather the facts at the scene.

AI dashcams such as CameraMatics record video automatically before, during and after an incident, and the companion app supports the claims process. Software can therefore fill in much of the report's evidence and data.

California law makes the driver responsible for filing the SR-1 accident report within 10 days, regardless of fault. An insurance agent, attorney or other representative may file it for the driver, but the account of what happened has to come from the driver.

In 2026, fleet driver-monitoring products (Netradyne, Motive, Fleetx) use AI dashcams to give real-time alerts for speeding, tailgating, distraction and extra passengers. Seatbelt detection appears in fewer products and is still in beta for some. These systems only alert. The licensed human driver still has to drive lawfully and make passengers comply.

In some places the law makes the driver personally responsible for passengers' seat belt use. Since 2013, Hawaii cites the driver if any passenger is unbelted, so legal responsibility sits with the licensed human operator.

Whether the driver must make adult passengers belt up varies by jurisdiction. In the UK the driver is responsible only for themselves and for children. Where it applies, the driver does it in person inside the vehicle, by asking and persuading passengers.

Courier AI agents handle the digital side of the work, such as dispatch, scheduling and pickup intake. A human driver still has to drive and carry the items, and the agent can only plan or coordinate the errand.
Courier support agents take pickup requests and quotes and then pass them to human dispatch. That covers only the coordination part of the errand.
Agent tools can schedule pickups through an API, which speeds up the planning step. Collecting and dropping off mail and packages still needs physical presence, and agents have no robotics.

In shuttle telematics systems, each vehicle's GPS unit reports when it enters or leaves stop and route geofences, and the server stores this as historical route and travel-time data. Route recording can therefore run with no manual entry.
Automatic logbook apps record each trip's start and end address, kilometres, date and start and end times, and sort trips by purpose. An agent could compile and format these records into route logs.

Commercial shuttle fleet platforms provide GPS tracking, schedule adherence monitoring and reporting exports. An agent needs access to these systems, and drivers must still note exceptions and detours the system misses and confirm the logs, so a human remains in the loop.

Telematics platforms such as Motive, CalAmp CrashBoxx and Mojio, combined with RapidSOS, detect crashes automatically. They alert fleet managers and send location and severity data to dispatch or 911. Some workflows still depend on a human to verify the crash or make a phone call.
CalAmp CrashBoxx gives fleet operators a first notice of loss within seconds. It uses context to filter out false alarms, so part of the reporting job is already automated.

The FMCSA bans commercial drivers from using hand-held phones while driving, but two-way radios are exempt. No law requires a human to make these reports. The driver's on-scene observation is still the main input.

A CRS report dated August 2026 says remote-control technologies are readily available but are not a fully autonomous train control system. Long-haul U.S. freight still has no driverless operation, and crews remain responsible for watching for obstacles because PTC handles only a few types of emergencies.

Locomotive automation pilots such as DB Cargo's ATO/RTO trial and Wabtec Teleops use dedicated onboard hardware with a driver aboard or a remote team ready to take control. General-purpose software agents cannot reach or control the cab.
Under 49 CFR Part 240, each railroad must run an FRA-approved program to certify the locomotive engineers who operate its trains, so a qualified human has to be at the controls.

In the US, FRA treats remote-control locomotive operators as locomotive engineers under 49 CFR Part 240. They need certification, including a skills test, and must keep line of sight to the equipment or work inside a zone where only one remote-control locomotive operates.

Fully automated yard locomotives are still prototypes. DB Cargo and Bosch trialled one at Munich North, expect regulatory approval at the end of 2027 and plan to deploy it from 2028. These are purpose-built onboard systems, not general software agents.
Under FRA guidance, anyone who moves a locomotive must hold certification. The only exceptions are moves inside a repair area and moves under 100 feet for inspection.

In early hump yards, brakemen rode cars down the hill and slowed them with hand-operated brakes. Mechanized retarders, controlled manually or by automatic feedback, later replaced this work. So the task is physical, and the automation that exists is trackside machinery, not a software agent.

Modern retarder systems, such as the one at Bailey Yard, set car speed automatically from car weight, distance, wind and temperature. This takes over the speed-control goal through physical yard equipment, not through an AI agent acting by software alone.

Under 49 CFR 218.99 and railroad operating rules, a crewmember physically on site protects and rides equipment during switching moves. The NTSB has urged a ban on riding cars after 14 deaths since 2020.

Yard inventory systems such as RailComm/Tracsis iTrack already keep a live railcar count automatically, using AEI readers, cameras and turnout sensors, and compare it with the car management system's records. An agent working through these systems could compile counts of available cars and cars sent to repair.

Under 49 CFR 215.9, a qualified person must physically find and tag defective (bad-order) cars before they move to repair. So someone has to be in the yard to identify cars and the type of service each needs before the numbers can be recorded.

Bad-order tag records can be electronic and must be kept for 90 days. The recordkeeping itself does not have to be done by a licensed human, though the tag carries the reporting person's signature or electronic ID.

Vendors say their camera-based AI can read container codes, track crane and grab states, and check load sequences against stowage plans. These are claims, not independent tests, and the systems run on fixed port or crane cameras, not on the ship officer's watch.
The master holds overall responsibility for cargo stowage. Supervision is usually delegated to the chief officer, who watches loading on deck and in the holds.
The master must make sure the approved Cargo Securing Manual is followed strictly. Only people with practical knowledge of that manual may take charge of stowage.

Ramp agent job postings require lifting up to 70 lbs, often in the cramped aircraft hold, and carrying baggage up and down jet-way stairs. One aircraft can mean more than 100 items, so the core of the task is physical work.

AI weight-and-balance software such as CHAMP Cargospot Autoload can build a cargo load plan in seconds. That is planning, though, not moving the bags, which is only a small part of the attendant's job. The timing figures come from the vendor and have not been independently checked.
Job postings also mention pushing and pulling loaded carts and working outdoors in all weather. A software-only agent with no body or robot cannot do any of that.

Machines that clean aircraft exteriors are physical robots that a person operates on site (for example, Nordic Dino's semi-automatic robots). They hold only about 5% of the exterior cleaning market. A software-only AI agent can't do this kind of hands-on work.
The vendor says its robotic washers can cut exterior cleaning of a wide-body aircraft from about 6 hours to 2. Either way, the work takes physical equipment and someone on the ramp.

An EU-funded project (Aerowash II) developed an automated washing system with preset patterns for each aircraft model. That is robotics, not software an AI agent could run on its own. My search found no products for polishing specifically.
Software for fueling crews only works out uplift quantities, converts units and logs meter tickets. The hose connection, bonding, nozzle handling and monitoring are all done by hand.
FAA AC 150/5230-4C treats line-service and supervisory fueling training under 14 CFR 139.321(e) as critical to safety. It assumes trained people do the fueling.
Fueling data is captured on rugged tablets at the point of fueling, which only digitizes the paperwork around the physical job.
Autonomous or remote-controlled aircraft tugs are still at the demonstration stage (a university prototype at Provo Airport). They are dedicated robotic vehicles, not software-only AI agents.
A semi-autonomous tug at JFK still needs federal approval, so a human tug operator remains the norm under aviation regulation.
Semi-autonomous towing is expected to arrive first in controlled areas such as hangars and closed ramp zones. Fully autonomous tugs are seen as some way off for busy airport operations.

Commercial cargo inspection tools such as OxMaint and Cargosnap say they record freight condition from photos taken at loading and unloading. They add timestamps and GPS, flag new damage automatically and link the record to the shipment. These are vendor claims with no independent benchmarks. Someone still has to be at the freight to take the photos or set up the cameras.

Mobile freight inspection platforms produce audit-ready photo records with timestamps and GPS. An agent could turn this evidence, plus the inspector's notes or voice memos, into a structured report, but a person on site has to collect the evidence.

US federal rules on vehicle inspection reports (49 CFR 396.11 and 396.13) require signatures from drivers and carrier officials for defects and repair certifications. They do not stop a human inspector from having an AI draft the record of freight condition and handling.

Commercial cold-chain platforms such as Emerson GO, ThingsBoard and ITRI stream temperature and humidity sensor data to the cloud. They send threshold alerts in real time and generate compliance reports automatically, so an agent could do the review and flagging work end to end when sensors are installed.

The FDA sanitary transportation rule accepts several ways to show temperature: manual periodic readings, reefer downloads, data loggers or telematics. Records must be auditable, so some checks still rely on physical readings or on downloads taken on site.

Under the rule the shipper sets the required conditions and carriers must show they met them when asked. An inspector's on-site check and sign-off therefore remains a human step where no sensors are installed or readings are disputed.

Automated piece-picking from bins is done by physical robot systems (for example Bastian SmartPick with machine vision and a six-axis arm), not by software-only AI agents. The reference agent has no body, so it cannot do this.
In 2026 warehouse picking still mixes robots with humans who handle items by hand. Software only guides pickers and verifies picks; it does not do the picking.
Order-picking automation relies on hardware such as mobile robots, goods-to-person systems and robotic piece pickers, so the task is mainly physical manipulation.

Stocking shelves means physically moving and placing goods. Shelf-stocking robots are dedicated robotic hardware, not software agents. Salling Group's October 2026 humanoid trial needs human operators to guide every movement.
Telexistence's TX SCARA restocks beverage shelves in Japanese convenience stores, but it is a physical robot rather than a software agent, and remote humans take over when it fails.
Software and AI help mostly with monitoring, such as shelf-scanning systems that report stock gaps. The physical placement of goods still falls to human associates.

ERP storeroom modules can create a pick list automatically when an approved requisition is released. This step tells the storeroom to start issuing items, but staff still have to issue them physically and then confirm the pick.

In asset-management software, the user builds pick lists from work orders or requisitions and issues the parts. The system then records the transactions and assigns costs, so the agent's share is the digital paperwork, not taking material out of the warehouse.

Pick processing includes physically retrieving items, checking them with barcode or RFID scans, and deducting them from inventory. The retrieval and hand-over steps need someone physically present, which an AI agent without a body cannot do.

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.22 requires storerooms, passageways and floors to be kept clean, orderly and free of hazards such as spills and protruding objects. Meeting it means physically sweeping, wiping, removing obstructions and inspecting the space.

Floor cleaning in warehouses is being automated by physical robots, such as Brain Corp's BrainOS scrubbers. Those are robotic hardware, which this rating excludes. A software-only agent can only draft cleaning checklists, schedules or compliance logs.
OSHA lets employers decide how often walking-working surfaces are inspected, and no licence or human sign-off is required. The barrier here is physical, not legal.
Retail pricing software already works out an item's current price from its regular price (cost plus markup), sale and advertised prices, and competitor prices.
Automated markdown systems work out item prices from markdown profiles and updated sales data without a person doing the math.
AI markdown tools work out prices and send them to point-of-sale systems and electronic shelf labels, so the price calculation itself is digital.

A 2026 preprint, Flowr, describes an agentic Procurement and Ordering Agent for supermarket chains. It writes structured purchase orders using replenishment signals, demand forecasts and supplier catalog data.
Vendors sell retail AI agents that watch stock levels, work out order quantities and send purchase orders to suppliers. These claims come from vendors and have not been checked independently.

Vendor material says retail inventory agents watch point-of-sale data in real time, spot demand spikes for individual products and decide whether to reorder. This covers the demand-based part of the task.
Lucas Dynamic Slotting is a commercial tool that uses machine learning to assign storage slots. It works from SKU velocity, SKU affinity, product and slot attributes, and pick paths.
Infios AI runs inside a warehouse management system. It keeps analyzing pick frequency, velocity and affinity data, then recommends and carries out location reassignments.

Slotting software takes item demand, physical attributes, handling methods and storage constraints into account. Its output is an item-to-location assignment and a list of relocations for staff to carry out. A human still has to check physical and environmental conditions on site.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(l), only trained and authorized operators may run powered industrial trucks. The employer must evaluate each operator in the actual workplace and certify the training. Operators are re-evaluated at least every 3 years.

Autonomous forklifts exist, such as Walmart's FoxBot units at four distribution centers and Fox Robotics, which Symbotic acquired. They are dedicated robotic hardware, though, which is outside the reference technology because it has no physical body. A software agent cannot drive a standard forklift.

Forklift work means physically steering and lifting loads in a warehouse. The only digital parts an agent could handle are small ones, such as checking a pick list or a work order on a scanner or WMS screen.

Commercial and research AI tools such as the OpenGrants AI Grant Writer Agent and GRAIL (IJCAI 2026) can already find grants and write first drafts. Industry guides say AI output is still a starting draft that a human checks, edits and submits. Fully autonomous tools that find, draft and submit applications are still early prototypes.

For EPA Brownfields grants, the organization must have an active SAM.gov registration and UEI. An Authorized Organization Representative approved by the organization's E-Business Point of Contact must submit the application through Grants.gov, so a named human has to submit and certify it.

EPA's Brownfields guidance (FY23 FAQs and the Grants.gov tip sheet) says the AOR must submit the complete application package. Applications are rejected if the SAM.gov account is inactive, which sets institutional and accountability limits on full delegation.

Accessory installs mean hands-on work: disconnecting the negative battery cable, removing cowls, connecting harnesses, securing them with wire ties and testing the lights. An AI without a body can't do any of that.

evidence.fact: Harley-Davidson harness kits need physical tools such as a heat gun and a Deutsch terminal crimp tool. They also carry electrical limits like fuse amperage and wire gauge per splice. An AI could look these up and check them, but it can't carry them out.

The manufacturer's instructions are digital documents. Here an agent can help by finding the right procedure, checking fitment and adding up electrical load. No law requires a licensed person to do the install itself.

MEX CMMS says its AI scheduler reviews all open work orders and assigns each to a technician by skills, trade and availability. Supervisors can preview and edit the schedule before applying it, so a human still reviews the result.
JLL describes Corrigo CMMS as using AI scheduling to assign tasks automatically by priority, technician skills and availability.

This overview of AI-powered CMMS describes AI scheduling as an assistant that recommends assignments by urgency, location and expertise, with final decisions left to human planners. It cites no licensing rule that requires a human to sign off on crew schedules.

Payroll platforms such as Gusto, QuickBooks and ADP already work out and e-file Form 941 and state and local payroll tax forms automatically each time payroll runs. Filing APIs also generate, validate, e-sign and send 94x forms to the IRS, so the preparation and transmission steps are already automated.
TaxBandits offers an API that automates 94x filings from start to finish: it generates, validates, e-signs and transmits the forms.

Form 941 has to be signed under penalty of perjury by the employer or by a Reporting Agent the taxpayer has authorized on Form 8655, which the taxpayer signs. The IRS generally rejects unsigned 94x returns, so an accountable human or firm must authorize and sign the return.

Most of the work happens on site: walking the scene, taking measurements from fixed points with tape, total station or a laser scanner, and drawing a rough sketch. An agent with no body cannot do this. Drawing the final diagram afterwards can be done in software that takes scanner point clouds and manual measurements as input. FARO Zone, for example, is sold as a replacement for hand-drawn sketches, so an agent could plausibly draft the final diagram from field data.

For a sketch to be admitted in court, it must name who made the rough and final versions and show case identifiers, scale, a north arrow, and evidence numbers that match the evidence log. The final version must also reflect the rough sketch. This means a human has to check and take responsibility for it.

Courts admit scene diagrams and laser-scan products based on testimony from the person who took the measurements: that the measurements are accurate and that the equipment was validated and calibrated. A human has to vouch for the work.

Running an excavator or backhoe without an operator needs robotic retrofit hardware installed on the machine, such as Built Robotics' Exosystem with radar, 360° cameras and GPS, or Bedrock Operator. That is physical robotics, which the reference agent does not have. A software-only agent cannot work the machine's controls.

OSHA has no general licence for heavy-equipment operators. 29 CFR 1926.20(b)(4) and 1926.21(b)(2) require employers to let only people qualified by training or experience operate equipment. This is an employer training duty, not a sign-off that must be done by a licensed person.
The task means working the machine controls on a job site and watching the surroundings in real time. Apart from small planning or locate lookups, it is entirely physical.
